What is the first precept of natural law according to Aquinas (Summa I-II, Q. 94)?
answer: 'Good is to be done and pursued, and evil is to be avoided' — from which more specific precepts derive
choices: 'Good is to be done and pursued, and evil is to be avoided' — from which more specific precepts derive
'Love God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself' — Aquinas's reduction of the Decalogue to its essence
'Treat others as you would have them treat you' — the Golden Rule applied as the basis of natural law
'Do no harm to any rational being' — the negative principle that Aquinas placed before any positive obligation
context: Aquinas's natural law theory provides the framework for Catholic moral teaching to this day. From the first precept, secondary precepts derive: preserve life, propagate the species, educate offspring, live in society, seek truth about God. The theory underlies Catholic positions on issues from just war to sexuality to environmental stewardship.

question: By tradition, on December 6, 1273, while celebrating Mass in Naples, Aquinas — the most prolific and ambitious systematic theologian of medieval Europe — experienced something that caused him to refuse to continue writing the Summa. When his secretary Reginald of Piperno pleaded with him to return to work, Aquinas replied. He died three months later, March 7, 1274, on his way to the Council of Lyon. What did he say?
answer: 'I cannot, because all that I have written seems like straw to me, compared with what I have seen and revealed to me'
choices: 'I cannot, because all that I have written seems like straw to me, compared with what I have seen and revealed to me'
'I cannot, for my hand has been struck by the angel; the words will no longer obey my mind in their wonted order'
'I cannot, because the council in Lyon awaits me; my reputation will suffice for what remains to be ordered'
'I cannot, for the rule of our order forbids that I should write what I have seen; obedience requires silence'
context: The Summa was completed posthumously by Aquinas's pupils using his earlier material (the Supplementum). His Dominican confreres dragged him from his bed weeping; he refused. The work ends mid-treatise. The mystical experience has been variously interpreted — visions some say, or possibly a small stroke. His refusal nevertheless became iconic in Catholic spirituality.

question: William of Ockham (c. 1287-1347) was an English Franciscan friar whose philosophical and theological work pushed late medieval thought in a sharply different direction from Aquinas. Where Aquinas was a 'realist' on universals (general categories like 'humanity' have real existence), Ockham was a 'nominalist' (only individuals exist; universals are names). He is also remembered for a methodological principle. What is 'Ockham's Razor'?
answer: 'Entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity' — the principle of explanatory parsimony in philosophical argument
choices: 'Entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity' — the principle of explanatory parsimony in philosophical argument
'God's omnipotence exceeds human understanding' — the principle that no logical limit applies to divine power
'Faith and reason are separate kingdoms' — the principle that theology cannot be demonstrated philosophically
'Tradition trumps speculation' — the principle of submitting to the church's teaching against novel philosophy
context: Ockham's Razor (the explanatory parsimony principle) was actually a general scholastic commonplace before him, but became associated with him. His nominalism and emphasis on God's absolute power (potentia absoluta) destabilized the synthesis of faith and reason that Aquinas had built. Some historians see his work as opening philosophical space for the Reformation a century later.

question: Hildegard of Bingen (1098-1179) was a German Benedictine abbess, visionary, composer, poet, natural philosopher, medical writer, and correspondent of popes and emperors. From age three she had experienced visions; at 42 a divine voice commanded her to write them down. She produced major mystical works (Scivias), composed liturgical music (Ordo Virtutum, earliest known morality play), and wrote on natural science. What modern recognition did she receive?
answer: Doctor of the Church — declared by Pope Benedict XVI in October 2012, only the fourth woman so honored
choices: Doctor of the Church — declared by Pope Benedict XVI in October 2012, only the fourth woman so honored
Co-patroness of Europe — added by Pope John Paul II in 1999 alongside Catherine of Siena and Edith Stein
Patroness of the Internet — declared by Pope Francis in 2013 for her early information networks across Germany
Co-patroness of musicians — alongside St. Cecilia, declared by Pope Pius XII in the mid-20th century
context: Hildegard was canonized in May 2012 and declared Doctor of the Church in October 2012 by Benedict XVI. Her music is widely performed and recorded today; her theology (the 'green' viriditas, the cosmic feminine wisdom) appeals to modern readers. She is the only one of four female Doctors (with Teresa of Ávila, Catherine of Siena, Thérèse of Lisieux) not formally canonized before her doctoral declaration.

question: Catherine of Siena (1347-1380) was a Dominican tertiary of Siena who fasted nearly to death, mystically married Christ, received the stigmata invisibly, and intervened in church politics. From 1309 the popes had resided not in Rome but in Avignon (a papal enclave in southern France) — the 'Babylonian Captivity.' Catherine wrote ferociously to Pope Gregory XI urging him to return. What did she accomplish?
answer: Personally persuaded Gregory XI to return to Rome in 1377, ending the Avignon papacy — though crisis returned with the Great Schism
choices: Personally persuaded Gregory XI to return to Rome in 1377, ending the Avignon papacy — though crisis returned with the Great Schism
Persuaded Pope Clement VII to remain in Avignon to avoid imperial pressure; the papacy returned to Rome only in 1408
Founded a women's preaching order that the papacy never approved formally; she died excommunicated in 1380
Personally translated the Vulgate into Italian; her bible became a forerunner of the Renaissance vernacular movement
context: Catherine's letters (over 380 survive) and Dialogue are major works of late medieval mysticism. Gregory XI did return to Rome in 1377, partly through her urging. Her death in 1380, at 33, came shortly after the Great Schism began (1378). Pope Paul VI declared her Doctor of the Church in 1970, alongside Teresa of Ávila — the first two women so honored.

question: Between roughly 1140 and 1300, an architectural revolution swept across France and then Europe — the Gothic cathedral. Beginning at the Abbey of Saint-Denis (Abbot Suger, dedicated 1144), the new style combined three structural elements that together allowed enormous windows of stained glass. Which three elements distinguish Gothic from Romanesque architecture?
answer: Pointed arch, ribbed vault, and flying buttress — together transferring weight outward, freeing the walls for windows
choices: Pointed arch, ribbed vault, and flying buttress — together transferring weight outward, freeing the walls for windows
Round arch, barrel vault, and thick walls — the Romanesque elements that the Gothic style deliberately retained
Columned portico, dome, and apse — features inherited from Roman basilica architecture and refined in Byzantine practice
Cruciform plan, central nave, and double aisles — features common to both Romanesque and Gothic without distinction
context: Chartres (begun 1194 after fire), Notre-Dame de Paris (1163-1345), Reims (1211-1275), Amiens (1220-1270) — the great French Gothic cathedrals reshape medieval Christianity in stone. The vast stained-glass windows (Chartres preserves 152 of 176 medieval glass panels) taught the Bible in light to the largely illiterate populace. Cologne Cathedral (started 1248) finished only in 1880.

question: The medieval university was a Christian invention of the 12th and 13th centuries. The earliest were Bologna (law, 1088), Paris (theology, c. 1150), Oxford (c. 1167, English scholars expelled from Paris). Each developed distinct organization — Bologna was student-controlled, Paris was master-controlled. What was the standard curriculum that all students completed before specializing in theology, law, or medicine?
answer: The seven liberal arts — trivium (grammar, logic, rhetoric) and quadrivium (arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, music)
choices: The seven liberal arts — trivium (grammar, logic, rhetoric) and quadrivium (arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, music)
The four humours (sanguine, phlegmatic, choleric, melancholic) — taught as the foundation of all natural philosophy
The five cardinal virtues plus the three theological virtues — taught as the foundation of all ethical reasoning
The eight beatitudes plus the ten commandments — taught as the unified moral foundation of Christian learning
context: The seven liberal arts (artes liberales — the studies fit for a free man) became the standard undergraduate curriculum. The structure persists: 'arts' degrees, the 'liberal arts' tradition. The medieval universities institutionalized intellectual life; cathedrals and monasteries had previously preserved learning, but universities created the systematic intellectual conversation that fed the Renaissance and Reformation.

question: The medieval Inquisition originated formally in 1184 with the bull Ad abolendam of Pope Lucius III, which authorized bishops to inquire (inquirere) into heresy in their dioceses. The papal Inquisition proper — staffed largely by Dominicans and Franciscans — was established by Pope Gregory IX in 1231. What was its principal procedural innovation that distinguished it from earlier ecclesiastical discipline?
answer: Inquisitio — actively investigating heresy by interrogating suspects, rather than waiting for accusations to be brought
choices: Inquisitio — actively investigating heresy by interrogating suspects, rather than waiting for accusations to be brought
Confessio — relying solely on voluntary confession from suspects without further interrogation or questioning
Probatio — relying on physical proofs (the appearance of stigmata, miracles) rather than verbal testimony
Excommunicatio — the bishops' traditional remedy used as the only and final punishment for heretics
context: The procedural shift from accusation to inquisition was the great medieval innovation — and the source of much subsequent abuse. Torture was authorized by Innocent IV (1252, Ad extirpanda). Convicted impenitent heretics were 'relaxed' to the secular arm for execution (typically burning), since the church could not shed blood directly. The medieval Inquisition was largely active 1230s-1300s in France and Italy.

question: The Spanish Inquisition was established in 1478 by Pope Sixtus IV at Ferdinand and Isabella's request — separate from the papal Inquisition, under Spanish royal rather than papal control. Its targets were initially conversos (Jewish converts suspected of secretly practicing Judaism) and later moriscos (Muslim converts). The first Grand Inquisitor was the Dominican Tomás de Torquemada. What was the scale of executions?
answer: About 2,000 executions during Torquemada's tenure 1483-1498 — much smaller than later Protestant propaganda claimed
choices: About 2,000 executions during Torquemada's tenure 1483-1498 — much smaller than later Protestant propaganda claimed
About 50,000 executions during Torquemada's fifteen years — among the worst religious massacres of European history
About 200 executions total during the entire 350-year history — the Inquisition was largely symbolic
About 500,000 executions — the figures from the most aggressive 16th-century Protestant pamphleteering
context: Modern scholarship (Henry Kamen, Edward Peters) has substantially revised downward the wilder Protestant 'Black Legend' figures. Total executions over 350+ years are estimated at 3,000-5,000 — still terrible, but far below propaganda figures of hundreds of thousands. The Spanish Inquisition was finally abolished in 1834. Its concentration on conversos was particularly brutal.

question: In 1633, the Roman Inquisition tried Galileo Galilei for 'vehement suspicion of heresy' regarding his defense of Copernican heliocentrism. Galileo had previously been warned in 1616 not to teach heliocentrism as fact. After his 1632 Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems, he was tried, forced to abjure, and placed under house arrest for the rest of his life. He died blind in 1642. What is the apocryphal phrase he allegedly muttered after the abjuration?
answer: 'E pur si muove' — 'and yet it moves' — referring to the Earth that he had just denied moves
choices: 'E pur si muove' — 'and yet it moves' — referring to the Earth that he had just denied moves
'Pater dimitte illis' — 'Father forgive them' — adapting Christ's words from the cross
'Vincit veritas' — 'truth conquers' — the motto of his correspondence with Kepler and others
'Per scientia ad libertatem' — 'through science to freedom' — anachronistic but widely attributed
context: The 'E pur si muove' attribution is first documented over a century after Galileo's death; it was almost certainly never said at trial. Pope John Paul II formally rehabilitated Galileo in 1992. The case became the iconic example (often oversimplified) of conflict between church and science — though Galileo was a believing Catholic throughout, and the Jesuit astronomers of his day were among his closest supporters.

question: On Friday, October 13, 1307, King Philip IV of France ordered the simultaneous arrest of every Knight Templar — perhaps 2,000 men. The Order, founded 1119 to protect pilgrims, had become enormously wealthy as the first international bankers of medieval Europe. Charges included heresy, idolatry, blasphemy, sodomy. What was Philip's principal motivation, according to modern historians?
answer: Massive royal debt to the Templars — the Templars were France's largest creditor, and Philip seized their assets
choices: Massive royal debt to the Templars — the Templars were France's largest creditor, and Philip seized their assets
Genuine theological concerns about Templar secret rituals — Philip was personally pious and feared cosmic punishment
Pressure from Pope Clement V — the papacy demanded the suppression which Philip reluctantly carried out
Defense of orthodoxy against Cathar revival — the Templars were accused of harboring Cathar refugees
context: Philip's bankruptcy and resentment of Templar wealth (he owed them a fortune from war costs) drove the suppression. Pope Clement V (resident in Avignon under French influence) dissolved the order in 1312. The last Grand Master Jacques de Molay was burned at the stake in Paris March 18, 1314. Templar property mostly went to the Hospitallers. The 'Friday the 13th' superstition is sometimes traced to this date, though that linkage is modern.

question: Around 1418-1427, an Augustinian canon of the Brothers of the Common Life in the Netherlands composed (or compiled) a small book of four parts that became, after the Bible, perhaps the most widely read Christian devotional book in history. The book is known as The Imitation of Christ (De Imitatione Christi). Who was its author, and what is its principal theme?
answer: Thomas à Kempis — and the theme is interior conversion through humble imitation of Christ, against worldly pomp
choices: Thomas à Kempis — and the theme is interior conversion through humble imitation of Christ, against worldly pomp
Gerard Groote — and the theme is church reform through education of clergy, against the abuses of the late medieval church
Erasmus of Rotterdam — and the theme is recovery of New Testament Christianity, against medieval scholastic accretions
Johannes Tauler — and the theme is mystical union through detachment, against the rationalism of the schoolmen
context: The Imitation of Christ (1418-1427) is the most widely circulated Christian devotional work after the Bible. Its style is direct, aphoristic, intensely interior. 'What good will it do you to debate profound matters of the Trinity if you lack humility and so displease the Trinity?' Read by Loyola, John Wesley, John Newton, Thomas More, Thomas Merton — across confessional lines.

question: John Duns Scotus (c. 1266-1308) was a Scottish Franciscan philosopher and theologian — the rival in stature to the Dominican Thomas Aquinas. Where Aquinas was called Doctor Angelicus ('Angelic Doctor'), Scotus earned the title Doctor Subtilis. He developed the philosophical doctrine of haecceitas (thisness, the principle of individuation) and defended a theological doctrine about Mary that the Catholic Church later defined as dogma. What was it?
answer: The Immaculate Conception of Mary — her preservation from original sin from the first instant of her conception
choices: The Immaculate Conception of Mary — her preservation from original sin from the first instant of her conception
The Bodily Assumption of Mary into heaven — her direct ascent without seeing corruption of the body
Mary as Theotokos — Mother of God — already defined at Ephesus in 431 AD against Nestorius
The Perpetual Virginity of Mary — defended against later Protestant denial that she had no other children
context: Scotus's defense of the Immaculate Conception (against Aquinas, who had argued Mary needed redemption) became the dominant Franciscan position. Pope Pius IX defined it as dogma in 1854 (Ineffabilis Deus). The Assumption (defined 1950) was the other Marian dogma of the modern era. Scotus died unexpectedly at 42 in Cologne; he was beatified in 1993.

question: Around 1450-1455, in Mainz, the goldsmith Johannes Gutenberg printed the first substantial book produced with movable metal type in Europe — about 180 copies of a Latin Vulgate Bible, 1,282 pages in two volumes. The technology was foundational to the Reformation seventy years later. What specifically made Gutenberg's printing transformative?
answer: Movable type cast in a hand mold — letters could be rapidly reset for each page, unlike the static woodblocks used in East Asia
choices: Movable type cast in a hand mold — letters could be rapidly reset for each page, unlike the static woodblocks used in East Asia
Paper made from wood pulp — replacing the expensive parchment that had limited medieval book production
Movable type carved from boxwood — a refinement of medieval woodblock printing rather than a radical new system
An oil-based ink applied with a rubber roller — superior to the water-based inks used by Korean and Chinese printers
context: The hand-cast metal movable type and the press itself (adapted from wine presses) revolutionized book production. Within fifty years (1500) over 1,000 print shops operated across Europe; perhaps 10 million books printed. Luther's pamphlets in the 1520s reached audiences impossible in the manuscript era — printing made the Reformation possible.

question: On October 31, 1517 — All Hallows' Eve — Martin Luther, Augustinian friar and theology professor at Wittenberg, sent his 95 Theses on indulgences to Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz. Tradition says he also nailed them to All Saints' Church door (a university bulletin board). The Theses attacked indulgence sales. What was the immediate trigger?
answer: Johann Tetzel's preaching tour selling indulgences in Saxony to fund construction of St. Peter's Basilica in Rome
choices: Johann Tetzel's preaching tour selling indulgences in Saxony to fund construction of St. Peter's Basilica in Rome
Pope Leo X's announcement of a general indulgence for the building of new universities across Holy Roman Empire
Emperor Charles V's introduction of a special tax for crusade against the Ottomans framed as indulgence
Cardinal Wolsey's preaching tour in northern Germany aimed at financing Henry VIII's military campaigns in France
context: Tetzel's preaching — 'as soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs' — was crude but effective. Albrecht of Mainz received Luther's letter; Rome saw the Theses in Latin and German translations within weeks. The printing press spread them across Germany in two months. The Reformation had begun.

question: Between May 1521 and March 1522, while hiding at Wartburg Castle under Elector Frederick the Wise's protection (disguised as 'Junker Jörg'), Luther translated the entire New Testament from Erasmus's Greek into vivid colloquial German — in eleven weeks. He continued with the Old Testament from Hebrew over twelve years. What was the lasting impact of the Luther Bible?
answer: It shaped modern High German as a standard literary language — comparable to Shakespeare's role in shaping English
choices: It shaped modern High German as a standard literary language — comparable to Shakespeare's role in shaping English
It introduced the chapter and verse divisions still used in all modern Bibles — these were Luther's own innovations
It was the first vernacular Bible in Europe — only Latin Bibles had existed in print before Luther's 1522 New Testament
It established the Lutheran liturgy that became the standard worship form of all Protestant denominations subsequently
context: Luther's German Bible (NT 1522, complete 1534) standardized German across regional dialects — 'a national-language Bible' that did for German what the King James did for English a century later. There had been 14 German vernacular Bibles before Luther (so his was not 'first'), but his became dominant. The chapter-and-verse divisions were medieval, not Lutheran.

question: On June 13, 1525, the 42-year-old Martin Luther married a 26-year-old former Cistercian nun named Katharina von Bora, who had escaped from the Marienthron convent two years earlier (smuggled out among empty herring barrels). Their marriage demonstrated practically a key Reformation principle. What was it?
answer: Clerical marriage — that priests and monks should be free to marry, against centuries of Western mandatory celibacy
choices: Clerical marriage — that priests and monks should be free to marry, against centuries of Western mandatory celibacy
Lay communion in both kinds — practiced openly at the wedding banquet to demonstrate Eucharistic Reformation principle
Justification by faith alone — that no priestly mediation was needed for the sacrament of marriage between believers
Sola scriptura — that the New Testament knew no monastic vows, and Katharina's escape was therefore legitimate
context: The Luther-Katharina marriage was a public statement that scripture nowhere forbade clergy to marry, despite medieval Catholic practice. The marriage was happy; six children, with Katharina managing the household, gardens, and Luther's correspondence. Luther called her 'Herr Käthe' ('Lord Katie') and dedicated his commentary on Galatians to her. She survived him by six years.

question: Beginning in 1519, Huldrych Zwingli (1484-1531) led the Reformation in Zurich. A humanist from Erasmus's circle, he reformed worship more radically than Luther — removing images, simplifying liturgy, rejecting real presence. He was killed in 1531 at the Battle of Kappel. His disagreement with Luther over the Eucharist split Protestantism. What was Zwingli's position on the Lord's Supper?
answer: Memorial view — the bread and wine are symbolic remembrances of Christ's death, not the body and blood of Christ
choices: Memorial view — the bread and wine are symbolic remembrances of Christ's death, not the body and blood of Christ
Consubstantiation — Christ is present 'in, with, and under' the elements, the Lutheran position that Zwingli shared
Transubstantiation — the elements actually become the body and blood, the Catholic position retained at Zurich
Spiritual real presence — Christ is genuinely present spiritually but not corporeally, the position later associated with Calvin
context: Zwingli's memorial view (interpreting 'this is my body' figuratively) became the dominant Protestant position in Reformed and Anabaptist circles, against Luther's insistence on Christ's bodily presence in the Eucharist. The disagreement was fundamental — the two could not agree at Marburg (1529) and Protestant unity was lost. Zwingli's reform spread through Swiss German-speaking cities.

question: John Calvin (1509-1564), a French lawyer-humanist who fled Catholic France around 1533 after a Protestant conversion, became the most influential Reformed theologian. After publishing the Institutes of the Christian Religion (1536), he was persuaded by Guillaume Farel to remain in Geneva. Calvin and Farel were expelled in 1538 but Calvin returned in 1541. What kind of city government did Calvin help establish in Geneva?
answer: A theocratic discipline — the Consistory of pastors and elders enforced moral and doctrinal discipline among citizens
choices: A theocratic discipline — the Consistory of pastors and elders enforced moral and doctrinal discipline among citizens
A democratic republic — Calvin restructured Geneva on the lines of Athenian democracy with universal male suffrage
An aristocratic oligarchy — Calvin entrenched power in the merchant families against Catholic episcopal control
A monastic city — Calvin established a quasi-monastic discipline requiring lay celibacy in religious congregations
context: Calvin's Geneva had a Consistory that disciplined morals — banned dancing, drunkenness, gambling, blasphemy. Calvin himself held no civic office; pastoral authority worked through the Consistory and the Company of Pastors. Geneva became known as 'the Protestant Rome' — John Knox called it 'the most perfect school of Christ that ever was in the earth since the days of the Apostles.'

question: John Calvin's Institutes of the Christian Religion went through multiple editions during his lifetime, growing from a small handbook in 1536 to a massive four-book systematic theology in its definitive 1559 Latin edition (translated into French 1560). It became the most influential single work of Protestant systematic theology. How is the final 1559 edition structured?
answer: Four books: Creator God, Redeemer Son, Holy Spirit and salvation, the Church and means of grace
choices: Four books: Creator God, Redeemer Son, Holy Spirit and salvation, the Church and means of grace
Three books: Father, Son, Holy Spirit — paralleling the Apostles' Creed in Trinitarian fashion
Five books: Bible, God, Christ, Salvation, Last Things — paralleling later evangelical fundamentalist systematics
Seven books: corresponding to the sacraments but reduced to two from the Catholic seven by Calvin's revision
context: Calvin's Institutes is the systematic counterpoint to Luther's polemical pamphlets — comprehensive, calm, scholastically rigorous. Its structure roughly follows the Apostles' Creed: God the Creator (Book I), Christ the Redeemer (II), the Holy Spirit's application of salvation (III), and the Church and sacraments (IV). It became the foundation of Reformed (Presbyterian, Reformed, Puritan) theology.

question: Among Calvin's most distinctive (and most controversial) teachings was his doctrine of predestination — that God from eternity has chosen some for salvation and others for damnation. Calvin held this not as the central doctrine but as a corollary of God's sovereignty: God's salvation must be entirely God's gracious initiative, not human will. What term did Calvin use for the rejected?
answer: Reprobation — God's eternal decree to pass over some, leaving them to the just consequence of their fallen sins
choices: Reprobation — God's eternal decree to pass over some, leaving them to the just consequence of their fallen sins
Damnation — Calvin denied any divine decree of damnation, holding only that God elected some and left others
Predetermination — Calvin used this term equally for both groups, treating salvation and damnation as parallel
Election unto reprobate — Calvin's term for the entire fallen race, with a remnant chosen by particular election
context: Calvin distinguished election (God's positive choice of some for salvation) from reprobation (God's passing over others). Whether this 'double predestination' is fair to Calvin or only to later 'high Calvinists' (Beza, Perkins, Owen) is debated. The doctrine animated the Synod of Dort (1618-19) producing the famous TULIP acronym. Critics call it determinism; defenders call it sovereign grace.

question: On October 27, 1553, the Spanish physician Michael Servetus was burned outside Geneva. He had denied the Trinity (Christianismi Restitutio, 1553) and infant baptism. Arrested by the Catholic Inquisition in Vienne, he escaped — then traveled through Geneva, where he was arrested. Calvin testified against him; the Council convicted him. What is this episode's significance for Calvin's legacy?
answer: The principal moral stain on Calvin's record — Calvin defended the execution; modern Calvinists acknowledge it as a tragic failure
choices: The principal moral stain on Calvin's record — Calvin defended the execution; modern Calvinists acknowledge it as a tragic failure
A vindication of Reformed orthodoxy — Calvin's actions are still defended unanimously by modern Reformed scholarship
A papal plot — Servetus was a Catholic agent provocateur, and Calvin's execution of him was self-defense
An invention of later Catholic propaganda — modern scholarship has shown Calvin never met Servetus or testified
context: The Servetus execution is the most-cited blot on Calvin's record. Calvin did defend it publicly (Defense of the Orthodox Faith, 1554). Most modern Calvinists acknowledge the act as a tragic failure of the Reformer to think outside the medieval Christendom framework. Sebastian Castellio's response Concerning Heretics (1554) was an early defense of religious toleration against Calvin's reasoning.

question: Thomas Cranmer (1489-1556), Archbishop of Canterbury from 1533, was principal architect of the English Reformation under Henry VIII and Edward VI. His most enduring achievement was a beautifully crafted English-language prayer book that has shaped Anglican worship for five centuries. What was it, and when was the first edition published?
answer: The Book of Common Prayer (1549) — first English liturgy, revised by Cranmer himself in 1552 toward a more Reformed shape
choices: The Book of Common Prayer (1549) — first English liturgy, revised by Cranmer himself in 1552 toward a more Reformed shape
The Articles of Religion (1549) — the doctrinal foundation of the Church of England, eventually finalized as the 39 Articles in 1571
The Great Bible (1549) — the first authorized English Bible for liturgical use, commissioned earlier under Henry VIII in 1539
The English Catechism (1549) — a question-and-answer summary of Anglican teaching for children and new believers
context: The 1549 Book of Common Prayer was the first English-language liturgy. Cranmer's prose — 'almighty God, unto whom all hearts be open, all desires known' — shaped English religious idiom for centuries. The 1552 revision was more Reformed; under Elizabeth (1559) it was moderated; the 1662 BCP after the Restoration became the classic Anglican text. Cranmer himself was burned by Mary I in 1556.

question: On March 21, 1556, the deposed Archbishop of Canterbury Thomas Cranmer was burned at the stake in Oxford by order of Queen Mary I. Under pressure of repeated examinations he had signed several recantations of his Protestant teachings. In his final speech at the stake — which the Catholic authorities expected to be his public submission — Cranmer surprised them. What did he do?
answer: Renounced his recantations; said the hand that had signed them would burn first; thrust his right hand into the flames
choices: Renounced his recantations; said the hand that had signed them would burn first; thrust his right hand into the flames
Read out his recantations aloud, signed them again before the crowd, and went to the stake reaffirming Catholic faith
Refused to speak entirely, weeping silently as the fire was kindled around him; his courage was praised by both sides
Demanded a trial before Parliament rather than execution by ecclesiastical court — and was burned for the demand alone
context: Cranmer's recantation of his recantations at the stake — the right hand burned first as the hand that had signed — was an extraordinary moment. Foxe's Book of Martyrs (1563) made it iconic for Protestant England. Mary I (r. 1553-1558) burned about 280 Protestants in five years, earning the nickname 'Bloody Mary' — a small figure compared to her sister Elizabeth's later executions of Catholics, but more concentrated and theological.

question: On November 3, 1534, Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy, separating the Church of England from papal jurisdiction. Henry VIII was declared 'the only Supreme Head in earth of the Church of England.' The immediate trigger was Henry's desire to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon and marry Anne Boleyn — which Pope Clement VII had refused. Who was executed in 1535 for refusing to acknowledge the Act?
answer: Sir Thomas More and Bishop John Fisher — both later canonized as Catholic saints in 1935 by Pope Pius XI
choices: Sir Thomas More and Bishop John Fisher — both later canonized as Catholic saints in 1935 by Pope Pius XI
Cardinal Wolsey and Thomas Cromwell — Wolsey actually died of natural causes 1530 before the Act was passed
Bishop Cranmer and Bishop Latimer — both actually supported the Act of Supremacy enthusiastically and lived on
Anne Boleyn and George Boleyn — the future queen actually supported the break and married Henry the next year
context: Thomas More (Henry's former Lord Chancellor) and John Fisher (Bishop of Rochester) were executed July 1535. More had resigned his chancellorship in 1532; he refused to swear to the Act and was beheaded July 6. Fisher had been the only bishop to oppose the break; he was beheaded June 22. Both were canonized 1935. Anne Boleyn was beheaded the following May 1536, charged with adultery, incest, and treason.

question: Between 1536 and 1541, Henry VIII's chief minister Thomas Cromwell oversaw the systematic dissolution of all monasteries, abbeys, friaries, and convents in England and Wales. The smaller houses went first (1536), then the larger. The action confiscated about a quarter of all land in the country — a transfer of wealth comparable to nothing in English history before or since. What did the Crown do with the seized monastic lands?
answer: Mostly sold them to the gentry and rising merchant class — creating a new property-owning class bound to the Protestant settlement
choices: Mostly sold them to the gentry and rising merchant class — creating a new property-owning class bound to the Protestant settlement
Returned them to the parishes for distribution to the poor through traditional charity organizations
Reserved them as Crown property — the lands remained in royal hands throughout the Tudor and Stuart periods
Granted them to universities — Oxford and Cambridge tripled in endowment from the monastic dissolution alone
context: The sale of monastic lands to gentry and merchants created a constituency with material interest in the Reformation's success — they would not return the lands to Rome. The dissolution destroyed centers of learning, charity, and welfare; tens of thousands of monks, nuns, and friars were turned out. Some monastic buildings survive as cathedrals or stately homes; many became ruins, picturesque memorials.

question: On taking the throne after the death of her Catholic half-sister Mary I in November 1558, Elizabeth I (r. 1558-1603) inherited a religiously divided kingdom. Her first Parliament in 1559 passed two Acts that established what became known as the 'Elizabethan Settlement.' What were these two Acts, and what was Elizabeth's overall religious strategy?
answer: Act of Supremacy + Act of Uniformity — establishing the monarch as Supreme Governor and the Book of Common Prayer as standard
choices: Act of Supremacy + Act of Uniformity — establishing the monarch as Supreme Governor and the Book of Common Prayer as standard
Act of Toleration + Act of Reconciliation — granting freedom of conscience to all denominations including Catholics and Puritans
Act of Settlement + Act of Succession — focused on dynastic continuity with religion left ambiguous and undecided
Act of Restoration + Act of Renunciation — fully restoring Catholic practice while renouncing papal political authority
context: The Elizabethan Settlement created the Anglican via media ('middle way') between Roman Catholicism and Continental Protestantism — Reformed in theology, traditional in liturgy, episcopal in government. Elizabeth was titled 'Supreme Governor' (not 'Head') in deference to Catholic sensibility; the 1559 BCP softened some 1552 Reformed elements. Elizabeth famously said she did not 'make windows into men's souls.'

question: By the 1580s, English Puritans — wanting to purify the Church of England of remaining Catholic elements — demanded more thorough reform. A smaller Separatist group concluded the Church of England was beyond reform and formed independent congregations. The Separatists faced fierce persecution. Where did they flee in 1608, and where did they later go?
answer: Holland — first to Amsterdam then Leiden — and from there a portion sailed on the Mayflower to New England in 1620
choices: Holland — first to Amsterdam then Leiden — and from there a portion sailed on the Mayflower to New England in 1620
Scotland — to Edinburgh under James VI's protection — but many returned south after James inherited England in 1603
Germany — to Frankfurt and the Palatinate — establishing the Lutheran-Reformed alliance later disrupted by the Thirty Years War
Switzerland — to Geneva and Zurich — joining the Calvinist establishment and absorbing into French and German congregations
context: The Pilgrim story begins with the Scrooby congregation under William Brewster and John Robinson. They fled to Amsterdam (1608), moved to Leiden (1609), and grew uneasy about their children becoming Dutch. A portion sailed on the Mayflower (1620) to Plymouth, Massachusetts. The Pilgrim Fathers were distinct from the larger non-Separatist Puritan migration to Massachusetts Bay starting 1630.

question: On September 6, 1620 (Old Style), the merchant ship Mayflower set sail from Plymouth, England with about 102 passengers — roughly half Separatist Pilgrims from Leiden, the rest 'strangers' (other settlers). After 66 days they sighted Cape Cod on November 9. Before disembarking, the male leaders signed a document establishing self-governance. What is the document called?
answer: The Mayflower Compact — a brief covenant establishing 'civil body politic' under God's authority for the colony's order
choices: The Mayflower Compact — a brief covenant establishing 'civil body politic' under God's authority for the colony's order
The Plymouth Charter — a royal document granted by James I in 1620 establishing the Plymouth Plantation legally
The Pilgrim Confession — a Puritan creedal statement separately written from the Westminster Confession decades later
The Cape Cod Articles — a series of practical agreements governing rations, hunting, and contact with the native peoples
context: The Mayflower Compact (signed November 11, 1620) is often called the first Western governing document based on consent of the governed. It bound the signers to enact 'just and equal laws' for the general good. About half the original passengers died during the first winter. The 'first Thanksgiving' with the Wampanoag came in autumn 1621.

question: John Wesley (1703-1791) and his brother Charles (1707-1788) were Anglican priests and Oxford fellows who had founded the disciplined 'Holy Club' for spiritual formation. After a failed missionary trip to Georgia (1735-1737), John returned spiritually depressed. On the evening of May 24, 1738, John attended a meeting on Aldersgate Street in London where someone was reading a Lutheran text. What happened?
answer: His heart was 'strangely warmed' as the reader expounded Luther's Preface to Romans — a moment that launched the Methodist revival
choices: His heart was 'strangely warmed' as the reader expounded Luther's Preface to Romans — a moment that launched the Methodist revival
He was ordained to a new bishopric in the New World — but declined the position to remain in England as missionary
He fell into a trance and saw the Last Judgment — recorded in his journal as the moment of his conversion
He met George Whitefield for the first time — the two then split before being reunited in the Methodist movement
context: Wesley's Aldersgate experience (May 24, 1738) was the spiritual turning point of his life. Reading Luther's Preface to Romans, he felt 'I did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation; and an assurance was given me that he had taken away my sins, even mine.' From that point, the Methodist revival spread across Britain — field preaching, class meetings, lay preachers, hymns by Charles.

question: George Whitefield (1714-1770) was the most spectacular preacher of the 18th century — preaching to crowds of 20,000+ in open fields (Franklin once measured his voice). He crossed the Atlantic 13 times and was instrumental in the First Great Awakening in the colonies (1730s-40s). He differed from John Wesley theologically on what major point?
answer: Predestination — Whitefield was a Calvinist insisting on election; Wesley was Arminian insisting on free human response
choices: Predestination — Whitefield was a Calvinist insisting on election; Wesley was Arminian insisting on free human response
Sacraments — Whitefield held a Reformed memorialist view; Wesley insisted on Anglican real presence in Communion
Bible — Whitefield insisted on plenary inspiration; Wesley accepted higher critical readings of the Old Testament
Church polity — Whitefield favored Congregationalist governance; Wesley insisted on episcopal succession through bishops
context: The Wesley-Whitefield disagreement (1739-40) over predestination divided the Methodist movement into Wesleyan (Arminian) and Calvinistic streams. Whitefield's Calvinist Methodism continued through Selina Hastings, Countess of Huntingdon. The 1739 controversy briefly broke their friendship but they were reconciled. Whitefield died at Newburyport, Massachusetts (1770), preaching to his last hour.

question: On July 8, 1741, the Congregationalist pastor Jonathan Edwards (1703-1758) preached a sermon at Enfield, Connecticut that became the most famous sermon in American history. Edwards — a Yale-trained theologian who was perhaps the most original metaphysical mind in colonial America — used vivid imagery of divine wrath to describe the unconverted soul's danger. What was the title?
answer: 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God' — drawing on the image of a spider suspended over the flame by God's mercy
choices: 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God' — drawing on the image of a spider suspended over the flame by God's mercy
'The Cup of God's Wrath' — drawing on Revelation 14's image of the great winepress of God's wrath against the wicked
'The Worm Dies Not' — drawing on Mark 9's image of unquenchable fire and undying worm as the punishment of the lost
'A Divine and Supernatural Light' — Edwards's positive sermon on conversion delivered earlier and printed widely
context: Edwards's Enfield sermon used the spider image — the unregenerate held over hell by God's hand alone. The First Great Awakening (1730s-40s) saw the colonies erupt with revival. Edwards's theological writings — The Religious Affections (1746), Freedom of the Will (1754) — established him as the major American theologian of the colonial era. He died 1758 of a smallpox inoculation soon after becoming president of Princeton.

question: Between 1790 and 1840, the US experienced a second wave of revivalism — the Second Great Awakening. Unlike the more Calvinist First, the Second was characterized by Arminian theology (free response to grace) and the camp meeting — outdoor revival gatherings drawing thousands. What event in August 1801 became iconic for the movement?
answer: The Cane Ridge Revival in Kentucky — perhaps 20,000 attended; manifestations included jerks, falling, holy laughter, hours-long preaching
choices: The Cane Ridge Revival in Kentucky — perhaps 20,000 attended; manifestations included jerks, falling, holy laughter, hours-long preaching
The Cumberland Presbytery Schism — Presbyterian split over uneducated frontier preachers eventually formed a new denomination
The Mormon First Vision in upstate New York — Joseph Smith's reported encounter with the Father and Son in a grove
The Burned-Over District Campaign — Charles Finney's series of revival meetings in upstate New York's evangelical heartland
context: Cane Ridge (August 6-12, 1801) outside Paris, Kentucky, drew an estimated 10,000-25,000 to a revival organized by Presbyterian Barton Stone. The 'jerks,' falling, and other physical manifestations astonished observers. The Second Great Awakening transformed American religion — Methodists, Baptists, and new denominations (Disciples of Christ, Adventists, Mormons) grew while traditional Calvinist denominations declined relatively.

question: Between February 1692 and May 1693, in Salem Village (modern Danvers) and surrounding towns, witchcraft accusations led to formal trials of over 200 people, imprisonment of 150, and execution of 20 (19 hanged, one pressed with stones for refusing to plea). What kind of evidence did Salem courts admit that especially troubled later observers?
answer: 'Spectral evidence' — testimony that the accused's spirit-form (specter) had tormented the witness, even if the accused was elsewhere
choices: 'Spectral evidence' — testimony that the accused's spirit-form (specter) had tormented the witness, even if the accused was elsewhere
Anonymous accusations — written charges against named individuals without any accuser publicly identified or cross-examined
Physical torture of suspects — extracted confessions through documented torture, against English common-law tradition
Catholic accusations — Catholic priests testifying against Protestants on the basis of confessional secrets they had heard
context: Spectral evidence was the defining failure of Salem. Increase Mather's Cases of Conscience (1693) ('it were better that ten suspected witches should escape than that one innocent person should be condemned') effectively ended the trials by attacking spectral evidence. Massachusetts officially apologized in 1697 (Samuel Sewall publicly); the colony made restitution to victims' families. The episode remains a touchstone for the dangers of moral panic.

question: Around 1647, an unschooled shoemaker's apprentice named George Fox (1624-1691) began preaching in northern England. He taught direct unmediated experience of Christ — the 'Inner Light' in every person — and rejected paid clergy, sacraments, and church buildings. His followers were nicknamed 'Quakers' by hostile observers. What movement did this become?
answer: The Religious Society of Friends — pacifist, egalitarian, contemplative; the principal 17th-century radical Protestant survival
choices: The Religious Society of Friends — pacifist, egalitarian, contemplative; the principal 17th-century radical Protestant survival
The Methodist Connexion — though it became this only a century later under Wesley with substantially different theology
The Baptist Union — though Baptists actually predated Fox by decades and held quite different doctrines on sacraments
The Anabaptist Mennonites — though these were Continental in origin and 16th-century in dating, not English 17th-century
context: Fox's Friends grew rapidly despite intense persecution under the Stuart Restoration (perhaps 15,000 imprisoned under the Conventicle Acts). Quaker testimonies — pacifism, plain dress, plain speech, refusal of oaths, religious equality for women — became distinctive marks. William Penn's Pennsylvania (1681) became a Quaker experiment in religious liberty. Quaker abolitionism preceded other Christian denominations by a century.

question: On March 4, 1681, Charles II granted William Penn (1644-1718) — a Quaker gentleman whose father had been an admiral owed money by the Crown — a vast tract of land in North America. Penn called it 'Sylvania' (woodland); Charles insisted on 'Penn-sylvania' to honor the admiral. Penn established the colony as a 'Holy Experiment.' What distinguished it from neighbors like Massachusetts?
answer: Universal religious toleration — Catholics, Jews, all Protestants welcome; no established church; fair dealings with Native Americans
choices: Universal religious toleration — Catholics, Jews, all Protestants welcome; no established church; fair dealings with Native Americans
Quaker theocracy — only Quakers could vote or hold office in Pennsylvania's government during the colonial period
Confiscatory taxation of non-Quakers — those refusing to embrace the Inner Light were taxed at double rates by statute
Mandatory pacifism — all male residents were required to swear off military service and weapons by colonial law
context: Pennsylvania's religious liberty made it perhaps the most pluralistic colony in early America. Penn's 'Great Treaty' with the Lenape at Shackamaxon (probably 1682) became famous for honoring rather than dispossessing native peoples — though later proprietors broke faith with his policies. Quaker Pennsylvania's pacifism eventually conflicted with British imperial wars, leading to Quaker withdrawal from majority political power by the 1750s.

question: On July 18, 1870, the First Vatican Council — meeting from 1869 under Pope Pius IX with about 700 bishops attending — promulgated the dogmatic constitution Pastor Aeternus. The decisive vote was 433 in favor with 2 opposed (the doubters had largely left). What did the constitution define?
answer: Papal infallibility — when speaking ex cathedra on matters of faith or morals, the pope is preserved from error
choices: Papal infallibility — when speaking ex cathedra on matters of faith or morals, the pope is preserved from error
Papal sovereignty — the pope holds full temporal jurisdiction over all kings and emperors regardless of their consent
Papal jurisdiction — the pope is the sole bishop and all other bishops merely his deputies in local dioceses
Papal succession — the pope must always be Italian and elected only by Italian cardinals to ensure continuity
context: Vatican I's definition of papal infallibility was carefully limited: the pope speaking ex cathedra (from the chair), defining a doctrine of faith or morals for the universal church. The doctrine has been invoked explicitly only twice: the Immaculate Conception (1854) and the Assumption of Mary (1950). The council was suspended when Italian troops took Rome in September 1870 ending the Papal States. Vatican II reopened the dialogue.

question: On October 16, 1978, after 33-day Pope John Paul I's sudden death, the Polish cardinal Karol Wojtyła was elected pope at age 58 — the first non-Italian since Adrian VI (1522) and the first Slavic pope ever. As John Paul II he reigned until April 2, 2005 — 27 years, second-longest in modern history. What is widely considered his most consequential geopolitical contribution?
answer: His support for Solidarity in Poland (from his June 1979 pilgrimage onward) helped delegitimize communist rule across Eastern Europe
choices: His support for Solidarity in Poland (from his June 1979 pilgrimage onward) helped delegitimize communist rule across Eastern Europe
His opening to Islam through visits to Egypt and Damascus, which substantially restored Catholic-Muslim relations after centuries
His ecological encyclicals, which made the Catholic Church the leading religious voice for environmental responsibility globally
His liberation theology reforms in Latin America, which embraced Marxist analysis as compatible with Catholic social teaching
context: John Paul II's 1979 Polish pilgrimage — 13 million Poles attending public Masses — broke through communist control. His support for Solidarity (founded 1980) and his diplomatic pressure (with Reagan) on the Soviet empire is widely credited with accelerating its collapse. Survived assassination attempt May 13, 1981 by Mehmet Ali Ağca. Canonized 2014 by Francis. His 1984 prayer at Auschwitz was historic.

question: On March 13, 2013, after the unprecedented resignation of Pope Benedict XVI (the first papal resignation since Celestine V in 1294), the Argentine cardinal Jorge Mario Bergoglio was elected pope at age 76. He took the name Francis — the first pope to use that name. What are several 'firsts' that mark his pontificate?
answer: First Jesuit pope, first pope from the Americas, first non-European since 8th-century Gregory III who was Syrian
choices: First Jesuit pope, first pope from the Americas, first non-European since 8th-century Gregory III who was Syrian
First married pope, first pope from Asia, first lay pope without ordination since the Renaissance era
First Anglican pope, first pope without a Roman seminary education, first pope to abolish papal infallibility
First pope to convene a fourth Vatican Council, first to reside outside the Apostolic Palace permanently
context: Francis's pontificate has emphasized humility (he chose to live at the Casa Santa Marta rather than Apostolic Palace), pastoral concern for the poor and marginalized, environmental responsibility (Laudato Si', 2015), and dialogue. His stances on contested issues have made him beloved by some Catholics and criticized by others. He continues to serve in the time period this bank covers.

question: On July 16, 1054, Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida — papal legate of the dead Pope Leo IX — laid a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, excommunicating Patriarch Michael Cerularius and his followers. Cerularius reciprocated. The mutual excommunications are conventionally dated as the start of the Great Schism between Catholic and Orthodox Christianity. What were the principal disputed issues?
answer: The filioque ('and from the Son') addition to the Nicene Creed by the West, and papal claims of universal jurisdiction
choices: The filioque ('and from the Son') addition to the Nicene Creed by the West, and papal claims of universal jurisdiction
The dating of Easter and the use of unleavened versus leavened bread in the Eucharist — both technically resolvable
Iconoclasm and the Marian dogmas — the Catholic-Orthodox dispute about images and the role of the Virgin
Indulgences and clerical celibacy — issues that actually became Reformation disputes between Catholics and Protestants
context: The Great Schism (1054) was the culmination of centuries of drift between Greek East and Latin West. The 1965 lifting of the mutual excommunications (by Paul VI and Athenagoras) was a major step toward reconciliation, but the substantive issues — particularly papal jurisdiction — remain unresolved. The 1204 sack of Constantinople by Western Crusaders deepened the rift beyond easy healing.

question: Around 988 AD, Prince Vladimir of Kiev (ruler of Kievan Rus') converted to Byzantine Christianity and ordered mass baptism in the Dnieper. According to the Russian Primary Chronicle, he had sent emissaries to investigate religions of his neighbors — Judaism (Khazars), Islam (Volga Bulgars), Western and Eastern Christianity. What did the emissaries report from Constantinople?
answer: 'We knew not whether we were in heaven or on earth' — the beauty of Hagia Sophia's liturgy decided Vladimir for Orthodoxy
choices: 'We knew not whether we were in heaven or on earth' — the beauty of Hagia Sophia's liturgy decided Vladimir for Orthodoxy
'Their God is severe but their treasury is full' — the wealth and discipline of Byzantium impressed the practical Vladimir
'Their books are many but their warriors are few' — the emissaries advised against Byzantine entanglement on military grounds
'Their saints are bones but their priests are gold' — the emissaries dismissed the Orthodox veneration of relics
context: The Hagia Sophia liturgy story is the foundational legend of Russian Orthodoxy — whatever the historical truth, it captures the centrality of liturgical beauty to Eastern Christian self-understanding. Vladimir's conversion brought Kievan Rus' into Byzantine Christian civilization; when Constantinople fell in 1453, Moscow eventually claimed the role of 'Third Rome.' Vladimir was canonized; he remains a major saint of the Russian Orthodox Church.

question: Around 301 AD — twelve years before Constantine's Edict of Milan legalized Christianity in the Roman Empire — King Tiridates III of Armenia converted to Christianity and made it the official state religion. The agent of his conversion was a man whom Tiridates had earlier imprisoned in a pit for 13 years. Who was this missionary, and what is significant about Armenia's conversion?
answer: Gregory the Illuminator — Armenia became the first nation in the world to adopt Christianity as state religion
choices: Gregory the Illuminator — Armenia became the first nation in the world to adopt Christianity as state religion
Patrick of Ireland — Armenia became the second nation after Ireland to convert; Irish missionaries reached the Caucasus
Mesrop Mashtots — Armenia became the first to develop a vernacular Christian alphabet which Mesrop invented in 405
Cyril of Jerusalem — Armenia became the first to use Greek as its liturgical language outside the Roman Empire
context: The Armenian Apostolic Church remains one of the oldest national churches in Christendom. Armenia's 301 conversion preceded any other state's. The Armenian alphabet (created 405 by Mesrop Mashtots) enabled biblical translation. Armenia rejected the Council of Chalcedon (451) and remains one of the Oriental Orthodox churches (with Coptic, Ethiopian, Syrian, Indian). The Armenian Genocide (1915-1923) killed perhaps 1.5 million.

question: G. K. Chesterton (1874-1936) was an English journalist and Christian apologist who converted from vague Anglicanism through Anglo-Catholicism to Rome (1922). His 1908 Orthodoxy is an autobiography of intellectual conversion. The book famously develops the image of a man who set out to discover a new island and discovered something specific. What did the man discover?
answer: England — Chesterton's metaphor for the journey of those who set out to invent a new religion and end at Christianity
choices: England — Chesterton's metaphor for the journey of those who set out to invent a new religion and end at Christianity
Atlantis — the lost civilization, used as a metaphor for paganism that turned out not to be lost after all
America — the metaphor for the journey toward what one expected to be radically new but turned out familiar
Avalon — the legendary British isle, used as a metaphor for the British religious imagination's homeward turn
context: Chesterton's 'discovered England' metaphor frames Orthodoxy: 'I am the man who with the utmost daring discovered what had been discovered before... I tried to invent a heresy of my own; and when I had put the last touches to it, I discovered that it was orthodoxy.' The Everlasting Man (1925) developed his apologetic with greater historical sweep. C. S. Lewis credited it with shaping his own Christian thought.

question: Søren Kierkegaard (1813-1855) was a Danish Lutheran philosopher and theologian whose pseudonymous works pioneered Christian existentialism. His 1843 Fear and Trembling, published under the pseudonym Johannes de Silentio, meditates on the Genesis 22 binding of Isaac. Kierkegaard introduces a famous category for Abraham's faith. What is it?
answer: The 'teleological suspension of the ethical' — Abraham's faith requires going beyond the universal ethical for God's particular command
choices: The 'teleological suspension of the ethical' — Abraham's faith requires going beyond the universal ethical for God's particular command
The 'dialectical synthesis of the rational' — Abraham reasons his way to a higher rationality that subsumes the ethical
The 'systematic absolution of the historical' — Abraham transcends the specific historical moment by abstraction
The 'phenomenological reduction of the immediate' — Abraham brackets the appearance to grasp the deeper essence
context: Fear and Trembling is one of the canonical texts of Christian existentialism. Kierkegaard's 'knight of faith' — Abraham who acts on the absurd command — became a foundational figure for theologians as diverse as Karl Barth, Reinhold Niebuhr, and Paul Tillich. Kierkegaard's pseudonymous authorship (Climacus, Anti-Climacus, Vigilius Haufniensis, etc.) complicates direct attribution; he himself published less famous edifying discourses.

question: In Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov (1880), the atheist Ivan tells his pious brother Alyosha a 'poem' set in 16th-century Seville during the Inquisition. Christ has returned and is performing miracles. He is arrested by the Cardinal-Inquisitor, who visits him in the cell and delivers a long monologue. What does the Grand Inquisitor argue?
answer: Christ's offer of freedom is unbearable to most humans; the Church has provided what people actually want — bread, mystery, and authority
choices: Christ's offer of freedom is unbearable to most humans; the Church has provided what people actually want — bread, mystery, and authority
Christ's miracles are inauthentic; only the Church's miracles validated by long tradition can be trusted by ordinary people
Christ's gospel is admirable but impractical; only the Inquisition's strict discipline can keep human nature from chaos
Christ's return is premature; the Antichrist must come first per the Apocalypse before the Second Coming proper
context: The Grand Inquisitor parable (Brothers Karamazov, Book 5, Chapter 5) is among the most influential passages in modern theology — read by Berdyaev, Solovyov, Romano Guardini, Joseph Ratzinger (Pope Benedict XVI), and many others. Christ silently listens; at the end, He kisses the Inquisitor on the lips. The kiss is the answer.

question: Dorothy Day (1897-1980), American journalist, after a bohemian youth (abortion, failed marriage, common-law relationships) converted to Catholicism in 1927. In 1933, with the French peasant Peter Maurin, she founded the Catholic Worker movement in New York — 'houses of hospitality' for the poor and a newspaper. What was the movement's distinctive integration?
answer: Voluntary poverty, hospitality to the poor, pacifism, and personalist Catholic social teaching against statism and capitalism
choices: Voluntary poverty, hospitality to the poor, pacifism, and personalist Catholic social teaching against statism and capitalism
Social services, registered Catholic charity status, government grant-receiving status, ecumenical Protestant cooperation
Evangelism, conversion-focused street preaching, traditional Latin Mass celebration, and Marian devotional practices
Liberation theology, Marxist analysis of class struggle, support for socialist revolutionary movements in Latin America
context: The Catholic Worker movement (still active in dozens of houses across the US and abroad) practices personalist Catholic anarchism — neither state welfare nor capitalist charity, but Christian hospitality from person to person. Dorothy Day refused tax-exempt status. Her cause for canonization was opened in 2000; she is currently 'Servant of God' on the way to formal sainthood.

question: Mother Teresa (1910-1997) — Albanian-born Catholic sister — in 1948, after seventeen years as a teaching sister, received 'a call within a call' to leave her Loreto convent and work with the poorest of the poor in Calcutta's slums. She founded the Missionaries of Charity in 1950. What is the order's distinctive fourth vow (in addition to poverty, chastity, and obedience)?
answer: Wholehearted free service to the poorest of the poor — codifying the order's specific charism as a binding religious vow
choices: Wholehearted free service to the poorest of the poor — codifying the order's specific charism as a binding religious vow
Strict enclosure within a single house — the Missionaries of Charity are technically a cloistered contemplative order
Total silence except during prayer — the Missionaries of Charity follow Cistercian silence as a fourth discipline
Permanent celibacy without exception for senior members — the order forbids any female religious life outside celibate orders
context: The fourth vow distinguishes the Missionaries of Charity. The order today has 4,500+ sisters in 130+ countries running 600+ houses for the dying, the disabled, AIDS patients, the disadvantaged. Mother Teresa won the Nobel Peace Prize 1979. Her private letters (published 2007) revealed decades of spiritual darkness — a dark night of the soul she endured silently. Canonized September 4, 2016 by Pope Francis.

question: Martin Luther King Jr. (1929-1968) was a Baptist minister, son of a Baptist minister, who became the central figure of the American civil rights movement from the Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955-1956) until his assassination in Memphis, Tennessee on April 4, 1968. His Christian theological formation was at Crozer Seminary and Boston University. His 1963 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' draws on what theological tradition for civil disobedience?
answer: Augustine and Aquinas — 'an unjust law is no law at all,' grounding civil disobedience in natural law tradition
choices: Augustine and Aquinas — 'an unjust law is no law at all,' grounding civil disobedience in natural law tradition
John Calvin — predestination required obedience to law against the unjust authority of segregation
Karl Barth — neo-orthodoxy required transcendence of all human authority including civil rights movements
Walter Rauschenbusch — Social Gospel required pragmatic accommodation with existing social structures
context: King's Letter from Birmingham Jail (April 16, 1963) cites Augustine's 'unjust law is no law at all' and Aquinas's articulation of natural law. King's 1963 'I Have a Dream' speech at the Lincoln Memorial drew on Isaiah 40 ('every valley shall be exalted') and Amos 5 ('let justice roll down as waters'). His theology was a blend of black church tradition, personalism, Niebuhrian realism, and Gandhi's nonviolent resistance.

question: The doctrine of the Trinity — that God is one being eternally existing in three persons — was hammered out through fierce 4th-century controversies. The decisive formula uses two key terms: ousia (Greek, 'being' or 'substance') and hypostasis (Greek, 'person' or 'subsistence'). One ousia, three hypostases. Which heresy did this formula specifically reject?
answer: Modalism (Sabellianism) — that the Father, Son, and Spirit are merely modes or roles of one undifferentiated God
choices: Modalism (Sabellianism) — that the Father, Son, and Spirit are merely modes or roles of one undifferentiated God
Adoptionism — that Jesus was a man whom God adopted as Son at his baptism, having been merely human before
Docetism — that Christ only seemed to have a body, his suffering and death therefore being merely apparent
Pelagianism — that humans can attain holiness without grace, making Christ's atoning death unnecessary
context: Modalism (taught by Sabellius c. 220 AD) collapsed the distinctions between persons. The Cappadocian Fathers (Basil the Great, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa) developed the 'one ousia, three hypostases' formula that became orthodox. The Filioque ('and from the Son') controversy — whether the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or from the Father and the Son — divided East and West permanently after 1054.

question: After the 4th-century Trinity controversies, the 5th century concerned the Person of Christ. Chalcedon (451) produced the classic definition: Christ is one Person in two natures — fully divine and fully human, 'without confusion, change, division, or separation.' Which patriarch is associated with the position that Christ has two persons, leading to the Nestorian controversy?
answer: Nestorius of Constantinople — accused of separating the natures into two persons; condemned at Ephesus 431
choices: Nestorius of Constantinople — accused of separating the natures into two persons; condemned at Ephesus 431
Eutyches of Constantinople — actually held the opposite view, that the two natures became one composite nature
Apollinaris of Laodicea — held that the divine Logos replaced Christ's human soul, a different heresy entirely
Cyril of Alexandria — was the orthodox opponent of Nestorius, defending the unity of Christ's person
context: Nestorius (c. 386-451) was Patriarch of Constantinople 428-431. He objected to calling Mary 'Theotokos' ('God-bearer'), preferring 'Christotokos' ('Christ-bearer'). Cyril of Alexandria led the opposition. The Council of Ephesus (431) condemned Nestorius. The Church of the East (sometimes called Nestorian) preserved his teachings; modern dialogue has clarified the dispute was partly verbal. Eutyches's opposite error (monophysitism) was condemned at Chalcedon (451).

question: The Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation was formally defined at the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) and reaffirmed at Trent (1551). It teaches that in the Eucharist, by the priest's words of consecration, the substance of the bread and wine is changed into the substance of Christ's body and blood, while the 'accidents' (appearance, taste, weight) remain as bread and wine. What philosophical framework does this doctrine use?
answer: Aristotelian metaphysics — the distinction between substance (essential nature) and accidents (sensible qualities)
choices: Aristotelian metaphysics — the distinction between substance (essential nature) and accidents (sensible qualities)
Platonic metaphysics — the distinction between form (true reality) and matter (illusory appearance) of an object
Stoic metaphysics — the distinction between active principle (logos) and passive principle in material reality
Cartesian dualism — the distinction between extended substance (body) and thinking substance (mind) of a being
context: Transubstantiation rests on Aristotelian substance-accidents metaphysics, made available to medieval theologians through the recovery of Aristotle in the 12th-13th centuries. Aquinas's articulation in the Summa is classic. Luther rejected transubstantiation but maintained Christ's real bodily presence (consubstantiation, sort of). Zwingli rejected real presence entirely. Calvin held a 'spiritual real presence.' Anglicans split.

question: The Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed (381 AD) originally stated that the Holy Spirit 'proceeds from the Father.' Beginning in the 6th century in Spain and gradually spreading throughout the Western (Latin) church, the phrase 'and the Son' (Latin: filioque) was added — 'proceeds from the Father and the Son.' The Eastern (Greek) church rejected this addition as unauthorized. What does the dispute concern theologically?
answer: Whether the Spirit's eternal procession involves the Son or only the Father — the Trinitarian relations themselves
choices: Whether the Spirit's eternal procession involves the Son or only the Father — the Trinitarian relations themselves
Whether Christ has authority to send the Spirit at his discretion or only as the Father commands him to
Whether the Spirit existed before the Incarnation or only after Pentecost as the church's distinctive gift
Whether the Spirit can be present in non-Christian religions, or whether the Spirit operates only through the Son
context: The filioque controversy was one of the principal theological causes of the 1054 schism between Catholic and Orthodox. Greek theologians objected both to the substantive theology (compromising the Father's unique role as source) and the procedure (a unilateral Western addition to a creed agreed by ecumenical council). The doctrinal dialogue continues; the procedural objection remains harder to resolve.

question: The atonement — Christ's reconciling work on the cross — is the central event of Christian faith, but Christian theology has offered several different theories of how it works. The 'classic' or 'Christus Victor' theory dominated for a millennium; Anselm's 'satisfaction theory' (Cur Deus Homo, 1098) shifted the framework; the Reformation 'penal substitution' theory developed Anselm in legal terms. Which of the following is NOT one of the major atonement theories?
answer: Reverse karma theory — Christ accumulated such positive karma he could distribute it to the underserving by request
choices: Reverse karma theory — Christ accumulated such positive karma he could distribute it to the underserving by request
Christus Victor — Christ's death defeated Satan and the powers of darkness, ransoming captive humanity
Satisfaction theory — Christ's death satisfied the offended honor of God against humanity's sin
Moral influence theory — Christ's death demonstrates God's love so as to move humans to responding love
context: The major atonement theories include: ransom (Origen, early church), Christus Victor (Aulén's 1931 retrieval of patristic motif), satisfaction (Anselm), penal substitution (Reformation), moral influence (Abelard, modern liberal theology), governmental (Grotius). No major Christian theory uses karma — that is Hindu/Buddhist. Each theory captures something the others miss; together they describe a many-sided event.

question: At the Reformation, Martin Luther articulated the doctrine of justification by faith alone — sola fide — as the article on which the church stands or falls. Justification is God's declaration that the sinner is righteous; it is received by trusting Christ's righteousness, not by any human merit. The Reformation's 'five solas' summarized its protest. Which of the following is NOT one of the five solas?
answer: Sola sacramenta — the sacraments alone are the means of grace, a position the Reformers explicitly rejected
choices: Sola sacramenta — the sacraments alone are the means of grace, a position the Reformers explicitly rejected
Sola scriptura — by scripture alone — that scripture is the supreme authority for faith and practice
Sola gratia — by grace alone — that salvation is entirely God's gracious gift apart from human merit
Soli Deo gloria — to God alone be glory — that all human effort serves God's glory rather than human pride
context: The five solas: sola scriptura, sola fide, sola gratia, solus Christus, soli Deo gloria. Sola sacramenta was not Protestant — the Reformers reduced sacraments from seven (Catholic) to two (baptism and Lord's Supper) and denied any automatic operation. The Roman Catholic Church's response at Trent (1547) affirmed justification by faith plus love expressed in works, not faith alone. The Catholic-Lutheran Joint Declaration on Justification (1999) found substantial agreement.

question: The Apostles' Creed is the oldest creedal statement of the Western church, traditionally said to be composed by the twelve apostles — though scholars place it as a development of the 2nd-century 'Old Roman Creed,' reaching its current form around the 8th century. It opens 'I believe in God the Father Almighty.' Which of the following clauses is NOT in the Apostles' Creed?
answer: 'And in the consubstantial Trinity of one essence' — this Trinitarian phrasing is from the Athanasian Creed, not the Apostles'
choices: 'And in the consubstantial Trinity of one essence' — this Trinitarian phrasing is from the Athanasian Creed, not the Apostles'
'He descended into hell' (descendit ad inferna) — a clause added in some Western forms around the 4th-5th centuries
'The communion of saints' (communionem sanctorum) — present in Latin and Greek forms of the Apostles' Creed
'The resurrection of the body' (carnis resurrectionem) — present from the earliest forms of the Apostles' Creed
context: The Apostles' Creed names propositions but does not elaborate Trinitarian metaphysics (left to Nicene and Athanasian Creeds). It is structured in three articles: Father, Son, Spirit. The 'descended into hell' clause is one of the more disputed elements — its meaning (Hades, the dead, hell proper) has been variously interpreted. The Apostles' Creed is used liturgically in Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran, Methodist, and many Reformed churches.

question: From 1643 to 1653, an assembly of Puritan divines met at Westminster (London) by order of the Long Parliament to advise on the reform of the Church of England. They produced four major documents: the Confession of Faith, the Larger and Shorter Catechisms, and the Directory for Public Worship. The Westminster Confession (1646) became the foundational doctrinal document for what tradition?
answer: Presbyterianism — adopted by the Church of Scotland in 1647 and by most English-speaking Presbyterian and Reformed churches
choices: Presbyterianism — adopted by the Church of Scotland in 1647 and by most English-speaking Presbyterian and Reformed churches
Anglicanism — adopted by the Church of England as superseding the 39 Articles of 1571 throughout the Cromwellian period
Methodism — adopted by John Wesley as the doctrinal foundation of the Methodist movement a century after publication
Congregationalism — adopted only by independent Congregationalist churches without conformity to the Westminster Assembly
context: The Westminster Confession remains the foundational doctrinal standard of the Church of Scotland, the Presbyterian Church (USA), the Orthodox Presbyterian Church, and dozens of other Reformed bodies. The Shorter Catechism's first question — 'What is the chief end of man?' Answer: 'To glorify God, and to enjoy him forever' — became one of the most-memorized texts in English-speaking Protestantism for three centuries.

question: Vatican I's 1870 definition of papal infallibility specified strict conditions. The pope is preserved from error only when he speaks ex cathedra ('from the chair'), defining a doctrine of faith or morals to be held by the universal church. Since 1870, the doctrine has been formally invoked exactly twice — both regarding Mary. What were the two ex cathedra definitions?
answer: Immaculate Conception (Pius IX, 1854) and Bodily Assumption (Pius XII, 1950)
choices: Immaculate Conception (Pius IX, 1854) and Bodily Assumption (Pius XII, 1950)
Bodily Assumption (Pius XII, 1950) and Co-Redemptrix (yet to be formally defined despite ongoing campaigns)
Perpetual Virginity (Pius IX, 1854) and Queen of Heaven (Pius XII, 1950)
Bodily Assumption (Pius XII, 1950) and the Sorrowful Heart doctrine (Pius XI, 1929)
context: The Immaculate Conception (defined December 8, 1854 in Ineffabilis Deus — sixteen years BEFORE Vatican I codified the infallibility doctrine the act exercised) and the Bodily Assumption (defined November 1, 1950 in Munificentissimus Deus) are the two undisputed ex cathedra definitions. Some Catholic theologians argue various other teachings should be considered infallible by ordinary magisterium even though not formally ex cathedra defined.

question: Catholic teaching on Mary developed gradually over the centuries, with four particular dogmas regarded as essential. Three are ancient — Theotokos (God-bearer, defined at Ephesus 431), Perpetual Virginity (universal patristic teaching), and her role in salvation history. The fourth is the Immaculate Conception. What does this dogma teach?
answer: Mary was preserved from original sin from the moment of her own conception in her mother's womb
choices: Mary was preserved from original sin from the moment of her own conception in her mother's womb
