Mary's conception of Jesus was without sexual union — the virginal conception of the Son rather than her own conception
Mary was sinless throughout her life by deliberate choice — moral perfection achieved by grace rather than by preservation
Mary was born without bodily defect — physical perfection corresponding to her spiritual unique calling
context: The Immaculate Conception (defined by Pius IX, 1854) refers to MARY's conception (in Anne's womb, traditionally), not Jesus's conception in Mary. The doctrine had been debated for centuries; Duns Scotus defended it against Aquinas's denial. Eastern Orthodoxy holds Mary's perpetual sinlessness but rejects the Western 'original sin' framework that requires preservation. Mary's bodily Assumption was defined in 1950.

question: Predestination has been bitterly disputed. Major positions: Augustinian-Calvinist (God predestines some, passes over others), Thomist (foreknowledge respects free choice), Molinist (God's 'middle knowledge' of counterfactuals allows predestination without violating freedom), Arminian (God predestines those he foreknows will believe). Who proposed the Molinist solution?
answer: Luis de Molina, 16th-century Spanish Jesuit — his De Concordia (1588) developed 'middle knowledge' to reconcile sovereignty and freedom
choices: Luis de Molina, 16th-century Spanish Jesuit — his De Concordia (1588) developed 'middle knowledge' to reconcile sovereignty and freedom
Cornelius Jansen, 17th-century Dutch theologian — his Augustinus revived strict Augustinian predestination against the Jesuits
Jacobus Arminius, 17th-century Dutch theologian — his Remonstrance (1610) named the position now called Arminianism
Theodore Beza, 16th-century French Reformed theologian — his Tabula Praedestinationis systematized supralapsarian Calvinism
context: Luis de Molina (1535-1600) developed 'middle knowledge' (scientia media) — God's knowledge of contingent counterfactuals (what every free creature would freely do in every possible situation). This allows God to ordain his providence without violating creaturely freedom. The Catholic Banez vs. Molina controversy raged 1582-1607; Pope Paul V suspended the dispute without resolution. Some Protestants (William Lane Craig) defend Molinism today.

question: Beginning in the late 1960s and especially after the 1968 Medellín bishops' conference, a movement called Liberation Theology emerged. Its founding text was Gustavo Gutiérrez's A Theology of Liberation (1971). It insisted on 'the preferential option for the poor' and used Marxist-influenced social analysis. How did the Vatican respond?
answer: Two CDF instructions under Cardinal Ratzinger (1984, 1986) cautioned against Marxist analysis while affirming concern for the poor
choices: Two CDF instructions under Cardinal Ratzinger (1984, 1986) cautioned against Marxist analysis while affirming concern for the poor
Pope John Paul II fully embraced liberation theology in his 1979 visit to Mexico — supporting Marxist class analysis
Pope Paul VI condemned liberation theology entirely in his 1971 encyclical Octogesima Adveniens issued just months after Gutiérrez
The Vatican made no formal response throughout the 20th century — liberation theology was allowed without correction
context: Cardinal Ratzinger's Libertatis Nuntius (1984) and Libertatis Conscientia (1986) for the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith cautioned against Marxist analysis while affirming the option for the poor. Several liberation theologians (Leonardo Boff, Jon Sobrino) were disciplined. Pope Francis as Cardinal Bergoglio engaged in this debate from the perspective of the Argentine 'theology of the people' — distinct from Marxist liberation theology.

question: In Hesiod's Theogony (c. 700 BC) — the most influential ancient Greek systematic account of the gods' origins — the cosmos does not begin with a creator god. Hesiod writes that first of all came something formless and primordial, from which other primordial entities then emerged: Gaia (Earth), Tartarus (the Abyss), and Eros (Desire). What did Hesiod call this first primordial reality?
answer: Chaos — not a place of confusion but a yawning void or chasm, the original gap from which other primordial beings issued
choices: Chaos — not a place of confusion but a yawning void or chasm, the original gap from which other primordial beings issued
Ouranos — the Sky, who actually came later as Gaia's offspring and was thus second-generation
Aether — the upper luminous air, who actually came later as Erebus's child by Nyx the Night
Pontos — the Sea, who actually came later as Gaia's offspring after Ouranos was generated
context: Hesiod's Chaos (Χάος) was etymologically a 'yawning gap' rather than disorder. Gaia, Tartarus, Eros emerged 'first of all' but after Chaos. Erebus (Darkness) and Nyx (Night) issued from Chaos; from them came Aether and Hemera (Day). The Theogony's structure parallels Near Eastern creation myths but with distinctively Greek features — no creator god, just emergence.

question: Per Hesiod's Theogony, the primordial Earth (Gaia) coupled with her son the Sky (Uranus) and bore the Titans, Cyclopes, and Hekatonkheires. Uranus, fearing or repulsed by the Hekatonkheires (hundred-handers), pushed his children back into Gaia's womb. Gaia in pain produced an adamantine sickle and asked her sons to use it. Only one was willing. What did he do?
answer: Cronus — the youngest Titan — castrated his father Uranus and threw the severed genitals into the sea
choices: Cronus — the youngest Titan — castrated his father Uranus and threw the severed genitals into the sea
Iapetus — the Titan of mortality — castrated his father Uranus and gave the genitals to Gaia for safekeeping
Hyperion — the Titan of light — castrated his father Uranus and burned the genitals on a great altar
Coeus — the Titan of intelligence — castrated his father Uranus and used the genitals to fashion the Moon
context: Hesiod's account: Cronus castrated Uranus; from the blood that fell on Gaia came the Furies, Giants, and Meliae (ash-tree nymphs); from the foam where the genitals fell in the sea came Aphrodite (born of the foam, 'aphros'). Uranus prophesied that Cronus would be overthrown by his own son — initiating the cycle of generational violence that runs through the Theogony.

question: After castrating his father Uranus, Cronus became king of the Titans. He married his sister Rhea; she bore him six children. Mindful of Uranus's prophecy that he would be overthrown by his own son, Cronus did something distinctive when each child was born. What did he do, and how did Rhea save the sixth?
answer: He swallowed each child whole; Rhea hid Zeus in a Cretan cave nursed by the goat Amalthea and gave Cronus a swaddled stone
choices: He swallowed each child whole; Rhea hid Zeus in a Cretan cave nursed by the goat Amalthea and gave Cronus a swaddled stone
He threw each child into Tartarus; Rhea hid Zeus among the Curetes of Crete who danced and clashed shields
He had each child killed by the Hekatonkheires; Rhea spirited Zeus to Egypt, where he grew up among Pharaoh's priests
He banished each child to the ends of the earth; Rhea hid Zeus among the Hyperboreans north of the wind
context: Hesiod records Cronus's serial cannibalism. Rhea, hiding her sixth pregnancy, bore Zeus on Mount Lyctus in Crete (or Mount Ida in some versions) and gave Cronus a stone wrapped in swaddling. The goat Amalthea nursed Zeus; her horn became the cornucopia. The Curetes (or Korybantes) clashed bronze shields to drown the infant's cries. The substitution stone was later set up at Delphi.

question: Having grown to adulthood in hiding, Zeus returned to Mount Olympus and forced Cronus to disgorge his swallowed siblings — Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, Poseidon. With these gods Zeus made war on Cronus and the Titans. The war lasted ten years. What was the decisive factor that turned the tide for the Olympians?
answer: Zeus freed the Cyclopes and Hekatonkheires from Tartarus; the Cyclopes forged thunderbolts for Zeus and the hundred-handers hurled rocks
choices: Zeus freed the Cyclopes and Hekatonkheires from Tartarus; the Cyclopes forged thunderbolts for Zeus and the hundred-handers hurled rocks
Zeus persuaded Cronus's mother Gaia to side with the Olympians; she withdrew her support from the Titans by withholding harvests
Zeus traveled to the underworld and bargained with Tartarus directly for the souls of dead Titan warriors to be released
Zeus discovered Cronus's swallow-trick had weakened him; one decisive battle in the open plains broke the Titans' army
context: The Titanomachy ended when Zeus, advised by Gaia, freed the Cyclopes (Brontes, Steropes, Arges) and Hekatonkheires (Briareus, Cottus, Gyges) who had been imprisoned by Uranus. The Cyclopes' thunderbolts, Hades's helmet of invisibility (gift of the Cyclopes), and Poseidon's trident together overcame the Titans. The defeated Titans were chained in Tartarus, guarded by the Hekatonkheires.

question: Among the Titans who sided with Zeus (rather than against him) in the Titanomachy was Prometheus ('Forethought'). Despite his alliance, Prometheus had a complex relationship with Zeus. After Zeus took fire away from humans, Prometheus stole it from Mount Olympus — concealed in a hollow fennel stalk — and gave it back to mortals. What was Zeus's punishment?
answer: Chained Prometheus to a rock in the Caucasus; an eagle ate his liver daily; the liver grew back each night
choices: Chained Prometheus to a rock in the Caucasus; an eagle ate his liver daily; the liver grew back each night
Banished Prometheus to Hyperborea beyond the north wind; he could neither see fire again nor speak of his crime
Forced Prometheus to swallow molten gold; the cooled metal would slowly choke him through the ages
Confined Prometheus to Tartarus with the other defeated Titans; he was given no special punishment beyond imprisonment
context: Aeschylus's Prometheus Bound (c. 460 BC) dramatized the punishment. Heracles eventually shot the eagle and freed Prometheus (with Zeus's consent, or against it depending on the version). Hesiod also tells the prior story of Prometheus's deception at Mecone — he tricked Zeus into accepting bones wrapped in fat for sacrifice, leaving the meat for humans (which is why Greeks burned bones to the gods).

question: After Prometheus's theft of fire, Zeus determined to punish humanity. He commanded Hephaestus to fashion the first woman from clay — beautiful and irresistible. Athena dressed her; Aphrodite gave her charm; Hermes gave her cunning and deceptive speech. Each god contributed (hence 'all-gifted'). Zeus sent her to Prometheus's brother Epimetheus with a sealed container. What was she instructed to do, and what was inside?
answer: She opened the jar (Greek 'pithos,' often translated 'box'); all evils flew out into the world; only Hope remained inside
choices: She opened the jar (Greek 'pithos,' often translated 'box'); all evils flew out into the world; only Hope remained inside
She gave the jar to Epimetheus to open; when he refused, she destroyed the jar; the trapped evils spread regardless
She buried the jar at her death; the contents leaked into the soil and emerged as crop blights and pestilences
She entrusted the jar to her daughter Pyrrha; Pyrrha kept it sealed; the evils within remain trapped to this day
context: Hesiod's Works and Days tells the story. Pandora ('all-gifted' — name reflects the gods' contributions) opened the pithos out of curiosity; hope (elpis) remained within. The 'Pandora's box' translation is from Erasmus's 1508 Adagia, which substituted 'pyxis' (box) for 'pithos' (storage jar). The myth's relationship to Genesis 3 (woman's curiosity, the introduction of evil) has long fascinated comparative mythologists.

question: Distinct from the Titanomachy (Olympians vs. Titans) is the Gigantomachy — the war between the Olympian gods and the Giants (gigantes), monstrous offspring of Gaia born from the blood that fell when Uranus was castrated. Gaia, angry that the Titans were imprisoned, incited the Giants to attack Olympus. A prophecy declared that the Giants could be killed only by a god and one specific other being. Who, and what was decisive?
answer: Only a god working with a mortal — Heracles fought alongside Zeus, Athena, and Poseidon to kill the Giants
choices: Only a god working with a mortal — Heracles fought alongside Zeus, Athena, and Poseidon to kill the Giants
Only Zeus and Hera together — no other gods could approach the Giants except in the cosmic king's presence
Only Apollo and Artemis as twins — the divine twins alone could break the Giants' immortality together
Only the Cyclopes' new weapons — the Olympians needed second-generation thunderbolts to overcome the Giants
context: The Gigantomachy is the subject of major Greek sculpture — the Pergamon Altar (c. 180 BC, now in Berlin) is the largest and most famous frieze. Heracles is essential because of the 'god plus mortal' prophecy. The Giants (Alcyoneus, Porphyrion, Enceladus, Mimas, others) were buried under volcanoes and mountains by the victorious Olympians.

question: After the Gigantomachy, Gaia bore a final monstrous opponent of the Olympians — Typhon (or Typhoeus), the most fearsome being in Greek myth. Hesiod describes him as having a hundred snake-heads from his shoulders, eyes shooting fire, voices producing all sounds from gods to bulls. Initially he routed the Olympians (who fled to Egypt in animal forms). Zeus eventually confronted him alone. Where was Typhon imprisoned?
answer: Under Mount Etna in Sicily — where his struggles to escape are said to cause the volcano's eruptions
choices: Under Mount Etna in Sicily — where his struggles to escape are said to cause the volcano's eruptions
Under Mount Olympus itself — where his chains pull the mountain down each time he stirs from sleep
Under the Aegean Sea floor near Lesbos — where his thrashing is said to cause earthquakes throughout the Aegean
Under the Pillars of Heracles at Gibraltar — where his head supports the meeting of Mediterranean and Atlantic
context: Hesiod's Theogony describes the battle. Apollodorus's Library tells the Egyptian flight. Mount Etna's eruptions — and other volcanic activity around the Mediterranean (Vesuvius, Stromboli, Thera) — were attributed to Typhon's struggles. He fathered with Echidna a brood of monsters: the Hydra, Cerberus, Chimera, Sphinx, Nemean Lion.

question: In Works and Days, Hesiod recounts not a single creation but a series of human races — successive ages of humanity. Each race was created by the gods, lived its time, and ended in some way. The races declined in nobility through the sequence. What is the order of races as Hesiod gives them?
answer: Golden, Silver, Bronze, Heroic, Iron — with the Heroic age (Trojan War, Theban war) inserted between the Bronze and Iron
choices: Golden, Silver, Bronze, Heroic, Iron — with the Heroic age (Trojan War, Theban war) inserted between the Bronze and Iron
Golden, Silver, Bronze, Iron — a straight four-fold descent, with no Heroic age intervening between Bronze and Iron
Golden, Bronze, Silver, Iron, Lead — a five-fold descent corresponding to the metal-hierarchy of Pythagorean tradition
Iron, Bronze, Silver, Golden — an ascending sequence indicating humanity's gradual moral perfection over the ages
context: Hesiod's five-age scheme (Works and Days 109-201) is unusual in inserting the Heroic age between Bronze and Iron — perhaps because he wanted to honor the great heroes of myth without breaking the descending nobility pattern. Hesiod placed himself in the Iron Age — already characterized by toil, conflict, and moral decline. The scheme influenced subsequent reflections on cyclical history (Vico, Spengler).

question: After several generations of human wickedness, Zeus determined to destroy mankind by a great flood. He warned only one couple in advance — the Titan Prometheus's son Deucalion and his wife Pyrrha (Epimetheus and Pandora's daughter). They built an ark, survived the nine-day flood, and landed on Mount Parnassus. They consulted the oracle of Themis. What did the oracle command, and what was the result?
answer: 'Cast the bones of your mother behind you'; they threw stones (the bones of Mother Earth); the stones became a new human race
choices: 'Cast the bones of your mother behind you'; they threw stones (the bones of Mother Earth); the stones became a new human race
'Lay seven garlands on the cold altar of Themis'; they did so; from the garlands sprang the new race of men and women
'Sail to Egypt with sweet water of the Nile'; they did so; the new humans grew from Pyrrha's tears in the river silt
'Plant olive saplings on every hilltop of Hellas'; they did so; the new race emerged from the cracking of olive seeds
context: The Deucalion-Pyrrha story parallels biblical Noah's flood, Sumerian Utnapishtim, and other Near Eastern flood myths. Stones from Deucalion became men; stones from Pyrrha became women — the pun on Greek 'laos' (people) and 'laas' (stone) is the etymology. Hellen (eponymous ancestor of the Hellenes) was their son. The myth was central to Greek self-understanding.

question: Zeus, king of the gods, was infamous in myth for his many liaisons with mortal and divine women — fathering numerous heroes and demigods. To escape Hera's jealousy (and sometimes the women's resistance), Zeus often appeared in disguised form. Match the lover to Zeus's disguise: which of the following is correct?
answer: Leda — a swan; Europa — a bull; Danaë — a shower of gold; Ganymede — an eagle
choices: Leda — a swan; Europa — a bull; Danaë — a shower of gold; Ganymede — an eagle
Leda — a bull; Europa — a swan; Danaë — an eagle; Ganymede — a shower of gold
Leda — an eagle; Europa — a shower of gold; Danaë — a bull; Ganymede — a swan
Leda — a shower of gold; Europa — an eagle; Danaë — a swan; Ganymede — a bull
context: Zeus's disguises are among the most-painted scenes in Western art. Leda + swan produced Helen and the twins Castor and Pollux; Europa + bull produced Minos; Danaë + golden shower produced Perseus; Ganymede (Trojan prince) + eagle was carried up to Olympus as cupbearer. These transformations have inspired Yeats's 'Leda and the Swan' (1924), countless Renaissance paintings.

question: King Tyndareus's wife Leda of Sparta caught Zeus's attention. Disguised as a swan — pursued by an eagle (in some versions) — Zeus came to her by the river Eurotas. Leda also lay with her husband the same night. She produced an unusual brood. What were the children, and what was their significance?
answer: Two eggs hatched four children: Helen, Clytemnestra, and the twins Castor and Pollux (Dioscuri)
choices: Two eggs hatched four children: Helen, Clytemnestra, and the twins Castor and Pollux (Dioscuri)
Two eggs hatched two children: Helen alone from Zeus's egg, Clytemnestra alone from Tyndareus's egg
Three eggs hatched six children: Castor, Pollux, Helen, Clytemnestra, Iphianassa, and Phoebe
One egg hatched three children: Helen, Polydeuces, and Achilles in a single divine birth
context: The traditional version: two eggs, four children. The twins Castor (mortal son of Tyndareus) and Pollux (immortal son of Zeus) became inseparable; when Castor died, Pollux shared his immortality, becoming the constellation Gemini. Helen's elopement (or abduction) with Paris caused the Trojan War. Clytemnestra married Agamemnon and murdered him on his return from Troy.

question: Europa was the daughter of King Agenor of Tyre (Phoenicia). Zeus fell in love with her as she played with friends by the shore. He transformed himself into a magnificent white bull — tame and beautiful — and approached. She climbed on his back. The bull plunged into the sea and swam, with Europa clinging to his horns, all the way to Crete. There Zeus assumed his true form and lay with her. What were the consequences?
answer: She bore three sons including Minos (king of Crete); the continent of Europe was named after her
choices: She bore three sons including Minos (king of Crete); the continent of Europe was named after her
She bore four daughters who founded Carthage; the continent of Europe takes its name from a different Europa
She fled back to Phoenicia after the encounter; Cadmus founded Thebes searching for her in Greece
She was returned to Tyre by Poseidon's intervention; the Phoenician alphabet later spread back to Greek lands
context: Europa's sons by Zeus: Minos, Rhadamanthus, Sarpedon. Minos became king of Crete and (with Rhadamanthus) judge of the dead. Her brother Cadmus, sent by Agenor to find her, gave up the search and founded Thebes — bringing the Phoenician alphabet to Greece. 'Europe' as continental name appears in Hesiod and after; the etymology connects to the Phoenician princess.

question: King Acrisius of Argos received an oracle that his daughter Danaë's son would kill him. To prevent this, Acrisius locked Danaë in a bronze tower (or underground chamber) with no possibility of male contact. Zeus, however, came to her in a form that could penetrate the tower. What was it, and who was their child?
answer: A shower of gold that fell through a roof aperture; their son was the hero Perseus
choices: A shower of gold that fell through a roof aperture; their son was the hero Perseus
A breath of wind that entered through a keyhole; their son was the hero Bellerophon
A column of light that descended through the ceiling; their son was the hero Heracles
A flowing stream that seeped under the door; their son was the hero Theseus
context: Acrisius, learning of Perseus's birth, placed Danaë and the infant in a chest and cast it into the sea. They drifted to the island of Seriphos, where the fisherman Dictys rescued them. Perseus grew up to behead Medusa, rescue Andromeda, and eventually kill his grandfather Acrisius (by accident with a discus) — fulfilling the prophecy. Klimt's painting 'Danaë' (1907) is among the most famous treatments.

question: The Trojan prince Ganymede was the most beautiful of mortals — son of King Tros (eponymous ancestor of Troy). Zeus saw him from Olympus and was struck by desire. What did Zeus do, and what role did Ganymede take on Olympus?
answer: Zeus took the form of an eagle, swooped down, and carried Ganymede up to Olympus; he became cupbearer of the gods
choices: Zeus took the form of an eagle, swooped down, and carried Ganymede up to Olympus; he became cupbearer of the gods
Zeus sent the goddess Iris to bring Ganymede; he became messenger of the gods alongside Hermes
Zeus appeared as a Trojan elder and persuaded Tros to let Ganymede train as a charioteer; he drove Zeus's chariot
Zeus disguised himself as a mortal hunter; Ganymede joined the hunt and was lifted up at the end; he became armorer
context: Ganymede became cupbearer to Zeus, replacing Hebe (goddess of youth) in that role. The myth was treated with explicit homoeroticism by ancient writers; pederasty in religious contexts (Zeus + Ganymede as paradigm) was a contested element of Greek religious practice. In compensation, Zeus gave Tros a herd of immortal horses. Ganymede became the constellation Aquarius.

question: Hera was Zeus's sister-wife and queen of Olympus. Their relationship was tempestuous — Zeus's many infidelities provoked Hera's furious vengeance, which usually fell on the women and their offspring rather than on Zeus himself. Hera famously persecuted Heracles (son of Zeus by Alcmene), nearly killing him in his cradle. What did the infant Heracles do?
answer: Strangled two serpents Hera sent into his cradle to kill him — astonishing his mortal parents Amphitryon and Alcmene
choices: Strangled two serpents Hera sent into his cradle to kill him — astonishing his mortal parents Amphitryon and Alcmene
Outran a great hare Hera sent to bite him — circling the cradle so swiftly his speed amazed the gods
Sang to two harpies Hera sent — his crying voice (already a divine baritone) charmed them into withdrawal
Threw two thunderbolts at the serpents — his prenatal divine power emerging spontaneously at the threat
context: The infant Heracles's strangling of the serpents (often depicted in art) was the first sign of his divine paternity. Hera's persecution of Heracles continued throughout his life — the Twelve Labors themselves were imposed because Hera's madness drove Heracles to kill his own children. The Greek name 'Heracles' means 'Glory of Hera' — possibly a sardonic name for the man whose suffering she caused.

question: Iris was the goddess of the rainbow and a messenger of the gods — particularly serving Hera (just as Hermes served Zeus). Daughter of the Titan Thaumas and the Oceanid Electra, she was the swift courier of divine commands between Olympus, the upper world, and the underworld. What is Iris's symbolic significance in Greek thought?
answer: The rainbow as a bridge connecting heaven and earth — divine messages from gods to mortals as light through rain
choices: The rainbow as a bridge connecting heaven and earth — divine messages from gods to mortals as light through rain
The rainbow as a curse mark on the world — the price humans paid for accepting Pandora's jar from the gods
The rainbow as a memorial of the great flood — the sign that Zeus would not destroy humanity by water again
The rainbow as Zeus's bowstring — the weapon used to subdue Typhon during the cosmic battle before Olympus rose
context: Iris connecting heaven and earth via the rainbow is a beautiful theological motif — distinct from Iris in Hesiod (who carries the water of the Styx for the gods' binding oaths). Iris remained relatively minor compared to Hermes, but appears frequently in Homer and the Homeric Hymns. The biological iris (eye, flower) is named for the goddess; iridescence retains the etymology.

question: Poseidon was one of the three brothers — sons of Cronus and Rhea — who drew lots after the Titanomachy to divide the cosmos. Zeus drew the sky, Hades the underworld, and Poseidon the sea. (Earth and Olympus were held in common.) Poseidon wielded a trident forged by the Cyclopes, with which he could shake the earth and raise storms. What was his epithet in Homer?
answer: Earth-shaker (Ennosigaios) — Poseidon's power extended to causing earthquakes, not just to the sea
choices: Earth-shaker (Ennosigaios) — Poseidon's power extended to causing earthquakes, not just to the sea
Cloud-gatherer (Nephelegereta) — actually Zeus's standard Homeric epithet, not Poseidon's
Far-shooter (Hekatebolos) — actually Apollo's standard Homeric epithet, not Poseidon's
Many-counseled (Polymetis) — actually Odysseus's standard Homeric epithet, not Poseidon's
context: Poseidon's Earth-shaker title connected him to earthquakes (which the Greeks understood as the sea's roots beneath the land disturbing). His son Polyphemus the Cyclops was blinded by Odysseus, provoking Poseidon's ten-year persecution. Horses were sacred to him; he supposedly created the horse (or the salt-water spring; versions vary) in his contest with Athena for Athens.

question: In the founding myth of Athens, Poseidon and Athena competed for the city's patronage. Each offered the city a gift; the people (or the gods, or king Cecrops) would judge whose gift was more valuable. What did each give, and who won?
answer: Poseidon — a salt-water spring; Athena — the olive tree; Athena won and the city was named for her
choices: Poseidon — a salt-water spring; Athena — the olive tree; Athena won and the city was named for her
Poseidon — the horse for warfare; Athena — the spear-shaft of bronze; Poseidon won and Athens armed itself first
Poseidon — the sea route to wealth; Athena — the loom for cloth; the gods split the city by halves between them
Poseidon — a fish that brought storms; Athena — the bee that made honey; the judges declared a tie that day
context: The olive (Athena's gift) provided oil for food, light, anointing, and athletic competition — central to the Mediterranean economy. The Erechtheion on the Acropolis incorporates marks attributed to Poseidon's trident strike. Poseidon's anger at losing manifested in periodic floods (according to myth, his salt-spring still flowed). The contest is depicted on the Parthenon's west pediment.

question: In Homer's Odyssey, Odysseus's ten-year wandering after the Trojan War is largely caused by Poseidon's enmity. The trigger was Odysseus's encounter with one of Poseidon's sons. Which son, and what did Odysseus do?
answer: Polyphemus the Cyclops — Odysseus blinded him to escape his cave; Polyphemus prayed to Poseidon for vengeance
choices: Polyphemus the Cyclops — Odysseus blinded him to escape his cave; Polyphemus prayed to Poseidon for vengeance
Triton the merman — Odysseus shipwrecked on his reef but did not propitiate him with proper offerings on landing
Pegasus the winged horse — Odysseus attempted to capture him for his own use against Poseidon's prohibition
Proteus the shape-shifter — Odysseus wrestled him for prophecy but did not pay the proper tribute afterward
context: Polyphemus's blinding (Odyssey Book 9) is one of the great set-pieces of Western literature. Odysseus called himself 'Nobody' (Outis) when asked his name; when Polyphemus called for help, his neighbors heard 'Nobody is hurting me' and ignored him. Odysseus's pride in shouting back his real name as he sailed away gave Polyphemus the information to curse him by name to Poseidon.

question: Hades — the third Olympian brother — drew the lot of the underworld in the post-Titanomachy division. He was god of the dead and of mineral wealth beneath the earth (silver, gold, ores). Greeks rarely named him directly, fearing to attract his notice; they used euphemisms. What was the most common?
answer: Plouton ('the wealthy one') — referring to mineral wealth; later Latinized as Pluto in Roman usage
choices: Plouton ('the wealthy one') — referring to mineral wealth; later Latinized as Pluto in Roman usage
Helios ('the bright one') — though this name actually belonged to the Titan of the sun, distinct from Hades
Zelos ('the zealous one') — a euphemism rejecting any association with the proper underworld god
Hyperion ('the high one') — a Titanic name used among certain Pythagorean schools but not generally
context: Plouton (Πλούτων) — 'Pluto' in Latin — was the favored euphemism. The English word 'plutocracy' (rule of wealth) preserves it. Hades was rarely worshipped openly; sacrifices to him used black animals at night with averted face. The underworld realm itself is sometimes also called Hades by metonymy. Hades shared with Demeter the realm of agricultural fertility through the Persephone story.

question: Persephone (Roman Proserpina), daughter of Demeter (goddess of grain) and Zeus, was gathering flowers in a meadow when the earth opened and Hades emerged in his chariot drawn by black horses. He seized her and carried her down to the underworld to be his bride. Demeter searched the earth for her daughter in mourning; nothing grew. Hermes was sent to negotiate her return. What was the catch?
answer: Persephone had eaten pomegranate seeds in the underworld; she had to spend that many months each year with Hades
choices: Persephone had eaten pomegranate seeds in the underworld; she had to spend that many months each year with Hades
Persephone had touched the asphodel meadows; she had to return for the equinox of each year going forward
Persephone had wept in Hades's presence; she was bound to comfort him for one season annually thereafter
Persephone had taken Hades's helmet of invisibility; she had to return every spring to give it back to him
context: The Persephone myth explains the seasons: she spends spring and summer with Demeter (the earth bears fruit) and autumn/winter with Hades (nothing grows). The pomegranate seeds (varies: 3, 4, or 6) became iconic. The myth was central to the Eleusinian Mysteries — Greek mystery religion's most famous initiation, focused on Demeter and Kore (Persephone). The mysteries were kept secret for nearly 2,000 years.

question: Demeter — goddess of grain, agriculture, and the harvest — was a major Olympian (one of Cronus's children, sister of Zeus). Her search for the abducted Persephone took her wandering across the earth in disguise as an old woman. Where did she rest, and what did the king and queen there do that became foundational for Greek religious practice?
answer: At Eleusis under King Celeus and Queen Metaneira; she was made nurse to Demophoön; her secret rites became the Eleusinian Mysteries
choices: At Eleusis under King Celeus and Queen Metaneira; she was made nurse to Demophoön; her secret rites became the Eleusinian Mysteries
At Athens under King Erechtheus; she taught the women to grind grain; the Thesmophoria women's festival began here
At Delphi under King Pelias; she taught the priestesses the chthonic prayers; the Pythian rites began here
At Olympia under King Pelops; she healed his shoulder of ivory; the agricultural games of Hera began here
context: The Homeric Hymn to Demeter (c. 600 BC) tells the Eleusis episode in detail. The Eleusinian Mysteries — initiated annually for two millennia (c. 1500 BC – 392 AD) — were among the most influential religious practices of antiquity. Cicero, Plutarch, and many others wrote of their transformative power. The hieron logos (sacred story) was so well-kept that we still do not know its content with certainty.

question: The Eleusinian Mysteries — held annually in autumn at Eleusis, fifteen miles from Athens — were the most prestigious mystery religion of the ancient Greek world. Initiated annually for almost two millennia (c. 1500 BC until 392 AD), they were open to anyone (men, women, slaves, foreigners — but not murderers or those who spoke Greek poorly enough to misunderstand the rites). What was their fundamental hope offered to initiates?
answer: Hope of a blessed afterlife — initiates would have a better fate among the dead than the uninitiated would have
choices: Hope of a blessed afterlife — initiates would have a better fate among the dead than the uninitiated would have
Hope of agricultural prosperity — initiates would have abundant crops on their own farms for the coming year
Hope of political success — initiates would advance in Athens's democratic offices through Demeter's blessing
Hope of erotic fulfillment — initiates would find spouses through the matchmaking sacred to Persephone
context: Sophocles wrote: 'Thrice happy are those mortals who, having seen these rites, depart for Hades; for them alone there is true life there.' The Greater Mysteries (autumn) and Lesser Mysteries (spring) involved a procession from Athens, ritual fasting, drinking the kykeon (perhaps psychoactive?), and culminated in a vision in the Telesterion. The Roman Emperor Theodosius closed Eleusis in 392 AD as part of his anti-pagan campaign.

question: Hestia — eldest child of Cronus and Rhea, sister of Zeus, Hera, Hades, Poseidon, and Demeter — was goddess of the hearth, home, and family. Though one of the twelve principal Olympians in older lists, she was eventually replaced in some accounts by a different god. Whom, and why?
answer: Dionysus — Hestia voluntarily yielded her seat among the Twelve when Dionysus's late addition required room
choices: Dionysus — Hestia voluntarily yielded her seat among the Twelve when Dionysus's late addition required room
Heracles — Hestia gave up her place when Heracles was deified after his death and ascended to Olympus
Helios — Hestia stepped aside when the sun-god's importance required formal Olympian status by acclamation
Themis — Hestia ceded her place when the goddess of divine law was formally added by Zeus's decree
context: Dionysus's late arrival on Olympus (as a 'newcomer' god) caused the twelve-throne problem. Tradition resolved it by having Hestia voluntarily yield. She was rarely depicted in art (no scandals, no adventures) but was central to Greek domestic religion — every household hearth was her shrine. The Roman counterpart Vesta retained more prominent public cult, with the Vestal Virgins guarding her perpetual flame in the Forum.

question: Athena was unique among Olympians for her birth. Zeus had swallowed his first wife Metis (Wisdom) when she became pregnant — fearing a prophecy that her son would overthrow him. The fetus continued to develop inside Zeus. Eventually he developed a terrible headache. What was the resolution, and what came forth?
answer: Hephaestus split open Zeus's head with an axe; Athena leaped out fully armed, with a war-cry shaking Olympus
choices: Hephaestus split open Zeus's head with an axe; Athena leaped out fully armed, with a war-cry shaking Olympus
Prometheus opened Zeus's head with a chisel; Athena emerged silent as an infant cradled in golden swaddling clothes
Apollo healed Zeus by a sacred chant; Athena was peacefully extracted as a sleeping maiden through the skull's pores
Hermes drilled a hole through Zeus's temple; Athena flowed out as a stream that hardened into the goddess on the ground
context: Athena's birth from Zeus's head — fully grown, fully armed (helmet, spear, aegis), with a war-cry — is among the most iconic Greek myths. The 'Hephaestus + axe' version is most common. Athena's parthenogenetic birth (no mother) reinforced her status as goddess of wisdom and strategic war (in contrast to Ares's blood-lust battle). She was the patron of Athens, hence her name (or the city's name; either etymology).

question: Arachne, a young Lydian woman, was renowned for her weaving — and proud enough to claim her skill matched the goddess Athena's. Athena, disguised as an old woman, warned her against such hubris; Arachne dismissed the warning. Athena revealed herself and challenged her to a contest. They wove. Arachne's tapestry depicted the gods' shameful seductions of mortal women — and was technically faultless. What did Athena do?
answer: Tore Arachne's tapestry, struck her with the shuttle; Arachne hanged herself; Athena transformed her into a spider
choices: Tore Arachne's tapestry, struck her with the shuttle; Arachne hanged herself; Athena transformed her into a spider
Praised Arachne's skill but admonished her humility; Arachne went back to weaving and lived a long life ashamed
Wept at Arachne's depictions of the gods' cruelties; turned to leave; Arachne died of exhaustion from the strain
Took Arachne to Olympus as an honored weaver of divine cloths; she became a minor goddess of fine textiles
context: Ovid's Metamorphoses Book 6 tells the story. Athena (Minerva) won not because of superior skill but because she could not abide Arachne's depiction of the gods' moral failings — and because Arachne's pride exceeded the limits of mortal propriety. Arachne's transformation to spider is etymologically retained in 'arachnid.' The myth treats artistic excellence and divine privilege ambiguously.

question: Apollo and his twin Artemis were children of Zeus by the Titaness Leto. Hera, jealous, forbade any place to give Leto refuge for birth. Eventually the floating island of Delos accepted her; she bore the twins there. Apollo, only a few days old, set off on his first divine mission. Where, and to do what?
answer: To Delphi, to kill the dragon Python that guarded the oracle of Mother Earth, and to establish his own oracle there
choices: To Delphi, to kill the dragon Python that guarded the oracle of Mother Earth, and to establish his own oracle there
To Olympus, to confront Hera over her persecution of his mother — establishing his honor as Zeus's son
To Troy, to begin the long protection of that city through its early generations — siding with future Priam
To Hyperborea beyond the north wind, to consult the elders about the proper rites for an oracle of his own
context: Apollo's killing of Python (a serpent or dragon) established his Delphic oracle on the site of an older earth-mother oracle. Apollo was thereafter called 'Pythian Apollo'; the priestess was the 'Pythia.' The Pythian Games (held at Delphi every four years) commemorated the slaying. Apollo's purification ceremony at Tempe after the killing established the Septerion ritual repeated every nine years.

question: Apollo mocked Eros (Cupid) for playing with archery, the boy god's bow against the great god's. Eros took revenge by shooting Apollo with a gold-tipped arrow of love and the nymph Daphne with a lead-tipped arrow of revulsion. Apollo pursued Daphne through forests. Just as he was about to catch her, she prayed to her father Peneus (a river god). What happened?
answer: She was transformed into a laurel tree (Greek 'daphne'); Apollo made the laurel his sacred plant and crowned victors with it
choices: She was transformed into a laurel tree (Greek 'daphne'); Apollo made the laurel his sacred plant and crowned victors with it
She was transformed into a cypress tree; Apollo wept and made the cypress sacred to mourning forevermore
She was transformed into a fountain; Apollo drank from her waters and they became sacred to poetic inspiration
She was transformed into a swan; Apollo's chariot was henceforth pulled by swans rather than by his earlier horses
context: Ovid's Metamorphoses tells the story. The Greek 'daphne' means 'laurel.' The laurel wreath became the symbol of Pythian Games victors, of poets (poet laureate), and of triumphant Romans. Bernini's marble Apollo and Daphne (1622-25) in the Galleria Borghese captures the moment of transformation — fingers turning to twigs, hair to leaves. The myth treats divine pursuit and consent ambiguously.

question: The oracle of Delphi was the most prestigious religious center of the Greek world for over a thousand years (c. 800 BC to 393 AD). Consultations went through a priestess called the Pythia (after Apollo's killing of Python). She sat on a tripod over a chasm in the inner sanctuary (adyton) of Apollo's temple. What was the proposed source of her inspiration, by ancient and modern accounts?
answer: Vapors rising from the chasm — possibly ethylene or other gases — recent geological work has partly confirmed this
choices: Vapors rising from the chasm — possibly ethylene or other gases — recent geological work has partly confirmed this
A sacred laurel branch she chewed and burned — providing a hallucinogen of which the bay leaf is now neutral
Pure psychological possession by Apollo — no physical cause; the priestess's spiritual qualification alone determined it
Wine mixed with snake venom — drunk before each consultation in a ritual the priests of Apollo kept secret
context: Recent geological studies (de Boer, Hale, Spiller 2001) found ethylene-containing gases at the Delphi temple site, supporting Plutarch's ancient account of pneuma. Ethylene in small doses produces euphoric states; large doses produce confusion. The Pythia would speak; priests translated her ravings into hexameter responses. Famous responses: to Croesus, 'a great empire shall fall' (his own); to Athens, 'wooden walls' (the navy at Salamis).

question: Inscribed at the entrance to Apollo's temple at Delphi were three famous maxims — attributed to the Seven Sages, the wisdom traditions of archaic Greece. These maxims encapsulated the moral wisdom that Apollo's worship was meant to teach. Which of the following is NOT one of the three principal Delphic maxims?
answer: 'Wealth is wisdom' (ho ploutos sophia) — actually a later Hellenistic cynical inversion, not a genuine Delphic maxim
choices: 'Wealth is wisdom' (ho ploutos sophia) — actually a later Hellenistic cynical inversion, not a genuine Delphic maxim
'Know thyself' (γνῶθι σεαυτόν) — gnothi seauton — the most famous of the three Delphic maxims
'Nothing in excess' (μηδὲν ἄγαν) — mēden agan — the second principal maxim of moderation and the mean
'Surety brings ruin' (ἐγγύα πάρα δ' ἄτη) — engya para d' atē — the warning against rash pledges and oaths
context: The three maxims (gnothi seauton, mēden agan, engya para d' atē) became foundational for Greek ethics. 'Know thyself' was central to Socrates's philosophical inquiry. 'Nothing in excess' grounded the Aristotelian mean. The maxims represented practical wisdom over against the heroic pride that brought tragedy. They were probably inscribed by the late archaic period (6th century BC).

question: Artemis — Apollo's twin sister, daughter of Zeus by Leto — was goddess of wild nature, the hunt, the moon (in later identification with Selene), and protector of virgins and young children. As a young goddess, she asked her father Zeus for a specific gift that would define her. What did she ask for?
answer: Eternal virginity, a bow and arrows, a band of nymph companions, mountains for hunting, lordship over towns
choices: Eternal virginity, a bow and arrows, a band of nymph companions, mountains for hunting, lordship over towns
Eternal youth, golden apples, fast deer, the right to choose which mortals would die in battle, and Olympus's eastern wing
Eternal joy, the keys to dawn, swift horses, the lordship over all springs of pure water, and a private hunting ground
Eternal beauty, a magical bow, the friendship of beasts, dominion over the constellations, and a sacred grove on Olympus
context: Callimachus's Hymn to Artemis records the wish list. Her eternal virginity (parthenia) was non-negotiable — she fiercely punished any who threatened it (Actaeon, who saw her bathing; Orion, in some versions). She and Apollo together slaughtered the children of Niobe for her boast. She was particularly worshipped at Ephesus (the famous temple, one of the Seven Wonders, was hers) and at Brauron in Attica.

question: The hunter Actaeon, grandson of Cadmus of Thebes, was hunting in the forest when he stumbled upon a clearing where Artemis was bathing with her nymphs in a pool. He saw the naked goddess. What did Artemis do, and what was Actaeon's fate?
answer: Transformed Actaeon into a stag; his own fifty hunting dogs caught and tore him to pieces, not recognizing their master
choices: Transformed Actaeon into a stag; his own fifty hunting dogs caught and tore him to pieces, not recognizing their master
Blinded Actaeon and gave him the gift of prophecy; he wandered the wilderness as a seer until he died of grief
Made Actaeon mute; he could never speak of what he had seen, but the trauma haunted him until his old age
Cursed Actaeon's whole house; his descendants died one by one until the line was extinguished without violence
context: Ovid's Metamorphoses Book 3 tells the story. Actaeon's transformation and death exemplified the danger of seeing what should not be seen — divine modesty enforced by lethal violence. The fifty hounds are named individually by Ovid. The myth resonates with the danger of any forbidden glimpse — paralleled biblically by Uzzah touching the ark (2 Samuel 6).

question: Ares — son of Zeus and Hera, god of war — was unusually unpopular among the Olympians. Zeus himself calls him 'most hateful to me of all the gods that hold Olympus' (Iliad 5.890). Even his mother Hera disliked him. What does Ares represent that the Greek pantheon distinguished from Athena's war-portfolio?
answer: Brute battle-frenzy and slaughter — distinguished from Athena's strategic warfare guided by reason
choices: Brute battle-frenzy and slaughter — distinguished from Athena's strategic warfare guided by reason
Defensive warfare and shield-craft — distinguished from Athena's pure offensive arts and weapon-making
Naval warfare and ship-craft — distinguished from Athena's land warfare and the chariot-making of Aphrodite
Sacrificial warfare and dueling — distinguished from Athena's mass conflict and Hera's siege-craft and walls
context: The Ares-Athena distinction is theologically interesting: Greek thought distinguished irrational bloodlust from rational strategy. Ares (Mars in Latin) was more popular in Rome (Romulus was supposedly his son). His Olympian unpopularity made him sometimes seem comically humiliated — caught with Aphrodite by Hephaestus's net (Odyssey 8), wounded by Diomedes (Iliad 5), bound by the Aloadae in a bronze jar for thirteen months.

question: Aphrodite — goddess of love, beauty, and sexual desire — had two competing origin myths. The Homeric tradition called her daughter of Zeus and Dione (a minor Titaness). The Hesiodic tradition gave her a far more dramatic origin. What did Hesiod tell?
answer: She arose from the sea foam (aphros) where the severed genitals of Uranus had fallen, drifting to Cyprus as a fully grown goddess
choices: She arose from the sea foam (aphros) where the severed genitals of Uranus had fallen, drifting to Cyprus as a fully grown goddess
She was born from the eastern wind blowing across Asia Minor, materializing in the moment Eros first descended from heaven
She emerged from a giant pomegranate that fell from Olympus to the island of Cythera and split open at her birth
She was carved by Hephaestus from purest sea-marble and breathed alive by Hera as the divine model of feminine beauty
context: Hesiod's etymology — Aphrodite from aphros (foam) — became the standard mythological account. She was carried on a scallop shell to Cyprus (Botticelli's Birth of Venus, c. 1486, captures the moment). Her cult centers were Paphos on Cyprus, Cythera, and Corinth (which had ritual prostitution as part of her worship). Her affairs (Ares, Anchises producing Aeneas, Adonis) feature in many myths.

question: At the wedding of Peleus and Thetis (the future parents of Achilles), the goddess Eris (Discord) — uninvited — threw a golden apple inscribed 'to the fairest' into the assembly. Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite each claimed it. Zeus refused to judge; he sent them to the Trojan prince Paris to choose. Each goddess offered him a bribe. What did each offer?
answer: Hera — empire over Asia and Europe; Athena — wisdom and skill in war; Aphrodite — the most beautiful woman in the world
choices: Hera — empire over Asia and Europe; Athena — wisdom and skill in war; Aphrodite — the most beautiful woman in the world
Hera — eternal youth; Athena — knowledge of every craft; Aphrodite — irresistible beauty and the love of Helen
Hera — kingdom of Troy intact; Athena — victory in war; Aphrodite — many fertile wives and countless children
Hera — wealth and gold mines; Athena — fame in song forever; Aphrodite — the most beautiful goddess as wife
context: Paris chose Aphrodite. The 'most beautiful woman' was Helen, queen of Sparta, wife of Menelaus. Aphrodite arranged for Paris to take her to Troy. The Trojan War followed. The Judgment of Paris is among the most painted mythological scenes — Rubens, Renoir, and many others. The Greek tradition reads it as the human choice that brought disaster.

question: Eros (Roman Cupid), son of Aphrodite, fell in love with the mortal princess Psyche — whose beauty rivaled Aphrodite's, provoking Aphrodite's jealousy. Eros came to Psyche only at night, in darkness, forbidding her ever to see his face. She was happy until her envious sisters convinced her he must be a monster. One night she lit a lamp to see. What happened?
answer: A drop of hot oil fell on Eros; he woke, was wounded, fled; Psyche then endured trials before being reunited with him
choices: A drop of hot oil fell on Eros; he woke, was wounded, fled; Psyche then endured trials before being reunited with him
She saw his beautiful face and the lamp went out; from then on they lived in light, with full mutual recognition
He turned away and forbade her presence; Psyche threw herself from a cliff but was rescued by Zephyrus the wind
The room was destroyed by a bolt of love-fire; Eros and Psyche were transformed together into the constellation Lyra
context: Apuleius's The Golden Ass (2nd century AD) preserves the fullest version. Psyche's tasks (sorting grain, fetching golden fleece, gathering Stygian water, descending to the underworld for a beauty box) parallel hero quests. They were eventually reunited; Psyche became immortal. The myth has been read as the soul's (psyche literally means 'soul') journey to union with Love itself — Platonized in C. S. Lewis's Till We Have Faces.

question: Hephaestus — son of Zeus and Hera (or in some versions of Hera alone) — was the divine smith and craftsman, god of fire and metalworking. He was lame, the only physically imperfect Olympian. The cause of his lameness varies. What is one account of how he became lame?
answer: Thrown from Olympus by Zeus (or Hera) and crippled by the fall — he fell for a day and landed on Lemnos
choices: Thrown from Olympus by Zeus (or Hera) and crippled by the fall — he fell for a day and landed on Lemnos
Born deformed from Hera's parthenogenesis — she made him alone in jealous response to Athena's birth from Zeus
Burned in his own forge as an apprentice — Hephaestus's lameness was the price of his early craftsmanship
Wounded in the Gigantomachy — the Giant Mimas struck his leg with a club before Heracles killed Mimas
context: Multiple versions exist; the throw from Olympus (whether by Zeus during the Hera-Zeus quarrel or by Hera when she saw him weak) is most common. He was raised by the sea-nymph Thetis on Lemnos (later Achilles's mother — long friendship). His forges were beneath volcanoes — Mount Etna especially. He was married to Aphrodite (an irony of the lame, ugly smith with the goddess of beauty) — she preferred Ares, leading to the famous net trap.

question: Hephaestus's greatest works of craft in myth were divine armor and other made objects. For which heroes did he forge their famous armor?
answer: Achilles (after Patroclus's death in Iliad 18) and Aeneas (at Venus/Aphrodite's request in Virgil's Aeneid 8)
choices: Achilles (after Patroclus's death in Iliad 18) and Aeneas (at Venus/Aphrodite's request in Virgil's Aeneid 8)
Hector and Priam — Hephaestus secretly armed the Trojans during the war's late stages out of Trojan piety
Heracles and Theseus — the divine smith provided armor for the two greatest heroes before the Trojan War
Odysseus and Diomedes — Hephaestus armed the Greeks' two most cunning warriors before the war began
context: Iliad Book 18 contains the elaborate description of Achilles's shield (ekphrasis — five scenes including a city at peace and a city at war). Virgil's Aeneid Book 8 echoes this with Aeneas's shield depicting future Roman history. Hephaestus also made: Pandora's body, the Necklace of Harmonia, Talos the bronze giant guarding Crete, the golden tripods that moved by themselves to Olympian feasts.

question: Hermes — son of Zeus and the Pleiad Maia, born in a cave on Mount Cyllene in Arcadia — was the god of boundaries, transitions, communication, commerce, thieves, and travelers. Among his unique roles, he served as messenger between the gods and as guide of souls. What is the technical Greek term for his soul-guiding function?
answer: Psychopompos — 'soul-guide' — the one who escorted the souls of the dead from the upper world to Hades
choices: Psychopompos — 'soul-guide' — the one who escorted the souls of the dead from the upper world to Hades
Theurgos — 'god-worker' — the title of the priest performing the rites for the dead, never a divine role
Pneumatikos — 'spirit-bearer' — the goddess of breath, not Hermes; this term properly belongs to Iris instead
Eumenides — 'kindly ones' — actually the euphemism for the Furies, not for Hermes the soul-guide
context: Hermes Psychopompos appears in Homer (Odyssey 24, leading the souls of the slain suitors) and in many vase paintings. His other domains: protector of merchants, herdsmen, travelers, thieves, athletes, oratory, and trickery. He invented the lyre (from a tortoise shell) and gave it to Apollo to settle a dispute. The caduceus — his wand with two intertwined snakes — became the symbol of medicine (often confused with the rod of Asclepius).

question: On the day of his birth, the infant Hermes climbed out of his cradle, traveled to the meadow where Apollo's sacred cattle grazed, and stole fifty of them. To conceal the theft, he had the cattle walk backward — leaving tracks that looked as though they had walked toward the meadow rather than away. He then returned to his cradle and pretended to sleep. What did he do next when Apollo confronted him?
answer: Gave Apollo a lyre he had invented from a tortoise shell that morning — Apollo accepted it in exchange for the cattle
choices: Gave Apollo a lyre he had invented from a tortoise shell that morning — Apollo accepted it in exchange for the cattle
Returned the cattle by tracing the backward tracks; Apollo was so amused he made Hermes the messenger god
Showed Apollo a flute he had carved from reeds; Apollo refused the trade and reported the theft to Zeus directly
Pretended ignorance until Apollo lost patience; Zeus intervened and ordered Hermes confined to his cradle a year
context: The Homeric Hymn to Hermes (c. 600 BC) tells the story. The tortoise-shell lyre was Hermes's invention — Apollo's instrument forever after. Hermes traded it for the cattle, demonstrating his trickster-trader nature from infancy. The myth establishes both Apollo as god of music (via the lyre Hermes invented) and Hermes as god of commerce, oratory, and clever bargaining.

question: Dionysus (Roman Bacchus) — god of wine, ecstasy, madness, ritual frenzy, and theater — was 'twice born.' His mother Semele was a Theban princess. Hera, jealous, tricked Semele into asking Zeus to appear in his full divine form. The sight killed her instantly. Zeus saved the fetal Dionysus from her dying body. What did Zeus do next?
answer: Sewed Dionysus into his own thigh, where the god completed gestation; thus Dionysus was 'born' a second time
choices: Sewed Dionysus into his own thigh, where the god completed gestation; thus Dionysus was 'born' a second time
Placed Dionysus in a cedar chest and sent him to Egypt, where he was raised by the gods of the Nile delta
Gave Dionysus to the Centaur Chiron to raise on Mount Pelion, alongside Heracles and other young heroes
Hid Dionysus on Olympus disguised as a girl, so Hera would not recognize him for many years to come
context: The 'twice born' Dionysus (from Semele's womb, then from Zeus's thigh) became one of his epithets. Semele was made a goddess after the resurrection of Dionysus. Hera continued to persecute him — driving him mad as a young man until he discovered wine. The myth was central to Dionysian initiation and to Greek theater (which developed from Dionysian rituals, the Dionysia festivals at Athens producing Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides).

question: The Homeric Hymn to Dionysus tells of his encounter with pirates. Sitting by the sea on Naxos, Tyrrhenian (Etruscan) pirates spotted him — a youth in purple, beautiful, easy to capture. They seized him and put him in their ship. They could not bind him; the ropes fell off. The ship began to fill with wine, ivy, vine-leaves. What happened to the pirates?
answer: Dionysus transformed into a lion; the terrified pirates leaped overboard and were transformed into dolphins by him
choices: Dionysus transformed into a lion; the terrified pirates leaped overboard and were transformed into dolphins by him
Dionysus called a great storm; the ship sank and only the helmsman (who had warned the others) survived to tell the tale
Dionysus called wild beasts onto the deck; the pirates were rent in pieces and only one boy was spared as worshipper
Dionysus walked off across the water; the pirates pursued him and were stranded on a deserted island for ten years
context: The Homeric Hymn (number 7) tells the dolphin transformation. The episode is depicted on the famous Exekias cup (c. 530 BC) showing Dionysus reclining on a vine-covered ship, dolphins around him. The myth illustrated Dionysus's transformative power and the danger of refusing recognition of the god. The Etruscans' renowned piracy made them stock villains in such stories.

question: Euripides's tragedy The Bacchae (405 BC, performed posthumously) dramatizes Dionysus's return to his mother's hometown of Thebes. King Pentheus — Dionysus's cousin (Cadmus's grandson) — refused to recognize the god's divinity and tried to suppress his worship. Dionysus disguised himself as a mortal priest and led Pentheus to spy on the Bacchic rites of his own mother Agave and her sisters on Mount Cithaeron. What happened?
answer: Agave and the Bacchants tore Pentheus apart; Agave returned to Thebes carrying her son's head, thinking it a lion's
choices: Agave and the Bacchants tore Pentheus apart; Agave returned to Thebes carrying her son's head, thinking it a lion's
Pentheus was seized by his soldiers and brought safely back to Thebes; the rites continued unimpeded thereafter
Pentheus was struck blind by Dionysus and led back to the city by Tiresias; he later repented and instituted the worship
Pentheus was transformed into a fawn and hunted by Agave; he escaped and returned to Thebes as Dionysus's high priest
context: The Bacchae is among the most disturbing of surviving Greek tragedies. Pentheus's dismemberment by his own mother — the 'sparagmos' (rending) at the heart of Dionysian ritual — embodied the god's terrible power over those who resisted him. Agave's recognition scene, in which she sees that the 'lion's head' she carries is her son's, is among the most devastating in ancient drama. The play asks what divinity demands of mortals.

question: The Muses — nine sisters, daughters of Zeus and the Titaness Mnemosyne (Memory) — were goddesses of inspiration for the arts. Hesiod, in the opening of the Theogony, claimed they had visited him while he tended sheep on Mount Helicon and inspired his poetry. Later tradition assigned specific arts to each Muse. Which Muse is associated with which art?
answer: Calliope — epic poetry; Clio — history; Erato — love poetry; Euterpe — flute music; Melpomene — tragedy
choices: Calliope — epic poetry; Clio — history; Erato — love poetry; Euterpe — flute music; Melpomene — tragedy
Calliope — astronomy; Clio — comedy; Erato — sculpture; Euterpe — painting; Melpomene — architecture
Calliope — dance; Clio — geometry; Erato — rhetoric; Euterpe — medicine; Melpomene — agriculture
Calliope — wisdom; Clio — gold-working; Erato — animal husbandry; Euterpe — weaving; Melpomene — pottery
context: The nine Muses: Calliope (epic poetry), Clio (history), Erato (love poetry), Euterpe (flute/lyric), Melpomene (tragedy), Polyhymnia (sacred poetry), Terpsichore (dance), Thalia (comedy), Urania (astronomy). The specific assignments were later (Hellenistic period); earlier Greeks named the nine without sharp specialization. The English 'music' derives from 'mousike' — the art of the Muses generally, not just instrumental music.

question: Pan — god of shepherds, flocks, mountain wilds, and rustic music — was depicted with goat legs, goat horns, and goat ears (a satyr-like figure). He played the panpipes (syrinx), which he created from the reeds into which the nymph Syrinx was transformed when fleeing his advances. He could induce a particular emotion in those who heard sudden cries in the wilderness. What is its name, derived from his?
answer: Panic — the sudden irrational terror Pan could inspire in lonely travelers or armies in wild places
choices: Panic — the sudden irrational terror Pan could inspire in lonely travelers or armies in wild places
Panacea — the universal remedy attributed to Pan's healing herbs found on remote mountainsides only
Panegyric — the elaborate praise speech delivered at religious gatherings in his honor
Pantheon — the gathered company of all gods that Pan was said to have summoned at his birth
context: 'Panic' from Pan's irrational fear (the cry of the god in the wilderness) is the standard English etymology. 'Panacea' is from pan + akos (universal remedy), unrelated to the god. Pan's death is the subject of a famous report in Plutarch — a voice was heard at sea: 'Great Pan is dead.' Christians (Eusebius) read this as marking Christ's redemption ending paganism; modern scholars debate its meaning.

question: Narcissus was a beautiful youth — son of the river god Cephissus and the nymph Liriope. The seer Tiresias prophesied at his birth that he would live long, 'if he never knows himself.' Narcissus grew up haughty, scorning all who fell in love with him — including the nymph Echo (whose tragic fate accompanied his). The avenging goddess Nemesis answered the prayers of his rejected lovers. What did she contrive?
answer: Narcissus saw his reflection in a pool, fell in love with the image, could not leave, and wasted away into a flower
choices: Narcissus saw his reflection in a pool, fell in love with the image, could not leave, and wasted away into a flower
Narcissus was struck by Eros's lead arrow and could love no one; he died alone in the forest at twenty-five years old
Narcissus was transformed into an owl by Nemesis; he flies still calling for the lovers he had scorned in life
Narcissus was wounded by his own pride and the goddess's silver arrow; he became the constellation Ophiuchus
context: Ovid's Metamorphoses Book 3 tells the story. Narcissus's name became the term for psychological self-love (narcissism, in Freud's vocabulary). The flower (narcissus, daffodil family) grew where he died. Echo — the nymph cursed by Hera to repeat only the words of others — pined away to a disembodied voice. The myth treats self-knowledge ambiguously: Tiresias's prophecy was fulfilled — Narcissus died from coming to know himself.

question: Pygmalion, a king (or sculptor) of Cyprus, was disenchanted with the women of his city — particularly the Propoetides (who had denied Aphrodite's divinity and been turned to prostitutes, then to stone by Aphrodite). He carved an ivory statue of an ideal woman — and fell in love with his own creation. He kissed it, dressed it, talked to it, slept beside it. He prayed to Aphrodite at the goddess's festival. What was the result?
answer: Aphrodite brought the statue to life; Pygmalion married her; she bore him a daughter named Paphos
choices: Aphrodite brought the statue to life; Pygmalion married her; she bore him a daughter named Paphos
Aphrodite turned Pygmalion himself into stone; the statues remained together forever in his palace as a warning
Aphrodite gave Pygmalion a real wife who looked like the statue; the statue itself remained marble and was destroyed
Aphrodite cursed Pygmalion with eternal longing; the statue would never live but he could love no one else
context: Ovid's Metamorphoses Book 10 tells the story. The name 'Galatea' for the statue is later (attested in Rousseau, 1772). The myth — the artist who falls in love with his creation — has inspired numerous literary adaptations: George Bernard Shaw's Pygmalion (1913), the musical My Fair Lady, the film Pretty Woman. The motif treats artistic creation as a form of erotic desire.

question: King Midas of Phrygia caught the drunken old satyr Silenus (Dionysus's foster father) wandering in his garden. Midas entertained Silenus royally for ten days and returned him to Dionysus. As a reward, Dionysus offered Midas any wish. Midas asked that everything he touched turn to gold. What unexpected problem did this cause?
answer: Food, drink, and his own daughter all turned to gold at his touch; he begged Dionysus to revoke the gift; Dionysus had him wash in the Pactolus river
choices: Food, drink, and his own daughter all turned to gold at his touch; he begged Dionysus to revoke the gift; Dionysus had him wash in the Pactolus river
His kingdom was overrun with treasures he could not move; thieves slaughtered his court; he was deposed within a month
His golden touch made everything inert; even his army's weapons turned to gold and could not be used in battle effectively
His mother turned to gold first; he cursed Dionysus and lost his life in punishment for the curse against the god
context: Ovid's Metamorphoses Book 11 tells the story. The Pactolus river (in Lydia, Asia Minor) carried gold dust in its sands — a real geological fact the myth explained. King Midas himself was a real Phrygian king (mid-8th century BC) — his tomb at Gordion has been excavated. The 'Midas touch' has entered English as the phrase for wealth-generating ability. The myth warns against unconsidered greed.

question: In a later episode, King Midas attended a musical contest between Apollo (lyre) and Pan (panpipes). The mountain god Tmolus judged Apollo the winner. Midas alone disagreed, favoring Pan. Apollo was offended. What did Apollo do, and how was the resulting secret kept and revealed?
answer: Gave Midas ass's ears; Midas hid them under a turban; his barber whispered the secret into a hole in the ground; reeds grew there and whispered 'Midas has ass's ears'
choices: Gave Midas ass's ears; Midas hid them under a turban; his barber whispered the secret into a hole in the ground; reeds grew there and whispered 'Midas has ass's ears'
Made Midas's tongue silver; he could no longer speak music, only mute prose; his court fled and his palace decayed
Took away Midas's hearing entirely; he became deaf to all music for the rest of his life as warning to all kings
Turned Midas into an actual ass; his queen led him in disgrace through the kingdom until he died of shame within a year
context: Ovid's Metamorphoses Book 11 tells the barber story. The reeds whispering the secret made the king's shame eternal — every wind through the riverbank reeds spoke of Midas's ears. The Midas of this story is the same Midas of the golden touch (or possibly his son in different versions). The myth illustrated the limits of royal power against divine displeasure and the impossibility of hiding what one fears to admit.

question: Heracles — son of Zeus by Alcmene, persecuted by Hera from birth — was the greatest hero of Greek mythology. In a fit of madness sent by Hera, he killed his own children. As penance, the oracle of Delphi instructed him to serve King Eurystheus of Tiryns for twelve years. Eurystheus assigned him twelve seemingly impossible tasks. Which of these is NOT one of the canonical Twelve Labors?
answer: Slaying the Sphinx of Thebes — actually a labor of Oedipus, who solved her riddle to free the city
choices: Slaying the Sphinx of Thebes — actually a labor of Oedipus, who solved her riddle to free the city
Slaying the Nemean Lion — the first labor; Heracles strangled the invulnerable beast and wore its hide
Slaying the Lernaean Hydra — the second labor; Heracles burned the necks to prevent new heads regrowing
Cleansing the Augean stables — the fifth labor; Heracles diverted two rivers through them in a single day
context: The Twelve Labors (in standard order): Nemean Lion, Lernaean Hydra, Ceryneian Hind, Erymanthian Boar, Augean Stables, Stymphalian Birds, Cretan Bull, Mares of Diomedes, Belt of Hippolyte, Cattle of Geryon, Apples of the Hesperides, Capture of Cerberus. The Sphinx is associated with Oedipus and Thebes, not Heracles. The labors made Heracles the prototype of the hero who overcomes monstrous obstacles by superhuman effort.

question: The first labor: Heracles was sent to slay a lion ravaging the region of Nemea. The lion was a monstrous offspring of Typhon and Echidna, with a hide impervious to all weapons — arrows, swords, clubs simply bounced off. How did Heracles kill it, and what did he do with the hide?
answer: Strangled it with his bare hands after trapping it in its cave; wore its hide as armor, with the head as a helmet
choices: Strangled it with his bare hands after trapping it in its cave; wore its hide as armor, with the head as a helmet
Struck it with his club until stunned, then drowned it in a river; tanned the hide as a cloak for traveling
Wrestled it into the sea where it drowned; gave the hide to King Eurystheus as proof of completion
Trapped it in a pit of fire; the lion died of heat; the impervious hide was burned and ash remained
context: The Nemean Lion's invulnerable hide became Heracles's signature armor. He cut the skin with the lion's own claws (the only thing that could pierce it). The image of Heracles wearing the lion's head as a helm, hide as cloak, with his club, became the canonical artistic representation. The Nemean Games (founded c. 573 BC at Nemea) were held in his honor.

question: The second labor: in the swamp of Lerna near Argos lived a monstrous water serpent — the Hydra, daughter of Typhon and Echidna. It had nine heads (numbers vary, one immortal). When Heracles cut off one head, two grew back from the stump. Eurystheus, when he learned Heracles had not done it alone, refused to count it. Who helped, and how?
answer: His nephew Iolaus drove a chariot and burned the stumps with torches after each beheading; the immortal head was buried
choices: His nephew Iolaus drove a chariot and burned the stumps with torches after each beheading; the immortal head was buried
His friend Theseus cut the heads; Heracles burned the bodies; together they worked through the night to finish
His mentor Chiron the Centaur provided a healing draught; the Hydra died of poisoning from within rather than wounds
His half-brother Apollo shot the heads with sun-arrows; Heracles only collected the heads after Apollo killed it
context: Iolaus's torching (with brands from a burning forest) prevented head regeneration. The immortal head was cut off and buried under a great rock. Heracles dipped his arrows in the Hydra's venomous blood — the source of many subsequent deaths (Chiron's accidental wounding, the centaur Nessus's revenge, eventually Heracles's own death). Eurystheus's refusal to count the labor led to a thirteenth task being substituted.

question: The fifth labor: King Augeas of Elis owned the largest herd of cattle in Greece — divinely blessed to never sicken — kept in stables that had not been cleaned in thirty years. Eurystheus assigned Heracles to clean them in a single day, expecting humiliating failure. How did Heracles accomplish it?
answer: Diverted the rivers Alpheus and Peneus through the stables; the water washed out thirty years of filth in a single day
choices: Diverted the rivers Alpheus and Peneus through the stables; the water washed out thirty years of filth in a single day
Set fire to the stables and burned the filth; Augeas's herd grazed on new grass when the ashes were swept away by wind
Carried each cow out by hand, scraped the stalls clean, and returned the cattle in a single very long day of labor
Summoned the dung beetles of Egypt by Apollo's blessing; the beetles devoured the filth in a single afternoon
context: The river-diversion solution showed Heracles's cleverness — and Eurystheus again refused to count the labor, because Heracles had been paid (Augeas had promised him 10% of the cattle). The Olympic Games were sometimes attributed to Heracles in honor of this labor. The Greek phrase 'cleansing the Augean stables' became a metaphor for any massive cleaning-up task.

question: The twelfth and final labor: Heracles was to capture Cerberus, the three-headed dog guarding the entrance to Hades, and bring him back to the upper world. This required descending alive into the underworld. Heracles was initiated into the Eleusinian Mysteries to prepare. He encountered the dead, freed Theseus (who was stuck to a chair) and Pirithous, and approached Hades. What did Hades demand?
answer: That Heracles capture Cerberus using only his bare hands without weapons; Heracles wrestled the dog into submission
choices: That Heracles capture Cerberus using only his bare hands without weapons; Heracles wrestled the dog into submission
That Heracles offer to drink a cup of poison; Persephone's pomegranate would revive him before the venom worked
That Heracles defeat the Furies in single combat first; he persuaded them to stand down by Apollo's mediation
That Heracles answer three riddles posed by the dead; Tiresias whispered the answers in his ear at each
context: Heracles strangled Cerberus into submission, brought him to Eurystheus (who hid in a jar), and returned him to Hades. The descent (katabasis) made Heracles, like Theseus, Orpheus, Odysseus, and Aeneas, one of the heroes who entered and emerged from the underworld alive — a paradigm of the hero's journey. The labor completed his twelve years of service; he was free.

question: After the Twelve Labors, Heracles married Deianira and was eventually poisoned through her. She had been given a 'love potion' by the dying centaur Nessus — actually poisoned blood from Hydra venom on Heracles's arrows. In agony from the poison shirt, Heracles built a pyre on Mount Oeta and commanded Philoctetes to light it (gifting him his bow). What happened?
answer: His mortal flesh burned away; his immortal part ascended to Olympus; Zeus made him a god and reconciled him with Hera
choices: His mortal flesh burned away; his immortal part ascended to Olympus; Zeus made him a god and reconciled him with Hera
His pyre would not light; Apollo descended and took him to Olympus directly without burning by personal divine command
The pyre transformed into a marble tomb; Heracles slept inside as a hero awaiting Greece's hour of greatest need
His funeral songs reached Hades; Persephone returned him to Deianira repentant; they lived together fifty more years
context: Heracles's apotheosis — the burning of the mortal part and elevation of the divine — made him the prototype of the deified hero. On Olympus he was reconciled with Hera (who became his mother-in-law when she gave him Hebe as wife). The myth shaped the conception of heroic divinization across Greek and later cultures. His pyre site on Mount Oeta became a cult center.

question: The Athenian hero Theseus volunteered for the third tribute to King Minos of Crete — fourteen youths (seven boys, seven girls) sent annually to be devoured by the Minotaur, a half-bull half-man monster confined in the labyrinth designed by Daedalus. Theseus intended to kill the Minotaur and end the tribute. Who helped him, and how?
answer: Ariadne, Minos's daughter, fell in love with him; she gave him a ball of thread to unwind through the labyrinth
choices: Ariadne, Minos's daughter, fell in love with him; she gave him a ball of thread to unwind through the labyrinth
Minos's queen Pasiphae (the Minotaur's mother) helped him out of compassion for the Athenian victims
Daedalus himself helped by giving Theseus a map of the labyrinth scratched onto a wax tablet
The Minotaur's twin (a kind, human-form son of Pasiphae) helped Theseus find his brother in the labyrinth
context: Ariadne's thread — unwound on entry, followed back on exit — allowed Theseus to escape after killing the Minotaur with his fists (or a sword Ariadne gave him). Theseus took Ariadne with him on the return journey but abandoned her on the island of Naxos (where Dionysus found her and married her). The black sails of his ship (he forgot to switch to white sails of victory) caused his father Aegeus to leap to his death, giving the Aegean its name.

question: Beyond the Minotaur adventure, Theseus's historical importance in Athenian self-conception was political. After becoming king of Athens, he carried out a major reform that the Athenians later credited him with. What was it?
answer: The synoikismos — political unification of the scattered villages of Attica into the single polis of Athens
choices: The synoikismos — political unification of the scattered villages of Attica into the single polis of Athens
The reform of the calendar — establishing the lunar-solar system that would govern Athenian religious life
The founding of the Athenian navy — building the first triremes that would later defeat the Persians at Salamis
The establishment of Athenian democracy — proto-democratic institutions that Cleisthenes later formalized in 508 BC
context: Theseus's synoikismos ('living together') made Attica a unified polity centered on Athens. The Synoikia festival (held annually in summer) commemorated the unification.
