Theseus was Athens's foundational political hero — Pericles invoked him; the Theseion (now identified as the Hephaesteum) was his memorial temple. His remains were supposedly brought from Skyros to Athens in 475 BC by Kimon.

question: Perseus was the son of Zeus (who came to Danaë as a shower of gold) and Danaë daughter of Acrisius of Argos. Acrisius placed mother and infant in a chest and cast them into the sea. They drifted to the island of Seriphos, ruled by King Polydectes. Polydectes desired Danaë but Perseus protected her. Polydectes contrived a plan to remove him. What did he demand?
answer: The head of Medusa — the most fearsome of the Gorgons; her gaze turned mortals to stone
choices: The head of Medusa — the most fearsome of the Gorgons; her gaze turned mortals to stone
The Golden Fleece of Colchis — guarded by a dragon Aeetes had set on a sacred oak tree
The Apples of the Hesperides — kept beyond the western edge of the known world
The Belt of Hippolyte — taken from the Amazon queen as proof of valor
context: Polydectes pretended to demand wedding-gifts for his (false) wedding to Hippodameia. Other guests brought horses; Perseus, having none, foolishly promised the head of Medusa. The quest gave Polydectes hope of being rid of him. The gods (Athena and Hermes) aided Perseus — providing a mirror-polished shield, winged sandals, a cap of invisibility, and a curved sword. Athena thus orchestrated the assault on her rival the Gorgon.

question: The three Gorgon sisters — Stheno, Euryale, and Medusa — were once beautiful (in some accounts; the older tradition has them monstrous from birth). Medusa was the only mortal of the three. She had been transformed (in Ovid's account) by Athena after Poseidon raped her in Athena's temple. Anyone who looked at her face directly was turned to stone. How did Perseus succeed?
answer: Looked at her reflection in his polished shield; cut off her head while she slept; flew away with winged sandals
choices: Looked at her reflection in his polished shield; cut off her head while she slept; flew away with winged sandals
Closed his eyes and felt his way to her by the smell of snakes; one blow severed the head before the eyes opened
Waited until daylight when she retreated to a cave; killed the sleeping monster from above through a chimney
Persuaded her two immortal sisters to look at her by mistake; the petrification of one Gorgon by another did the work
context: From Medusa's severed neck sprang the winged horse Pegasus and the giant Chrysaor (Poseidon's offspring fathered in their assault). Perseus put the head in a special bag (kibisis). On the return journey he used the head to turn King Atlas to stone (the mountain), to rescue Andromeda by petrifying the sea monster Cetus, and finally to turn Polydectes to stone. The head became part of Athena's aegis.

question: Returning from killing Medusa, Perseus passed over the kingdom of Aethiopia (Ethiopia). King Cepheus and Queen Cassiopeia had boasted that their daughter Andromeda's beauty exceeded the Nereids' (sea nymphs). Poseidon, offended, sent a sea monster to ravage the coast. An oracle declared the only remedy was to sacrifice Andromeda. Perseus saw her chained to a rock as the monster approached. What did he do?
answer: Killed the sea monster (with his sword, or with Medusa's head); freed Andromeda; married her after defeating her rival suitor
choices: Killed the sea monster (with his sword, or with Medusa's head); freed Andromeda; married her after defeating her rival suitor
Carried her away on his winged sandals; the sea monster destroyed the kingdom; they fled to Argos and never returned
Sacrificed himself instead — Athena resurrected him after the monster died of choking on his sword in its throat
Used Medusa's head on Andromeda's parents who had ordered the sacrifice; he then freed her and ruled Aethiopia
context: Perseus killed the sea monster Cetus. Andromeda's parents had promised her to her uncle Phineus; at the wedding, Phineus arrived with armed men, and Perseus turned them all to stone with Medusa's head. Perseus and Andromeda had several children, including Perses (eponymous ancestor of the Persians, per legend). The four became constellations: Perseus, Andromeda, Cassiopeia, Cepheus.

question: Bellerophon, prince of Corinth, was sent (after Stheneboea's false accusation) with a sealed letter to King Iobates of Lycia instructing the king to kill the bearer. Iobates, unwilling to kill a guest directly, sent Bellerophon to slay the Chimera, a fire-breathing hybrid (lion in front, goat in middle, serpent behind). What did Bellerophon use, and what was his eventual fate?
answer: Rode Pegasus the winged horse (caught with Athena's golden bridle); thrust a lead-tipped spear into the Chimera's flaming throat
choices: Rode Pegasus the winged horse (caught with Athena's golden bridle); thrust a lead-tipped spear into the Chimera's flaming throat
Wore the helmet of Hades for invisibility; stabbed the Chimera through the heart in the cave where it slept
Trapped the Chimera in a forest fire it could not escape; the heat melted its serpent half by metaphysical irony
Solved a riddle the Chimera posed; the monster died of shame at being outwitted by a mortal as legend prescribes
context: Athena gave Bellerophon a golden bridle to tame Pegasus (who had sprung from Medusa's neck). Iliad 6 (Glaucus's speech to Diomedes) and later sources tell the tale. Bellerophon's hubris eventually destroyed him: he tried to ride Pegasus up to Olympus to live with the gods. Zeus sent a gadfly to sting Pegasus; Bellerophon fell, was crippled and blinded, and wandered alone until death.

question: Jason was rightful heir to Iolcus in Thessaly. His uncle Pelias had usurped the throne. An oracle warned Pelias to beware a man with one sandal; Jason arrived with one sandal (having lost the other helping an old woman — Hera in disguise — across a stream). Pelias sent Jason on a quest expected to be fatal: to fetch the Golden Fleece from Colchis on the eastern shore of the Black Sea. What was Jason's ship called?
answer: The Argo — built by Argus, with Athena's help; the heroes who sailed in it were called the Argonauts
choices: The Argo — built by Argus, with Athena's help; the heroes who sailed in it were called the Argonauts
The Hyperion — built by Apollo for the journey eastward into the rising sun toward Colchis on the morning shore
The Phoenix — built by Hephaestus to carry fire across the sea for the dragon-guardian at Colchis directly
The Cyclops — built by the Cyclopes themselves for the heroes' return journey from the eastern lands of darkness
context: The Argo carried a famous crew — Heracles, Theseus, Castor and Pollux, Atalanta, Orpheus, Peleus (father of Achilles), and many others. Argus built it with Athena's guidance; some versions include a beam from the talking oak of Dodona in the prow. The voyage included encounters with the Harpies, the Symplegades (clashing rocks), and the dragon at Colchis. Apollonius of Rhodes's Argonautica (3rd century BC) preserves the fullest version.

question: At Colchis, King Aeetes demanded Jason perform impossible tasks before he could have the Fleece: yoke fire-breathing bronze-hoofed bulls, plow a field, sow it with dragon's teeth, and defeat the warriors that sprang up. Aeetes's daughter Medea, a sorceress who had fallen in love with Jason (Aphrodite's doing), helped him with her magic. What did she give him, and what did Jason promise her in return?
answer: Magic ointment for fire-immunity; potion to put the dragon to sleep at the Fleece; Jason promised to marry her
choices: Magic ointment for fire-immunity; potion to put the dragon to sleep at the Fleece; Jason promised to marry her
A second sword to fight the warriors; a magical bridle for the bulls; Jason promised her half his kingdom
Wine to drug Aeetes himself; lethal poison for the warriors; Jason promised her the throne of Colchis
Wax wings to fly over the bulls; an invisibility cloak; Jason promised her his eternal devotion and tomb beside him
context: Medea's magic was indispensable. She also killed her own brother Apsyrtus (in some versions) to delay her father's pursuit. Jason and Medea returned to Iolcus with the Fleece — Medea then arranged Pelias's death (his daughters dismembered him on her trickery). The two fled to Corinth. Years later, Jason planned to abandon Medea to marry the princess Glauce. Medea's revenge is the subject of Euripides's tragedy.

question: In Euripides's Medea (431 BC), Medea responds to Jason's planned abandonment with a terrible vengeance. She sends Glauce a poisoned robe and crown that burst into flame, killing her and her father King Creon. Then she does something more terrible. What?
answer: Kills her own two sons by Jason — to deprive him of all descendants and inflict the maximum suffering on him
choices: Kills her own two sons by Jason — to deprive him of all descendants and inflict the maximum suffering on him
Curses Jason's bloodline; his descendants died one by one until his line was extinguished within generations
Burns the palace of Corinth; thousands die in the fire; Medea escapes by ship to Athens unharmed
Casts Jason into a year-long sleep of nightmares; he awakens to find his fleet destroyed and his fame forgotten
context: Medea's killing of her own children is among the most disturbing acts in Greek tragedy. She escapes in a dragon-drawn chariot (gift of her grandfather Helios). Euripides's Medea was first performed 431 BC at the Dionysia; he placed third — the audience was apparently uncomfortable. Modern productions have made it a feminist tragedy of patriarchal betrayal. Jason died alone, sleeping under the rotting hull of the Argo when a beam fell on him.

question: Oedipus was the son of King Laius and Queen Jocasta of Thebes. At his birth an oracle warned that Laius would be killed by his own son. The infant was exposed with pierced ankles (hence 'Oedipus' — 'swollen-foot') but was rescued and raised in Corinth. Learning a different oracle (he would kill his father and marry his mother), he fled Corinth. At a crossroads he met an arrogant old man in a chariot. What happened?
answer: Oedipus killed the old man (who was actually Laius) and his retinue in a quarrel about right-of-way
choices: Oedipus killed the old man (who was actually Laius) and his retinue in a quarrel about right-of-way
Oedipus turned aside in respect and lost his way; he later met Laius again at Thebes and was wounded by him
Oedipus was attacked by the old man and his retinue; he was wounded and left for dead but recovered by Apollo
Oedipus solved a riddle the old man posed; the old man revealed himself to be the seer Tiresias and warned of fate
context: Sophocles's Oedipus Rex (c. 429 BC) traces the slow revelation of Oedipus's identity. After killing Laius at the crossroads, Oedipus continued to Thebes, solved the Sphinx's riddle, was made king, married the widowed queen Jocasta (his mother), and fathered children with her. Years later, a plague forced inquiry; he discovered the truth. The play has been foundational for Western tragic theory (Aristotle's Poetics) and depth psychology (Freud's Oedipus complex).

question: Approaching Thebes after killing Laius, Oedipus encountered the Sphinx — a winged lion with the face of a woman — who guarded the road. She killed all who could not answer her riddle. What was the riddle, and what was Oedipus's answer?
answer: 'What walks on four legs in the morning, two at noon, three in the evening?' Answer: Man (infant crawling, adult walking, old man with cane)
choices: 'What walks on four legs in the morning, two at noon, three in the evening?' Answer: Man (infant crawling, adult walking, old man with cane)
'What has one voice but four shapes through life?' Answer: A river (springs, brooks, rivers, deltas in the day's course)
'What was created at the dawn but seen only at dusk?' Answer: The shadow (born with light but visible only with sunset)
'What walks alone but speaks of many?' Answer: The poet (one voice but many lives recounted in his songs)
context: Oedipus's answer destroyed the Sphinx, who threw herself from the cliff. The grateful Thebans made him king. The riddle of Man embodied the human life cycle — the very Man (Oedipus) whose own identity through the cycle would prove tragic. The Sphinx episode is the proximate cause of Oedipus's downfall — without it, he would not have become king of Thebes and met his mother.

question: When the truth of Oedipus's parentage and crimes was finally revealed — through the testimony of the shepherd who had been ordered to expose the infant — what did the two royals do?
answer: Jocasta hanged herself in her chambers; Oedipus, finding her body, blinded himself with the pins from her dress
choices: Jocasta hanged herself in her chambers; Oedipus, finding her body, blinded himself with the pins from her dress
Jocasta drank poison prepared by the seer Tiresias; Oedipus exiled himself with his daughters to Colonus
Jocasta jumped from the palace walls into the Theban plain; Oedipus was struck blind by lightning from Apollo
Jocasta sealed herself in the temple and starved; Oedipus pierced his eyes with a sword and continued ruling Thebes
context: Sophocles's Oedipus Rex shows the catastrophe. Oedipus's daughters Antigone and Ismene are left to face the consequences (Antigone takes up the next play, Antigone, in which she defies her uncle Creon to bury her brother Polyneices). Oedipus's blinding was self-punishment — having lived in moral blindness, he made the physical condition match. His daughters guided him to exile at Colonus, where his mystical death is depicted in Sophocles's Oedipus at Colonus.

question: After Oedipus's death, civil war erupted at Thebes between his two sons Eteocles and Polyneices over the throne. They killed each other in single combat. Their uncle Creon, taking power, decreed that Eteocles (who defended Thebes) should receive full burial, but that Polyneices (who attacked) should be left unburied — a profound religious offense for a Greek. What did Antigone do?
answer: Buried Polyneices in defiance of the decree; Creon condemned her to be entombed alive; she hanged herself in the tomb
choices: Buried Polyneices in defiance of the decree; Creon condemned her to be entombed alive; she hanged herself in the tomb
Pleaded with Creon for proper burial; he relented after Tiresias's warning, and the family was reconciled fully
Fled to Athens with Ismene; King Theseus received them and arranged proper burial of Polyneices himself
Pretended compliance while secretly burying her brother; was never discovered and lived to old age in Thebes peacefully
context: Sophocles's Antigone (c. 441 BC) explores the conflict between divine law (familial duty, proper burial) and civic law (Creon's decree). Antigone's principled defiance and tragic end made her a foundational figure for ethical reflection on conscience versus authority — invoked by Hegel, Sophocles's namesake, modern playwrights. Creon's son Haemon (Antigone's fiancé) and wife Eurydice also die. Tiresias's warning came too late.

question: Daedalus — the master craftsman who built the labyrinth for Minos — fell out of favor with Minos when he helped Pasiphae satisfy her unnatural lust for the bull (resulting in the Minotaur) and helped Theseus escape. Minos imprisoned Daedalus and his son Icarus in the labyrinth. How did Daedalus contrive their escape?
answer: Built wings of feathers and wax; warned Icarus not to fly too close to the sun; Icarus did and fell into the sea
choices: Built wings of feathers and wax; warned Icarus not to fly too close to the sun; Icarus did and fell into the sea
Built a ship in secret and sailed away by night; Icarus drowned in a storm on the journey; Daedalus survived
Tunneled through the labyrinth into a sea cave; Icarus drowned in the tide pools at the cave's mouth on escape
Bribed the guards with golden trinkets he had forged; Icarus was killed by the guards when his bribe was insufficient
context: Ovid's Metamorphoses Book 8 tells the story. Icarus, exhilarated, flew too high; the wax melted; he fell into the sea (the Icarian Sea, between the Cyclades and Anatolia). Daedalus reached Sicily and was protected by King Cocalus. Minos pursued him; Daedalus killed Minos by pouring boiling water through a pipe into his bath. The myth of Icarus has been central to reflections on hubris and the limits of human aspiration — Bruegel's Landscape with the Fall of Icarus.

question: Tantalus — a king (variously of Lydia, Phrygia, or Argos), son of Zeus — was honored as a friend by the gods and invited to dine on Olympus. He committed two grave offenses (the second worse): he stole nectar and ambrosia to share with mortals, and he served his own son Pelops at a banquet to test whether the gods would notice. What is his eternal punishment in Tartarus?
answer: Stands in a pool of water beneath fruit-laden branches; water recedes when he stoops; fruit lifts when he reaches
choices: Stands in a pool of water beneath fruit-laden branches; water recedes when he stoops; fruit lifts when he reaches
Pushes a boulder up a hill; it rolls back down just as he reaches the summit (actually Sisyphus's punishment)
Bound to a fiery wheel that turns eternally (actually Ixion's punishment, not Tantalus's, in Tartarus)
Forced to fill a leaky jar with water forever (actually the Danaides' punishment for killing their husbands)
context: Tantalus's punishment gives English 'tantalize.' The gods detected the cannibal feast — only Demeter, in grief over Persephone, absent-mindedly ate Pelops's shoulder. The gods restored Pelops (with an ivory shoulder replacing the one Demeter ate); he later won Hippodameia in the chariot race and gave the Peloponnese its name. The Tantalid curse persisted across generations: Atreus and Thyestes, Agamemnon, Orestes — the House of Atreus tragedies.

question: Sisyphus, founder and king of Corinth, was famously cunning and deceitful. Among other transgressions, he revealed Zeus's seduction of the nymph Aegina to her father Asopus (the river god). He also bound Thanatos (Death) when sent to fetch him — so that no one died until Ares freed Death. As a final cleverness, he persuaded Persephone to let him return to the upper world to punish his wife (whom he had instructed to leave him unburied). What is his eternal punishment?
answer: Pushing a boulder up a steep hill; it always rolls back down just as he reaches the top, forever
choices: Pushing a boulder up a steep hill; it always rolls back down just as he reaches the top, forever
Sleeping in a cave guarded by Argos the hundred-eyed; awakened every hour by stinging insects forever
Filling a vast jar with water with broken cups; the water leaks out faster than he can pour, forever
Standing in icy water while flames lick at his face; neither extreme can be escaped, forever
context: Albert Camus's The Myth of Sisyphus (1942) made the figure central to existentialist philosophy — the absurd hero who knows the futility of his task and yet 'one must imagine Sisyphus happy.' The Greek myth itself was a punishment for hubris against divine prerogatives (especially the binding of Death). The boulder image has entered English as the metaphor for any unrewarded labor.

question: Ixion, king of the Lapiths, killed his father-in-law (the first kin-slayer in Greek myth). Zeus took pity on him, purified him, and invited him to Olympus. Ixion, grateful, tried to seduce Hera. Zeus discovered the plan and created a cloud (Nephele) in Hera's likeness; Ixion lay with the cloud, fathering the Centaurs. Zeus banished him to Tartarus. What is his eternal punishment?
answer: Bound to a fiery wheel that turns eternally — he can never rest, never escape the burning rotation
choices: Bound to a fiery wheel that turns eternally — he can never rest, never escape the burning rotation
Hung upside down over a fire; the smoke and heat blind him while pitch drips constantly on his face below
Tied to a stake with serpents constantly biting his limbs; their venom never kills but ensures eternal agony
Buried beneath Mount Etna with Typhon; his struggles to escape cause Mediterranean volcanic eruptions to this day
context: Ixion's wheel — sometimes described as wreathed in flame — is among the most distinctive eternal punishments in Tartarus. The myth illustrated the special offense of violating hospitality (xenia) by attempting to seduce one's host's wife — the same offense the Trojan War punished (Paris's seduction of Helen, his host Menelaus's wife). The Centaurs (Ixion's offspring with Nephele) became a tribe in Thessaly.

question: The Trojan War began with a wedding — that of Peleus (king of the Myrmidons) and the sea-goddess Thetis. Eris (Discord) was not invited and threw a golden apple inscribed 'to the fairest' into the assembly. Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite each claimed it. Zeus, refusing to judge, sent them to a Trojan shepherd. Who was the shepherd, and why him?
answer: Paris, son of Priam king of Troy — exposed at birth because of a prophecy of doom, raised as a shepherd
choices: Paris, son of Priam king of Troy — exposed at birth because of a prophecy of doom, raised as a shepherd
Aeneas, son of Anchises and Aphrodite — chosen because of his mother's parental concern in the judgment
Hector, eldest son of Priam — chosen because of his reputation for piety and prudent judgment in disputes
Tros, eponymous ancestor of Troy — chosen because the judgment of the city's founding ancestor would bind it morally
context: Paris had been exposed because of his mother Hecuba's dream that she would bear a firebrand consuming Troy. He survived on Mount Ida as a shepherd. The Judgment of Paris (already discussed in the Olympian section) led to Aphrodite's victory and his choice of Helen as reward — and thus to the Trojan War. The story is told in the lost epic Cypria and alluded to in Iliad 24.

question: Helen — daughter of Zeus (as swan) and Leda — was the most beautiful woman in the world. Her suitors had been so numerous and so powerful that, on Odysseus's advice, all swore an oath to defend whichever one she chose. She chose Menelaus, king of Sparta. Years later Paris arrived as a Trojan ambassador and was Menelaus's guest. What followed?
answer: Paris took Helen back to Troy (with or without her consent, depending on the version); Menelaus invoked the suitors' oath
choices: Paris took Helen back to Troy (with or without her consent, depending on the version); Menelaus invoked the suitors' oath
Helen herself rejected Paris's overtures; Paris kidnapped her by force; the suitors swore the oath only after the abduction
Paris had been sent to retrieve a princess promised to him; Helen was that princess; the oath was unrelated to her marriage
Helen and Paris fled together by night; Menelaus did not pursue but called the suitors' oath only after a year of mourning
context: The 'Helen problem' — was she willing or forced? — has divided poets from Homer onward. Iliad 6 and 24 show her as remorseful, blaming herself. Stesichorus and Euripides developed the 'phantom Helen' tradition: the real Helen never went to Troy at all but waited in Egypt. The oath of the suitors (called the Oath of Tyndareus) is what bound all the Greek kings to mount the expedition to Troy.

question: The Greek fleet (perhaps 1,000+ ships) gathered at Aulis in Boeotia for the voyage to Troy. The winds were contrary. The seer Calchas declared that Artemis was angry — Agamemnon (commander-in-chief) had killed a sacred deer (or boasted of his hunting prowess). To appease her, Agamemnon must sacrifice his own daughter. Iphigenia was summoned from Mycenae under false pretenses (told she would marry Achilles). What happened?
answer: She was sacrificed by Agamemnon (in some versions, Artemis substituted a deer at the last moment and saved her)
choices: She was sacrificed by Agamemnon (in some versions, Artemis substituted a deer at the last moment and saved her)
Clytemnestra, Iphigenia's mother, smuggled her daughter away; the army sacrificed a deer in her place at midnight
Achilles himself intervened and refused to allow it; the army then voted to abandon the expedition entirely
Apollo descended in person and forbade the sacrifice; Artemis accepted a hundred oxen instead of the maiden
context: Versions vary: Aeschylus's Agamemnon describes the slaughter; Euripides's Iphigenia at Aulis ends with the substitution; in Iphigenia in Tauris, Artemis carries her to the land of the Taurians, where she becomes a priestess of human sacrifice (later rescued by her brother Orestes). The sacrifice motivated Clytemnestra's later murder of Agamemnon on his return — the House of Atreus tragedies.

question: Achilles — son of King Peleus and the sea-goddess Thetis — was the greatest of Greek warriors at Troy. His mother, knowing he was destined for either a short and glorious life or a long obscure one, tried to make him invulnerable. According to the most popular post-Homeric tradition (Statius's Achilleid, c. 95 AD), what did she do, and where was the weak point?
answer: Dipped him in the river Styx holding him by the heel; the heel remained mortal because it was untouched by the water
choices: Dipped him in the river Styx holding him by the heel; the heel remained mortal because it was untouched by the water
Coated him in immortal oil from Olympus; the oil pooled in the soles of his feet, leaving them vulnerable
Hid him from death itself; one mortal day of his life remained unprotected — the day of his death
Disguised him as a girl among King Lycomedes's daughters; one of them seduced him and made him mortal
context: The Styx-dipping is post-Homeric (not in Homer; Homer's Achilles is mortal without specified weak point). Statius's Achilleid (unfinished) gave the heel motif. Achilles was killed at Troy by an arrow shot by Paris (guided by Apollo) into his heel. The phrase 'Achilles heel' for any uniquely vulnerable point has entered all modern languages. The anatomical Achilles tendon is also named for him.

question: The Iliad — Homer's epic of the tenth year of the Trojan War — opens with one of the most famous lines in Western literature. The first word in Greek (mēnin, accusative case) sets the theme. What does it mean, and what is the rage about?
answer: 'Rage' — the rage of Achilles against Agamemnon, who has taken Achilles's war-prize Briseis in dishonor
choices: 'Rage' — the rage of Achilles against Agamemnon, who has taken Achilles's war-prize Briseis in dishonor
'Glory' — the glory of the Trojan War heroes, whose deeds Homer recounts for all generations to remember
'Mourning' — the mourning of Priam over Hector's body that begins and structures the entire poem's narrative
'Wandering' — the wandering of Greeks after Troy that the Odyssey will continue when the Iliad concludes
context: Mēnin (μῆνιν) opens the Iliad: 'Sing, goddess, of the rage of Peleus's son Achilles' (Lattimore). The Iliad is the story of how that rage unfolds — Achilles's withdrawal from battle, Patroclus's death wearing Achilles's armor, Achilles's terrible vengeance on Hector, and finally the ransoming of Hector's body. The whole epic is about anger, honor, death, mourning, and reconciliation — all in 51 days of the tenth year of the war.

question: The plot of the Iliad turns on Agamemnon's quarrel with Achilles. Apollo, angered by Agamemnon's refusal to return the captive Chryseis to her father Chryses (Apollo's priest), sent a plague on the Greek camp. Agamemnon, forced to return Chryseis, demanded compensation. He took Achilles's war-prize — the captive Briseis. What did Achilles do?
answer: Withdrew from battle with his Myrmidons; prayed to his mother Thetis to ask Zeus to bring defeat upon the Greeks
choices: Withdrew from battle with his Myrmidons; prayed to his mother Thetis to ask Zeus to bring defeat upon the Greeks
Killed Agamemnon's herald and prepared for civil war within the Greek camp until Odysseus intervened
Sailed home to Phthia immediately; the gods later compelled him to return for Patroclus's funeral games
Challenged Agamemnon to single combat; Athena descended and disarmed both kings before the duel could occur
context: Achilles's withdrawal — and Thetis's prayer to Zeus, who agreed to give the Trojans the upper hand to demonstrate Achilles's value — drives the Iliad's plot for many books. Without Achilles, the Greeks suffer. Books 11-15 show their suffering. Book 16 brings Patroclus's death; Book 18 brings Achilles's grief and decision to return. The poem is structured around the consequences of one man's anger.

question: In Iliad Book 16, with the Greeks pressed back to their ships and Hector about to set them ablaze, Achilles's beloved companion Patroclus begged to take Achilles's armor and lead the Myrmidons into battle to terrify the Trojans into retreat. Achilles consented but warned him only to drive the Trojans from the ships, not to pursue them to the walls of Troy. What happened?
answer: Patroclus drove the Trojans back but then pursued them to the walls; Apollo struck him; Hector finished him
choices: Patroclus drove the Trojans back but then pursued them to the walls; Apollo struck him; Hector finished him
Patroclus saved the ships and returned to camp safely; Hector killed him in a separate engagement days later
Patroclus was wounded but escaped to Achilles's tent; he died of his wounds three days later despite Apollo's healing
Patroclus single-handedly killed Hector; in the subsequent triumph, the Trojan archers shot him down in revenge
context: Patroclus's death is the turning point of the Iliad. His pursuit beyond what Achilles allowed brought him into the path of Apollo (who stripped him) and then Hector (who finished him). The armor was lost; Hephaestus forged Achilles new armor (Iliad 18). Achilles returned to battle in terrible grief and rage, killing many Trojans, eventually killing Hector outside the walls. Patroclus's funeral games occupy Book 23.

question: In Iliad Book 22, Achilles — wearing the new armor Hephaestus made him — confronted Hector outside Troy's walls. Hector's family watched from the walls; he chose to stand. After a brief flight (three times around the walls), Athena tricked Hector and Achilles caught him. They fought; Achilles killed Hector with a spear-thrust through the throat. What did Achilles do with the body?
answer: Tied it to his chariot and dragged it around the walls of Troy and then around Patroclus's tomb for days
choices: Tied it to his chariot and dragged it around the walls of Troy and then around Patroclus's tomb for days
Burned it on a pyre with the slaughtered Trojan captives as offerings to Patroclus's shade in the afterlife
Cut it into pieces and scattered them in the sea to deny the Trojans any possibility of decent burial
Returned it immediately to Priam; the funeral was held at once and the war paused for nine days for the rites
context: Achilles's mutilation of Hector's body was extreme even by Bronze Age standards — and the gods objected. Iliad 23 contains Patroclus's funeral and games. Iliad 24 — the climactic final book — has Priam, ancient king of Troy, traveling alone to Achilles's tent in the Greek camp to beg for his son's body. The scene of Priam kissing Achilles's hands (the hands that killed his son) is one of the most powerful moments in ancient literature.

question: In Iliad Book 24, Priam — king of Troy, aged father of fifty sons (Hector the firstborn now dead) — undertook a perilous nighttime journey to the Greek camp to beg Achilles for Hector's body. Hermes guided him in disguise. Priam slipped past sentries and entered Achilles's tent unannounced. What does Priam do when he enters?
answer: Falls at Achilles's feet, kisses the hands that killed his son, and asks Achilles to remember his own father Peleus
choices: Falls at Achilles's feet, kisses the hands that killed his son, and asks Achilles to remember his own father Peleus
Demands the body as right of war; threatens Achilles with the wrath of all the Trojan gods if it is denied
Offers an enormous ransom in gold and bronze; sits before Achilles in silence until accepted
Curses Achilles in the name of Apollo; promises that Apollo will avenge Hector before the year is out
context: Priam's plea — 'remember thy father' (Iliad 24.486) — moved Achilles to weep. The two men wept together, Priam for Hector, Achilles for his own father Peleus (whom he would never see again) and for Patroclus. Achilles returned Hector's body. The Iliad ends with Hector's funeral at Troy — twenty-four books that began with Achilles's rage now close on the bitter compassion possible even in war. Among the greatest scenes in literature.

question: After the Iliad's events (Achilles dying soon after killing Hector, Paris and many others killed in the continuing siege), the Greeks could not take Troy by force. Athena (or Odysseus alone) devised a stratagem. The Greeks built a giant wooden horse, hid the best warriors inside, and pretended to sail away leaving the horse as an offering to Athena. What was the role of Sinon?
answer: Sinon was a Greek planted as fake deserter; he persuaded the Trojans the horse was an offering and should be brought inside the walls
choices: Sinon was a Greek planted as fake deserter; he persuaded the Trojans the horse was an offering and should be brought inside the walls
Sinon was the Greek warrior in the horse who would open the gates; his name became proverbial for the hidden enemy
Sinon was the carpenter who built the horse; his lieutenants were the warriors who emerged at midnight to open the gates
Sinon was Odysseus's pseudonym used at Troy when posing as a deserter to confuse the Trojan defenders
context: The Trojan Horse episode is told in Virgil's Aeneid Book 2 (Aeneas's recounting to Dido) and in the lost Greek epic Iliupersis ('Sack of Troy'). Sinon's lie persuaded the Trojans. The priest Laocoön ('I fear the Greeks even bearing gifts') tried to warn them; sea serpents (sent by Athena or Apollo) strangled him and his sons. The Trojans brought the horse inside. By night the Greeks emerged, opened the gates, and sacked the city.

question: Cassandra, daughter of Priam and Hecuba, was a princess of Troy and a prophetess. Apollo had granted her the gift of true prophecy in exchange for her promised sexual favor. When she refused after receiving the gift, Apollo could not revoke it — but added what curse?
answer: That she would always prophesy truly, but no one would ever believe her
choices: That she would always prophesy truly, but no one would ever believe her
That she could foresee only ill omens and never good news for her family or city
That her prophecies would always come true only after the prophesied disasters occurred
That she would prophesy only in incomprehensible riddles no one could decode in time
context: Cassandra's tragedy was she foresaw the Trojan War's outcome, the Trojan Horse, her own death — and could persuade no one. Aeschylus's Agamemnon (458 BC) gives her the most powerful voice; she sees her own murder by Clytemnestra (after Agamemnon takes her as captive) before she enters. The figure has become archetypal for the prophet whose true warnings go unheeded — 'Cassandra warnings' for ignored prophecies.

question: Aeneas — son of Aphrodite and the mortal Anchises, Trojan prince of the royal line — was one of the few major Trojan warriors not killed in the war. When Troy fell, his mother (Venus, in Virgil's Aeneid) appeared to him and commanded him to flee. What did Aeneas do, and what was his destiny?
answer: Carried his father Anchises on his shoulders and led his son Ascanius by the hand; eventually founded Rome's ancestral line in Italy
choices: Carried his father Anchises on his shoulders and led his son Ascanius by the hand; eventually founded Rome's ancestral line in Italy
Threw himself onto the funeral pyre of Troy; Aphrodite intervened and bore him to Olympus as a god
Stayed to die with Troy; his mother spirited him away unconscious to Carthage where he founded that city instead
Took the Palladium (sacred statue of Athena) from the temple; carried it to Asia Minor and founded the kingdom of Phrygia
context: Virgil's Aeneid (29-19 BC) is the Roman national epic, casting Rome as the destined successor to Troy. Aeneas carrying Anchises (with Ascanius) is one of the iconic images of Roman piety — pietas, the duty to gods, family, and country. He wandered the Mediterranean (Carthage, where he loved and abandoned Dido), descended to the underworld, fought wars in Italy, and the Julii (Julius Caesar's family) traced their descent from his son Ascanius/Iulus.

question: Homer's Odyssey tells of Odysseus's ten-year return journey (nostos) from Troy to his home island of Ithaca. The poem is named for him — Odysseus = Odyssey. His wanderings, his eventual return, and his slaughter of the suitors who have been courting his wife Penelope form the plot. How is the Odyssey organized in narrative time?
answer: Books 1-4 Telemachus's search; 5-8 Odysseus from Calypso to Phaeacians; 9-12 Odysseus's recounted adventures; 13-24 return and revenge
choices: Books 1-4 Telemachus's search; 5-8 Odysseus from Calypso to Phaeacians; 9-12 Odysseus's recounted adventures; 13-24 return and revenge
Books 1-12 chronological wanderings from Troy; 13-24 chronological events on Ithaca after homecoming
Books 1-6 Penelope on Ithaca; 7-12 Telemachus's voyage; 13-18 Odysseus's wanderings; 19-24 the family reunion
Books 1-8 the gods' debate on Odysseus's fate; 9-16 his physical journey; 17-24 his recovery of the kingdom
context: The Odyssey's narrative structure is sophisticated. Books 9-12 are Odysseus's first-person account to the Phaeacians of his earlier adventures (Cyclops, Circe, the underworld, sirens, Scylla and Charybdis) — flashback within the larger narrative. The poem returns home in books 13-24 for the recognition scenes (with his swineherd Eumaeus, dog Argos, son Telemachus, nurse Eurycleia) and slaughter of the suitors.

question: In Odyssey Book 9, Odysseus and twelve companions explored the island of the Cyclopes and entered the cave of one — Polyphemus, son of Poseidon. Polyphemus returned, rolled a great stone across the cave mouth (trapping the Greeks), and began to eat them two at a time. What was Odysseus's escape plan?
answer: Got Polyphemus drunk on strong wine; told him 'my name is Nobody'; blinded him with a heated stake; escaped tied under the rams' bellies
choices: Got Polyphemus drunk on strong wine; told him 'my name is Nobody'; blinded him with a heated stake; escaped tied under the rams' bellies
Crept past while Polyphemus slept; the bronze stone could not be moved; only Odysseus escaped by stealth alone
Persuaded Polyphemus they were gods; the Cyclops freed them; only Odysseus's later mockery brought down Poseidon's wrath
Killed Polyphemus by Athena's spear; Poseidon's wrath came from the killing of his son, not from the trickery employed
context: When Polyphemus, blinded, cried 'Nobody is hurting me' to his Cyclops neighbors, they ignored him. Odysseus and his men escaped by clinging under the bellies of Polyphemus's rams as he let them out to pasture. Odysseus's mistake came as they sailed away — pride drove him to shout back his real name, allowing Polyphemus to curse him by name to Poseidon. The episode is among the most famous in Western literature.

question: After leaving the Cyclops, Odysseus's ship eventually reached the island of Aeaea, home of the sorceress Circe — daughter of Helios. She invited the men in for a feast, drugged their food with a magic potion, and transformed them with her wand. What happened, and how did Odysseus avoid the same fate?
answer: She turned them into swine; Hermes gave Odysseus the herb moly to resist; Odysseus drew his sword and threatened her
choices: She turned them into swine; Hermes gave Odysseus the herb moly to resist; Odysseus drew his sword and threatened her
She turned them into wolves; Athena warned Odysseus in a dream; he refused the food and overpowered her
She turned them into birds; Apollo descended in person to break the spell; the men flew home as swallows
She turned them into stone; Dionysus's wine on Odysseus's lips countered the spell; he chiseled them free
context: The Circe episode (Odyssey Book 10) follows the standard pattern: Hermes (Olympic protector) intervenes; Odysseus resists the spell; Circe transforms the men back. He then stayed with her for a year. She advised him on the journey to the underworld (the Nekyia, Book 11). The transformation into swine has been allegorized — humans become beasts when they yield to appetite (Joyce's Ulysses, Atwood's Circe).

question: Among the dangers Circe warned Odysseus about were the Sirens — two (or three) bird-women on a rocky island whose song was so beautiful that all sailors heard it died, their ships dashed on the rocks. The shore was littered with bones. Odysseus wanted to hear the song and survive. What did he and his crew do?
answer: Put wax in the crew's ears; bound Odysseus to the mast with orders not to release him no matter what; rowed past
choices: Put wax in the crew's ears; bound Odysseus to the mast with orders not to release him no matter what; rowed past
Sang counter-songs to the Sirens until they tired of competing; the Sirens fell into the sea and drowned themselves
Sacrificed a bull to Poseidon for safe passage; the Sirens' island was hidden by a fog Athena sent for protection
Sailed by night when the Sirens slept; the moonlight allowed silent passage without temptation arising at all
context: The Sirens episode (Odyssey 12) is among the most-recalled images in Western literature. Odysseus heard the song and survived only because his crew (deafened by wax) could not be persuaded to release him. The Sirens in some versions died at being passed — being unable to bear that any man had heard them and survived. Their later association with mermaid imagery is iconographic confusion; Greek Sirens were bird-women.

question: While Odysseus was away (ten years of war plus ten years of return), the great hall of his palace on Ithaca was filled with 108 suitors — young aristocrats of Ithaca and surrounding islands — feasting on his herds and pressing his wife Penelope to remarry. Penelope held them off with what stratagem?
answer: She would marry when she finished weaving a shroud for her father-in-law Laertes; she unwove it nightly for three years
choices: She would marry when she finished weaving a shroud for her father-in-law Laertes; she unwove it nightly for three years
She would marry when her son Telemachus came of age; she postponed his coming of age with delays as long as possible
She would marry only the man who could string her husband's bow; the suitors tried and failed throughout the years
She would marry whoever brought her the head of her husband; the suitors searched the sea but found nothing for years
context: The web-weaving deception (Odyssey 19) bought Penelope three years. A maid betrayed her; she was forced to finish. Penelope is among the most admired figures in Greek literature for her cunning loyalty — 'periphron Penelopeia' (circumspect Penelope) Homer's epithet. The bow-stringing contest comes at the end (Book 21), but only after Odysseus has returned in disguise. Penelope herself proposes it as the test, having (perhaps) recognized her husband.

question: Odysseus arrived on Ithaca disguised as an old beggar. He revealed himself first to his swineherd Eumaeus and his son Telemachus. He entered his hall as a beggar; the suitors mocked him. Penelope proposed the contest: she would marry whoever could string Odysseus's great bow and shoot through twelve axe-helves. None of the suitors could even string the bow. The beggar asked to try. What happened?
answer: Odysseus strung the bow, shot through the axes, then killed all 108 suitors with Telemachus, Eumaeus, and the herdsman Philoetius
choices: Odysseus strung the bow, shot through the axes, then killed all 108 suitors with Telemachus, Eumaeus, and the herdsman Philoetius
Odysseus strung the bow; the suitors fled; he killed only the ringleaders Antinous and Eurymachus and pardoned the rest
Odysseus failed to string the bow at first; Athena descended visibly to give him strength; the suitors then attacked
Odysseus revealed himself with the bow but did not fight; the suitors surrendered and left Ithaca peacefully forever
context: The slaughter of the suitors (Odyssey 22) is among the most violent scenes in Greek literature — 108 dead, plus 12 maids hanged for fraternizing with the suitors. The recognition scene with Penelope (Book 23) follows — she tests Odysseus by referring to their bed, which he had carved from a living olive tree (an unmovable secret only the two of them knew). The Odyssey closes with a fragile peace negotiated by Athena.

question: The two great epics traditionally attributed to Homer are the Iliad and the Odyssey. Each is divided into 24 books (corresponding to the 24 letters of the Greek alphabet — though this division was post-Homeric, by Alexandrian scholars). Roughly how many lines does each contain?
answer: Iliad about 15,700 lines; Odyssey about 12,100 lines — both in dactylic hexameter (six metrical feet per line)
choices: Iliad about 15,700 lines; Odyssey about 12,100 lines — both in dactylic hexameter (six metrical feet per line)
Iliad about 8,000 lines; Odyssey about 6,000 lines — both shorter than other ancient epics like the Mahabharata
Iliad about 25,000 lines; Odyssey about 20,000 lines — longer than Virgil's Aeneid but shorter than Dante's Comedy
Iliad about 3,500 lines; Odyssey about 2,800 lines — concise even by ancient standards of epic poetry
context: Iliad ≈ 15,693 lines; Odyssey ≈ 12,109 lines. Both in dactylic hexameter, the standard meter of Greek epic. The Alexandrian librarians (3rd-2nd century BC) divided each into 24 books. The 'Homeric Question' — whether one poet, two, oral tradition, etc. — has been debated since antiquity. Most modern scholars accept a strong oral tradition synthesized by one or more major poets in the 8th century BC.

question: Hesiod — the second great archaic Greek poet alongside Homer, traditionally dated to the late 8th or early 7th century BC — wrote two major surviving works. His Theogony ('birth of the gods') is the most systematic account of the gods' genealogy and the cosmic order. The poem opens with the Muses inspiring him on Mount Helicon. What does the Theogony cover?
answer: From Chaos through the generations of primordial beings, Titans, and Olympians, to Zeus's establishment of cosmic order
choices: From Chaos through the generations of primordial beings, Titans, and Olympians, to Zeus's establishment of cosmic order
Only the deeds of Zeus from his birth on Crete to his establishment as king of Olympus after the Titanomachy
Only the lineages of the major Olympian gods from Cronus and Rhea forward to the heroic generations of mortals
Only the conflicts of the gods with each other, beginning with the Titanomachy and ending with the Trojan War
context: Theogony is the foundational text for Greek mythology — over 1,000 lines tracing cosmic genealogy. The poem ends with the heroic generation that bridges gods and mortals (the catalogue of heroines, which becomes the basis for the lost Ehoeae). The Theogony's account of Cronus, Zeus, Prometheus, Typhon was authoritative for later Greek thought. Hesiod's other surviving work, Works and Days, is a moral and agricultural poem.

question: Hesiod's Works and Days — also surviving — was addressed to his (perhaps fictional) brother Perses. The poem combines moral instruction, the myth of the five ages (Golden, Silver, Bronze, Heroic, Iron), the Prometheus and Pandora stories, and detailed practical advice on what?
answer: Farming and seafaring — the calendar of agricultural tasks and good days for various activities throughout the year
choices: Farming and seafaring — the calendar of agricultural tasks and good days for various activities throughout the year
Hunting and metallurgy — the practical arts of the rural household other than agriculture, in lavish detail
Trade and diplomacy — the practical arts of city-state engagement that Hesiod claims his ancestors mastered
Athletics and music — the practical arts of the leisure class, addressed to Perses as the brother of nobler upbringing
context: Works and Days's agricultural calendar — when to plow, when to harvest, when to prune, when to sail, when to marry — preserves an irreplaceable picture of archaic Greek rural life. The dispute with Perses over their father's inheritance frames the moral instruction. Themes include the necessity of work, the dangers of injustice, and the moral order of Zeus's world. The poem combines myth, ethics, and economics in distinctively Greek fashion.

question: Mount Olympus — the highest mountain in Greece (2,917 meters / 9,570 feet) in northern Thessaly — was the home of the gods. The peaks are often hidden in cloud. In Homer, Olympus is both the actual mountain and a heavenly realm above the visible clouds. What was the central feature of Olympus in Greek imagination?
answer: Zeus's throne room — where the gods gathered for council and banquets of nectar and ambrosia
choices: Zeus's throne room — where the gods gathered for council and banquets of nectar and ambrosia
Apollo's oracle chamber — the primary oracular location until Delphi was established below in the lowlands
Hera's gardens of golden apples — the source of the gods' immortality through her cultivation
Hephaestus's central forge — where divine weapons and armor for both gods and chosen mortals were made
context: Olympus's central feature in Homer (Iliad, Odyssey) is Zeus's throne and the council chamber where the gods meet, drink nectar, eat ambrosia, and debate the affairs of mortals. Their houses were arranged around the peak — Hephaestus's forge was actually on Lemnos or beneath Mount Etna, the Hesperides' garden at the world's western edge. Olympus is a heavenly realm of light above weather; the mountain is its earthly anchor.

question: Delphi — on the southern slope of Mount Parnassus in central Greece — was the most prestigious religious center in the Greek world. The Greeks regarded it as the geographical center of the world. According to legend, Zeus released two eagles from the ends of the earth; they met at Delphi. A sacred stone in the inner sanctuary of Apollo's temple marked this center. What was the stone called?
answer: Omphalos — 'navel' — the navel of the world; an ovoid stone wrapped in carved netting, still preserved at Delphi
choices: Omphalos — 'navel' — the navel of the world; an ovoid stone wrapped in carved netting, still preserved at Delphi
Tholos — 'round shrine' — the architectural form of the building; the stone itself was actually unnamed in antiquity
Pythos — 'serpent' — referring to the dead Python under which the stone supposedly rested as a tomb marker
Adyton — 'inner sanctuary' — the name of the chamber rather than the stone; the stone was simply called 'rock'
context: The Omphalos (literally 'navel') marked Delphi as the world's center. The original may have been a meteorite or a sacred natural stone. Several copies exist; the most famous is now in the Delphi Archaeological Museum. The carved net surrounding it may represent the woolen wrappings of sacred bandages. The 'navel of the world' concept is shared with other ancient cultures (Jerusalem's Foundation Stone, Mecca's Black Stone).

question: The priestess of Apollo at Delphi was called the Pythia — after Python, the dragon Apollo killed on the spot. The Pythia sat on a tripod over a chasm in the inner sanctuary (adyton). She entered a trance state and uttered the oracle. By the historical period, what were the standard practices around consulting the oracle?
answer: Consultation only on the 7th day of each month for nine months a year; preliminary purification rites and a substantial fee
choices: Consultation only on the 7th day of each month for nine months a year; preliminary purification rites and a substantial fee
Consultation only at the festival of Apollo at the spring equinox; once-yearly responses delivered to all clients in turn
Consultation only by registered priests of Apollo on behalf of clients; no direct dialogue with the Pythia herself
Consultation only in person and in dactylic hexameter Greek; clients composed and delivered their questions in verse
context: The Delphic oracle operated nine months a year (the three winter months Apollo was said to be visiting Hyperborea, when Dionysus presided). Pilgrims came from across the Mediterranean world. They purified themselves with water from the Castalian Spring, paid a fee (the pelanos), sacrificed a goat. The Pythia's responses were often ambiguous (Croesus's 'great empire will fall' — his own). The historical Delphi operated c. 800 BC – 393 AD.

question: Among the most famous oracle responses was the one given to King Croesus of Lydia (c. 560-547 BC), the wealthiest king of his time, when he asked whether to attack the rising Persian Empire under Cyrus. The Delphic oracle's reply became the paradigm of ambiguous prophecy. What did it say?
answer: 'If you cross the Halys River, a great empire will fall' — Croesus crossed; the empire that fell was his own, not Persia's
choices: 'If you cross the Halys River, a great empire will fall' — Croesus crossed; the empire that fell was his own, not Persia's
'The Persians shall flee at the first arrow of the Lydian bow' — they did flee, but only briefly, and Croesus was eventually defeated
'Beware a man with a single shoe at the gates of Sardis' — Cyrus's herald arrived with one sandal, and the city fell
'When the mules ride on golden horses' — Croesus thought this impossible, but Cyrus's Persians later did become 'mules of empire'
context: Herodotus tells the Croesus story (Histories 1). The Halys River was the boundary between Lydia and Persian territory. Croesus, interpreting 'a great empire will fall' favorably, attacked. Cyrus defeated him 547 BC at Pteria and again at Sardis. Croesus on his pyre invoked Solon's earlier wisdom ('call no man happy until he is dead'). Cyrus pardoned him; Croesus became his advisor. The story shaped Greek thinking about the danger of ambiguous prophecy.

question: Orpheus — son of the Muse Calliope and Apollo (or the Thracian king Oeagrus) — was the greatest musician in Greek myth. His lyre could charm wild animals, move stones, and stop rivers. He married the nymph Eurydice; she was bitten by a snake on their wedding day and died. Grief-stricken, Orpheus descended into the underworld to retrieve her. What did Hades grant, and what was the condition?
answer: Eurydice could return with him to the upper world; Orpheus must not look back at her until both were out — he looked back and lost her
choices: Eurydice could return with him to the upper world; Orpheus must not look back at her until both were out — he looked back and lost her
Eurydice could return for one year of each three; she would spend two-thirds of her time in Hades and one-third with Orpheus
Eurydice's shade could speak with him but not return; they conversed for one full year before he ascended alone
Eurydice would be made a goddess; she would be lost to Orpheus but would live forever as a minor deity of dawn
context: Orpheus's failure to follow the rule (his impatience or doubt as they neared the upper world's exit) lost Eurydice permanently. He returned alone and rejected all other women; the maenads (Bacchic women) in their frenzy tore him apart. His head, still singing, floated to the island of Lesbos. The Orphic mysteries — distinct mystery religion focused on the soul's rebirth and the underworld — developed from his legendary descent and teachings.

question: The Orphic mysteries — a distinctive Greek mystery religion attributed to Orpheus's teachings — diverged from mainstream Greek religious thought in important ways. While most Greeks expected the same dim afterlife in Hades for nearly all dead, Orphism taught something different. What was its distinctive eschatology?
answer: Reincarnation of the soul; the goal was to purify the soul through ritual and ascetic life to escape the cycle and ascend to a blessed state
choices: Reincarnation of the soul; the goal was to purify the soul through ritual and ascetic life to escape the cycle and ascend to a blessed state
Resurrection of the body at the end of the cosmic cycle; all souls awaited the renewal of the world at the next Great Year
Immediate translation to Elysium for initiates; the uninitiated remained in Hades but with consoling memories
Annihilation of the soul at death for all but Orpheus's own descendants; only his bloodline survived in any form
context: Orphism's reincarnation doctrine resembled some Indian thought (Pythagoras may have learned from Orphic traditions). The famous Orphic gold tablets (found in tombs in southern Italy and Crete) contain instructions for the soul's journey: 'I am a child of earth and starry heaven, but my race is of heaven alone.' Plato adopted Orphic motifs (Phaedo, Republic). The body was tomb of the soul (sōma sēma, the famous play on words).

question: The Parthenon — temple of Athena Parthenos ('the virgin') on the Athenian Acropolis — was built between 447 and 432 BC during the leadership of Pericles. The architects were Ictinus and Callicrates; the chief sculptor was Phidias. It is the canonical example of the Doric architectural order. What was the temple's principal image?
answer: A 12-meter chryselephantine (gold-and-ivory) statue of Athena Parthenos by Phidias, holding a Nike and a spear
choices: A 12-meter chryselephantine (gold-and-ivory) statue of Athena Parthenos by Phidias, holding a Nike and a spear
The original wooden cult statue of Athena Polias, transferred from the older Erechtheum during the rebuilding period
A bronze equestrian statue of Athena, mounted on horseback to commemorate her victory in the contest with Poseidon
A great mosaic of the Birth of Athena from Zeus's head, covering the floor of the inner sanctuary completely
context: Phidias's gold-and-ivory Athena Parthenos (now lost; the original was probably destroyed in late antiquity) stood 12 meters tall. Roman copies and ancient descriptions allow reconstruction (Nashville, Tennessee has a full-scale copy). The Parthenon also held the city's treasury. Its frieze depicted the Panathenaic procession; pediments showed Athena's birth and her contest with Poseidon. Major reconstructions: Roussel, Korres. The marbles taken by Lord Elgin remain a contested artifact.

question: Phidias's other great chryselephantine statue — even more famous than Athena Parthenos — was at Olympia. The Statue of Zeus at Olympia (c. 435 BC) was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. It stood about 12 meters tall, seated on a throne, holding a Nike and a scepter. What is its eventual fate?
answer: Destroyed or removed in late antiquity; possibly burned in Constantinople 475 AD; no original copy survives in any form
choices: Destroyed or removed in late antiquity; possibly burned in Constantinople 475 AD; no original copy survives in any form
Buried in a landslide in 522 AD; recovered in 1875 by German archaeologists; now in the Olympia Archaeological Museum
Melted down for coinage by Constantine in the 4th century; the gold was used to fund Constantinople's founding
Preserved intact in a temple at Olympia until 1456; then dismantled by the Ottoman Turks for transport to Istanbul
context: The Statue of Zeus's exact fate is uncertain. Olympia was closed by Theodosius I (393 AD) when he banned pagan games; the statue was perhaps moved to Constantinople and lost in the fire of 475 AD. Ancient writers (Pausanias, Strabo, Quintilian) describe it. Phidias's workshop at Olympia has been excavated (showing his tools and a cup inscribed 'I belong to Phidias'). Pausanias considered it one of the supreme works of human art.

question: Greek religious practice centered on animal sacrifice. The largest type of sacrifice — typically for great festivals or major civic events — was the hecatomb. What did the name literally mean, and what was the typical scale?
answer: Hekatombē — 'a hundred oxen' — though the term came to mean any large sacrifice; actual numbers varied widely
choices: Hekatombē — 'a hundred oxen' — though the term came to mean any large sacrifice; actual numbers varied widely
Hekatombē — 'a hundred priests' — referring to the number officiating rather than to the animals offered up
Hekatombē — 'a hundred altars' — the temple complex required for a single grand state sacrifice in the polis
Hekatombē — 'a hundred days' — the duration of preparation required before such a major sacrifice could occur
context: Hekatombē combined hekaton (hundred) and bous (ox). Real hecatombs were sometimes literally a hundred oxen; sometimes the term meant a large sacrifice. Plutarch records Athenian hecatombs at the Panathenaia. The meat from sacrifices was distributed to the citizens — religion and civic feasting were inseparable in Greek practice. The bones and fat were burned for the gods; the meat went to the people.

question: The Greek underworld was bounded by five rivers. The most famous was the Styx (Hatred), by which the gods swore inviolable oaths. To cross from the world of the living to Hades, the dead had to be ferried across by Charon. What did each soul need to pay?
answer: An obol (a small copper coin) placed in the mouth of the corpse at burial — Charon would not transport the unpaid
choices: An obol (a small copper coin) placed in the mouth of the corpse at burial — Charon would not transport the unpaid
A drop of pomegranate juice on the lips at death — derived from Persephone's seeds, the underworld's symbol
A small clay amulet of Hermes carried in the hand — Charon recognized the soul's safe-conduct from the gods
A few drops of olive oil poured on the funeral pyre — Charon could not refuse a soul properly anointed by oil
context: Charon's obol was placed in the mouth (or on the eyes) of corpses across the Greek and Roman worlds. Souls of the unburied — or of those without a coin — wandered the riverbank for a hundred years. The custom is archaeologically attested. The famous Charon's obol — a coin in the mouth — has been found in tombs from Greece to Roman Britain. The Styx was real (a real river in Arcadia named for the goddess); the underworld river was its supernatural counterpart.

question: The five rivers of the Greek underworld each had a distinct association. Acheron was the river of woe; Styx, hatred; Lethe, forgetfulness; Phlegethon, fire; Cocytus, lamentation. What was the function of the Lethe?
answer: Souls drank from it to forget their previous lives before being reincarnated into new bodies
choices: Souls drank from it to forget their previous lives before being reincarnated into new bodies
Souls drank from it to remember everything they had forgotten in life before being judged
Souls had to cross it before reaching the judgment hall; only those without sin could pass dry-shod
Souls drank from it to forget the pain of death before entering the asphodel meadows of the neutral dead
context: Lethe's role in forgetting before reincarnation was particularly developed in Orphic-Pythagorean and Platonic traditions (Republic Book 10's myth of Er). Mainstream Greek religion did not necessarily emphasize reincarnation, but the river of forgetfulness fit naturally with whatever specific eschatology. Mnemosyne (memory) had a counter-spring; some Orphic initiates were instructed to ask for water from Mnemosyne, not Lethe.

question: For ordinary Greeks, the afterlife was a dim and joyless existence in Hades — even Achilles preferred to be a slave on earth rather than king among the dead (Odyssey 11). But for a special few — heroes, the elect of the gods, in some accounts the righteous — there was a different destination. What was it called?
answer: The Elysian Fields (or Elysium) — the realm of the blessed, where heroes feasted with the gods in eternal happiness
choices: The Elysian Fields (or Elysium) — the realm of the blessed, where heroes feasted with the gods in eternal happiness
The Hyperborean Lands — beyond the north wind, where Apollo lived among the favored mortals six months yearly
The Isles of Atlantis — the lost civilization to which only the philosophically pure could return after death
The Pillars of Heracles — the western edge of the world, where the bravest heroes were transported by Poseidon
context: Elysium developed in Greek religious thought over time. Homer mentions it only briefly (Odyssey 4); later writers (especially in mystery religion contexts) elaborated it. Plato's myths (Gorgias, Phaedo, Republic) developed the moral judgment of souls — Elysium for the righteous, Tartarus for the wicked. The Elysian afterlife became one of the elements of Christian heaven (etymology of 'Elysian Fields' for Paris's Champs-Elysées).

question: At the center of Norse cosmology stands a great tree — the cosmic ash tree from which all the Nine Worlds depend. The name means 'Odin's horse' (yggr = a name for Odin, drasil = horse) — a reference to Odin's self-sacrifice hanging on its branches for nine nights to win the runes. What is this tree?
answer: Yggdrasil — the world-tree whose branches reach to heaven and whose three roots descend to three wells in three realms
choices: Yggdrasil — the world-tree whose branches reach to heaven and whose three roots descend to three wells in three realms
Mjolnir — the cosmic hammer; this is actually Thor's weapon, not the world-tree, despite their poetic associations
Bifrost — the rainbow bridge; this is the connection between Asgard and Midgard but not the tree itself
Glasir — the golden grove in front of Valhalla; smaller than Yggdrasil but often confused with it in poetry
context: Yggdrasil's three roots reached the Well of Urd (in Asgard), the Well of Mímir (near the giants' land), and Hvergelmir (in Niflheim). The Eddas describe creatures inhabiting it: the dragon Niðhöggr at its base, the eagle at its top, the squirrel Ratatosk carrying messages between them, four stags eating its leaves. The tree's eventual fate (shaking but surviving Ragnarok) framed Norse cosmic vision.

question: Yggdrasil's three roots descend to three wells — each in a different realm. The most famous is the Well of Urd (Urðarbrunnr) in Asgard, where the three Norns — Urd (past), Verdandi (present), Skuld (future) — sit and water the root. What were the other two wells, and where were they?
answer: The Well of Mimir (wisdom) by the giants; Hvergelmir (the seething cauldron) in icy Niflheim
choices: The Well of Mimir (wisdom) by the giants; Hvergelmir (the seething cauldron) in icy Niflheim
The Well of Saga (poetry) in Vanaheim; the Well of Eir (healing) in the realm of the light elves
The Well of Freyr (fertility) in Alfheim; the Well of Andvari (gold) in Svartalfheim of the dwarves
The Well of Hod (winter) in Niflheim; the Well of Baldr (light) in Asgard near the great hall of Breidablik
context: The Well of Mimir — Mimir's head guarded its wisdom-giving water. Odin sacrificed an eye to drink from it. The Well of Hvergelmir was the source of the eleven rivers that flowed into Ginnungagap at the beginning of creation. The Norns at Urd's Well also wove the threads of fate from beneath Yggdrasil's roots. The water of the wells fed the tree and the tree fed the wells in cyclical exchange.

question: Norse cosmology organized reality into nine worlds, all connected by Yggdrasil. The worlds include realms of gods, mortals, giants, elves, dwarves, and the dead. Which of the following is NOT one of the standard Nine Worlds?
answer: Pandemonium — actually from Milton's Paradise Lost (1667), capital of Hell, not a Norse realm at all
choices: Pandemonium — actually from Milton's Paradise Lost (1667), capital of Hell, not a Norse realm at all
Asgard — the home of the Aesir gods (Odin's family), highest of the Nine Worlds
Midgard — the home of humans, the 'middle enclosure' in the cosmic order
Niflheim — the realm of mist and ice, primordial realm and home of the dishonored dead
context: The Nine Worlds (with some textual variation): Asgard (Aesir), Vanaheim (Vanir), Alfheim (light elves), Midgard (humans), Jotunheim (giants), Svartalfheim (dwarves/dark elves), Muspelheim (fire), Niflheim (ice/mist), Helheim (dishonored dead). Pandemonium is from Christian Milton, not Norse myth. The Yggdrasil tree connected all nine.

question: Asgard — the highest of the Nine Worlds — was the home of the principal family of Norse gods, the Aesir. Located above Midgard, connected by the rainbow bridge Bifrost, it contained twelve great halls. What was the most famous of Asgard's halls, and to which god did it belong?
answer: Valhalla — Odin's hall where the slain warriors (einherjar) feasted and fought until Ragnarok
choices: Valhalla — Odin's hall where the slain warriors (einherjar) feasted and fought until Ragnarok
Sessrumnir — actually Freyja's hall in Folkvangr, not in Asgard proper despite its grandeur
Thrudheim — actually Thor's farmstead realm rather than a hall in Asgard's central complex
Breidablik — actually Baldr's hall in Asgard, though less famous than Odin's and not central
context: Valhalla ('hall of the slain') — Odin's hall with 540 doors, roof of golden shields. The einherjar (chosen warriors) feasted on the boar Saehrimnir (slaughtered and resurrected daily) and drank mead from the goat Heidrun. By day they fought in the practice yard; wounds healed by evening. They prepared for Ragnarok when they would fight beside the Aesir against the forces of chaos.

question: The Vanir were a second family of Norse gods — distinct from the Aesir but eventually merged with them after the Aesir-Vanir war. They were associated with fertility, prosperity, the sea, and certain forms of magic (seidr). Their realm was Vanaheim. Who were the three principal Vanir who came to live with the Aesir as hostages after the war?
answer: Njord (sea), Freyr (fertility), Freyja (love and seidr magic) — among the most popular gods in Norse worship
choices: Njord (sea), Freyr (fertility), Freyja (love and seidr magic) — among the most popular gods in Norse worship
Mimir (wisdom), Hoenir (silent), Kvasir (poetry) — actually the Aesir hostages sent to the Vanir, not the reverse
Surt (fire), Loki (trickster), Aegir (sea) — actually three giant or part-giant figures, not Vanir at all
Bragi (poetry), Idun (apples), Forseti (justice) — actually pure Aesir, not Vanir hostages from the war
context: After the Aesir-Vanir war (a major prehistorical event in Norse cosmology), hostages were exchanged. From the Vanir came Njord and his children Freyr and Freyja. From the Aesir to the Vanir went Hoenir and Mimir (whom the Vanir later beheaded in anger). The Aesir-Vanir merger created the unified Norse pantheon; Freyr and Freyja became among the most worshipped Norse deities.

question: Midgard — 'middle enclosure' — was the realm of humans, situated in the middle of Yggdrasil. According to the Eddas, it was created by Odin and his brothers Vili and Ve from the body of the slain primordial giant Ymir. What was the surrounding feature of Midgard, and what does its name imply about Norse cosmology?
answer: An encircling ocean inhabited by the world-serpent Jormungandr — Midgard is bounded by chaos that it must contain
choices: An encircling ocean inhabited by the world-serpent Jormungandr — Midgard is bounded by chaos that it must contain
An encircling forest of iron trees — Midgard's wood-shield protects the human realm from Jotunheim's giants
An encircling wall of ice from Niflheim's mists — Midgard is defended by the frozen waste from invasion
An encircling sea of fire from Muspelheim — Midgard's heat-shield prevents the frost giants from approaching
context: Midgard was surrounded by ocean; Jormungandr the World Serpent lay in that ocean, biting his own tail (his name means 'huge monster'; he is Thor's destined enemy at Ragnarok). The cosmic structure — humans in the middle, gods above, chaos surrounding — is theologically significant. The name 'Middle Earth' (Tolkien) is a direct translation of Miðgarðr.

question: Jotunheim was the realm of the giants (jötnar — singular jötunn) — the great enemies of the Aesir, but also their frequent lovers and (in some cases) parents. The relationship between Aesir and giants is complex — Odin's mother Bestla was a giantess; Loki was a giant; Thor's mother was Earth (Jord), a giantess. What is the principal feature of Jotunheim?
answer: Wild, mountainous, forested wilderness — full of monstrous beings and dangerous magic
choices: Wild, mountainous, forested wilderness — full of monstrous beings and dangerous magic
Burning desert — a vast arid land where only the fire giants could survive comfortably
Underground caverns — connected to Svartalfheim and ruled by king of dwarves rather than giants
Floating islands of ice — drifting in primordial chaos, accessible only via Yggdrasil's branches
context: Jotunheim's wild geography contrasted with Asgard's orderly halls — the giants represented chaos, the primordial powers older than the Aesir. Many key Norse myths involve Aesir-giant encounters: Thor's journey to Utgard-Loki, the building of Asgard's wall, the kidnapping of Idun, Skadi's marriage to Njord. The boundary between gods and giants was permeable; descent was rarely pure.

question: At the opposite cosmic extreme from the icy Niflheim was Muspelheim — the primordial realm of fire. In the Eddas, the meeting of Muspelheim's heat and Niflheim's ice in the void of Ginnungagap initiated creation. Who was the principal being of Muspelheim, and what is his role in Norse cosmology?
answer: Surt — the fire giant who will lead Muspelheim's forces at Ragnarok, his sword brighter than the sun, burning the world
choices: Surt — the fire giant who will lead Muspelheim's forces at Ragnarok, his sword brighter than the sun, burning the world
Logi — the fire giant who appeared in Thor's adventure at Utgard-Loki; primarily a folk figure rather than cosmic
Loki — the trickster god is sometimes confused with fire, but Loki was actually a giant of mixed parentage
Vidar — actually the silent god of vengeance who kills Fenrir at Ragnarok, not a fire being at all
context: Surt's role at Ragnarok is to burn the world. His flaming sword (which he wields outward at the final battle) will consume Yggdrasil and the Nine Worlds. Muspelheim's existence from before creation gives Norse cosmology its dualistic primordial structure (fire/ice → existence). Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda is the principal source for Surt's role.

question: Before the Nine Worlds existed, the Norse cosmos was structured around three primordial realities: a great void between two extremes. What were they?
answer: Ginnungagap (the void) between Niflheim (ice/mist) to the north and Muspelheim (fire) to the south
choices: Ginnungagap (the void) between Niflheim (ice/mist) to the north and Muspelheim (fire) to the south
Ginnungagap (the void) between Asgard (gods) above and Helheim (dead) below in the original cosmos
Ginnungagap (the void) between Jotunheim (giants) east and Vanaheim (Vanir) west of the primal world
Ginnungagap (the void) between Midgard (humans) on the surface and the underworld beneath the rivers
context: The Voluspa (Prophecy of the Volva, in the Poetic Edda) describes Ginnungagap as the primordial void. The encounter of fire and ice in the void produced the first being — the giant Ymir, formed from the melting ice. Audhumla, the primordial cow, emerged also; she licked salt-ice and revealed Buri (ancestor of the gods). The myth contains striking parallels with Hesiod's Chaos and ancient Near Eastern creation accounts.

question: Ymir — the first being in Norse cosmogony — was a giant formed when the heat of Muspelheim met the ice of Niflheim in Ginnungagap. From his armpits sprouted male and female giants; from one of his legs another giant grew. Ymir was nourished by what creature, and what happened to him eventually?
answer: Audhumla, the primordial cow; Odin and his brothers Vili and Ve killed Ymir and made the world from his body
choices: Audhumla, the primordial cow; Odin and his brothers Vili and Ve killed Ymir and made the world from his body
Hvergelmir, the boiling spring; Ymir died of exposure when the spring's heat exhausted itself overnight
Surt, the fire giant; Ymir was burned to ash and the Nine Worlds emerged from the smoke and embers later
The serpent Niðhöggr; Ymir was eaten alive by the dragon and the Nine Worlds emerged from his bones
context: Audhumla licked salt-ice for nourishment, revealing the proto-god Buri. Buri's son Bor (Odin's father) married the giantess Bestla. Odin, Vili, and Ve killed Ymir. The flood of his blood drowned almost all the giants except Bergelmir (Norse Noah figure) and his wife. The brothers made the world from Ymir's body — flesh became earth, bones became mountains, blood became sea, skull became sky, brains became clouds.

question: Per Snorri Sturluson's account in the Prose Edda, when Odin and his brothers killed the giant Ymir, they used his body to create the world. Which body part became which feature of the cosmos?
answer: Flesh → earth; blood → sea; bones → mountains; teeth → rocks; skull → sky; brain → clouds; hair → trees
choices: Flesh → earth; blood → sea; bones → mountains; teeth → rocks; skull → sky; brain → clouds; hair → trees
Flesh → mountains; blood → rivers; bones → trees; teeth → stars; skull → earth; brain → fog; hair → grass
Flesh → sky; blood → underworld rivers; bones → seabed; teeth → moon and sun; skull → sea; brain → soil; hair → smoke
Flesh → fire; blood → ice; bones → wind; teeth → lightning; skull → thunder; brain → snow; hair → mist
context: The Ymir cosmogony parallels Mesopotamian (Marduk slaying Tiamat) and Indo-European (Purusha hymn in Rigveda) patterns of cosmogony from a primordial sacrifice. Snorri's exact correspondences may be his systematization of older traditions. The four dwarves Nordri, Sudri, Austri, Vestri (North, South, East, West) held up the sky-skull at the four corners; their names became the Norse cardinal directions.

question: In Norse cosmic prehistory, the Aesir gods and the Vanir gods waged war. The cause is uncertain — Snorri Sturluson tells of a Vanir witch (Gullveig/Heid) tortured three times by the Aesir for her magic. The war ended in stalemate. How was peace established?
answer: Exchange of hostages: Njord, Freyr, Freyja came from the Vanir to Aesir; Hoenir, Mimir, Kvasir came from Aesir to Vanir
choices: Exchange of hostages: Njord, Freyr, Freyja came from the Vanir to Aesir; Hoenir, Mimir, Kvasir came from Aesir to Vanir
Marriage alliance: Odin married a Vanir princess and the Vanir king married the goddess Frigg as bonded queens
Treaty of peace and trade: the two pantheons opened a market on the borders of Asgard and Vanaheim each year
Total assimilation: all the Vanir became Aesir by oath; the Vanir realm Vanaheim was incorporated into Asgard
context: The hostage exchange is the standard account (Voluspa, Snorri's Heimskringla). Kvasir was made from the spit of all the gods (sealing the truce); he became the wisest being and was killed by dwarves who made his blood into the mead of poetry. The Aesir-Vanir war reflects an early conflict perhaps between two cult traditions among the Germanic peoples — eventually unified.
