Auschwitz received transports from across Europe — Hungary alone sent 437,000 Jews (most killed within weeks) in summer 1944. The Soviet liberation (January 27, 1945) found 7,000 survivors. International Holocaust Remembrance Day falls on this date. Primo Levi (If This Is a Man) and Elie Wiesel (Night) survived to write about it.

question: In 622 AD, after twelve years of preaching in Mecca and facing increasing persecution, Muhammad and his followers emigrated to Yathrib (later renamed Medinat al-Nabi, 'City of the Prophet,' or simply Medina) about 200 miles north. This emigration is called the Hijra. What is its significance in Islamic history?
answer: Year 1 of the Islamic calendar (Anno Hegirae, AH) — the lunar calendar Muslims use for religious dating
choices: Year 1 of the Islamic calendar (Anno Hegirae, AH) — the lunar calendar Muslims use for religious dating
The year of the first Caliph's reign — actually Abu Bakr's caliphate began ten years later in 632
The year of Muhammad's death — actually 632, ten years after the Hijra; the dates are sometimes confused
The year of the Quran's compilation — actually under Uthman c. 650, three decades after the Hijra
context: The Hijra marks Islam's transformation from a persecuted Meccan minority into a politically governed religious community at Medina. The Islamic calendar dates from 16 July 622 (1 Muharram, AH 1). Caliph Umar formalized this dating c. 638 AD. The Hijra was not a flight (Muhammad arranged it carefully) but a planned migration. The Quran refers to the muhajirun (emigrants) and ansar (helpers in Medina) — the two original Muslim social categories.

question: Ibn Sina (Avicenna, 980-1037) — Persian polymath born near Bukhara — was the most influential Islamic philosopher and physician. His Canon of Medicine (al-Qanun fi al-Tibb) was the standard medical textbook in both the Islamic world and medieval Europe for centuries. What were his philosophical contributions?
answer: Synthesizing Aristotelian philosophy with Islamic theology; theory of essence and existence; the 'Floating Man' thought experiment
choices: Synthesizing Aristotelian philosophy with Islamic theology; theory of essence and existence; the 'Floating Man' thought experiment
Translation of the entire Greek philosophical corpus into Arabic; his original works were summaries of his translations
Compilation of all Quranic exegesis from earlier scholars; his philosophy was primarily theological exegesis rather than original
Founding of Sufism; his philosophical works were actually mystical poetry rather than systematic philosophy
context: Avicenna's Kitab al-Shifa ('Book of Healing,' a philosophical encyclopedia) and al-Ishara ('Book of Pointers') were major works. His 'Floating Man' argument (a person suspended in air, deprived of all sensation, would still know he existed) anticipated Descartes's cogito by 600 years. His distinction of essence (mahiyya) and existence (wujud) influenced Aquinas. Translated into Latin in the 12th century, Avicenna became a major reference for European scholastic philosophy.

question: Ibn Rushd (Averroes, 1126-1198) — born in Cordoba, Andalusia — was the greatest commentator on Aristotle in the medieval world. His Latin translations made Aristotle available to medieval European universities. He served as judge and physician in the Almohad court but eventually fell from favor. What is his philosophical relationship to al-Ghazali?
answer: Wrote 'Incoherence of the Incoherence' rebutting al-Ghazali's 'Incoherence of the Philosophers' point by point
choices: Wrote 'Incoherence of the Incoherence' rebutting al-Ghazali's 'Incoherence of the Philosophers' point by point
Was al-Ghazali's student and disciple; the two are sometimes confused as the same person
Predated al-Ghazali; al-Ghazali wrote against Averroes's positions in his own later treatise
Was unrelated to al-Ghazali; the two worked in different fields with no philosophical engagement
context: The al-Ghazali / Ibn Rushd exchange is one of the great intellectual confrontations of medieval Islam. Al-Ghazali (1058-1111) attacked the philosophers' use of Greek rationalism in 'Incoherence of the Philosophers' (Tahafut al-Falasifa). Averroes responded in 'Incoherence of the Incoherence' (Tahafut al-Tahafut). Al-Ghazali's position won in the Islamic world; the philosophical tradition declined. Averroes was banned in his last years. Yet in Latin Europe, his commentaries on Aristotle became foundational for scholasticism.

question: Al-Ghazali (1058-1111) is among the most influential Islamic thinkers — a theologian, philosopher, and Sufi mystic. His 'Incoherence of the Philosophers' (Tahafut al-Falasifa, c. 1095) attacked the Aristotelian philosophical tradition associated with Avicenna and al-Farabi. What was his most controversial argument?
answer: Causation is illusory — what looks like cause and effect is actually God's repeated direct creation; fire does not cause burning
choices: Causation is illusory — what looks like cause and effect is actually God's repeated direct creation; fire does not cause burning
Mathematics is impossible — the philosophers' use of geometry leads inevitably to atheism by mathematical determinism
Logic is heretical — Aristotelian syllogism is incompatible with Islamic theology and must be entirely rejected
Philosophy is forbidden entirely — no rational engagement with Greek thought is permissible in Islamic culture
context: Al-Ghazali's occasionalism (God as the direct cause of every event; what appears as natural causation is actually God's customary action) had major theological consequences. He did not reject philosophy entirely but bounded it sharply. His mystical turn in 'The Revival of Religious Sciences' (Ihya' Ulum al-Din) made Sufism mainstream. His influence shifted the Islamic intellectual tradition away from the rationalism of the Golden Age. Some modern scholars debate whether he 'closed the gates of ijtihad.'

question: The Ottoman Empire — founded by Osman I in 1299, dissolved 1923 — was the longest-lasting Islamic empire and at its height controlled territory from Vienna to Yemen, Algeria to Iraq. Key events include the conquest of Constantinople (1453) by Mehmet II, the height of power under Suleiman the Magnificent (r. 1520-1566). What was the principal Islamic institution within the Ottoman political system?
answer: The Sultan was also Caliph (after 1517); Islamic law (sharia) governed civil life through ulama hierarchy and qadi judges
choices: The Sultan was also Caliph (after 1517); Islamic law (sharia) governed civil life through ulama hierarchy and qadi judges
The Sultan was always secular; Islamic affairs were handled by an independent Caliphate in Mecca throughout Ottoman rule
The Sultan was Shia; the Ottoman Empire was Shia until 1500, then converted entire to Sunni under Selim I
The Sultan rejected the title of Caliph; Islamic affairs were handled by Iran's Safavid dynasty by treaty agreement
context: After Selim I conquered Egypt (1517), the Ottoman Sultans claimed the Caliphate (the last Abbasid Caliph supposedly transferred the title). The Sultan-Caliph dual role lasted until 1924 when the Turkish Republic abolished both offices. The Ottoman religious institution included the Shaykh al-Islam (chief Islamic scholar), millets (religious communities of non-Muslims with internal autonomy), and a vast system of religious endowments (waqf).

question: In February 1979, the Iranian monarchy under Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi collapsed; the cleric Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini returned from exile in Paris and established the Islamic Republic of Iran. What political system did Khomeini institute?
answer: Velayat-e Faqih ('guardianship of the jurist') — a Shia clerical theocracy with a Supreme Leader above an elected president
choices: Velayat-e Faqih ('guardianship of the jurist') — a Shia clerical theocracy with a Supreme Leader above an elected president
Constitutional monarchy under a different royal line — actually the system the revolutionaries replaced, not what they created
Secular democracy modeled on the French Republic — Khomeini was actually opposed to clerical rule despite his own status
Direct democracy without leaders — the revolution was anarchist in inspiration and rejected hierarchical structures
context: Khomeini's 1979 revolution established a unique political form — a constitutional system with elected institutions subordinated to a clerical supreme leader. The Iranian Revolution shocked the world: the Carter administration was unprepared; the US embassy hostage crisis (1979-1981) defined American relations with revolutionary Iran. Khomeini's regime suppressed leftists, secularists, and religious minorities. The 1979 Iran is sometimes called the start of modern political Islamism (Sunni Islamism — Muslim Brotherhood — was earlier).

question: On September 11, 2001, al-Qaeda terrorists — under the leadership of Osama bin Laden — carried out coordinated attacks on the United States. They hijacked four airliners; two struck the World Trade Center in New York; one struck the Pentagon; one crashed in Pennsylvania after passenger resistance. What was the death toll?
answer: About 2,977 killed; the worst foreign attack on American soil in history; precipitated the 'War on Terror'
choices: About 2,977 killed; the worst foreign attack on American soil in history; precipitated the 'War on Terror'
About 800 killed — actually a substantial underestimate of the true death toll
About 15,000 killed — actually an overestimate, though early estimates of WTC casualties were higher than final
About 50 killed — actually a substantial underestimate of the true death toll
context: 9/11 killed 2,977: about 2,606 in the WTC and surrounding area, 184 at the Pentagon, 40 on UA Flight 93, plus the 19 hijackers. The attacks led to US invasions of Afghanistan (2001) and Iraq (2003), the Patriot Act, the Department of Homeland Security, and dramatic changes in air travel and surveillance. Osama bin Laden was killed by US Navy SEALs in Abbottabad, Pakistan on May 2, 2011. Al-Qaeda was weakened but inspired subsequent jihadist movements (ISIS).

question: In June 2014, the leader of an extremist group operating in Iraq and Syria — Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi — declared a 'caliphate' over the territories his forces had seized, calling himself caliph of all Muslims. What was the group, and what did it become known for?
answer: Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) / Islamic State (Daesh) — known for extreme brutality, genocide of Yazidis, beheadings, terror
choices: Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) / Islamic State (Daesh) — known for extreme brutality, genocide of Yazidis, beheadings, terror
Al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) — actually a Yemen-based al-Qaeda affiliate, not the ISIS group
Al-Shabaab — actually the Somalia-based jihadist group, not the Iraq-Syria caliphate of 2014
Boko Haram — actually the Nigeria-based jihadist group, not the Iraq-Syria caliphate of 2014
context: ISIS held substantial territory 2014-2017, including major cities (Mosul, Raqqa). At peak it controlled territory of about 10 million people. The international coalition (including US, Iraq, Kurdish forces, Iran) drove ISIS from territory by 2019. Al-Baghdadi was killed by US Special Forces in October 2019. ISIS committed documented genocide of the Yazidi religious minority in Iraq (UN finding 2016). The group's extreme violence — beheadings, mass executions, sexual slavery — exceeded even al-Qaeda's brutality.

question: Siddhartha Gautama (traditionally dated 563-483 BC, though modern scholarship debates) was the historical Buddha. Born to a royal Shakya family in Lumbini (modern Nepal), prince of Kapilavastu, his father (King Suddhodana) sheltered him from suffering. He married Yashodhara at 16, had a son Rahula. At 29, he encountered four sights that changed his life. What were they?
answer: An old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a wandering ascetic — revealing aging, sickness, death, and the spiritual path
choices: An old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a wandering ascetic — revealing aging, sickness, death, and the spiritual path
A king, a soldier, a merchant, and a slave — revealing the four social castes of ancient India and their separate fates
Four flames in a sacred grove — symbols of fire, water, earth, and air to be reconciled in spiritual practice
Four animals — a lion, a snake, a peacock, and an ox — symbols of his future Buddha-titles and disciples
context: The Four Passing Sights are traditional. Encountering them shattered Siddhartha's sheltered existence. He left his palace, wife, and son in the Great Renunciation (mahabhinishkramana), cut his hair and beard, exchanged his royal clothes for ascetic robes. He studied with two teachers, then practiced severe asceticism for six years. He realized asceticism would not bring liberation. He sat under the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya determined to find enlightenment or die.

question: After his enlightenment, Buddha walked to Sarnath (near Varanasi) and preached his first sermon to five ascetics who had been his earlier companions. This sermon is called 'Setting in Motion the Wheel of Dharma' (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta). What did he teach?
answer: The Four Noble Truths: dukkha exists; dukkha arises from craving; cessation is possible; the Eightfold Path is the way
choices: The Four Noble Truths: dukkha exists; dukkha arises from craving; cessation is possible; the Eightfold Path is the way
The Three Refuges: Buddha, Dharma, Sangha — the foundational vow of Buddhist practice for laypeople and monastics
The Five Precepts: no killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, intoxicants — the lay ethical code
The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination — the cycle of how suffering arises through ignorance and grasping
context: The Four Noble Truths form the foundation of Buddhist thought: (1) dukkha (suffering, unsatisfactoriness) is the nature of existence; (2) the cause of dukkha is tanha (craving); (3) cessation of craving leads to cessation of dukkha (nirvana); (4) the path to cessation is the Noble Eightfold Path. The Eightfold Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.

question: Buddhism developed into several major schools over its 2,500-year history. The three principal traditions today are Theravada, Mahayana, and Vajrayana. What are their geographic distributions and emphases?
answer: Theravada (SE Asia: Sri Lanka, Thailand, Burma, Cambodia, Laos); Mahayana (E Asia: China, Japan, Korea, Vietnam); Vajrayana (Tibet, Mongolia, Himalayas)
choices: Theravada (SE Asia: Sri Lanka, Thailand, Burma, Cambodia, Laos); Mahayana (E Asia: China, Japan, Korea, Vietnam); Vajrayana (Tibet, Mongolia, Himalayas)
Theravada (Tibet, Mongolia); Mahayana (Sri Lanka, Thailand); Vajrayana (China, Japan) — actually the distributions are reversed
Theravada (China, Japan); Mahayana (Tibet, Mongolia); Vajrayana (Sri Lanka, Thailand) — actually all reversed
Theravada (Korea); Mahayana (Burma, Cambodia); Vajrayana (Vietnam) — actually none of these are correct geographic mappings
context: Theravada ('Teaching of the Elders') — the older, more conservative tradition emphasizing monastic discipline and individual arahant-realization; Mahayana ('Great Vehicle') — emerged c. 1st century BC, emphasizes the bodhisattva ideal (postponing personal liberation to save all beings); Vajrayana ('Diamond Vehicle') — tantric Buddhism emphasizing rapid enlightenment through ritual, mantra, mandala. All three preserve different canons of scripture.

question: The Dalai Lama — the most prominent figure of Tibetan (Vajrayana) Buddhism — heads a tulku (reincarnated lama) lineage that has continued for fourteen lives. The institution was established when Sonam Gyatso (1543-1588) received the title 'Dalai Lama' ('Ocean Teacher') from the Mongol khan Altan Khan in 1578. What is the current Dalai Lama's role, and what is his political history?
answer: Tenzin Gyatso (b. 1935) — 14th Dalai Lama; fled Tibet 1959 after Chinese suppression; Nobel Peace Prize 1989
choices: Tenzin Gyatso (b. 1935) — 14th Dalai Lama; fled Tibet 1959 after Chinese suppression; Nobel Peace Prize 1989
Lobsang Gyatso (b. 1900) — 13th Dalai Lama; ruled Tibet until 1933; the 14th has not yet been formally identified
Tenzin Gyatso (b. 1935) — 14th Dalai Lama; rules Tibet from Lhasa as both political and religious leader
Sonam Gyatso (b. 1935) — the 14th is also the founder of the institution, recently identified as a reincarnation
context: The 14th Dalai Lama, Tenzin Gyatso, was recognized at age 2 (in 1937 by 1939 enthronement). After China's 1950 invasion and the 1959 Tibetan uprising, he fled to India where he established the Tibetan Government in Exile at Dharamsala. He has been an international advocate for Tibet, won the 1989 Nobel Peace Prize, and is widely respected for his teaching and ethical leadership. The succession to the 15th is contested — China has claimed authority over the next incarnation.

question: The Bhagavad Gita ('Song of the Lord') — perhaps the most famous Hindu scripture — is a 700-verse poem within the much longer Mahabharata epic. The setting: the great battlefield of Kurukshetra, where the Pandava prince Arjuna is about to fight his Kuru cousins. He hesitates before slaughtering his own relatives. Who is his charioteer, and what does he say?
answer: Krishna (an avatar of Vishnu) explains the eternal soul, dharma, paths of action, knowledge, and devotion as duty
choices: Krishna (an avatar of Vishnu) explains the eternal soul, dharma, paths of action, knowledge, and devotion as duty
Yudhishthira (Arjuna's elder brother) explains the rules of war and the moral cost of family bloodshed
Vyasa (the sage and author of the Mahabharata) intervenes personally to teach Arjuna in the moment of crisis
Bhishma (the patriarch fighting against the Pandavas) urges Arjuna to refuse battle on grounds of honor
context: The Bhagavad Gita is the great philosophical-religious dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna. Three principal yogas are presented: karma yoga (path of action without attachment to results), jnana yoga (path of knowledge), bhakti yoga (path of loving devotion). The Gita's teaching that dharma (duty) sometimes requires action that seems morally troubling — that one acts without attachment to outcomes — has been read by everyone from Gandhi to Oppenheimer (who quoted it at Trinity).

question: Vedic-Hindu society was traditionally organized into four varnas (classes). What were they, and what is their relationship to the later caste (jati) system?
answer: Brahmin (priests), Kshatriya (warriors/rulers), Vaishya (merchants/farmers), Shudra (servants) — varnas idealized; jatis hereditary subdivisions
choices: Brahmin (priests), Kshatriya (warriors/rulers), Vaishya (merchants/farmers), Shudra (servants) — varnas idealized; jatis hereditary subdivisions
Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra — only the first three were respectable; Shudras were untouchables before British rule
Brahmin, Shudra, Vaishya, Kshatriya — the order is reversed; warriors were lower than priests in old practice
Vaishya (priests), Brahmin (warriors), Kshatriya (merchants), Shudra (servants) — actually these names mean different things
context: The four varnas (described in Rigveda 10.90, the Purusha Sukta — society as the divided body of the cosmic Purusha) provide the theoretical framework. Jatis (birth groups) are the actual social units — thousands of them, hereditary, regional. Below the Shudras were the Dalits (formerly called untouchables — Hindi achuta, Sanskrit asprushya), excluded from the varna system entirely. Caste discrimination was officially abolished in India's 1950 constitution; in practice it persists. The system has been a major Hindu social-ethical problem.

question: Sati was the Hindu practice of a widow burning herself on her dead husband's funeral pyre. While never universal — and contested by reformers within Hinduism throughout history — the practice persisted in some regions. The colonial British administration eventually banned it. When, and who was the principal Hindu reformer who advocated the ban?
answer: 1829 — banned by Governor-General William Bentinck; Raja Ram Mohan Roy was the principal Hindu reformer behind the ban
choices: 1829 — banned by Governor-General William Bentinck; Raja Ram Mohan Roy was the principal Hindu reformer behind the ban
1860 — banned after the Indian Rebellion; Swami Vivekananda was the principal Hindu reformer of the Brahmo Samaj movement
1875 — banned by the Indian Civil Service; Mahatma Gandhi was the principal Hindu reformer of the movement
1947 — banned only after Indian independence; the British had tolerated sati throughout their imperial rule
context: William Bentinck's Regulation XVII of 1829 banned sati in British India; the principal Hindu intellectual advocacy came from Raja Ram Mohan Roy (1772-1833), founder of the Brahmo Samaj — a Hindu reform movement. The ban was extended to princely states over subsequent decades. Modern sati incidents have been rare but occasionally documented; the 1987 case of Roop Kanwar in Rajasthan provoked national outrage and stricter laws.

question: Vishnu — among the principal Hindu gods (Trimurti: Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver, Shiva the destroyer) — has descended into the world ten times as avatars (incarnations) to restore dharma when it falters. What are some of the ten classic avatars?
answer: Matsya (fish), Kurma (turtle), Varaha (boar), Narasimha (man-lion), Vamana (dwarf), Parashurama, Rama, Krishna, Buddha, Kalki
choices: Matsya (fish), Kurma (turtle), Varaha (boar), Narasimha (man-lion), Vamana (dwarf), Parashurama, Rama, Krishna, Buddha, Kalki
Brahma, Shiva, Indra, Agni, Surya, Varuna, Soma, Yama, Kubera, Saraswati — actually these are other gods, not Vishnu's avatars
Ganesha, Hanuman, Kali, Durga, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati, Sita, Radha, Kartikeya — these are family members or consorts
Rama and Krishna alone — Vishnu has only two avatars, not ten; the ten-avatar tradition is a later modification
context: The Dashavatara (Ten Avatars) of Vishnu: Matsya saved Manu from the flood; Kurma supported Mount Mandara during the churning of the ocean; Varaha rescued the earth; Narasimha killed the demon Hiranyakashipu; Vamana subdued Bali; Parashurama destroyed corrupt kshatriyas; Rama (hero of the Ramayana); Krishna (Mahabharata, Bhagavad Gita); Buddha (in Hindu tradition); Kalki (yet to come at the end of the present age, Kali Yuga). Different lists exist.

question: The Ramayana — attributed to the sage Valmiki — is one of the two great Hindu epics (with the Mahabharata). It tells of Rama, prince of Ayodhya and avatar of Vishnu, his wife Sita, his brother Lakshmana, and his ally Hanuman the monkey-general. Who is the principal antagonist, and what is the central conflict?
answer: Ravana, the ten-headed demon-king of Lanka, who abducted Sita; Rama waged war with Hanuman's monkey army to rescue her
choices: Ravana, the ten-headed demon-king of Lanka, who abducted Sita; Rama waged war with Hanuman's monkey army to rescue her
Bhishma, the patriarch of the Kuru dynasty; actually the antagonist of the Mahabharata, not the Ramayana
Duryodhana, the eldest Kaurava prince; actually the antagonist of the Mahabharata, not the Ramayana
Karna, the warrior-prince of mysterious birth; actually a Mahabharata figure, not from the Ramayana
context: The Ramayana (composed c. 5th-4th century BC, with additions) is a foundational story for Hindu ethics, devotion (bhakti), and conjugal ideals. Hanuman's leap across the ocean to find Sita; Rama's eventual war and victory; Sita's purification by fire — all became iconic. The Ramleela (annual dramatic performances) culminate at Diwali (Rama's return to Ayodhya). The epic shaped Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain literature across Asia.

question: Among the most influential Egyptian myths is the story of Osiris — god of the dead and judge of the afterlife. His brother Set, jealous, killed and dismembered him into fourteen pieces and scattered them across Egypt. What did Osiris's wife Isis do?
answer: Gathered the pieces (could not find one) and resurrected Osiris long enough to conceive Horus from him
choices: Gathered the pieces (could not find one) and resurrected Osiris long enough to conceive Horus from him
Cursed Set and pursued him through the dynasties; the conflict became the dispute of Upper and Lower Egypt
Created the first mummy from Set's blood; the technique of mummification descended from this revenge
Sailed the pieces down the Nile to the sea; the body of Osiris became the river flowing through Egypt itself
context: Isis's gathering of Osiris's pieces (she found all but the phallus; she fashioned a replacement) and resurrection became foundational for Egyptian afterlife belief. Osiris became king of the dead. Horus (the falcon-headed son) avenged his father against Set. The myth structured Egyptian funerary practice — the dead identified with Osiris in their journey through the afterlife. Mummification preserved the body for resurrection by analogy with Osiris's restoration.

question: In Egyptian afterlife belief, the dead person was led through a series of tests in the Duat (the underworld). The most famous test was the weighing of the heart against a feather. What feather, and what was the consequence?
answer: The feather of Ma'at (truth, cosmic order) — if the heart was lighter or equal, the soul passed to the afterlife; if heavier, devoured
choices: The feather of Ma'at (truth, cosmic order) — if the heart was lighter or equal, the soul passed to the afterlife; if heavier, devoured
The feather of Ra (sun) — actually Ra's symbol was the sun disk, not a feather; the weighing is associated with Ma'at
The feather of Horus (falcon) — actually Horus's symbol was the falcon, not a feather; the weighing is Ma'at's role
The feather of Isis (mother) — actually Isis's symbol was the throne, not a feather; the weighing is Ma'at's role
context: Ma'at (the goddess and concept of cosmic truth, order, and justice) wore a single ostrich feather in her hair. In the weighing scene depicted in the Book of the Dead (c. 1550 BC onward), Anubis (jackal-headed god of embalming) weighed the heart against Ma'at's feather. Thoth (ibis-headed god of writing) recorded the verdict. If the heart was heavier (heavy with sin), it was eaten by Ammut (the devourer — crocodile-lion-hippopotamus hybrid).

question: Around 1353 BC, the 18th-dynasty pharaoh Amenhotep IV embarked on a dramatic religious revolution. He changed his name to Akhenaten ('beneficial to the Aten'), moved his capital from Thebes to a new city Akhetaten (modern Amarna), and promoted the worship of a specific deity above all others. What was the deity, and what was the nature of this religion?
answer: The Aten — the sun disk — worshipped as the sole god; Akhenaten's revolution is sometimes called the first monotheism
choices: The Aten — the sun disk — worshipped as the sole god; Akhenaten's revolution is sometimes called the first monotheism
Amun-Ra — the traditional king of the gods, simply restored to chief position under a moralistic reformer
Osiris — the god of the dead, elevated to position of supreme creator by Akhenaten's theological speculation
Aten and Apophis (the chaos serpent) — Akhenaten taught a dualism of light versus darkness in cosmic struggle
context: Akhenaten's Atenism is sometimes called the world's first monotheism (or at least monolatry — worship of one god without denying others' existence). The pharaoh closed temples of other gods, defaced their inscriptions, established a new naturalistic art style (the Amarna style). His reign ended with his death (c. 1336 BC); his successor Tutankhamun ('living image of Amun,' originally Tutankhaten) restored traditional religion. Atenism was vigorously erased from official memory.

question: The Epic of Gilgamesh — Sumerian/Akkadian poem about the legendary king of Uruk — is among the oldest surviving works of literature. Earliest tablets c. 2100 BC; the canonical Standard Babylonian version c. 1300 BC. What is the central plot?
answer: Gilgamesh and his friend Enkidu have adventures; Enkidu dies; Gilgamesh seeks immortality and fails; learns wisdom of human limits
choices: Gilgamesh and his friend Enkidu have adventures; Enkidu dies; Gilgamesh seeks immortality and fails; learns wisdom of human limits
Gilgamesh fights the gods directly; defeats them in single combat; becomes ruler of heaven and earth alike
Gilgamesh builds the walls of Uruk; the entire epic is a building-poem celebrating engineering achievements
Gilgamesh and his friend Enkidu invent agriculture; the poem is the founding myth of Mesopotamian farming
context: Gilgamesh's quest after Enkidu's death is the heart of the epic. He travels to Utnapishtim (Mesopotamian Noah, survivor of the great flood). Utnapishtim recounts the flood. Gilgamesh learns the plant of immortality exists; he obtains it but loses it to a serpent. He returns to Uruk with the realization that his lasting work is the city he has built. The epic explores mortality, friendship, kingship, and the limits of heroism. Discovered in modern times by George Smith in 1872.

question: Within the Epic of Gilgamesh (Tablet XI) is recounted the Babylonian flood story. The gods decided to destroy humanity in a great flood. One man was warned by the god Ea (Sumerian Enki). The hero built a ship, took his family and animals, and survived the seven-day flood. After the waters subsided, the gods (Enlil, Ishtar) gave him a unique reward. Who was he, and what was the reward?
answer: Utnapishtim — granted immortality alone among humans; he and his wife dwell apart at the mouth of the rivers
choices: Utnapishtim — granted immortality alone among humans; he and his wife dwell apart at the mouth of the rivers
Atrahasis — granted only mortality; the Atrahasis flood is a separate Mesopotamian tradition predating Utnapishtim
Ziusudra — granted godhood and inclusion in the divine council; he became a minor god of grain in Sumerian belief
Gilgamesh — actually the seeker of immortality, not the recipient; he failed to obtain it from Utnapishtim
context: The Utnapishtim flood account in Gilgamesh Tablet XI predates the biblical Noah by perhaps 800-1500 years. Earlier Sumerian versions (Ziusudra) and Atrahasis tradition share the basic narrative — flood, ark, survivor, divine judgment. The parallels with Genesis 6-9 are striking and have been studied since George Smith's 1872 discovery shocked Victorian England. The Mesopotamian flood myth probably came from a Tigris-Euphrates flood event preserved in cultural memory.

question: Huitzilopochtli — 'Hummingbird of the South' — was the patron deity of the Aztec city of Tenochtitlan and god of war, sun, and human sacrifice. The Aztecs believed he had to be sustained by a particular substance to keep the sun moving. What was it, and what was the scale of practice?
answer: Human blood and hearts; the Aztecs sacrificed perhaps 20,000 per year at the empire's peak; ~80,000 at the rededication of Templo Mayor 1487
choices: Human blood and hearts; the Aztecs sacrificed perhaps 20,000 per year at the empire's peak; ~80,000 at the rededication of Templo Mayor 1487
Maize and pulque only; the Aztecs were vegetarians whose sacrifices were always plant-based offerings
Animal blood from jaguars and eagles only; human sacrifice was forbidden in Aztec religion despite Spanish accusations
Fire and incense alone; the substance was atmospheric rather than material, and required no physical sacrifice
context: Aztec human sacrifice is among the most-documented in world history — Spanish conquistadors' eyewitness accounts (Bernal Díaz, Sahagún), Aztec codices (Codex Mendoza, Codex Magliabechiano), archaeology of Templo Mayor. The 1487 rededication (perhaps four days of continuous sacrifice; numbers in tens of thousands) is contested but well-attested. Modern apologetics that minimize the practice are not consistent with the evidence. The theology — sun-god needing blood — was real and central to Aztec religion.

question: Quetzalcoatl — 'feathered serpent' — was the principal pan-Mesoamerican deity (Aztec Quetzalcoatl; Maya Kukulkan; among others). He was god of wind, wisdom, the morning star, and patron of priests. According to one Aztec tradition, what was his eventual fate, and how did it relate to the arrival of Cortés in 1519?
answer: He sailed east in a raft of serpents; some Aztecs believed Cortés was Quetzalcoatl returning, though this is debated by historians
choices: He sailed east in a raft of serpents; some Aztecs believed Cortés was Quetzalcoatl returning, though this is debated by historians
He was killed by Huitzilopochtli; the war-god replaced him as supreme deity in the imperial Aztec pantheon
He withdrew to Mictlan (the underworld); he had no expected return, despite Spanish chroniclers' claims
He became the god of cultivation; his ritual departure was annual rather than once-for-all in Aztec tradition
context: Whether Moctezuma II genuinely believed Cortés was Quetzalcoatl returning has been disputed since the Conquest itself. Some accounts (especially Sahagún's Spanish-influenced collection, c. 1555) say yes; modern scholars (Camilla Townsend, others) doubt the legend predated the Conquest's outcome. Quetzalcoatl was certainly a major god, his return prophesied in some traditions, his temple central to many cities. Toltec / Aztec / Maya traditions about him vary.

question: Among the principal Celtic festivals of pre-Christian Ireland and Britain was Samhain (pronounced 'Sah-win'), held at the end of October / beginning of November. What was it, and what is its principal cultural legacy in the modern world?
answer: End-of-summer festival marking the start of winter; the dead were thought to walk the earth; ancestor of Halloween
choices: End-of-summer festival marking the start of winter; the dead were thought to walk the earth; ancestor of Halloween
Spring planting festival; the dead were thought to bring fertility to the fields; ancestor of May Day
Midwinter festival; the dead were thought to be especially restless; ancestor of Christmas without religious content
Harvest festival of the first fruits; the dead were thought to bless the gathering; ancestor of Thanksgiving
context: Samhain (October 31 - November 1) marked the Celtic year's end and beginning. The veil between living and dead was thinnest; ancestors could return; fires were extinguished and rekindled from the central sacred fire. Christianized as All Saints' Day (November 1) and All Souls' Day (November 2). Halloween (All Hallows' Eve) preserves many Samhain practices — costumes, divination, bonfires, the dead walking. Irish immigrants brought Halloween to America in the 19th century.

question: The Druids — priestly class of the ancient Celts in Gaul, Britain, and Ireland — are described by classical authors (Julius Caesar, Pliny the Elder, Posidonius). What were their principal functions and characteristics?
answer: Priests, judges, teachers, ritualists; held knowledge orally for 20 years of training; practiced sacrifices including human victims
choices: Priests, judges, teachers, ritualists; held knowledge orally for 20 years of training; practiced sacrifices including human victims

Farmers and herders; the Druids were the agricultural class blessed by chieftains as sacred laborers
context: Caesar's account in The Gallic War describes Druids as holding power equal to the warrior class. They taught for 20 years memorizing material (refusing to write it down). They performed religious functions and judged disputes. Roman writers describe Druidic human sacrifice — wicker men burned with victims inside (Caesar), divination from the death-throes of stabbed victims. The Druids resisted Roman conquest and were eventually suppressed (massacre at Mona / Anglesey, 60 AD).

question: Amaterasu — 'Heaven-Shining Great Deity' — is the chief deity of Shinto, the indigenous religion of Japan. Goddess of the sun, she is said to be the divine ancestor of the Japanese imperial family. What was her famous mythological episode involving a cave?
answer: She hid in a cave (after her brother Susanoo's outrages); the world went dark; the other kami lured her out to restore sunlight
choices: She hid in a cave (after her brother Susanoo's outrages); the world went dark; the other kami lured her out to restore sunlight

She traveled to a cave under the sea; she returned with the pearls that became the islands of Japan when she emerged
context: The Cave of Heaven (Ama-no-Iwato) episode is a foundational Shinto myth. Susanoo, the storm-god, had committed various offenses; Amaterasu hid; the world darkened. The other kami (gods) lured her out with the dance of Ame-no-Uzume, a mirror, jewels, and a curious sound. The myth establishes the imperial regalia (mirror, jewel, sword) and the divine descent of the imperial line — which continued unbroken (by tradition) from Emperor Jimmu (c. 660 BC) to the present.

question: Among the most influential African religious traditions is that of the Yoruba people of West Africa (Nigeria, Benin). What are the orisha, and how have they influenced religion in the African diaspora?
answer: Orisha — the principal Yoruba deities (Shango, Oya, Ogun, Yemaya, others) — became central to Cuban Santería, Brazilian Candomblé, Haitian Vodou

context: The orisha pantheon includes hundreds of deities. Major ones: Shango (thunder, lightning, dance), Oya (wind, storms, rebirth), Ogun (iron, war, smithing), Yemaya (mother of all, ocean), Oshun (love, beauty, fresh water), Eshu (trickster, crossroads). Enslaved Yoruba carried these deities to the Americas. Syncretized with Catholic saints (Shango = Santa Barbara; Yemaya = Virgin of Regla), they became Santería (Cuba), Candomblé (Brazil), Vodou (Haiti), each with millions of contemporary practitioners.

question: Vodou (or Voodoo, Vodun) is a religion practiced in Haiti, parts of Louisiana, and West Africa (Benin, Togo). It combines West African Vodun (especially from the Fon and Ewe peoples) with Catholic elements imposed during the slave era. What is the central pantheon called, and what role does Papa Legba play?

The 1791 Bois Caïman ceremony — where slaves under the leadership of Dutty Boukman and Cecile Fatiman swore an oath to overthrow the French — is often credited as the spiritual start of the Haitian Revolution (1791-1804), the only successful slave revolution in history.

question: On November 18, 1978, at a remote agricultural settlement in Guyana called Jonestown, 909 people died — the largest single deliberate loss of American civilian life until 9/11. The settlement was the relocated headquarters of the Peoples Temple cult led by Jim Jones. What had Jones organized that day?

'Drinking the Kool-Aid' entered American slang (though it was actually Flavor Aid). Jonestown shaped subsequent American attitudes toward cults.

question: In 1478 Pope Sixtus IV authorized Ferdinand and Isabella to appoint inquisitors investigating the orthodoxy of conversos and moriscos. The first Grand Inquisitor, the Dominican Tomás de Torquemada, established procedures lasting until Queen Isabella II abolished the Spanish Inquisition by royal decree in 1834. question: On April 9, 1945, two weeks before American troops arrived, a 39-year-old German Lutheran pastor was hanged at Flossenbürg on direct orders from Himmler. He had been arrested in April 1943 for Operation 7 (smuggling Jews to Switzerland) and later implicated in the July 20, 1944 plot to assassinate Hitler. question: After Worms in April 1521 the 38-year-old friar Martin Luther was staged-kidnapped on Frederick the Wise's orders and hidden at the Wartburg, disguised as Junker Jörg. In about eleven weeks from December 1521 to March 1522, working from Erasmus's Greek New Testament, he translated the entire New Testament into German. What is the wider significance?

question: On July 16, 1054, Cardinal Humbert, a legate of Pope Leo IX, walked into the Hagia Sophia during the Divine Liturgy and placed a bull of excommunication on the altar against Patriarch Michael Cerularius. The patriarch excommunicated the cardinal in return. The mutual excommunications were not lifted until December 1965 by Paul VI and Athenagoras I. What were the two principal theological issues?

The East regarded it as theologically wrong AND as an unauthorized alteration of an ecumenical creed. Papal supremacy claims were equally unacceptable.

question: Around 411 AD the British monk Pelagius arrived in Carthage teaching that humans could, by their own effort, choose the good and earn salvation without a special infusion of grace — grace being free will plus Christ's example plus Scripture. The 57-year-old Augustine recognized a fundamental threat to Pauline grace. What did Augustine establish?
answer: Original sin from Adam, the bondage of the will apart from grace, the prevenient and irresistible character of grace, and predestination — shaping Luther, Calvin, Jansenism

question: Between February 1692 and May 1693, in Massachusetts Bay, accusations of witchcraft spread from Salem outward — over 200 accused, 30 convictions, 19 hangings, farmer Giles Corey pressed to death under stones for refusing to plead. The trials collapsed partly because an influential Boston pastor published Cases of Conscience condemning 'spectral evidence.' Who was he, and what does Salem reveal?

question: On Good Friday, April 12, 1963, a 34-year-old Baptist pastor was arrested during planned Birmingham, Alabama protests. From his cell, on newspaper margins, he composed an open letter responding to eight white moderate clergymen who had called the protests 'unwise and untimely.' He cited Augustine, Aquinas, Buber, Tillich, Niebuhr, and Amos. What was its central theological argument?
answer: Augustine and Aquinas: an unjust law is no law at all — Christians have a moral duty to disobey nonviolently, the suffering of nonviolent resistance being redemptive

The Birmingham campaign — children's march, fire hoses and dogs, the bombing of the 16th Street Baptist Church killing four girls — broke open the public moral case. King was assassinated April 4, 1968.

question: On August 11, 1492 — the same year Columbus sailed and the Reconquista ended — cardinals elected the 61-year-old Spanish cardinal Rodrigo Borja to the papacy. He took the name Alexander VI. He had at least four children by his mistress Vannozza dei Cattanei before becoming pope. His son Cesare served as both cardinal and general; Lucrezia was used three times in dynastic marriage. His pontificate provided Savonarola's reform preaching its target in Florence (Savonarola burned 1498). Erasmus, Luther, and every later Catholic reformer drew on the Borgia example.

question: On February 23, 1807, after 18 years of parliamentary effort, the House of Commons voted 283 to 16 to abolish the British slave trade. question: On November 11, 1620, forty-one adult male passengers of a 100-foot English merchant ship at anchor off Cape Cod signed a brief document drafted that morning. question: In August 1562 in Avila a 47-year-old Discalced Carmelite nun opened the first house of her reformed order — Saint Joseph's, with four sisters. Spanish mystical literature of this generation is among the great Catholic achievements.

question: In September 1561 the 47-year-old Scottish Reformer John Knox — recently returned from Genevan exile, principal author of the Scots Confession (1560) — was summoned to Holyroodhouse for the first of four direct interviews with the newly returned 18-year-old Catholic queen of Scots, Mary Stuart, who had been raised in France and returned to a country whose parliament had just declared itself Protestant. question: In Mainz between 1450 and 1455, a goldsmith and inventor named Johannes Gutenberg completed printing of approximately 180 copies of a two-volume Latin Bible — 1,286 pages, 42 lines per column, two columns per page, set in Gothic black-letter type. About 49 copies survive. Gutenberg used movable metal type cast from individual matrices, oil-based ink, and a wine-press converted for printing. He went bankrupt in 1455. answer: Within fifty years printing had spread to over 250 European cities, perhaps 20 million books printed, the cost of books fallen 80%, and the conditions created for the Reformation

question: In 1864, an Anglican clergyman-turned-Catholic-priest, 63 years old, published a serialized public response to a malicious accusation by the novelist Charles Kingsley that Catholic clergy taught truthfulness was no virtue for itself. question: On April 9, 1906, in a small house at 214 North Bonnie Brae Street in Los Angeles, during a prayer meeting led by a 36-year-old African American minister blind in one eye and trained at a Houston Bible school, a parishioner began speaking in glossolalia. question: The greatest musician in Greek myth — son of the Muse Calliope, his lyre could move stones and tame wild animals — lost his bride Eurydice on their wedding day when she stepped on a serpent. question: In Ovid's Metamorphoses Book 6, a Lydian woman from Hypaepa, daughter of the dyer Idmon, boasted that her weaving was finer than any goddess's — even Athena's. Athena, in disguise as an old woman, warned her. She refused to recant. Athena revealed herself and a contest began. Athena wove four scenes of gods punishing mortals who challenged them. question: After Hera drove him mad and he killed his own wife Megara and their children, Heracles consulted the Delphic oracle. The oracle told him to serve King Eurystheus of Tiryns for twelve years, performing any labor Eurystheus assigned. The labors began with the Nemean lion (its hide impenetrable to weapons, killed by strangulation) and ended with the capture of Cerberus, the three-headed dog of Hades. What was the deeper purpose?

question: On the slopes of Mount Parnassus in central Greece, in the ravine where Apollo had killed the python whose decomposing body gave the place its name, a small Doric temple housed the omphalos — the navel stone marking the center of the world. Who was she called, and what does modern science suggest?

question: In Ovid's Metamorphoses Book 11, the Phrygian king Midas helped Dionysus's foster-father Silenus when the satyr wandered drunk into Midas's rose garden. The wine and bread turned to gold. He grew hungrier and thirstier. What ultimately destroyed his delight?

The gods restored Pelops (Demeter, mourning Persephone, had absentmindedly eaten the shoulder, which had to be replaced with ivory). What was his punishment?

question: For roughly 2,000 years, from at least the seventh century BC until the late fourth century AD, an annual nine-day ritual was performed each September at the small town of Eleusis on the Bay of Salamis, about fourteen miles from Athens. Initiates fasted, drank a special barley-and-mint potion called the kykeon, processed by torchlight along the Sacred Way, entered the Telesterion (initiation hall), and witnessed something that changed their understanding of life and death. question: After his twelve labors and many other adventures, Heracles had married Deianira and was crossing a river with her. The centaur Nessus offered to carry her across. In midstream he tried to assault her. Heracles shot Nessus with an arrow dipped in the Hydra's blood. Dying, Nessus told Deianira to save some of his blood as a love charm — if Heracles ever loved another, smearing the blood on his clothes would restore his love. question: In Euripides's Bacchae (405 BC), the new god Dionysus arrived in Thebes from the East. The young king Pentheus, son of Agave and grandson of Cadmus, refused to recognize him, calling him a foreign fraud. The women of Thebes — Pentheus's own mother Agave foremost among them — were already roaming Mount Cithaeron in Bacchic ecstasy, wearing fawn-skins, suckling wild animals, tearing apart calves with their bare hands. Dionysus persuaded Pentheus to spy on the rites disguised as a woman. What happened?

question: From at least the sixth century BC, Greek-speaking communities around the Mediterranean — Egyptian Greeks, Magna Graecia in southern Italy and Sicily, Crete — practiced mystery initiations attributed to the legendary singer Orpheus. Small gold leaves with verses (the so-called 'Orphic gold tablets') have been found in graves, guiding the dead through the underworld. They tell the dead to drink from the lake of Memory (not from Lethe, forgetfulness) and to say specific words to the gatekeepers. What was the underlying theology?
answer: Reincarnation through cycles of birth and death (the soul fallen from divinity into the body as punishment) and the possibility of escape through purification

The poem is set in the tenth year of the Greek siege of Troy. The wrath is the hero's anger at being deprived of his prize Briseis by the commander-in-chief Agamemnon. He withdraws from battle. His best friend Patroclus, wearing his armor, is killed by the Trojan prince Hector. He returns to the war, kills Hector, drags the body. Whose wrath?

What did Circe advise Odysseus to do, and what is the modern phrase?

context: Penelope is one of the great figures of world literature: clever, patient, faithful, politically savvy. The giant drank, grew drunk, asked Odysseus his name. Odysseus answered. What did he say, and what was the strategy?

question: Every four years, beginning by tradition in 776 BC and continuing without major interruption for over a thousand years until the Christian emperor Theodosius shut them down in 393 AD, athletes from across the Greek-speaking world gathered at the sanctuary of Zeus in the northwestern Peloponnese for a religious-athletic festival. A truce halted wars between Greek poleis for the duration. The footrace ('stadion') was the original event. What did victors receive, and what is the wider significance?
answer: A wreath of wild olive from the sacred grove of Zeus — no material prize — but immense honor at home, statues at Olympia, victory odes commissioned from

question: Between 447 and 432 BC, under the political leadership of Pericles and the artistic direction of Phidias, the Athenian democracy used tribute money from its Delian League allies to build a massive Doric temple on the Acropolis in honor of the city's patron goddess. Iktinos and Kallikrates were the architects. It had 8 columns on the short ends, 17 on the long sides. Inside stood a 38-foot gold-and-ivory statue of the goddess. What temple, and what was Phidias's other Wonder?
answer: The Parthenon — and Phidias's other Wonder of the Ancient World was the seated gold-and-ivory Zeus of Olympia (c. 435 BC), housed in Zeus's temple at the

question: Greek funerary practice across many regions involved placing a small coin in the mouth of the dead before burial. The coin was payment for a specific service in the underworld. question: The Viking settlement of northwestern France began in 911 AD when the Frankish king Charles the Simple granted lands in the lower Seine valley to the Viking leader Rollo (Old Norse: Hrólfr) by the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, in exchange for Rollo's conversion to Christianity and defense against further Viking raids. question: After the gods killed her father Thiazi (who had stolen Idun and her apples of youth), the giantess Skadi came to Asgard armed for war. Zeus and Apollo together drove Typhon into Tartarus through the Delphic chasm — the source of the python Apollo would later kill in his consolidation of the oracle
Zeus turned Typhon to stone with the Gorgoneion on his aegis — the petrification motif borrowed from the Perseus myth and applied to cosmic combat by Pindar's Pythian Ode 1
context: Hesiod's Theogony 820-880, and Apollodorus 1.6.3. Typhon's offspring with Echidna — Cerberus, the Hydra, the Chimera, the Sphinx, the Nemean Lion — generate most of Greek monstrous mythology. The eruptions of Etna were attributed to Typhon thrashing beneath the mountain.

question: After the Titanomachy, Prometheus — one of the few Titans who had sided with Zeus — was assigned the task of creating mortal beings. According to Plato's Protagoras (and Ovid), he fashioned the first humans from a particular material. His brother Epimetheus had already used up the better traits on the animals. What did Athena contribute?
answer: Athena breathed life and reason into the figures Prometheus had molded from clay mixed with water — the divine aspect that distinguished humans from the animals Epimetheus had given fur, claws, speed
choices: Athena breathed life and reason into the figures Prometheus had molded from clay mixed with water — the divine aspect that distinguished humans from the animals Epimetheus had given fur, claws, speed
Athena wove the first cloak for the naked humans — the act that established weaving as her domain and made the loom the central image of women's labor in Greek religious practice
Athena planted the first olive tree among the new humans — the gift she had previously given Athens in her contest with Poseidon, now extended as universal grant to humanity
Athena gave them the first laws on bronze tablets — the political art that distinguished human community from animal aggregation, the gift Hesiod assigned to her in Works and Days
context: Plato's Protagoras 320d-322a and Ovid's Metamorphoses 1.78-88. Hesiod's earlier tradition (Theogony, Works and Days) makes humanity simply 'arise' from the earth without Prometheus as creator. The clay-molding version became dominant in Hellenistic and Roman times and shaped European art and theology.

question: The Delphic site had been sacred before Apollo — earlier traditions place there an oracle of Gaia, Themis, or Phoebe. A great serpent (drakon) called Python guarded the site, sent by Hera to torment Leto when she was pregnant with Apollo and Artemis. When Apollo grew to maturity he came to Delphi armed. What did he do with the body of Python?
answer: Left it to rot beside the omphalos so the place name Pytho derived from Greek pythein, to rot; he then established the Pythian Games to atone for the slaying and the oracle as expiation
choices: Left it to rot beside the omphalos so the place name Pytho derived from Greek pythein, to rot; he then established the Pythian Games to atone for the slaying and the oracle as expiation
Burned it on a pyre at Castalia spring and used the ashes in his shrine — the cremation-purification rite later imposed on Delphi's priests after any blood-killing on the sacred precinct
Buried it under the adyton — the inner chamber where the Pythia would later prophesy seated over the chthonic vapors that rose from the serpent's grave
Fed it to the river Cephissus — the offering by which Apollo claimed the river as his sacred boundary and the river acquired its prophetic power on Boeotian shrines
context: Homeric Hymn to Apollo and various accounts including Plutarch's Moralia. Apollo retreated to Tempe in Thessaly for ritual purification after the killing — the basis of the Septerion ritual at Delphi every nine years. The Pythian Games (founded c. 586 BC in historical times) commemorated the slaying.

question: Held annually for almost 2000 years at Demeter's sanctuary at Eleusis, the Greater Mysteries took place over nine days each autumn (Boedromion 15-23). Initiates fasted, drank a barley-mint potion called kykeon, processed by torchlight along the Sacred Way from Athens, and witnessed something in the Telesterion forbidden to disclose. What did the initiate obtain?
answer: A vision (epopteia) of the sacred grain — Demeter's gift — and promise of better afterlife destiny than the uninitiated, conferred by witnessing the Persephone enactment
choices: A vision (epopteia) of the sacred grain — Demeter's gift — and promise of better afterlife destiny than the uninitiated, conferred by witnessing the Persephone enactment
An ecstatic identification with the goddess herself — initiation conferring divinity rather than afterlife promise, the version Plotinus and the Neoplatonists later read back into the rite
Sexual union with a temple priestess representing Demeter — the sacred marriage (hieros gamos) late Roman Christian critics ascribed to the mysteries to discredit them as obscene
Public confession of personal sins and ritual purification by water — the Mithraic-influenced rite Plutarch's Isis and Osiris had retrojected onto older Eleusinian practice
context: Plutarch, Pindar's threnodes, the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, and Christian polemicists like Clement of Alexandria preserve fragments. Theodosius I banned the Mysteries in 392 AD; the Visigoths under Alaric destroyed Eleusis in 395-96 AD. Cicero called the Mysteries the most important gift Greece gave the world.

question: The smith of the gods who forged Zeus's thunderbolts, Helios's chariot, Achilles's armor, was a lame god. Two traditions explained how. In Iliad 18 his mother Hera, ashamed of his weak feet, threw him from Olympus and he fell a whole day landing on Lemnos. In Iliad 1 Zeus threw him out for taking Hera's side. How did he avenge himself?
answer: He made Hera a golden throne with invisible chains; when she sat she was held fast and no god could release her; Hephaestus was brought back to Olympus, drunk by Dionysus, to free her
choices: He made Hera a golden throne with invisible chains; when she sat she was held fast and no god could release her; Hephaestus was brought back to Olympus, drunk by Dionysus, to free her
He forged the bonds in which Aphrodite and Ares were caught — his earlier vengeance for Aphrodite's adultery being indirect revenge on the Olympus that had cast him out
He withdrew his craft from the gods for nine generations — the period in which mortals were forced to invent their own metallurgy and bronze-age Greece climbed to its peak
He returned to Olympus disguised as a beggar — the first of the divine disguise plots Athena would later replicate when she returned the wandering Odysseus to Ithaca
context: Pausanias 1.20.2 preserves the throne-trap story; Hephaestus's lameness made him the divine analogue of the Greek metalworker (often physically restricted to the workshop). His main cults were on Lemnos (volcanic) and at Athens, where the temple now called the Theseion above the Agora was actually his.

question: On his first day of life — born to Maia in a cave on Mount Cyllene in Arcadia — a remarkable infant climbed out of his cradle and stole fifty of Apollo's cattle from Pieria. He drove them backward to confuse the tracks and made himself the first shoes. Returning to his cradle, he played innocent. Apollo tracked him by augury. What happened when the brothers met before Zeus?
answer: Hermes had invented the lyre that morning from a tortoise shell; he played, charmed Apollo; the brothers swapped cattle and wand for lyre, and Apollo named him god of thieves and heralds
choices: Hermes had invented the lyre that morning from a tortoise shell; he played, charmed Apollo; the brothers swapped cattle and wand for lyre, and Apollo named him god of thieves and heralds
Hermes had eaten the cattle in a single sitting — the unprecedented gluttony forcing Zeus to confine him to the underworld realm where he would become psychopomp by default
Hermes had hidden the cattle inside Cyllene itself — the mountain that became sacred to him and the source of the cult title Cyllenian Hermes that dominated Arcadian worship
Hermes had carved the first caduceus from the herdsman's staff — the symbol of medicine and reconciliation Apollo accepted as payment for transformation into divine doctor
context: The Homeric Hymn to Hermes 4 (c. 600 BC) is the source. Hermes became messenger of the gods, patron of travelers, traders, thieves, heralds, athletes, and psychopomp — guide of souls. His Roman equivalent Mercury gave us the name of the planet, the metal, and the gas-station chain.

question: In Demodocus's song on the island of Phaeacia (Odyssey 8), the lame smith god learned from Helios the sun (who sees all) that his wife Aphrodite was sleeping with Ares. He forged invisible chains so fine they could not be seen and stretched them above the bed. The lovers met. He caught them in the act. He called the Olympians to witness. What was the response?
answer: Inextinguishable laughter — the Homeric phrase asbestos gelos — though Apollo asked Hermes if he'd accept those chains to share Aphrodite's bed; Hermes said three times over yes
choices: Inextinguishable laughter — the Homeric phrase asbestos gelos — though Apollo asked Hermes if he'd accept those chains to share Aphrodite's bed; Hermes said three times over yes
Solemn outrage and judgment — Zeus convened the council, fined Ares, and instituted the divine law against adultery the Olympians would now enforce on each other and humanity
Embarrassed silence — the gods, recognizing their own affairs, refused to comment; the matter was resolved privately when Poseidon agreed to surety for Ares's good behavior
Demand for capital punishment by the Olympian wives — Hera, Demeter, and the rest insisted on the death of Aphrodite, only spared when Zeus reminded them of their own family pact
context: Odyssey 8.266-366. The scene is one of the earliest surviving Greek comedies — Demodocus is the blind bard at Alcinous's court, an obvious self-portrait by 'Homer.' The Olympians are anthropomorphic and undignified in early epic; Plato's later anger at this depiction launched the philosophical critique of poetry.

question: In the Homeric Hymn to Dionysus, the young god appeared on a promontory — a beautiful youth with dark hair, dressed in purple. Tyrrhenian pirates seized him intending to sell him as a slave. The helmsman alone recognized a god and warned them. They refused. Bonds fell off the god. Wine flowed across the ship; vines climbed the mast and wreathed the sail. What followed?
answer: Dionysus turned into a lion; a bear appeared on deck; the pirates leaped overboard and were transformed into dolphins — the helmsman alone was spared and made a steersman of the god
choices: Dionysus turned into a lion; a bear appeared on deck; the pirates leaped overboard and were transformed into dolphins — the helmsman alone was spared and made a steersman of the god
Dionysus drowned the pirates in a sudden wine-flood that filled the hold and rose above the deck — the pious helmsman alone floating clear and becoming the priest of the new cult
Dionysus turned the pirates to stone where they stood and set the ship adrift carrying their petrified figures around the Mediterranean as a warning to other would-be enslavers
Dionysus caused the pirates to murder one another in a sudden bacchic frenzy — the first instance of maenadic violence that would later kill Pentheus and Orpheus in his cult
context: Homeric Hymn 7 (perhaps 6th century BC). Dionysus crossed seas constantly in his cult — coming from Asia, returning from journeys. The hymn pairs with Euripides's Bacchae (c. 405 BC) — both showing what happens to those who refuse the god. Caravaggio painted the scene; the Exekias kylix (c. 530 BC) shows the dolphins around the ship.

question: When the Thracian musician Orpheus's bride Eurydice stepped on a viper and died on their wedding day, he descended living to the underworld. His lyre softened Cerberus; the wheel of Ixion paused; the stone of Sisyphus rested; even Hades and Persephone wept. They granted his wish on a single condition. What was the condition, and what did Orpheus do?
answer: He must lead Eurydice up to daylight without looking back — but at the last step before the sunlight he turned to be sure she followed, and she was drawn back into the underworld forever
choices: He must lead Eurydice up to daylight without looking back — but at the last step before the sunlight he turned to be sure she followed, and she was drawn back into the underworld forever
He must play continuously for the ascent — but his lyre broke as he stepped into the sunlight and Eurydice, still in the underworld, faded into shadow at the silence
He must not speak her name on the journey — but in joy at the threshold he called out her name, breaking the silence the underworld had required and losing her at the gate
He must trade his own life for hers at the threshold — Orpheus agreed and reached the sunlight only to be torn apart by Maenads who would not let him surrender to the gods
context: Virgil's Georgics 4.453-527 and Ovid's Metamorphoses 10. Orpheus was later torn apart by Maenads in Thrace; his head floated to Lesbos still singing. The Orphic mystery cult took its name from him and taught reincarnation, dietary restrictions, and a soul-body dualism the later Pythagoreans and Plato absorbed.

question: After Achilles killed Hector outside Troy's walls and dragged the body around the city behind his chariot, he refused to surrender the corpse. For twelve days the gods preserved Hector's flesh. On the twelfth night, guided by Hermes, an old man slipped into Achilles's tent and fell at Achilles's knees, kissing the hands that had killed his son. Who was he?
answer: Priam, king of Troy and father of Hector — bringing a ransom of gold; the encounter ended in mutual weeping (Priam for Hector, Achilles for his own father Peleus) and the body's return
choices: Priam, king of Troy and father of Hector — bringing a ransom of gold; the encounter ended in mutual weeping (Priam for Hector, Achilles for his own father Peleus) and the body's return
Polydorus, Priam's youngest son — sent in disguise because Priam was too aged to make the journey, and intercepting Achilles in his rage before his father could face him
Aeneas, son of Anchises and cousin of Hector — leading a delegation of Trojan nobles authorized by Priam to negotiate the ransom on the king's behalf since the king was too proud
Antenor, the wise counselor — the Trojan who had argued throughout the war for returning Helen to the Greeks, now the natural envoy to break the deadlock after Hector's death
context: Iliad 24, often called the most humane scene in any epic. Priam offers his son's weight in gold; Achilles agrees to a twelve-day truce for Hector's funeral. The Iliad ends with Hector's burial — not the fall of Troy. Auerbach used the scene in Mimesis as paradigmatic of epic's measured ethical depth.

question: In Iliad 6, Hector returns briefly from battle to Troy to ask the women of the city to pray to Athena. He meets his wife Andromache and infant son Astyanax on the city wall. Andromache pleads with him not to return to the field — her father, brothers, and mother all dead; he is everything to her. He reaches for his son. The boy cries in fright. Why?
answer: Hector's bronze helmet with its horsehair crest terrified the baby; Hector laughed, removed the helmet, kissed his son, and prayed he would grow to be a better man than his father
choices: Hector's bronze helmet with its horsehair crest terrified the baby; Hector laughed, removed the helmet, kissed his son, and prayed he would grow to be a better man than his father
Astyanax wept at his mother's grief, not Hector's armor — the precise observation of poetic detail that the Hellenistic scholiasts used to refute the historicity of the entire scene
The baby's nurse fell as Hector approached and dropped him; Hector caught the child mid-air, which the gods read as a sign that the city's future would survive the war intact
Hector first lifted Astyanax to a temple statue of Athena where the marble eyes terrified him; the substitution of helmet for statue was a Roman re-reading of the original epic moment
context: Iliad 6.466-481. After Troy fell, Astyanax was thrown from the walls by Neoptolemus (Achilles's son) to prevent any future heir of Hector from rising against the Greeks. Andromache became Neoptolemus's slave-concubine. The Iliad scene's tenderness is set against this future the reader knows is coming.

question: The Iliad ends with Hector's funeral and not Troy's fall. The death of Achilles comes in the Aethiopis (Cyclic epic, now lost), preserved in later summaries. In one of the most famous deaths in ancient literature, the greatest of the Greeks fell at the Scaean Gate of Troy. Who killed him, and how?
answer: Paris shot an arrow guided by Apollo into Achilles's heel — the only part vulnerable because Thetis had dipped him in the Styx held by that heel, the version Statius and post-classical poets fixed
choices: Paris shot an arrow guided by Apollo into Achilles's heel — the only part vulnerable because Thetis had dipped him in the Styx held by that heel, the version Statius and post-classical poets fixed
Apollo himself in his own form struck Achilles down — the version Aethiopis preserved, with Paris named only as the secondary instrument and the Olympian Apollo as the true agent
Polyxena, Priam's daughter, lured Achilles to the temple of Apollo Thymbraeus where Paris struck — the betrayal-by-lover variant that Hyginus and Dictys later canonized
Aeneas, fighting beside Hector's brothers — the Trojan combat that preceded Aeneas's flight to Italy, the version Virgil would have to suppress to make Aeneas a hero rather than killer
context: Achilles's body became contested ground; Ajax carried it off while Odysseus fought back the Trojans. The arms of Achilles were awarded to Odysseus over Ajax, who killed himself in shame — the subject of Sophocles's Ajax. The heel as sole vulnerability is later than Homer (who has Achilles entirely vulnerable).

question: After ten years of siege, the Greeks built a hollow wooden horse. Epeius the carpenter assembled it; Odysseus conceived the plan. Inside hid the best Greek warriors. The army sailed to Tenedos, just out of sight. A man named Sinon was left on the beach, captured and brought before Priam. What story did he tell that persuaded the Trojans?
answer: He had been left as sacrifice but escaped; the horse was a gift to Athena for the Greeks' theft of the Palladium; if Trojans damaged it they would suffer, if they brought it inside they would be safe
choices: He had been left as sacrifice but escaped; the horse was a gift to Athena for the Greeks' theft of the Palladium; if Trojans damaged it they would suffer, if they brought it inside they would be safe
He was a deserter who had quarreled with Odysseus; the horse was an attempt to scare the Trojans into surrender that had failed; if the Trojans destroyed it the Greeks would return in shame
He was the brother of Achilles, exiled after the death; the horse was a votive thank-offering for the Greek dead, and burning it would summon their vengeful ghosts on Troy
He was the son of Aeneas, a hostage; the horse was a guarantee of the truce the Greeks had offered; bringing it into Troy would seal the peace the Trojans had wanted for a decade
context: Virgil's Aeneid 2 (Aeneas's narrative to Dido) is the source — Greek epic cycle traditions are largely lost. Laocoön the priest warned 'Equo ne credite, Teucri' — do not trust the horse — and was killed by sea-serpents the Trojans took as divine confirmation that he was wrong.

question: Sailing back from Troy, Odysseus reached the island of Aeaea where the sorceress Circe — daughter of Helios the sun and the ocean-nymph Perse — lived in a palace surrounded by tame lions and wolves (men she had transformed). Eurylochus led half the crew to her hall. She gave them a drink and struck them with her wand. They became swine. What saved Odysseus?
answer: Hermes gave him moly — a black-rooted, white-flowered herb protecting against Circe's drug; Odysseus drank her cup without effect; when she struck he drew his sword, and she swore an oath not to harm him
choices: Hermes gave him moly — a black-rooted, white-flowered herb protecting against Circe's drug; Odysseus drank her cup without effect; when she struck he drew his sword, and she swore an oath not to harm him
Odysseus had Athena's aegis in his pack — the goddess having given it to him at Troy as protection against witchcraft and snake-poison, the moly being a later interpolation
Eurylochus brought to him the transformed swine before they fully forgot — Odysseus drank from a horn made of one of their tusks and gained immunity by the partial transformation
Odysseus held an iron knife between his teeth as he entered — the apotropaic iron-tooth-trick taught by Athena that Circe could not penetrate with bronze-age sorcery
context: Odyssey 10.275-405. Odysseus stayed a year with Circe before resuming his voyage. She advised him to consult the dead Tiresias in Hades — the katabasis episode of Book 11. The moly was identified by Pliny and others (probably the snowdrop or wild garlic).

question: Around 547 BC the Lydian king Croesus, considering war against Cyrus the Great of Persia, sent envoys to consult the Delphic oracle (and to test it). The Pythia answered ambiguously, and Croesus understood the response one way. He invaded Persia, lost the Battle of Pteria (and the Battle of Thymbra), lost Sardis his capital, and was deposed. What did the oracle say?
answer: If Croesus crosses the Halys he will destroy a great empire — which he took to mean Persia's, but the empire destroyed was his own; the classic example of oracular ambiguity
choices: If Croesus crosses the Halys he will destroy a great empire — which he took to mean Persia's, but the empire destroyed was his own; the classic example of oracular ambiguity
If Croesus crosses the Halys with cavalry the Persians cannot stand — which proved true for one engagement but did not prevent the strategic Persian victory in the larger war
If Croesus consults the oracle a third time he will be told the truth — the restriction the Pythia placed on her own response, which Croesus failed to invoke before his invasion
If Croesus offers a hecatomb at Apollo's temple of Tegyrae he will be invincible — the substitute oracle Croesus consulted in Boeotia after his initial Delphic consultation
context: Herodotus 1.46-92 records the consultations. Croesus had earlier tested oracles by asking what he was doing on a particular day (cooking tortoise and lamb in a bronze cauldron); only Delphi answered correctly. When captured, Cyrus put Croesus on a pyre but spared him after he cried out 'Solon, Solon' three times.

question: By the Eratosthenic date August 12, 1184 BC (more likely the late Bronze Age collapse), Agamemnon returned to Mycenae from Troy with Cassandra as concubine. His wife Clytemnestra received him with public honor — she rolled out crimson tapestries for his feet. Cassandra prophesied her own death. Agamemnon was killed in his bath. What was the murder weapon?
answer: An axe — and Clytemnestra had thrown a net over him so he could not strike back; her lover Aegisthus assisted; Cassandra was killed next; the killing was both vengeance for Iphigenia and treason
choices: An axe — and Clytemnestra had thrown a net over him so he could not strike back; her lover Aegisthus assisted; Cassandra was killed next; the killing was both vengeance for Iphigenia and treason
A sword stolen from Agamemnon's own armory — the irony Aeschylus reused for Orestes's later vengeance against Clytemnestra in a deliberate cycle of mirroring weapons
Poison in the wine she handed him as he stepped from the bath — the silent killing that Pindar's earlier tradition assigned before Aeschylus reframed it as physical violence
Snake-venom on the lip of the bath itself — the curse Hera was said in some local Argive traditions to have placed on the line, the bath being the actual site of the killing
context: Aeschylus's Agamemnon (458 BC), first play of the Oresteia trilogy. Aegisthus was Thyestes's surviving son, raised for vengeance. Orestes returned, killed both his mother and Aegisthus, was pursued by Furies, took refuge at Athens, was tried before the Areopagus with Athena breaking the tie — the founding myth of trial by jury.

question: In approximately 435 BC, in the temple of Zeus at Olympia (built 472-456 BC), the Athenian sculptor Phidias completed a colossal seated statue of Zeus. The god sat on a cedarwood throne inlaid with gold, ebony, ivory, and precious stones. He was about 12-13 meters (40 feet) tall — his head nearly grazed the temple ceiling. What was the material technique that made him?
answer: Chryselephantine — gold and ivory plates over a wooden core; the same technique Phidias had used for the Athena Parthenos in Athens; one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World
choices: Chryselephantine — gold and ivory plates over a wooden core; the same technique Phidias had used for the Athena Parthenos in Athens; one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World
Bronze cast in lost-wax over an iron armature — the technique used for the standing Athena Promachos and most Olympian temple statues outside Phidias's special commissions
Pentelic marble carved in situ — the same material as the Parthenon's pediments, which Phidias had directed before traveling to Olympia for the Zeus commission
Solid silver with gold detailing — the wealth-display technique used for Persian royal statues that Hellenistic Greek artists later copied for cult images in eastern temples
context: The Zeus stood until c. 391-393 AD, taken to Constantinople around 394 AD, destroyed in a fire (perhaps the 475 AD Lauseion fire). Phidias's workshop at Olympia has been excavated; a cup inscribed 'I belong to Phidias' confirms the site. The Athena Parthenos (also chryselephantine) was likewise lost.

question: On 12 September 490 BC at Marathon, about 9000 Athenian hoplites under Miltiades and 1000 Plataean allies faced a Persian force probably double that size under Datis and Artaphernes. The Athenians charged at a run across the last 200 meters under arrow fire. They won — 6400 Persians dead, 192 Athenians. What is the legendary postscript?
answer: Pheidippides ran the ~40 km from Marathon to Athens to announce the victory, gasped 'we have won' (nenikēkamen), and dropped dead — the legend whose date and modern marathon distance trace back to this run
choices: Pheidippides ran the ~40 km from Marathon to Athens to announce the victory, gasped 'we have won' (nenikēkamen), and dropped dead — the legend whose date and modern marathon distance trace back to this run
The Athenian army marched the ~40 km back to Athens that same evening — preventing the Persian fleet from landing at Phalerum, the historical kernel of the running legend
Pan appeared at Marathon causing the Persians to panic ('panic' coming from Pan) — the religious interpretation of victory that produced the Athenian Pan cult after the battle
Theseus's ghost rose from his tomb to lead the Athenian charge — the vision Plutarch records in his Life of Theseus that became central to fifth-century Athenian self-imagining
context: Herodotus records Pheidippides running from Athens to Sparta (about 250 km) before the battle to request Spartan reinforcement; the Marathon-to-Athens run appears only in Plutarch and Lucian centuries later. The Battle of Marathon held off the first Persian invasion. Pheidippides's name lives on as an ultramarathon distance.

question: Inscribed on the pronaos of the Apollo temple at Delphi were three terse maxims attributed to the seven sages of archaic Greece (Plato's Protagoras names Thales, Pittacus, Bias, Solon, Cleobulus, Myson, Chilon). The maxims were brief, clipped — the foundation of later Greek and Stoic ethics. What were the famous three?
answer: Know thyself (gnothi seauton); nothing in excess (meden agan); pledge brings ruin (eggue para d'ate) — the Delphic maxims framing measure, self-knowledge, and the dangers of binding oneself
