choices: Know thyself (gnothi seauton); nothing in excess (meden agan); pledge brings ruin (eggue para d'ate) — the Delphic maxims framing measure, self-knowledge, and the dangers of binding oneself
Know thyself; nothing in excess; the unexamined life is not worth living — the third being Socrates's later contribution falsely attributed to the temple by Platonic tradition
Honor the gods; respect parents; pity the suppliant — the social-ethical maxims the Hellenistic Stoics retrojected onto the older Delphic inscription as piety eroded
Live unnoticed; remember death; cherish friendship — the Epicurean maxims attributed to Delphi by Diogenes Laertius to give them an antique pedigree they did not have
context: Pausanias 10.24.1 lists the three. Plutarch's De E apud Delphos discusses a fourth marker, the letter E or epsilon. Socrates made gnothi seauton the foundation of his philosophy. The wider Delphic maxim tradition includes ~147 sayings recorded by Stobaeus and other anthologists.

question: Beneath the second root of Yggdrasil, in Jotunheim, lay a well of wisdom guarded by the wise giant Mimir. To drink required a sacrifice of equivalent worth. Odin came seeking wisdom. He had already endured nine nights of his hanging on the tree for the runes. Now he asked Mimir what price would buy a drink. What did Odin give?
answer: One of his eyes — he plucked it out and dropped it in the well; the eye still glitters at the bottom; he drank deeply and became wisest among the Aesir though one-eyed forever
choices: One of his eyes — he plucked it out and dropped it in the well; the eye still glitters at the bottom; he drank deeply and became wisest among the Aesir though one-eyed forever
His hand — to be cut off and given to Mimir as Tyr later gave his hand to Fenrir; the Aesir story-cycle pairing the two sacrifices in its dual structure of war and wisdom
His firstborn son Thor — to remain by the well as Mimir's apprentice until Ragnarok; the unfulfilled promise being the reason Thor's destiny was bound up with the world-serpent
His knowledge of the runes — Odin paid in poetry rather than flesh, the bard-version of the myth Snorri Sturluson reconstructed from older skaldic sources lost to us
context: Voluspa and Gylfaginning preserve the tale. Mimir was later beheaded in the Aesir-Vanir war; Odin preserved his severed head with herbs and consulted it for counsel. The well at Yggdrasil's root is one of three — Urd's well of fate, Mimir's well of wisdom, Hvergelmir of cold roaring water.

question: By the giantess Angrboda in Jotunheim, Loki fathered three monstrous children whose existence terrified the Aesir. The gods dealt with each according to the threat each posed. The wolf was bound in Lyngvi until Ragnarok. The serpent was thrown into the deepest sea where he grew until he circled the world biting his tail. What of the third?
answer: Hel was cast down to Niflheim and given dominion over all who died not in battle; she had a corpse-half (livid blue) and a living-half body; her hall was Eljudnir, her threshold Stumbling-Block
choices: Hel was cast down to Niflheim and given dominion over all who died not in battle; she had a corpse-half (livid blue) and a living-half body; her hall was Eljudnir, her threshold Stumbling-Block
Sleipnir was given to Odin as his steed; the eight-legged horse who would carry the Allfather between the worlds and to Hel and back at every emergency the Aesir would face
Garm the hellhound was chained at the cave of Gnipa; he would howl free at Ragnarok and fight Tyr to mutual destruction in the final battle on the plain of Vigrid
Vidar the silent god of vengeance was set apart in his hall of branches; he wore the iron shoe that would split Fenrir's jaw at Ragnarok and avenge Odin's death
context: Gylfaginning chapter 34. Vidar and Sleipnir are unrelated to Angrboda. Garm is a separate hellhound. Loki's monstrous children — Fenrir, Jormungandr, Hel — are the three. Loki himself was both Aesir and jotunn-blooded, the trickster whose mother Laufey was Aesir and whose father Farbauti was a giant.

question: When Baldr the most beloved of the Aesir began having dreams of his death, Odin rode to Hel to consult a dead seeress. Returning, the gods determined to protect Baldr. Frigg his mother went throughout the worlds extracting an oath from every thing — water, fire, metal, sickness, every plant and beast — not to harm her son. She made one omission. What did she leave out, and why?
answer: Mistletoe — she judged it too young to require an oath; Loki learned this, made a dart of mistletoe, put it in blind Hodr's hand to throw at Baldr in the gods' sport, killing him
choices: Mistletoe — she judged it too young to require an oath; Loki learned this, made a dart of mistletoe, put it in blind Hodr's hand to throw at Baldr in the gods' sport, killing him
Iron — the metal Aesir weapons were made from; Frigg considered the oath unnecessary since gods knew not to attack each other, an oversight Loki exploited at the Aesir's games
Stone — judging that stones were too dumb to swear an oath; Loki then turned himself to stone and crushed Baldr at the next opportunity, the version in some skaldic kennings
Saltwater — judging that the sea had already sworn through Aegir at the Vanir-Aesir treaty; Loki turned to a fish and drowned Baldr in the next bath, the variant in Saxo
context: Gylfaginning 49. The mistletoe is small, parasitic, and overlooked. Loki gave the dart to blind Hodr and aimed his throw — Baldr fell dead. The gods burned him on the ship Hringhorni with his wife Nanna (who died of grief) and his horse. Hermod rode Sleipnir to Hel to plead for Baldr's return.

question: After Baldr's death, the Aesir burned him on the great ship Hringhorni so heavy that only the giantess Hyrrokin could launch it. They desired Baldr back. Hermod, son of Odin, volunteered to ride Sleipnir down the road to Hel — nine days and nights through dark valleys. He found Baldr enthroned. He pleaded with Hel. What condition did Hel set for releasing Baldr?
answer: Every creature in all worlds must weep for Baldr — if one did not, Hel would keep him; messengers went out and all wept, except one giantess Thokk (Loki disguised) who refused
choices: Every creature in all worlds must weep for Baldr — if one did not, Hel would keep him; messengers went out and all wept, except one giantess Thokk (Loki disguised) who refused
Baldr must defeat Hel's hound Garm in single combat — the test Hel imposed on every dead warrior who wished to leave the underworld, and which Baldr refused as inappropriate
Frigg must descend in Baldr's place — the substitution-bargain Hel offered that Hermod refused on Odin's behalf without consulting his wife, the variant in Saxo's Latin retelling
Loki must be sacrificed — the obvious condition Hermod could not fulfill since Loki had escaped, and which prefigured the binding-of-Loki episode the Aesir would later impose anyway
context: Gylfaginning 49. The Thokk-as-Loki identification is implied: 'old Thokk shall weep dry tears for Baldr; let Hel keep what she has.' The Aesir then bound Loki under the venom-dripping serpent with the entrails of his own son Vali (transformed into a wolf), where he remains until Ragnarok.

question: In the Eddic poem Rigsthula, the white god Heimdall traveled the world under the alias Rig. He visited three households — first poor, then middling, then wealthy. At each he ate, slept three nights between master and mistress, and went on. Nine months later three sons were born. What were they, and why does it matter?
answer: Thrall (slave), Karl (free farmer), and Jarl (noble) — Heimdall established the three classes of Norse society from his divine seed; the youngest son of Jarl was Kon (king), who learned runes from his father
choices: Thrall (slave), Karl (free farmer), and Jarl (noble) — Heimdall established the three classes of Norse society from his divine seed; the youngest son of Jarl was Kon (king), who learned runes from his father
Aesir, Vanir, and Jotnar — Heimdall fathered the three great tribes of supernatural beings, the genealogy explaining why Aesir and Vanir intermarry while Jotnar remained outside
The three Norns Urd, Verdandi, Skuld — Heimdall as primordial father of the fates, the version in Saxo Grammaticus mistakenly retrojected onto the older mythological source
Odin, Vili, and Ve — the three brothers who would kill Ymir and create the world from his body; Heimdall fathering his own future colleagues, the cyclical variant
context: Rigsthula in the Poetic Edda. The poem's social charter justifies hereditary stratification — divine origin for all three classes but with the noble's son alone destined for kingship. The 'mead' of Aesir-Vanir war and the ordering of human society both pass through Heimdall's foundational journey.

question: The goddess Idunn — wife of Bragi, god of poetry — kept apples in an ash box. When an Aesir bit one, age fell away. Without these apples the gods aged like mortals. The giant Thiazi, in eagle form, captured Loki and forced him to deliver Idunn. Loki agreed. Idunn was carried off to Jotunheim. What happened to the gods?
answer: They began to age — gray, withered; the Aesir threatened Loki with death; he borrowed Freyja's falcon-cloak, flew to Jotunheim, turned Idunn to a nut, flew her back; Thiazi in eagle form died in Asgard's fires
choices: They began to age — gray, withered; the Aesir threatened Loki with death; he borrowed Freyja's falcon-cloak, flew to Jotunheim, turned Idunn to a nut, flew her back; Thiazi in eagle form died in Asgard's fires
They lost their power to age the world's seasons — winter came permanently in Midgard; the famine and ice forced humans to acclaim Bragi as new chief god in some Saxon traditions
They became unable to make the runes that bound the world — cosmic order began dissolving; Heimdall's horn sounded for the first time since creation summoning all Aesir to council
They turned to stone — the apples having sustained their flesh; only Odin (already wise) and Loki (no Aesir to begin with) retained motion, the variant in Saxo Grammaticus
context: Skaldskaparmal in the Prose Edda. Thiazi's daughter Skadi came to Asgard for vengeance; she was given marriage to a god whom she chose by his feet alone (hoping for Baldr, getting Njord). The story explains seasons (Skadi loves mountains, Njord the sea — they live apart). Thiazi's eyes Odin set in the sky as stars.

question: After Baldr died and Hel refused to release him, the Aesir wanted vengeance against blind Hodr who had thrown the dart. But Hodr was innocent — Loki had guided his hand. Still, blood vengeance was required. Odin came in disguise to a giantess named Rind and (in some accounts) raped or magically seduced her. She bore him a son who at one day old did what?
answer: Vali killed Hodr — washing neither hands nor combing hair until the deed was done; the child grew to a full-grown warrior in a day for the single purpose of executing the blood vengeance
choices: Vali killed Hodr — washing neither hands nor combing hair until the deed was done; the child grew to a full-grown warrior in a day for the single purpose of executing the blood vengeance
Vali avenged Loki by hunting Skadi — the parallel revenge for the killing of Loki's parents at her hand, the misattribution Saxo Grammaticus introduces in the Latin retelling
Vali bound Loki under the venom-dripping serpent — the chains made from the entrails of Narfi (Loki's other son) as Vali grew to manhood in an hour to carry out the punishment
Vali fought Garm — the hellhound at Gnipa, prefiguring the Ragnarok combat between Tyr and Garm, the variant Snorri suppresses but later mythographers preserve in Eddic glosses
context: Voluspa stanzas 33-34 and Baldrs draumar. The one-day-old vengeance is one of the strangest motifs in Norse mythology. Vali survives Ragnarok with Vidar — they will live in the new world after the destruction. Saxo recasts the story in Book 3 of the Gesta Danorum as the contest of Balder and Hother for Nanna's hand.

question: From before creation, on the southern edge of Ginnungagap, lay Muspelheim — pure fire and heat. Its guardian was a giant brighter than the sun, flaming sword in hand. He stood at his post since before Ymir was. At Ragnarok he would lead the sons of Muspell across Bifrost (which would break). What is the final role of this fire giant?
answer: Surt would burn the nine worlds — his flame consuming Yggdrasil itself, earth sinking into the sea, the sky cracking; he would kill Freyr in single combat after Freyr had given up his sword for love of Gerd
choices: Surt would burn the nine worlds — his flame consuming Yggdrasil itself, earth sinking into the sea, the sky cracking; he would kill Freyr in single combat after Freyr had given up his sword for love of Gerd
Surt would be killed by Heimdall at Bifrost — the two cosmic guardians neutralizing each other in the prelude to the central Aesir-Jotnar combat that determined the outcome
Surt would join the Aesir at Vigrid — the fire-giants having reconciled with the gods after the killing of Ymir, a variant Snorri suppressed but earlier skalds had taught
Surt would be defeated by Thor's hammer and bound below Etna — the variant modeled on the Greek Typhon myth that Snorri rejected as foreign contamination
context: Voluspa stanzas 50-58 and Gylfaginning 51. Surt is the most ancient cosmic being still active in Norse cosmogony. After Ragnarok the world is reborn green and fair; Lif and Lifthrasir emerge from the wood Hoddmimir to repopulate; the younger gods Vidar, Vali, Modi, Magni inherit the new world.

question: The Norse vision of cosmic destruction is uniquely paired with rebirth. After Surt has burned the worlds and the earth has sunk — after Thor has killed Jormungandr and died of venom in nine steps, Odin has been swallowed by Fenrir and Vidar avenged him — the earth rises green again. Where do the two humans who repopulate the world come from?
answer: Lif and Lifthrasir survive Ragnarok hidden in the wood Hoddmimir; they have eaten only the morning dew through the conflagration; from them new humanity descends in the renewed world
choices: Lif and Lifthrasir survive Ragnarok hidden in the wood Hoddmimir; they have eaten only the morning dew through the conflagration; from them new humanity descends in the renewed world
Ask and Embla return from Hel released by the renewed Baldr; the first humans of the old world being reincarnated to populate the new, the variant in some Faroese fragments
Vidar fathers them on a giantess named Skuld; the new generation of gods sharing in the human creation as the old Aesir had done at the beginning of the previous cycle
They are made anew from logs by the renewed Odin in some southern Saxon variant; the second creation paralleling Ask and Embla's first creation in the destroyed earlier world
context: Vafthrudnismal stanza 45 and Gylfaginning 53. The optimism of Norse eschatology distinguishes it from many traditions — the world does not end in final destruction but in cyclical renewal. Vidar, Vali, Magni, Modi, and the returned Baldr (with Hodr) populate the new Aesir generation in the renewed Idavoll.

question: Aegir, the sea-giant, held a great feast for the gods in his undersea hall. All the Aesir came except Thor (who was off fighting trolls in the east). Loki, who had been excluded after killing one of Aegir's servants, returned uninvited and was rebuffed. He then went around the hall systematically. What did he do?
answer: He insulted each god and goddess in turn — naming each Aesir's hidden sin, particularly the goddesses' sexual conduct; the gods could not strike him because the hall was sanctified, until Thor finally arrived and threatened him out
choices: He insulted each god and goddess in turn — naming each Aesir's hidden sin, particularly the goddesses' sexual conduct; the gods could not strike him because the hall was sanctified, until Thor finally arrived and threatened him out
He poisoned the mead with adder-venom — the act that began the Ragnarok prophecy fulfilling itself, the cause of the binding-of-Loki punishment that followed immediately
He stole the Mead of Poetry from Aegir's table — the second theft of the same mead Odin had brought from Suttung in the older cycle, the act that doubled the cosmic poetic gift
He revealed the gods' hidden weaknesses to the giants — sending messengers to Jotunheim with the catalog of vulnerabilities he had compiled, the act that doomed Asgard's defenses
context: Lokasenna in the Poetic Edda. The poem is a flyting — a ritualized exchange of insults common in early Germanic literature (cf. the Beowulf flytings). Each god has a hidden shame; Loki names it. Thor arriving threatens Mjolnir; Loki departs with prophecies of Ragnarok in his teeth.

question: In the branches of the world-tree Yggdrasil sat an eagle whose unmoving eye was Odin in disguise (or, in another reading, an unnamed eagle). At the lowest root of the tree, gnawing constantly, was the dragon Nidhogg. Between these two there ran constantly a third creature, climbing up and down. What was its role?
answer: Ratatoskr the squirrel carried insults between eagle and dragon — bearing the eagle's contempt down to Nidhogg and the dragon's threats up to the eagle; an emblem of poetic strife and slander between high and low
choices: Ratatoskr the squirrel carried insults between eagle and dragon — bearing the eagle's contempt down to Nidhogg and the dragon's threats up to the eagle; an emblem of poetic strife and slander between high and low
Ratatoskr was Yggdrasil's groundskeeper — eating the parasites that would otherwise weaken the tree; the Aesir kept him fed with nuts so he would maintain the cosmic vegetation
Ratatoskr was Odin's spy in his squirrel-form — reporting all the doings of Nidhogg and the eagle back to Asgard, the role assigned to Huginn and Muninn in other source-traditions
Ratatoskr was Loki's transformed shape — taking the squirrel form to carry intelligence between the high and low worlds during his exile, the variant Snorri suppresses as Christian-influenced
context: Grimnismal stanza 32. Yggdrasil suffers from creatures at every level: Nidhogg gnaws the root, four stags (Dain, Dvalin, Duneyr, Durathror) eat the leaves, Ratatoskr fans the strife. The tree is cosmic and besieged — it will burn at Ragnarok before rising new in the renewed world.

question: The Germanic runic alphabet appears on inscriptions from roughly the 2nd century AD onward. The earliest form had 24 runes named after their first phonetic value — fehu (cattle/wealth), uruz (aurochs), thurisaz (thurs/giant). By the late 8th century Viking-age Scandinavia had simplified to 16 runes. What is the technical name distinction?
answer: Elder Futhark (24 runes, 2nd-8th century AD, Continental Germanic) versus Younger Futhark (16 runes, Viking Age Scandinavia); the name comes from the first six runes f-u-th-a-r-k
choices: Elder Futhark (24 runes, 2nd-8th century AD, Continental Germanic) versus Younger Futhark (16 runes, Viking Age Scandinavia); the name comes from the first six runes f-u-th-a-r-k
Anglo-Saxon Futhorc (33 runes, England) versus Elder Futhark (24, Continental); the Younger Futhark being a regional variant of the Anglo-Saxon form rather than a distinct Scandinavian script
Codex Regius Futhark (the script of the surviving Eddas) versus Snorri's Reformed Futhark (the 18-rune scheme Snorri proposed); the Younger being Snorri's later artificial reduction
Hallristningar Futhark (the Bronze Age proto-runes) versus the Christian-era Futhark; with the 24-rune system being post-Christian and the 16-rune system pre-Christian
context: The Anglo-Saxon Futhorc expanded to 33 runes for the additional sounds of Old English; Younger Futhark contracted as Old Norse phonology shrunk and merged. Stones like Rok (Sweden, c. 800), Jelling (Denmark, c. 970), and the Maeshowe inscriptions (Orkney) preserve runic literature.

question: The chief Norse pagan ritual was a sacrificial feast: animals (and at major sanctuaries occasionally humans) were killed, blood sprinkled on participants and idols, flesh boiled and eaten communally. Adam of Bremen (c. 1075) described it at Uppsala every nine years. What was its technical name?
answer: Blot — related to blotha (to worship by sacrifice); the priest sprinkled the blot-blood (hlaut) on assembled worshippers with bundled twigs and on the cult statues
choices: Blot — related to blotha (to worship by sacrifice); the priest sprinkled the blot-blood (hlaut) on assembled worshippers with bundled twigs and on the cult statues
Sumbel — the ritual drinking and oath-taking ceremony at chieftain's halls; a ceremonial meal without animal sacrifice, the term Tacitus had used for Germanic feasts
Galdr — the chanting-spell of seidr practitioners; sometimes accompanying blot but a separate ritual category in the Old Norse classification of sacred acts
Heitstrenging — the heroic boasting at midwinter feasts in which warriors swore oaths over the Yule-boar; ceremonial but not sacrificial in Norse pagan vocabulary
context: Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis 4.27. The Uppsala temple held nine-day rites every ninth year, with nine of each kind of male creature (men, horses, dogs) hanged in the sacred grove. Iceland's blot rituals are documented in Eyrbyggja saga. Christianization gradually replaced blot with Christian liturgical rites.

question: A particular Norse magic carried strong gender associations. It involved trance-divination, fate-shaping, and shamanic work with spirits. Freyja the Vanir goddess of love and war was the principal divine practitioner; she had taught it to the Aesir. Even Odin learned it, despite the shame attached to a man practicing a woman's art. What was its name?
answer: Seidr — the witchcraft of fate-spinning, prophecy, and curse; men who practiced it were called ergi (effeminate), the worst social insult in Norse society; Odin's practice is one of his stranger attributes
choices: Seidr — the witchcraft of fate-spinning, prophecy, and curse; men who practiced it were called ergi (effeminate), the worst social insult in Norse society; Odin's practice is one of his stranger attributes
Galdr — the chanting magic of charms and runes; performed standing rather than seated in trance, the male-coded variant of Norse magical practice without the ergi associations
Volva-work — the technical name for the seeress's trance from the volr (staff) carried by practitioners; specifically female and without the male-shame component of seidr
Skaldr — the poetic magic of the court bard, of which seidr was a subset; the ergi associations being attached to skaldr generally in pre-Christian Norse vocabulary
context: Ynglinga saga and various Eddic and saga sources. Volva (seeress) practitioners staged elaborate ceremonies — the Volva description in Eirik the Red's saga is the most detailed. Tacitus (Germania 8) had recorded the German pre-Christian respect for female divinatory powers. Seidr was banned after Christianization.

question: The opening poem of the Poetic Edda is spoken by a dead seeress raised from the grave by Odin to prophesy the cosmic past and future. Beginning 'Hljods bid ek allar' — 'Hearing I ask of all the holy races' — the poem narrates the creation from Ymir, the Aesir's golden age in Idavoll, the murder of Baldr, the binding of Loki, and ends in Ragnarok with rebirth. What is its title?
answer: Voluspa — the Seeress's Prophecy; the most ambitious surviving Norse mythological poem, probably composed in the late 10th century, preserved in the Codex Regius and Hauksbok
choices: Voluspa — the Seeress's Prophecy; the most ambitious surviving Norse mythological poem, probably composed in the late 10th century, preserved in the Codex Regius and Hauksbok
Havamal — the Sayings of the High One; Odin's didactic poetry on wisdom and travel, the second longest poem in the Poetic Edda but a different genre from the cosmological Voluspa
Vafthrudnismal — Odin's contest of wisdom with the giant Vafthrudnir; a riddle-poem in the Edda that competes with Voluspa in cosmic scope but in dialogue form
Grimnismal — Odin's revelation to King Geirrod's son Agnar; the catalog of Yggdrasil's creatures and the halls of the gods, broader than Voluspa in detail but lacking the future-prophecy
context: Voluspa is preserved in the Codex Regius (c. 1270, the manuscript holding the Poetic Edda) and the Hauksbok (c. 1334). Snorri's Prose Edda Gylfaginning systematizes its narrative. The Christian additions in Voluspa's final stanzas (the coming of a great one to judge) reflect 10th-11th century syncretism.

question: One of the greatest Icelandic family sagas tells of a complicated, often murderous, supremely gifted poet who served both Eirik Bloodaxe (whom he hated but composed Hofudlausn for to save his head) and Athelstan of England. He killed his first man at age 6. The saga is traditionally attributed to Snorri Sturluson. Who is the protagonist?
answer: Egil Skallagrimsson — the great 10th-century Icelandic poet-warrior, whose saga is one of the longest and most psychologically complex of the Islendingasogur; his Sonatorrek mourns his sons' deaths
choices: Egil Skallagrimsson — the great 10th-century Icelandic poet-warrior, whose saga is one of the longest and most psychologically complex of the Islendingasogur; his Sonatorrek mourns his sons' deaths
Gunnar of Hlidarend — the central hero of Njal's saga, the great bowman and friend of Njal who refused exile and was killed in the burning of his hall, the most famous Icelandic warrior
Olaf the Peacock — the half-Irish gentleman-farmer of the Laxdaela saga, son of an Irish princess sold into slavery; his family saga is the great love-triangle saga of medieval Iceland
Grettir Asmundarson — the outlaw-hero of Grettis saga who lived 19 years in the wilderness, fought trolls, and was killed on Drangey by hired men at the saga's tragic close
context: Egils saga Skallagrimssonar (c. 1220-1240). The character bears the marks of Snorri's literary intelligence — but the attribution remains contested. The Battle of Brunanburh (937) where Egil fought is the same battle commemorated in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle's most famous Old English poem.

question: One of the great Icelandic family sagas tells of a love triangle ending in tragedy. The woman at the center marries four men in succession; the sworn-brothers Kjartan and Bolli compete for her; one kills the other; she lives long and in old age, asked which man she had loved best, gives her famous answer: 'I was worst to the one I loved most.' Who was she?
answer: Gudrun Osvifrsdottir — the heroine of the Laxdaela saga, whose four marriages and unrequited love for Kjartan Olafsson made the central narrative; she became a Christian anchoress in old age
choices: Gudrun Osvifrsdottir — the heroine of the Laxdaela saga, whose four marriages and unrequited love for Kjartan Olafsson made the central narrative; she became a Christian anchoress in old age
Hallgerd Long-Legs — the proud wife of Gunnar in Njal's saga, whose refusal of a single lock of her hair to make a bowstring led directly to her husband's death at the siege of Hlidarend
Aud the Deep-Minded — the early Christian Irish-Scottish widow who settled in Iceland with her freedmen and granddaughters, the founder of one of the great Icelandic family lines
Bergthora Skarphedinsdottir — Njal's wife in Njal's saga, whose quarrel with Hallgerd led to the rising blood-feud that ended in the burning at Bergthorshvol
context: Laxdaela saga (c. 1240s), about 80 chapters, set in the Dales of West Iceland. The 'I was worst to the one I loved most' line is one of the most famous in Icelandic literature. The saga's possible female authorship has been argued from its sympathetic treatment of women's experience.

question: Around 982 AD a hot-tempered Norwegian-born Icelander was outlawed from Iceland for three years over a series of killings. With no good options he sailed west to a land sighted decades earlier by Gunnbjorn Ulfsson. He spent his three years exploring, named it craftily to attract settlers, and returned to Iceland to recruit. What was his name?
answer: Eirik Thorvaldsson, called Eirik the Red — who named the green-coated southern coast 'Greenland' as a recruiting tactic; in 985 he led 25 ships of which 14 arrived to found the Eastern and Western Settlements
choices: Eirik Thorvaldsson, called Eirik the Red — who named the green-coated southern coast 'Greenland' as a recruiting tactic; in 985 he led 25 ships of which 14 arrived to found the Eastern and Western Settlements
Bjarni Herjolfsson — who in 986 was blown off course and sighted but did not land on three coasts west of Greenland that Leif Eriksson would later visit as Helluland, Markland, Vinland
Floki Vilgerdarson — the discoverer of Iceland (which he named after the ice he saw drift past in spring); his exploration occurred a century earlier than the Greenland venture
Thorfinn Karlsefni — Eirik's son-in-law and later Vinland explorer, who supplied the colonists in 1010 for the longer-lasting attempt at permanent Vinland settlement
context: The Greenland colony lasted from about 985-986 to the mid-15th century. Climate cooling (Little Ice Age), Inuit pressure, and isolation from Norway's collapse during the Black Death all contributed. The Eastern Settlement's Hvalsey Church marriage record of September 16, 1408 is the last attested document.

question: From the late 9th century onward Scandinavian (and after 1066, also Anglo-Saxon) warriors served as the personal bodyguard of the Byzantine emperor in Constantinople. They received high pay, gold, and the right to plunder the imperial palace on an emperor's death. They left runic graffiti — 'Halfdan was here' in Hagia Sophia. What is the technical name?
answer: The Varangian Guard — established by Basil II around 988 with 6000 Rus warriors sent by Vladimir of Kiev; Harald Hardrada served in it (1034-1043) and rose to command before returning to claim Norway
choices: The Varangian Guard — established by Basil II around 988 with 6000 Rus warriors sent by Vladimir of Kiev; Harald Hardrada served in it (1034-1043) and rose to command before returning to claim Norway
The Hetaireia — the broader corps of imperial bodyguards that included Varangians as one of three subdivisions but was not specifically Scandinavian by historical convention
The Athanatoi — the Immortals, the heavy cavalry corps Nikephoros II established in the 960s that included some Scandinavian volunteers but was not the institutional descendant
The Numera — the prison-guard regiment of the imperial palace some Varangians served in before promotion to the bodyguard proper, regularly confused in later western chronicles
context: Constantinople was 'Miklagard' (the Great City) in Old Norse. The runic graffiti in Hagia Sophia remain readable. The Varangian-Russian trade route 'from the Varangians to the Greeks' was the great medieval north-south commercial axis, replacing the older silk-road as the source of Islamic silver in northern Europe.

question: In 1190 a Sephardic Jewish physician serving as personal doctor to Saladin and his vizier al-Fadil in Egypt completed in Arabic the most influential work of medieval Jewish philosophy. He had fled Almohad persecution in Cordoba (1148) and Fez before settling in Fustat. Earlier he had composed the Mishneh Torah codifying Jewish law. What is his Arabic-titled work, and what shaped Aquinas?
answer: The Guide for the Perplexed (Dalalat al-Ha'irin) — reconciling Aristotelian philosophy with Torah; Aquinas drew on it extensively, citing 'Rabbi Moyses' in the Summa as one of his foremost sources
choices: The Guide for the Perplexed (Dalalat al-Ha'irin) — reconciling Aristotelian philosophy with Torah; Aquinas drew on it extensively, citing 'Rabbi Moyses' in the Summa as one of his foremost sources
The Kuzari — Judah Halevi's earlier dialogue between the king of the Khazars and a rabbi, which Aquinas confused with Maimonides in some early manuscripts of his commentary
The Or Adonai of Crescas — Hasdai Crescas's later 1410 critique of Aristotle, mistakenly antedated by some Christian scholastic readers to Maimonides's lifetime
The Sefer ha-Bahir — the early kabbalistic Book of Brightness that Maimonides explicitly rejected, attributed to him by mistaken later scribes citing Aquinas
context: Maimonides (Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon, 1138-1204) is the central Jewish philosopher. His 13 Principles of Faith (in the Mishnah commentary) became the basis of the Yigdal hymn. Aquinas drew on him for the doctrine of divine names, the proof of God from motion, and many other questions in the Summa.

question: Around 1280 in Castile a rabbi named Moses ben Shem Tov de León began circulating a mystical commentary on the Torah in Aramaic that he attributed to the 2nd-century rabbi Shimon bar Yochai (who had been hidden in a cave with his son for 13 years). The work systematized the doctrine of the ten Sefirot — emanations through which the infinite (Ein Sof) becomes the world. What is its name?
answer: The Zohar (Book of Splendor) — the foundational text of kabbalah; Gershom Scholem's modern scholarship attributed it to Moses de León himself rather than ancient Shimon bar Yochai
choices: The Zohar (Book of Splendor) — the foundational text of kabbalah; Gershom Scholem's modern scholarship attributed it to Moses de León himself rather than ancient Shimon bar Yochai
The Sefer Yetzirah (Book of Formation) — the older 2nd-6th century mystical text on the 32 paths of wisdom and the letters of creation that the Zohar built upon
The Bahir (Book of Brightness) — the 12th-century proto-kabbalistic work from Provence that introduced the Sefirot before the Zohar systematized them
The Etz Chaim (Tree of Life) — Hayyim Vital's 16th-century systematization of his teacher Isaac Luria's kabbalah; the work that the Zohar's later Safed-school followers produced
context: Kabbalah deeply influenced later Jewish mysticism (Lurianic 1500s, Hasidic 1700s), the Renaissance Hermetic tradition (Pico della Mirandola, Reuchlin), and modern thinkers from Walter Benjamin to Gershom Scholem. Christian Kabbalah read it as confirming the Trinity through the Sefirot.

question: Between May 1940 and January 1945, in Polish Upper Silesia annexed to the German Reich, the largest Nazi extermination camp operated. About 1.1 million people died there — approximately 960,000 Jews, 74,000 non-Jewish Poles, 21,000 Roma, 15,000 Soviet POWs, and others. The complex included Auschwitz I, the larger Birkenau, and Monowitz. When was it liberated, and by whom?
answer: January 27, 1945 — by the Soviet 322nd Rifle Division of the 60th Army, finding about 7000 prisoners alive (most had been force-marched west); the date is now International Holocaust Remembrance Day
choices: January 27, 1945 — by the Soviet 322nd Rifle Division of the 60th Army, finding about 7000 prisoners alive (most had been force-marched west); the date is now International Holocaust Remembrance Day
April 11, 1945 — by the US 3rd Armored Division, simultaneous with the Buchenwald liberation; the camp's gas chambers had been demolished by the SS in November 1944
May 5, 1945 — by the 11th Armoured Division of the British Second Army, who found mass burials still being filled in by guards as the troops approached
March 29, 1945 — by Free Polish forces under Anders, who recaptured the camp from the SS rear-guard during the broader Vistula-Oder offensive in winter 1944-45
context: Rudolf Hoss the commandant testified at Nuremberg. The estimate of 1.1 million dead (down from older 3 million figures) is from Polish historian Franciszek Piper's 1990s work. Primo Levi (a Monowitz prisoner) wrote 'If This Is a Man' (1947). The Auschwitz Album of photographs captures the May-June 1944 Hungarian transports.

question: On April 11, 1961, an Israeli court tried a Nazi captured by Mossad in Buenos Aires the previous May. He had organized the Final Solution's logistics — the train schedules, the deportations. He sat in a bulletproof glass booth, was convicted, and hanged May 31, 1962 — the only judicial execution in Israeli history. Whose famous report shaped his reception?
answer: Hannah Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem (1963) — coining 'banality of evil'; her argument he was not a monster but a thoughtless functionary provoked intense Jewish-intellectual backlash
choices: Hannah Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem (1963) — coining 'banality of evil'; her argument he was not a monster but a thoughtless functionary provoked intense Jewish-intellectual backlash
Elie Wiesel's Night (1958) — the literary memoir of the camps that became the standard literary work; mistakenly identified as the report on the Eichmann trial in some early sources
Simon Wiesenthal's The Murderers Among Us (1967) — the Nazi-hunter's account that included the Eichmann capture as one chapter; preceded Arendt's report by some years
Raul Hilberg's The Destruction of the European Jews (1961) — the comprehensive scholarly account that became the standard reference but was not specifically a report on the Eichmann trial
context: Arendt's report appeared in five New Yorker essays (Feb-March 1963) before publication as a book. Her thesis remains controversial — Bettina Stangneth's Eichmann Before Jerusalem (2014) used new sources to argue Eichmann was a committed ideologue, not just a bureaucrat.

question: According to Islamic tradition, in approximately 621 AD (during the 'year of sorrow' after Khadija's death), the Prophet Muhammad experienced a miraculous journey in a single night. He was awoken by Gabriel, mounted Buraq (a winged steed), and traveled from the Kaaba in Mecca to a holy site, then ascended through seven heavens. Where did he travel to before the ascent?
answer: The Furthest Mosque (al-Masjid al-Aqsa) in Jerusalem — established as Islam's third holiest site; the Dome of the Rock (built 691 by Abd al-Malik) marks the spot from which the ascent (Mi'raj) began
choices: The Furthest Mosque (al-Masjid al-Aqsa) in Jerusalem — established as Islam's third holiest site; the Dome of the Rock (built 691 by Abd al-Malik) marks the spot from which the ascent (Mi'raj) began
Mount Hira at Mecca — the cave of his first revelation, mistakenly transposed to Jerusalem by later traditions that read the Quran's vague reference politically
The Kaaba's interior — the Night Journey being interior rather than spatial, the Mu'tazilite rationalist interpretation that was suppressed under the Asharite dominance
Yathrib (later Medina) — anticipating the Hijra of the following year; the political-allegorical reading mainstream Shia tradition has sometimes preferred
context: Quran 17:1 (Surat al-Isra) references the Night Journey. The Mi'raj details (meeting prophets in each heaven — Adam, Jesus, John, Moses, Aaron, Joseph, Idris — and receiving the prescription of five daily prayers) appear in the Hadith. The Dome of the Rock is built over the rock from which the Mi'raj ascent occurred.

question: Born in Cordoba in 1126 and dying in Marrakesh in 1198, an Andalusian qadi and physician composed the most influential medieval commentaries on Aristotle. He served the Almohad caliph but was briefly banished in 1195 for excessive rationalism. His commentaries circulated in Latin from the 13th century; Aquinas called him 'The Commentator.' What was his Arabic name?
answer: Ibn Rushd (Latin Averroes) — Aristotle commentaries in three formats (short, middle, long); 'Latin Averroism' was condemned by Bishop Tempier at Paris in 1277
choices: Ibn Rushd (Latin Averroes) — Aristotle commentaries in three formats (short, middle, long); 'Latin Averroism' was condemned by Bishop Tempier at Paris in 1277
Ibn Sina (Latin Avicenna) — earlier (980-1037) Persian polymath whose Canon of Medicine dominated European medical schools until 1700; not Averroes the Aristotelian commentator
Al-Farabi (Latin Alpharabius) — the 10th-century Persian Aristotelian (the 'second teacher' after Aristotle himself), who preceded Averroes by two centuries in the same tradition
Al-Kindi (Latin Alkindus) — the 9th-century Arab philosopher in Baghdad who introduced Greek philosophy into Arabic but did not specifically commentate on Aristotle as Averroes did
context: Averroes was the last great Andalusian philosopher; the Almohads' turn to anti-rationalism (following al-Ghazali a century earlier) closed his school in the Muslim world. But his books shaped Latin Christendom through translations made in Toledo by Michael Scot and Hermann the German. Dante placed him in Limbo.

question: In 1324-1325 a West African emperor made a pilgrimage to Mecca that became legendary. He brought 60,000 men including 12,000 slaves carrying gold bars, and 80 camels carrying 50-300 pounds of gold each. He gave away so much in Cairo that the price of gold there fell for over a decade. Who was he, and what empire did he rule?
answer: Mansa Musa of Mali — emperor c. 1312-1337; his empire stretched from the Atlantic to the upper Niger; he founded the Sankore madrasa in Timbuktu and brought back al-Sahili to design the Djinguereber Mosque
choices: Mansa Musa of Mali — emperor c. 1312-1337; his empire stretched from the Atlantic to the upper Niger; he founded the Sankore madrasa in Timbuktu and brought back al-Sahili to design the Djinguereber Mosque
Askia Muhammad of Songhai — the later (1493-1528) ruler of the successor empire that displaced Mali; his hajj of 1497 was similarly opulent but a generation after Mali's collapse
Sundiata Keita — Mansa Musa's predecessor and founder of the Mali Empire (c. 1235-55); his epic preserved in Mande oral tradition does not include a documented Mecca pilgrimage
Idris Aluma of Bornu — the 16th-century ruler of the Bornu Empire in Lake Chad whose hajj is sometimes confused with Mansa Musa's in popular West African history surveys
context: Mansa Musa appears on the 1375 Catalan Atlas seated on a throne holding a golden nugget — proof his fame reached Europe within his lifetime. By some calculations he is the richest person who has ever lived. Timbuktu became a major center of Islamic learning, with the University of Sankore at one point housing 25,000 students.

question: The longest epic in any language (about 200,000 verses, ten times the Iliad and Odyssey combined) narrates a war between two branches of a royal family. The five Pandava brothers — Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula, Sahadeva — fight the hundred Kauravas led by Duryodhana. The decisive 18-day battle was fought on a sacred field. What field, and what dialog occurs there before the fighting?
answer: Kurukshetra ('field of the Kurus') — site of the Bhagavad Gita, in which Krishna teaches Arjuna duty (dharma) and devotion to action without attachment as Arjuna hesitates to fight his kinsmen
choices: Kurukshetra ('field of the Kurus') — site of the Bhagavad Gita, in which Krishna teaches Arjuna duty (dharma) and devotion to action without attachment as Arjuna hesitates to fight his kinsmen
Hastinapur — the imperial capital from which both sides set out for the battle; mistakenly identified as the battle-site in some popular adaptations of the Mahabharata
Vrindavan — the pastoral land of Krishna's youth on the Yamuna; the location of the Krishna-Radha romance but not the Mahabharata war's location
Indraprastha — the Pandava capital (founded on land cleared of the Khandava forest); not the battlefield but the political center the Kauravas had won at dice from the Pandavas
context: The Bhagavad Gita (700 verses, in Book 6 of the Mahabharata) is the most famous single text of Hinduism. Krishna reveals himself as God in chapter 11. The Pandavas win the war but at terrible cost; only Yudhishthira reaches heaven directly, with his dog (who is Dharma in disguise). Kurukshetra is in modern Haryana state.

question: From the 10th-12th centuries in Tamil country, the Chola dynasty produced bronze sculptures of Shiva dancing inside a circle of flame. He has four arms — one holds a damaru drum (rhythm of creation), one holds agni (fire of destruction), one is in abhaya mudra (fearlessness), one points to his raised foot (release). What is this image called?
answer: Nataraja — Lord of the Dance; the dance is the cosmic cycle of creation, preservation, destruction, illusion, and liberation; he stands on the dwarf Apasmara (forgetfulness, ignorance) whom his dance subdues
choices: Nataraja — Lord of the Dance; the dance is the cosmic cycle of creation, preservation, destruction, illusion, and liberation; he stands on the dwarf Apasmara (forgetfulness, ignorance) whom his dance subdues
Trimurti — the three-formed god combining Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva; the iconography Ellora and Elephanta sculptures show but distinct from the dancing Shiva of Chola bronze
Ardhanarishvara — Shiva combined with his consort Parvati in one body, half male and half female; a separate Shaiva iconography from the dancing Nataraja form
Lingaraja — Shiva as the great linga (phallic emblem); the older aniconic form that the Nataraja iconography replaced in popular Tamil devotion under the Cholas
context: The 11th-12th-century Chola bronzes are among the supreme achievements of Indian art. Coomaraswamy's 'Dance of Shiva' (1918) introduced the iconography to Western readers. Fritjof Capra's 'Tao of Physics' (1975) used Nataraja as an image of cosmic energy. CERN has a Nataraja statue outside the headquarters in Geneva.

question: The Hindu goddess Kali — whose name comes from kala (time, death) — emerged from the third eye of Durga during a battle against demons. She is typically depicted with dark blue or black skin, a tongue protruding, four arms (one holding a sword, one a severed head), a garland of 51 severed heads (one for each Sanskrit letter), and dancing on the prone body of her husband. Who is the husband she dances on?
answer: Shiva — when she would not stop destroying after killing the demon Raktabija, Shiva lay before her; recognizing her husband she protruded her tongue in embarrassment, the gesture frozen in iconography
choices: Shiva — when she would not stop destroying after killing the demon Raktabija, Shiva lay before her; recognizing her husband she protruded her tongue in embarrassment, the gesture frozen in iconography
Brahma — the creator god, in the version that emphasizes Kali's destruction overcoming creation, a reading associated with the Devi Mahatmya text
Yama — the god of death whom Kali defeats in her aspect as the conqueror of death itself, a reading associated with later tantric mortuary traditions
Indra — the older king of the gods whom the rising power of the goddess movement supplanted, the reading associated with feminist-Hindu scholarship since the 1980s
context: The Devi Mahatmya (4th-6th century AD) is the foundational text. Kali is central in Bengali tradition — Ramakrishna's 19th-century mysticism, the Dakshineswar temple in Kolkata. Western readers often find Kali frightening, but her devotees see fierce mother-love that destroys what we cling to. She is benevolent terror.

question: The Aztec capital Tenochtitlan was founded around 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco. By the 1480s it housed perhaps 200,000 — the largest city in the Americas. The Templo Mayor in the center served two gods on its summit. In February 1487 its rededication under emperor Ahuitzotl saw an estimated 20,000 prisoners sacrificed in four days. Who were the two gods of the twin pyramid?
answer: Huitzilopochtli (war and sun) and Tlaloc (rain and storm) — south and north halves of the same pyramid; the political-economic foundation of Aztec life required prisoner-tribute for the cosmic order
choices: Huitzilopochtli (war and sun) and Tlaloc (rain and storm) — south and north halves of the same pyramid; the political-economic foundation of Aztec life required prisoner-tribute for the cosmic order
Quetzalcoatl (feathered serpent, wisdom) and Tezcatlipoca (smoking mirror, fate) — the older Toltec pair the Aztecs had inherited but did not place atop the Templo Mayor itself
Coatlicue (mother-earth) and Mictlantecuhtli (lord of the dead) — major Aztec deities with their own shrines but not co-housed atop the Templo Mayor
Chalchiuhtlicue (water) and Xipe Totec (the flayed one, spring renewal) — important deities but neither paired atop the Templo Mayor in the 1487 dedication
context: The Templo Mayor excavation (begun 1978 under Matos Moctezuma after the discovery of Coyolxauhqui's monolith) confirmed extensive sacrificial activity. The numbers from Spanish chroniclers (Sahagun) are disputed (20,000 in four days may be overstated by 5x), but the practice's scale is no longer doubted by serious scholars.

question: Julius Caesar's Gallic War describes the religious elite of the Gauls as an organized priesthood maintaining shrines, sitting as judges, teaching the doctrine of soul-transmigration, and meeting annually in central Gaul. Tacitus describes Roman troops massacring them on the island of Mona (Anglesey) in 60 AD. What were they called, and what is the etymology?
answer: Druids — from a probable proto-Celtic root meaning 'oak-knower' (drus = oak, wid = to know); they had a 20-year training, taught orally, avoided writing their sacred lore
choices: Druids — from a probable proto-Celtic root meaning 'oak-knower' (drus = oak, wid = to know); they had a 20-year training, taught orally, avoided writing their sacred lore
Vates — a different Celtic priestly class (seers and diviners) less prominent than druids in classical sources; subordinate to the druids in Caesar's hierarchical scheme
Bards — the poetic and genealogical class within the Celtic learned elite, distinct from druids who served the religious function; medieval Welsh sources kept the distinction
Fili — the Irish term for the learned poet-class, post-druidic and Christian-era; mistakenly applied to pre-Roman druids by 17th-century antiquarians and Romantic enthusiasts
context: Caesar's Gallic War book 6 is the longest surviving classical account, supplemented by Pliny, Diodorus, and Strabo. The Roman conquest of Gaul and Britain (1st century BC-1st century AD) destroyed druidic institutions. Irish druidism survived until Patrick's mission (c. 432 AD). Modern 'Druidism' (18th century onward) is reconstruction.

question: Developed in Haiti during the 17th-18th centuries from West African Yoruba, Fon, and Kongo religious traditions blended with Catholic iconography by enslaved people, this religion centers on intermediary spirits between humanity and the distant high god Bondye (from French Bon Dieu). Each spirit has a Catholic saint correspondent. Which spirit is the gatekeeper invoked first at any ceremony?
answer: Papa Legba — the gatekeeper at the crossroads; first to be saluted in any ceremony, corresponding to Saint Peter (keys of the kingdom) and the Yoruba Eshu/Elegba; opens the gate to the other spirits
choices: Papa Legba — the gatekeeper at the crossroads; first to be saluted in any ceremony, corresponding to Saint Peter (keys of the kingdom) and the Yoruba Eshu/Elegba; opens the gate to the other spirits
Baron Samedi — the gravedigger lord of the dead; central in death-cults but invoked after others rather than as the gatekeeper at the start of ceremonies
Erzulie Freda — the spirit of love and luxury, corresponding to the Virgin Mary in some pairings; central but not the gatekeeper of the rite
Ogou Feray — the warrior-blacksmith spirit corresponding to Saint James the Greater; powerful but not the gate-opener of the ritual order
context: Vodou (the preferred spelling; 'voodoo' is the older anglicized form) is recognized as Haiti's national religion. The Bois Caiman ceremony (August 14, 1791) is the foundational moment of the Haitian Revolution — Boukman Dutty and Cécile Fatiman invoked the loa for the slave revolt that founded the first Black republic.

question: In 1559 the most influential Reformed theologian completed the definitive edition of his master work, the Institutes of the Christian Religion. Begun 1536 as a six-chapter handbook dedicated to Francis I of France, it had grown to 80 chapters in four books. What is the doctrine on which Calvin most parted from Lutheran orthodoxy?
answer: Double predestination — God from before creation elects some to salvation and reprobates others; both decrees flow from God's sovereign will, not from foreseen human merit
choices: Double predestination — God from before creation elects some to salvation and reprobates others; both decrees flow from God's sovereign will, not from foreseen human merit
Transubstantiation — Calvin held a memorialist view; actually Calvin held a spiritual real-presence position (sursum corda) distinct from both Lutheran consubstantiation and Zwinglian memorialism
Total depravity as bondage of the will — actually Calvin agreed with Luther on this, the Augustinian position both reformers defended against Erasmus's Diatribe on Free Will (1524)
Justification by faith alone — the central point of agreement between all Reformers; Calvin's distinctive emphasis was the imputed righteousness of Christ in particular formulations
context: The Synod of Dort (1618-19) codified five-point Calvinism (TULIP: Total depravity, Unconditional election, Limited atonement, Irresistible grace, Perseverance) against the Remonstrants (Dutch Arminians). Calvinist predestinationism flowed into Puritan, Reformed, and Presbyterian traditions across Britain and the Americas.

question: From 1739 to 1770 a Calvinistic Methodist priest preached from Georgia to Massachusetts and across England, Scotland, Wales, Ireland — perhaps the most-listened-to person of his century. Franklin estimated 30,000 could hear his voice. He crossed the Atlantic 13 times and died preaching at Newburyport, September 30, 1770. Who?
answer: George Whitefield — central figure of the First Great Awakening (1730s-40s), Calvinistic counterpoint to John Wesley's Arminianism; buried under the pulpit at Newburyport
choices: George Whitefield — central figure of the First Great Awakening (1730s-40s), Calvinistic counterpoint to John Wesley's Arminianism; buried under the pulpit at Newburyport
Jonathan Edwards — the great New England theologian and Northampton pastor whose 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God' (1741) is the famous Awakening sermon; but Edwards was American-resident
Gilbert Tennent — the Awakening's leading Presbyterian preacher (Log College founder); not the transatlantic itinerant who covered Britain and America the way Whitefield did
Theodore Frelinghuysen — the Dutch Reformed pioneer of awakening preaching in the Raritan Valley (1720s); preceded the broader Awakening but geographically circumscribed
context: Whitefield's slave-holding (the Bethesda orphanage used slave labor) and his support for the legalization of slavery in Georgia (1751) are honestly part of the picture. He was a complex figure whose evangelistic genius is paired with deep entanglement in the colonial slave economy.

question: On February 23, 1807, after 18 years of parliamentary effort, Parliament passed the Slave Trade Act abolishing the trade throughout the British Empire. The campaign leader was a Yorkshire-born evangelical MP, friend of Pitt the Younger, converted 1785, committed to slave trade abolition and reformation of manners. What was the name of his evangelical circle?
answer: The Clapham Sect — evangelical Anglican reformers including Thornton, Sharp, Hannah More, Macaulay, and Clarkson living around Holy Trinity Clapham, organizing abolitionism and social reforms
choices: The Clapham Sect — evangelical Anglican reformers including Thornton, Sharp, Hannah More, Macaulay, and Clarkson living around Holy Trinity Clapham, organizing abolitionism and social reforms
The Holy Club — John and Charles Wesley's Oxford undergraduate circle of the 1720s-30s; predecessor of Methodism rather than the abolitionist Clapham group two generations later
The London Missionary Society — founded 1795 by Anglican and Nonconformist evangelicals to support overseas mission; included Wilberforce but not specifically his political base
The Society for the Reformation of Manners — an older (1690s) Anglican moral-reform organization Wilberforce supported but did not use as his abolitionist political base
context: The 1807 Act ended the trade; the 1833 Slavery Abolition Act ended slavery throughout the empire (compensating slave-owners about £20 million, an enormous sum). Wilberforce died three days after the abolition bill passed second reading. He is buried in Westminster Abbey. Adam Hochschild's Bury the Chains (2005) is a fine modern account.

question: In the 1920s mainline American Protestants split between two parties. One held traditional doctrines (virgin birth, bodily resurrection, biblical inerrancy, substitutionary atonement) essential. The other accommodated higher-critical scholarship and Darwinian science. Names came from a 1910 publication and 1922 sermon. What were the two sides called?
answer: Fundamentalists (after The Fundamentals 1910-15) versus Modernists (after Fosdick's 'Shall the Fundamentalists Win?' 1922); the Presbyterian and Northern Baptist denominations split most painfully
choices: Fundamentalists (after The Fundamentals 1910-15) versus Modernists (after Fosdick's 'Shall the Fundamentalists Win?' 1922); the Presbyterian and Northern Baptist denominations split most painfully
Premillennialists versus Postmillennialists — an eschatological dispute about Christ's return that crossed but did not define the modernist-fundamentalist split of the 1920s
Calvinists versus Arminians — a theological dispute about predestination dating from the 1600s, not the early 20th-century American controversy specifically
Holiness versus Pentecostal — a dispute about the role of tongues and sanctification within the evangelical world, distinct from the modernist-fundamentalist controversy
context: The Scopes Trial (Dayton, Tennessee, July 1925) made fundamentalists seem foolish in the press (H.L. Mencken's reporting). But fundamentalism rebuilt institutionally — Westminster Theological Seminary (1929), Dallas Theological Seminary (1924), Wheaton, Moody Bible Institute. By the 1970s 'evangelicalism' was the public face of the rebuilt movement.

question: From July 10-21, 1925 a 24-year-old substitute biology teacher in Tennessee was tried for violating the Butler Act, which forbade teaching human descent from lower animals. The case was a publicity-arranged test (ACLU had advertised for a defendant). The lead prosecutor was a three-time Democratic presidential candidate; the defense star was a famous criminal lawyer. What were their names?
answer: William Jennings Bryan (prosecution, the Great Commoner who took the stand to be cross-examined on the Bible) versus Clarence Darrow (defense, the agnostic criminal lawyer who had defended Leopold and Loeb)
choices: William Jennings Bryan (prosecution, the Great Commoner who took the stand to be cross-examined on the Bible) versus Clarence Darrow (defense, the agnostic criminal lawyer who had defended Leopold and Loeb)
Bourke Cockran versus Robert Ingersoll — late 19th-century debaters on religion and morality; Cockran died in 1923 and Ingersoll in 1899, predating the trial
Frank Norris versus Charles Norris — two unrelated controversialist Baptist preachers and a Texas pastor; not connected to Scopes
John W. Davis versus John R. Brennan — Democratic politicians of the 1920s and 30s but not the Scopes attorneys; the names are fabrications
context: Scopes was found guilty and fined $100 (overturned on technicality). Bryan died five days after the trial ended. Inherit the Wind (1955 play, 1960 film) heavily fictionalized the case. The Butler Act remained on Tennessee's books until 1967; the Edwards v. Aguillard (1987) decision struck down a Louisiana 'creation science' equal-time law.

question: On April 9, 1906, in a stable-mission at 312 Azusa Street in Los Angeles, a one-eyed black holiness preacher began a revival lasting nearly nine years. Speaking in tongues, ecstatic worship, interracial congregations (in a Jim Crow era), and Spirit-baptism as a distinct work attracted thousands. The Apostolic Faith newspaper began publication. What was the leader's name?
answer: William J. Seymour — son of former slaves, blinded by smallpox; under his ministry modern Pentecostalism (hundreds of millions) was launched; the Apostolic Faith Mission was the base
choices: William J. Seymour — son of former slaves, blinded by smallpox; under his ministry modern Pentecostalism (hundreds of millions) was launched; the Apostolic Faith Mission was the base
Charles F. Parham — the white Topeka teacher who had taught Seymour the tongues-evidence doctrine; visited Azusa, broke with Seymour over racial mixing, is the founding theologian
Aimee Semple McPherson — the later (1920s-30s) founder of the Foursquare Gospel Church and Los Angeles Pentecostal celebrity; a generation after Azusa Street's beginning
Oral Roberts — the great mid-20th-century healing evangelist whose ministry began in the 1940s; influential in second-wave Pentecostalism but decades after Azusa Street
context: Pentecostalism is now perhaps the fastest-growing form of Christianity globally — major presence in Brazil, sub-Saharan Africa, China, the Philippines, and elsewhere. The Assemblies of God (1914), Church of God in Christ (1907, Mason), International Church of the Foursquare Gospel are major denominations.

question: In 1937 a 31-year-old German Lutheran pastor, heading an underground Confessing Church seminary at Finkenwalde in Pomerania, published a book attacking what he called the great enemy of contemporary Christianity. The enemy was 'cheap grace' — grace as doctrine without discipleship, forgiveness without repentance. What was the title?
answer: The Cost of Discipleship (Nachfolge, 'Following') — became the most-read 20th-century Protestant ethics; demanded grace must be costly and centered on the Sermon on the Mount
choices: The Cost of Discipleship (Nachfolge, 'Following') — became the most-read 20th-century Protestant ethics; demanded grace must be costly and centered on the Sermon on the Mount
Letters and Papers from Prison — his posthumous 1951 collection edited by Eberhard Bethge from Tegel prison correspondence (1943-44); after Discipleship, addressing different questions
Ethics — Bonhoeffer's unfinished systematic ethics, posthumous (1949); broader than Discipleship and focused on the church's role in modernity rather than discipleship
Life Together — Bonhoeffer's 1939 short work on Christian community based on his Finkenwalde experience; after Discipleship and treating the spiritual life of the seminary
context: Bonhoeffer was arrested April 5, 1943 in connection with Operation 7 (smuggling Jews to Switzerland), later implicated in the July 20, 1944 plot to kill Hitler. Transferred to Flossenburg, executed April 9, 1945 with Admiral Canaris, General Oster, and other Abwehr conspirators just two weeks before Allied liberation.

question: Genesis 22: Abraham climbed Mount Moriah carrying wood and a knife. His son, the long-awaited child of promise, carried the fire. 'Where is the lamb for the offering?' the boy asked. As Abraham raised the knife, an angel stopped him. What appeared in a thicket?
answer: A ram caught by its horns
choices: A ram caught by its horns
A lamb tied to a stake
A goat wandering free
A bull with golden horns
context: Hebrew tradition calls this the Akedah ('the binding'). Kierkegaard's 'Fear and Trembling' wrestled with what Abraham's obedience to a horrifying command could mean.

question: At Meribah the people raged at Moses for water. God told him to speak to the rock. Moses, exasperated, struck the rock twice with his staff — and the water flowed. But God told him he had not believed enough to honor him. What was the punishment?
answer: He would not enter the promised land
choices: He would not enter the promised land
He would lose his prophetic office
His staff would crack
His sister Miriam would die
context: Numbers 20. Moses saw Canaan from Mount Nebo but Joshua led the people in. Aaron also died on Mount Hor before the crossing. Both punished for the Meribah failure.

question: 1 Kings 3: two women brought a baby to Solomon, each claiming it. He called for a sword: 'Divide the living child in two.' The true mother cried 'Give her the child!' — the false one said 'Cut it.' What had Solomon asked God for at Gibeon?
answer: An understanding heart to judge
choices: An understanding heart to judge
Long life and victory
Riches above all kings
The peace of Jerusalem
context: God was pleased he asked not for self but for the people, and gave him wisdom, riches, and honor besides. Solomon's wisdom drew the Queen of Sheba from afar with spices and gold.

question: Matthew 2: wise men from the east followed a star to Bethlehem, where they fell down and worshipped the child Jesus. They opened their treasures and offered three gifts. Gold honored him as king. Frankincense was for the temple. What was the third?
answer: Myrrh, used for burial
choices: Myrrh, used for burial
Cinnamon, a spice of joy
Silver, mark of kingship
Wine for libations
context: Myrrh's funereal use foreshadowed the cross. Tradition named the magi Caspar, Melchior, and Balthasar from the three gifts. They warned Joseph in a dream and went home by another way, evading Herod.

question: Luke 2: at the Passover when Jesus was twelve, Joseph and Mary lost him on the road home. Three days they searched. They found him in the temple — sitting among the teachers, listening and asking questions. What did he say to his mother?
answer: 'Did you not know I must be in my Father's house?'
choices: 'Did you not know I must be in my Father's house?'

context: Luke 2:49. The only canonical scene of Jesus between infancy and his baptism. The teachers were 'amazed at his understanding'. Luke notes he then went home and was obedient to his parents.

question: John 2: at a wedding in Galilee, the wine ran out. Mary told Jesus; he protested 'My hour has not yet come,' but she instructed the servants to do whatever he said. He had them fill six stone water jars. The master of the feast tasted what?
answer: Wine — the best kept for last
choices: Wine — the best kept for last
Honey-mead of unusual sweetness
Spiced wine of the temple
Bread blessed and broken
context: John calls this the first of Jesus's 'signs'. The six jars were for Jewish purification rites — water of the old covenant becoming wine of the new. Each held 20-30 gallons.

question: Mark 6: a crowd of 5,000 men plus women and children followed Jesus into a remote place. Evening came; they were hungry. Andrew brought a boy with five barley loaves and two small fish. Jesus blessed, broke, and distributed. How much was left over?
answer: Twelve baskets full

Seven baskets full
Three baskets full
Five baskets full
context: The only miracle in all four gospels. Twelve baskets — one per disciple, perhaps one per tribe of Israel. John 6 builds the 'Bread of Life' discourse from it. A second feeding of 4,000 left seven baskets.

question: John 11: Mary and Martha of Bethany sent for Jesus when their brother fell sick. Jesus delayed. By the time he arrived the brother had been in the tomb four days. 'Jesus wept' — the shortest verse in scripture. What did he then cry?
answer: 'Lazarus, come out!'

'Awake, sleeper, and arise!'
'Damsel, I say to you, arise!'
'Young man, I say to you, get up!'
context: Lazarus came out bound hand and foot in graveclothes. Jesus said 'Unbind him and let him go.' This sign so alarmed the Sanhedrin that Caiaphas advised Jesus's death — better one man die than the nation perish.

question: After Jesus's arrest, a servant girl at the high priest's courtyard fire asked if Peter knew Jesus. He denied it. Two more accused him; he denied with curses. Then a cock crowed. What did Jesus do that broke Peter's heart?
answer: Turned and looked at him
choices: Turned and looked at him
Called him by name
Healed the high priest's servant
Spoke from across the courtyard
context: Luke 22:61. Peter went out and wept bitterly. After the resurrection, by the lakeshore, Jesus thrice asked 'Do you love me?' and thrice commissioned him: 'Feed my sheep.' Three denials, three restorations.

question: From the cross Jesus spoke seven times in the gospels combined. 'Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.' 'Today you will be with me in Paradise.' 'Woman, behold your son.' What was the cry of dereliction at the ninth hour?
answer: 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?'
choices: 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?'
'Into your hands I commit my spirit'
'I thirst'
'It is finished'
context: Mark 15:34, quoting Psalm 22:1 in Aramaic ('Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani'). Bystanders thought he was calling Elijah. The final words were 'It is finished' (John 19:30) and the commendation of his spirit (Luke 23:46).

question: On the first day of the week at early dawn, women came with spices to anoint Jesus's body. They found the great stone rolled away. An angel said 'He is not here, he is risen.' Which woman ran first to tell Peter and John?
answer: Mary Magdalene
choices: Mary Magdalene
Mary the mother of Jesus
Martha of Bethany
Salome the wife of Zebedee
context: John 20. Mary Magdalene became the 'apostle to the apostles' — first witness of resurrection. She did not at first recognize Jesus in the garden until he said her name. He told her, 'Do not cling to me.'

question: Genesis 22 has Abraham climbing Moriah with his son Isaac and firewood for a sacrifice. Isaac asks where the lamb is. At the last moment, what stays the father's hand?
answer: An angel calling from heaven, with a ram caught by its horns in a nearby thicket as the substitute offering.
choices: An angel calling from heaven, with a ram caught by its horns in a nearby thicket as the substitute offering.
A dove descending onto the altar stones, recognized as a sign the human sacrifice must not proceed.
A voice from a whirlwind identical to the one that answered Job out of his suffering.
A trembling of the earth that toppled the altar before the knife could be raised to strike.
context: The Akedah — 'binding of Isaac' — became the central proof-text in Jewish and Christian thought for tested faith. Paul's letters read the ram as foreshadowing the substitutionary death of Christ.

question: 1 Kings 18: Elijah on Mount Carmel against 450 prophets of Baal — each side prepares a bull, the god who answers by fire is God. The Baalists fail. What does Elijah do to make his test harder?
answer: Drenches the altar with twelve jars of water until a trench overflows, then prays — and fire falls and consumes it.
choices: Drenches the altar with twelve jars of water until a trench overflows, then prays — and fire falls and consumes it.
Builds the altar of twelve uncut stones rolled from the riverbed, refusing the dressed stones the Baalists use.
Stands silent through the morning, refusing to compete in noise, so the sky's silence is sharper.
Slaughters the bull only after the Baalists have cut themselves bloody, proving zeal summons nothing.
context: After the fire fell, Elijah had the prophets of Baal seized and killed at the Brook Kishon. One of the Hebrew Bible's most theatrical confrontations between YHWH-worship and Canaanite cult.

question: Daniel 3: three Jewish exiles refuse to bow before Nebuchadnezzar's golden image. The furnace is heated seven times hotter. The soldiers who throw them in die of the heat. What does the king see in the flames?
answer: Four figures walking unbound — three are the Hebrews, and a fourth 'like a son of the gods' walks with them.
choices: Four figures walking unbound — three are the Hebrews, and a fourth 'like a son of the gods' walks with them.
Three pillars of smoke where the men had stood, gradually rising and dispersing into the upper air.
Three lions prowling around an empty space, the men having been taken up in a chariot of fire.
Two angels with drawn swords holding the fire back from the men whose names the king pronounced.
context: Shadrach, Meshach, Abednego. The king pulls them out unharmed — not a hair singed — and decrees that no one shall speak against their God. A touchstone for Christian martyrs facing Roman fires.

question: Daniel 5: at Belshazzar's feast, temple vessels are used for drinking; fingers of a hand write on the wall. What words does Daniel read?
answer: Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin — numbered, weighed, divided: God has ended your reign and given it to the Medes and Persians.
choices: Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin — numbered, weighed, divided: God has ended your reign and given it to the Medes and Persians.
Maranatha, Sabaoth, Elohim — the Lord of hosts has come, and Babylon shall be remembered no more.
Selah, Selah, Adonai — pause, pause, the Lord — even now in feasting, judgment passes over you.
Anathema, Maranatha, Korban — accursed offering — the temple goblets are claimed back, and the city.
context: That very night Belshazzar was slain and Darius the Mede took the kingdom. The English phrase 'the writing on the wall' for inevitable doom traces to this scene, dated traditionally to the fall of Babylon in 539 BC.

question: 1 Kings 19: Elijah, fleeing Jezebel after Carmel, reaches Mount Horeb. A wind, an earthquake, and a fire pass — but God is in none. Where is God?
answer: In 'a still small voice' (or 'sound of sheer silence') that follows the wind, earthquake, and fire.
choices: In 'a still small voice' (or 'sound of sheer silence') that follows the wind, earthquake, and fire.
In the wind that splits the rocks — the older sign by which God had spoken to Moses on the same mountain.
In all three together — wind, quake, and fire — repeating the Sinai theophany that gave Moses the Law.
In the silence beforehand, when Elijah had first reached the cave and the wilderness fell quiet.
context: *Qol demamah daqqah* — Hebrew literally 'a voice of thin silence.' Centuries of Jewish and Christian spirituality have located God's intimate presence in this quietness, cut against the spectacular Carmel theophany.

question: Genesis 37: Joseph, his father's favorite, tells his brothers two dreams — sheaves bowing, sun and moon and stars bowing. They already hate him for his coat. What do they do when he reaches Dothan?
answer: Throw him into a dry pit, then sell him for twenty pieces of silver to Ishmaelite traders bound for Egypt.
choices: Throw him into a dry pit, then sell him for twenty pieces of silver to Ishmaelite traders bound for Egypt.
Bind him to a tree for wild beasts, but a passing caravan finds and ransoms him for grain.
Stage his death by spilling lamb's blood on his coat, then keep him as a household slave in their tents.
Cast lots over who will kill him; Reuben wins and instead frees him to return alone to Canaan.
context: Joseph becomes Pharaoh's vizier, reads the seven-fat-cows / seven-lean-cows dream, and saves Egypt from famine — feeding the brothers who sold him. The longest sustained narrative in Genesis.

question: 1 Kings 3: young Solomon at Gibeon is granted a wish. He does not ask for wealth, long life, or his enemies' defeat. Two prostitutes later claim the same baby. How does he settle it?
answer: Orders the baby cut in two with a sword; the true mother cries to spare the child even if the rival keeps it.
choices: Orders the baby cut in two with a sword; the true mother cries to spare the child even if the rival keeps it.
Asks each woman to name the hour of the birth, knowing the false mother will hesitate at a specific detail.
Commands them to nurse the child in turn; the true mother is the one the infant suckles peacefully.
Sends them away with the child until the new moon, when the true mother will return weeping.
context: Solomon had asked God for 'an understanding heart' — wisdom to judge. The judgment of Solomon became Western culture's archetype of judicial cleverness. His later turn to foreign wives' idolatry is the tragic counterweight.

question: Jonah, ordered to Nineveh, sails the opposite direction toward Tarshish. A storm threatens the ship. The lots fall on Jonah. What do the sailors do?
answer: Throw him overboard at his own instruction — a great fish swallows him, then spits him out three days later.
choices: Throw him overboard at his own instruction — a great fish swallows him, then spits him out three days later.
Tie him to the mast as the storm peaks, so the gods will see they did not surrender their cargo lightly.
Set him adrift in a small boat — expecting the sea to calm once the offender is separated from the rest.
Throw the ship's idols overboard one by one, until none remain and the storm relents from emptiness.
context: Jonah preaches in Nineveh; the city repents; God spares it. Jonah sulks under a withering plant. The book ends with God's question — should I not pity the city of 120,000 who do not know their right hand from their left?

question: Job opens with a wager: Satan tells God that Job is righteous only because he is prosperous. God lets Satan strip Job of children, livestock, and health. Three friends arrive to comfort him. What do they end up insisting?
answer: That Job must have sinned to suffer like this — the standard 'retributive justice' theology Job repeatedly rejects.
choices: That Job must have sinned to suffer like this — the standard 'retributive justice' theology Job repeatedly rejects.
That suffering is an illusion and the wise man learns to feel nothing — a Stoic doctrine the book introduces.
That Job's wife is the source of his misery, and casting her out will restore the favor of heaven within a year.
That Job should swear allegiance to the regional gods, since the God of Abraham has forgotten him.
context: Job 38 — God answers out of a whirlwind: 'Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?' Job repents in dust and ashes. The book leaves the wager unmentioned in the divine speech, and the friends are rebuked.

question: Numbers 21: Israel grumbles; God sends venomous serpents. The people repent. Moses prays and is told to make something — whoever looks at it after being bitten will live. What does he make?
answer: A bronze serpent on a pole — preserved later in the temple until King Hezekiah destroyed it for becoming an idol.
choices: A bronze serpent on a pole — preserved later in the temple until King Hezekiah destroyed it for becoming an idol.
A staff that drips honey, around which the serpents will themselves coil and lose their venom.
A breastplate of polished silver showing the names of the twelve tribes carved across its surface.
An ark of acacia wood smaller than the tabernacle's, to be carried at the head of the wilderness camp.
context: Nehushtan — the bronze serpent. Jesus refers to it in John 3:14 — 'as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up' — making the desert object a foreshadowing of the crucifixion.

question: Joshua 6: Israel circles Jericho once each day for six days, seven priests blowing rams' horns before the ark. On the seventh day they circle seven times. What happens when the priests give a long blast and the people shout?
answer: The walls of Jericho fall down flat and the army goes straight in, every man before him.
choices: The walls of Jericho fall down flat and the army goes straight in, every man before him.
The gates of the city open of their own accord, and the defenders flee through the streets in confusion.
A great hailstorm scatters the city's archers from the parapets, leaving the walls undefended at dawn.
The river behind the city floods its banks, sweeping away the foundations and undermining the towers.
