context: Joshua spares only Rahab the prostitute, who had hidden the Israelite spies. Christian tradition names her in Matthew 1 in the genealogy of Christ. The Battle of Jericho passed into spiritual song as a figure of barriers falling before faith.

question: Judges 16: Samson, betrayed by Delilah and captured by the Philistines, has his eyes put out and is bound to grind grain at Gaza. At a feast in the temple of Dagon he is brought out to mock. What does he do?
answer: Asks the boy leading him to place his hands on the two central pillars, prays for strength, and pulls them down.
choices: Asks the boy leading him to place his hands on the two central pillars, prays for strength, and pulls them down.
Recovers his speech long enough to prophesy the Philistines' destruction by an enemy from the south.
Lifts his blinded face to heaven and a sudden fire from above devours the temple, leaving him standing alone.
Tears the chains from his wrists and slays a thousand of them with the jawbone he had hidden in his belt.
context: Three thousand Philistines die in the collapse — more, the text says, than Samson killed in his lifetime. His hair had grown back; his strength returned. He is buried by his brothers in his father's tomb.

question: Matthew 2: magi from the East come asking where the king of the Jews has been born. Herod consults his scribes. What city do they identify from Micah?
answer: Bethlehem of Judea — 'and you, Bethlehem, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah.'
choices: Bethlehem of Judea — 'and you, Bethlehem, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah.'
Hebron of Judea — the city of David's anointing, where the line of kings had begun a thousand years before.
Jerusalem itself — Micah's prophecy was understood to set the birth at the very gate of the temple.
Nazareth of Galilee — Micah's reference to the despised town in the north was read as a Nazarene.
context: Matthew cites Micah 5:2. The visit of the magi — Epiphany, January 6 — is when much of Eastern Christianity exchanges gifts. Herod's response is the slaughter of the innocents at Bethlehem.

question: Matthew 4: Jesus, fasting in the wilderness for forty days after his baptism, faces three temptations. First: turn stones to bread. Second: throw yourself off the temple pinnacle. What is the third?
answer: On a high mountain, all the kingdoms of the world: 'all this I will give you if you fall down and worship me.'
choices: On a high mountain, all the kingdoms of the world: 'all this I will give you if you fall down and worship me.'
In a vision of glory, to seize Rome by acclamation before completing his ministry in Galilee.
Through a voice from a cave, to identify himself as the prophet Elijah returned and claim a kingdom.
By the appearance of his image in a still pool, to mistake the reflection for a second person and divide.
context: Each temptation Jesus answers with a verse from Deuteronomy. The pattern frames Jesus as the true Israel passing the test where the wilderness generation failed. The devil departs 'until an opportune time.'

question: John 2: at a wedding in Cana, the wine has run out. Jesus's mother tells the servants to do whatever he says. Jesus has them fill six stone water-jars used for purification rites. What do the servants then draw?
answer: Wine — and the steward says it is better than what was served first, when the guests' palates were sharp.
choices: Wine — and the steward says it is better than what was served first, when the guests' palates were sharp.
Olive oil — used to anoint the bridegroom's head, a sign of consecration over the wine.
Honey mixed with milk — symbol of the promised land, served only at the most important table.
Pure spring water that had become sweet to the tongue, recognized by the steward as a sign of blessing.
context: About 120 to 180 gallons of wine — the volume of the six stone jars. John uses 'signs' (semeia). The Cana sign is the first; the raising of Lazarus is the seventh, just before the Passion.

question: John 4: Jesus sits at Jacob's well in Sychar of Samaria around noon. A Samaritan woman comes to draw water. He asks her for a drink. What is her surprised reply?
answer: 'How is it that you, a Jew, ask a drink of me, a woman of Samaria?' — for Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.
choices: 'How is it that you, a Jew, ask a drink of me, a woman of Samaria?' — for Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.
'Why does a teacher of Israel come to a well in Samaria when there are clearer wells inside Judea?'
'Are you of the house of David, that you come asking water of the daughters of those who left the temple?'
'Is the time of the Messiah at hand, that the prophets are sent to wash among the despised gentiles?'
context: Jesus offers her 'living water' welling up to eternal life. She fetches her village; many believe. The Samaritan woman is among the earliest evangelists in John, and the encounter became a touchstone for breaking ethnic and gender barriers.

question: Mark 6: a vast crowd has followed Jesus to a remote place. As evening comes, the disciples want to send them away. Jesus tells the disciples to feed them. There are five loaves, two fish, 5,000 men. What follows?
answer: Jesus blesses and breaks the loaves; everyone eats and is satisfied; twelve baskets of leftovers are gathered.
choices: Jesus blesses and breaks the loaves; everyone eats and is satisfied; twelve baskets of leftovers are gathered.
Jesus distributes the bread first to the women and children, who give thanks aloud, and then the men receive.
A flock of quail descends as it did for Israel in the wilderness; the crowd eats from the sudden flight.
The disciples find that as they walk among the crowd, each family's own bag of food becomes full of bread.
context: Recorded in all four gospels — the only miracle besides the resurrection found in every gospel. John uses it as the lead-in to the Bread of Life discourse: 'I am the bread of life.'

question: Mark 9: Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain. His clothes become dazzling white, brighter than any earthly bleach. Two figures appear and speak with him. Who?
answer: Moses and Elijah — the Law and the Prophets — speaking with Jesus about his coming departure at Jerusalem.
choices: Moses and Elijah — the Law and the Prophets — speaking with Jesus about his coming departure at Jerusalem.
Abraham and David — the patriarch of the covenant and the king of the promise — confirming the lineage.
John the Baptist and the prophet Samuel — the last of the prophets and the first of the kingmakers.
Isaiah and Daniel — the prophets of suffering and of vision — flanking Jesus on left and right.
context: The Transfiguration. A voice from a cloud: 'This is my beloved Son; listen to him.' Peter wants to build three tents. Often paired with Sinai (Moses) and Carmel/Horeb (Elijah) — both mountain theophanies.

question: John 11: Jesus arrives near Bethany. Lazarus has been dead four days. He asks for the stone to be taken away. What does Martha object?
answer: 'Lord, by this time he stinks, for he has been dead four days' — there is decay, not merely death.
choices: 'Lord, by this time he stinks, for he has been dead four days' — there is decay, not merely death.
'The Sabbath approaches and the rolling of the stone will require more hands than the village can spare.'
'The Pharisees are watching from the road — if you raise him here, you will be reported to the Sanhedrin.'
'The tomb is in the hill — none of us has the strength to move the stone before the sun has set.'
context: Jesus weeps before the tomb (John 11:35, the shortest verse in the Bible) and calls Lazarus out. The Sanhedrin's resolve to kill Jesus crystallizes after this sign. 'I am the resurrection and the life' is read at most Christian funerals.

question: Mark 14: Jesus in Gethsemane after the Last Supper. He takes Peter, James, and John deeper and asks them to stay awake while he prays. He prays the same thing three times. What does he ask?
answer: That the cup pass from him — yet not what he wills, but what the Father wills, be done.
choices: That the cup pass from him — yet not what he wills, but what the Father wills, be done.
That the cup be shared among the disciples — so the burden of betrayal not fall on any one apostle.
That the angels of the wilderness who served him after the temptation now return to strengthen him.
That Peter's denial — already foreseen — be remitted, since the apostle would weep bitterly in repenting.
context: Luke 22:44 adds that his sweat became 'as great drops of blood' (the medical term hematidrosis fits this). The agony in the garden became a major subject of medieval and Counter-Reformation devotional art and music.

question: John 18: Pilate examines Jesus. Jesus says his kingdom is not of this world. Pilate asks: 'So you are a king?' Jesus answers with a claim about truth. What does Pilate famously then ask?
answer: 'What is truth?' — turns away, goes back outside, and tells the Jews he finds no case against the man.
choices: 'What is truth?' — turns away, goes back outside, and tells the Jews he finds no case against the man.
'Whose truth?' — meaning, which judge's verdict shall hold, Caesar's or the Sanhedrin's or his own.
'Where is truth?' — gesturing at the temple platform visible from his palace window across the city.
'When was truth?' — alluding to the Greek schools' doctrine that truth had ceased with the founders.
context: Pilate's question has echoed through Western literature — Francis Bacon, T. S. Eliot. John gives the question without an answer; the answer, in John's gospel, has already been given: 'I am the way, the truth, and the life.'

question: Matthew 27: after Jesus was crucified at the third hour, darkness covered the land. At the ninth hour Jesus cried out in Aramaic. The cry is preserved in the text. What does it mean?
answer: 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' — the opening line of Psalm 22.
choices: 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' — the opening line of Psalm 22.
'Father, into your hands I commend my spirit' — the opening line of Psalm 31.
'Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do' — the prayer over the soldiers casting lots.
'It is finished' — the single Greek word *tetelestai*, used elsewhere to mark a paid-up debt.
context: *Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani.* Bystanders thought he was calling Elijah. Psalm 22 — 'they pierce my hands and my feet... they divide my garments' — is read by Christian tradition as foreshadowing the crucifixion in startling detail.

question: John 20: Mary Magdalene weeps outside the empty tomb on Easter morning. She turns and sees someone she takes to be the gardener. He says her name. What is her response?
answer: She turns and says 'Rabboni!' — Aramaic for 'my teacher' — recognizing Jesus from a single word.
choices: She turns and says 'Rabboni!' — Aramaic for 'my teacher' — recognizing Jesus from a single word.
She falls at his feet to wash them with her hair as she had done at the supper in Bethany before his death.
She runs without speaking to find Peter and the beloved disciple, who race each other back to the tomb.
She kneels to gather the linen wrappings, which she will bring as proof to the eleven still in hiding.
context: Jesus tells her not to cling to him because he has not yet ascended. Magdalene becomes *apostola apostolorum* — apostle to the apostles — bearing the resurrection news. John's most intimate resurrection scene.

question: John 20: a week later. Thomas was absent at the first appearance and refused to believe without seeing. Jesus comes through locked doors again. He turns to Thomas. What does he invite him to do?
answer: 'Put your finger here and see my hands; reach your hand and put it in my side; do not disbelieve but believe.'
choices: 'Put your finger here and see my hands; reach your hand and put it in my side; do not disbelieve but believe.'
'Stand by the window and watch as I leave through the wall, that you may know the body is truly raised.'
'Sit with me at table and eat fish, that you may know I am not a phantom of the disciples' grief.'
'Walk with me to Bethany where Lazarus still lives, that you may see who else has risen from the dead.'
context: Thomas answers: 'My Lord and my God!' — the strongest Christological confession in the gospels. Jesus replies: 'Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed' — the gospel's farewell to the eyewitness generation.

question: Luke 10: a lawyer asks Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life. Jesus draws love-God-and-neighbor from him. The lawyer presses: who is my neighbor? Jesus tells a parable of a man left half-dead on the road. Three pass him. Who stops?
answer: A Samaritan — a member of the ethnic group the audience most despised — who tends the wounds himself.
choices: A Samaritan — a member of the ethnic group the audience most despised — who tends the wounds himself.
A Roman centurion off-duty, who has the man carried back to his own quarters at his personal expense.
A young rabbinical student returning from his teacher, who studies the wounds before binding them up.
A widow leading a donkey, who gives her last coin and remaining cloak before walking on barefoot.
context: The 'Good Samaritan' parable has shaped Western charity language — Good Samaritan laws, hospitals. Samaritans were considered religiously corrupt half-Jews; making one the moral hero is the parable's central scandal.

question: John 8: scribes and Pharisees bring a woman caught in adultery and stand her in the middle of the temple court. Moses commanded stoning. They ask Jesus what he says. What does he do?
answer: Bends down and writes on the ground; then says 'let him who is without sin among you cast the first stone.'
choices: Bends down and writes on the ground; then says 'let him who is without sin among you cast the first stone.'
Asks where the man caught with her is, since the Law required both adulterers to be brought for judgment.
Declares the temple grounds unsuitable for any execution, deferring the case to the Roman procurator's court.
Calls for the high priest to be summoned, knowing the Sanhedrin alone could prescribe the manner of stoning.
context: The accusers leave one by one, oldest first. Jesus: 'Neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more.' This passage (John 7:53–8:11) is absent from the oldest manuscripts but has been canonical in church use for many centuries.

question: Acts 9: Saul of Tarsus rides toward Damascus with letters authorizing him to arrest Christians. A light flashes; he falls. A voice asks why he is persecuting *him*. Saul asks who is speaking. What does the voice answer?
answer: 'I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting' — and Saul rises blinded, to be led into Damascus by the hand.
choices: 'I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting' — and Saul rises blinded, to be led into Damascus by the hand.
'I am the angel of the Lord, sent ahead of you' — and Saul rises with his sight intact but his commission revoked.
'I am the prophet Elijah returned' — and Saul rises with a new prophecy concerning the kingdom of Israel.
'I am the spirit of Stephen, whom you stoned' — and Saul rises remembering each face that died at his order.
context: Three days blind in Damascus, then healed by Ananias. Paul becomes the first great Christian missionary and writer of half the New Testament. The Damascus road remains the archetypal sudden conversion in Western thought.

question: Acts 16: Paul and Silas, jailed in Philippi after a beating, sing hymns at midnight. An earthquake shakes the prison; the doors fly open. The jailer prepares to kill himself. What does Paul shout?
answer: 'Do not harm yourself, for we are all here' — leading the jailer to ask what he must do to be saved.
choices: 'Do not harm yourself, for we are all here' — leading the jailer to ask what he must do to be saved.
'The Lord has set us free — do not detain us, for we go now to Thessalonica and Berea by morning.'
'The doors are not for us — bring forth the women and children imprisoned for unpaid debts and let them flee.'
'A house unlit cannot keep its prisoners — call for torches and write down what you have seen.'
context: The jailer is baptized that same night with his whole household. Philippi was Paul's first European mission. A Roman jailer joining a movement of crucified Jewish God-worship is the kind of border-crossing that defined apostolic Christianity.

question: On October 28, 312 AD, Roman armies met at the Milvian Bridge. The night before, the western emperor saw something — in a dream or sky — and ordered his soldiers to mark their shields. He won; Maxentius drowned in the Tiber. What did he see?
answer: A cross of light above the sun, with the words *in hoc signo vinces* — 'in this sign you will conquer.'
choices: A cross of light above the sun, with the words *in hoc signo vinces* — 'in this sign you will conquer.'
A dove with an olive branch flying westward from Rome over the Tiber, settling on the imperial standard.
A field of stars arranged in a Chi-Rho monogram, which his court soothsayer interpreted as a victory sign.
An eagle gripping a labarum, the standard he had captured from his rival earlier that summer in Verona.
context: Constantine. The Edict of Milan in 313 ended the persecution; the Christianization of the empire began. Whether the vision was genuine, political, or both has been debated — but its civilizational consequences are not in doubt.

question: In August 386 AD, a North African rhetorician sat weeping in a Milan garden, torn between his old life and a Christian conversion he could not make. He heard a child's voice from a nearby house chanting. What did the voice say?
answer: *Tolle, lege* — 'take up and read.' He opened Paul's letters at Romans 13 and his hesitation ended.
choices: *Tolle, lege* — 'take up and read.' He opened Paul's letters at Romans 13 and his hesitation ended.
*Veni, redi* — 'come, return.' He took it as a call from the religion of his mother Monica.
*Audi, vide* — 'hear, see.' He took it as a vision of the Christ his teacher Ambrose had preached.
*Lege, ora* — 'read, pray.' He took it as a command to seek meaning in the Psalms.
context: Augustine's *Confessions*, Book 8. The Milan garden conversion is one of the most influential single scenes in Western literature — the founding act of Christian autobiography, model for every spiritual narrative from Dante to Bunyan to C. S. Lewis.

question: William Tyndale translated the Bible directly from Hebrew and Greek into English in defiance of church law. Betrayed in Antwerp, he was strangled and burned in 1536. His final reported words were a prayer. What was it?
answer: 'Lord, open the King of England's eyes' — fulfilled within three years when Henry VIII authorized an English Bible.
choices: 'Lord, open the King of England's eyes' — fulfilled within three years when Henry VIII authorized an English Bible.
'Father, into your hands I commend my spirit' — borrowed directly from Christ's words on the cross.
'The Word of God endureth forever' — the verse he had taken as the motto of his translation work.
'Forgive them, for they know not what they do' — borrowed directly from Christ's prayer over the soldiers.
context: Roughly 75% of the KJV New Testament and 85% of the Pentateuch is Tyndale's wording. 'Let there be light,' 'the powers that be,' 'my brother's keeper,' 'salt of the earth,' and 'fight the good fight' entered English through Tyndale.

question: Genesis 11–12 traces Abram's family from Ur of the Chaldeans north through Haran, where his father Terah dies. There the LORD calls Abram, then 75 years old, to leave his country and kindred for a land God will show him. What does God promise?
answer: 'I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you... in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.'
choices: 'I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you... in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.'
'You shall be a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek, ruling beside me on Zion's holy hill.'
'Your hand shall be on the necks of your enemies, and they shall worship at the gates of your house.'
'You shall walk before me, and I shall give you the cattle of a thousand hills for your inheritance.'
context: Genesis 12:1–3 — the call of Abram. Paul (Romans 4, Galatians 3) reads this as the foundational moment of justification by faith: Abram believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness, before circumcision and before the Mosaic Law.

question: Exodus 14 has Pharaoh's army pursuing Israel to the edge of the sea. Moses, told by God to stretch out his hand, divides the waters. Israel walks across on dry ground. When the Egyptians pursue between the walls of water, what happens?
answer: The waters return at Moses' signal, and the chariots and horsemen are drowned in the closing sea.
choices: The waters return at Moses' signal, and the chariots and horsemen are drowned in the closing sea.
The angel of the LORD turns the chariot wheels backward so they cannot pursue further.
A pillar of fire descends between Egypt and Israel, repelling the chariots until daylight.
A whirlwind from heaven seizes the horsemen, scattering them to the wilderness behind them.
context: Exodus 15 — the Song of Moses ('I will sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously') — is among the oldest pieces of Hebrew poetry. The Red Sea crossing became the central image of redemption in Jewish memory, reread by Christian tradition as a type of baptism.

question: Leviticus 16 prescribes the rituals of Yom Kippur. The high priest enters the Holy of Holies once a year with the blood of a young bull, and then two goats are presented at the tent of meeting. What is done with the second goat?
answer: Lots are cast: one for the LORD (slaughtered), one for Azazel (sent into the wilderness bearing Israel's sins).
choices: Lots are cast: one for the LORD (slaughtered), one for Azazel (sent into the wilderness bearing Israel's sins).
Both are slaughtered, the first by the priest and the second by the Levites at the entrance to the camp.
One is burned and the other is given to the priests to eat as their portion of the day's sacrifice.
Both are released alive into the wilderness, the people gathering at the camp's edge to watch them flee.
context: The 'scapegoat' (from the Tyndale rendering of Azazel) is the source of the English word. Hebrews 9–10 reads Christ as both high priest and sacrifice, entering the heavenly Holy of Holies once and for all with his own blood, fulfilling and replacing the annual Yom Kippur ritual.

question: 1 Samuel 3: in the days when 'the word of the LORD was rare,' the child Samuel sleeps in the temple at Shiloh near the ark. A voice calls him in the night. He goes to Eli the high priest, thinking Eli has called. After the third time, Eli tells him what to say if it comes again. What?
answer: 'Speak, LORD, for your servant is listening' — the prayer of attentive readiness.
choices: 'Speak, LORD, for your servant is listening' — the prayer of attentive readiness.
'Here am I, LORD' — the same words Moses had spoken at the burning bush.
'O LORD, my heart is open' — borrowed by the medieval Sarum liturgy at the start of the Mass.
'Send your servant, O LORD' — the call to mission that opens Isaiah 6.
context: The Lord then reveals to Samuel the judgment on Eli's house — his sons would die because of their corruption at the sanctuary. The opening of 1 Samuel turns on the failure of Eli's priestly line and the rise of Samuel as prophet, judge, and kingmaker of Saul and David.

question: 2 Kings 5 tells of Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Aram, a great man but a leper. A captive Israelite girl tells his wife of a prophet in Samaria. Naaman comes with gifts. What does Elisha tell him to do?
answer: Wash seven times in the Jordan — and his flesh will be restored like that of a young boy.
choices: Wash seven times in the Jordan — and his flesh will be restored like that of a young boy.
Bathe in the well of Bethel — where the angel of God appeared to Jacob in his dream.
Drink water from the temple spring at Jerusalem — over which the priest will speak the Name.
Fast seven days in the wilderness — and his servants will return for him at the new moon.
context: Naaman, offended that Elisha does not even come out to him, almost refuses. His servants persuade him. He becomes the first foreign convert healed in the prophetic narratives. Jesus cites this scene at his hometown sermon (Luke 4) to illustrate the prophets' welcome of outsiders — and is nearly thrown off a cliff.

question: Ezekiel 37 places the prophet in the middle of a valley full of bones — 'very dry.' The LORD asks 'can these bones live?' Ezekiel answers 'O LORD, you know.' The LORD commands him to prophesy. What happens?
answer: The bones come together with a rattling sound, sinews grow, flesh covers them, and breath enters them.
choices: The bones come together with a rattling sound, sinews grow, flesh covers them, and breath enters them.
A great wind blows the bones together into a single white mountain at the center of the valley.
A flame rises from each bone, and the fires merge into a pillar that rises toward the sky.
Twelve graves open in the floor of the valley, and twelve white horses emerge bearing the bones.
context: The vision of the dry bones is read as a promise of the restoration of Israel after the Babylonian exile — and in Christian tradition as a figure of resurrection. The spiritual 'Dry Bones' rendered the chapter into one of the best-known African-American sacred songs.

question: 1 John opens with a strange first-person witness — 'that which we have heard, that which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands.' What is the witness about?
answer: 'The word of life' — what John has handled becoming the basis of his proclamation of Christ.
choices: 'The word of life' — what John has handled becoming the basis of his proclamation of Christ.
'The bread of life' — the eucharistic body shared in the church John founded.
'The light of life' — the inward illumination that John inherits from his teacher Christ.
'The water of life' — the baptismal mystery John celebrates as central to his Gospel.
context: The Johannine corpus (Gospel of John, 1–3 John, Revelation) shares vocabulary about 'life,' 'light,' 'love,' 'truth,' 'world.' 1 John's polemic against early docetic Christians — who denied that Christ had truly come 'in the flesh' — sharpened the doctrine of the incarnation against gnostic-leaning views.

question: The Norse warrior cult of *berserkers* fought in a frenzied state — howling, biting their shields, untouched by fire or iron. Their name reveals their dress. What does 'berserker' mean?
answer: Bear-shirt — *ber* (bear) + *serkr* (shirt) — warriors wearing bearskins, possibly with totemic identification.
choices: Bear-shirt — *ber* (bear) + *serkr* (shirt) — warriors wearing bearskins, possibly with totemic identification.
Bare-shirt — fighting naked or near-naked, as some classical sources reported.
Bare-foot — fighting unshod, ready for instant action regardless of terrain.
Battle-shaman — *ber* (battle) + *serkr* (priest), a wild-magic warrior of Odin.
context: Ulfhednar — 'wolf-coats' — were a parallel cult, fighting in wolfskins. The berserkers were dedicated to Odin and may have used hallucinogens (debated — perhaps fly agaric mushrooms). Their existence as both real warriors and quasi-religious figures is well-attested in saga literature. The English 'berserk' for uncontrolled rage descends from these Viking-age warriors.

question: King Hammurabi of Babylon (ruled c. 1792–1750 BC) inscribed a famous law code on a basalt stele topped by a relief of the king receiving the laws from a god. The stele is now in the Louvre. What god is the king shown receiving the laws from?
answer: Shamash — the Babylonian sun god, also god of justice.
choices: Shamash — the Babylonian sun god, also god of justice.
Marduk — chief god of Babylon, who in the *Enuma Elish* defeats Tiamat to make the world.
Anu — the sky god, traditionally chief of the Mesopotamian pantheon at older sites.
Enlil — wind and storm god of Sumer, prominent before Marduk's rise.
context: Hammurabi's Code (c. 1754 BC) is among the oldest substantial written legal codes. Its famous 'an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth' (*lex talionis*) limits private revenge by establishing proportionality. The code distinguishes treatment by class — penalties differ for offenses against nobles, freemen, and slaves. The stele's survival is a precious window into ancient Near Eastern legal culture.

question: On November 1, 1755, an earthquake estimated at magnitude 8.5–9 struck off the coast of Lisbon, Portugal, on All Saints' Day morning. The cathedral fell. A tsunami struck the harbor. Fires raged for days. About 30,000–50,000 people died. What was the theological response in Europe?
answer: Voltaire's *Candide* (1759) — a brutal satire on the optimistic doctrine that 'all is for the best.'
choices: Voltaire's *Candide* (1759) — a brutal satire on the optimistic doctrine that 'all is for the best.'
Calvin's *Institutes* — but Calvin had been dead nearly 200 years by the Lisbon earthquake.
Leibniz's *Theodicy* — but Leibniz had died decades before the earthquake, in 1716.
Locke's *Reasonableness of Christianity* — but Locke had died decades before the earthquake, in 1704.
context: The Lisbon earthquake was a defining moment for the Enlightenment's confrontation with the problem of evil. Voltaire's *Poem on the Lisbon Disaster* (1755) preceded *Candide*. Rousseau replied to Voltaire that humans had built their cities in unsafe places — an early environmental theodicy. The earthquake marked the cultural turning point at which traditional providential explanation began to weaken in elite European thought.

question: The story of Eros (Cupid) and Psyche is told by the Roman writer Apuleius in *The Golden Ass* (c. 160 AD) — a comic novel with a long inset myth. Eros visited Psyche in a darkened chamber, allowing her to feel him but not see him. Why?
answer: He had told her it was forbidden — his mother Aphrodite would punish them if Psyche saw his form.
choices: He had told her it was forbidden — his mother Aphrodite would punish them if Psyche saw his form.
He was disfigured by Aphrodite's curse and ashamed; only darkness made love possible.
He was a god and his radiance would consume any mortal who saw him in full form.
Aphrodite had set the condition; Psyche was being tested to see if she could trust without seeing.
context: Psyche broke the prohibition (urged by her sisters), looked at Eros by lamplight, was abandoned, and underwent four impossible tasks set by Aphrodite to be reunited with him. She was eventually deified. The tale shaped countless 'beauty and the beast' narratives and the philosophical reading of soul (*psyche*) and love (*eros*).

question: The Norse term *hamr* described what?
answer: A body or shape — an animal or human form that a sorcerer could change into in shape-shifting magic.
choices: A body or shape — an animal or human form that a sorcerer could change into in shape-shifting magic.
A horse — distinct from *jor* (mare); the masculine horse used by Norse warriors.
A hall — the building where a Norse chieftain held feasts and dealings.
A homestead — the farm and outbuildings of a Norse rural family.
context: *Hamr* and the related concept of *fylgja* (animal-shape soul-double) point to a layer of Norse religion that long predated and outlasted the formal Aesir pantheon. Norse magic — *seidr* — involved shifting into animal forms. The Eddic story of Loki becoming a mare (and giving birth to Sleipnir) is one prominent example. Norse shape-shifting is part of a broader Eurasian shamanic tradition.

question: 1 Samuel 16: God told Samuel that Saul had failed as king, and to anoint another. He went to Bethlehem and Jesse's house. Jesse paraded his seven older sons. What did God say?
answer: 'The Lord does not look on outward appearance but on the heart' — the youngest, watching sheep, was anointed.
choices: 'The Lord does not look on outward appearance but on the heart' — the youngest, watching sheep, was anointed.
'Bring me wine and bread; I will choose tomorrow once I have considered.'
'None of these; I will look to Egypt for the next king of Israel.'
'Anoint the eldest; the kingship requires birthright above all.'
context: The choice of David — the youngest, the shepherd — over the older brothers became Western culture's archetypal narrative of unexpected election. The story is a literary masterpiece: Samuel's protests, Jesse's confusion, the boy left in the fields. David's anointing eventually founded the messianic line that Christians read as fulfilled in Jesus 'son of David.'

question: 1 Kings 3: Solomon, newly king, asked God for one gift. What did he ask for?
answer: An understanding heart to judge the people — a request that pleased God so much that he was also granted riches and long life.
choices: An understanding heart to judge the people — a request that pleased God so much that he was also granted riches and long life.
Wealth great enough to build the temple his father David had planned but had not been allowed to build himself.
Victory over Israel's surrounding enemies — the Philistines, Moabites, Edomites — in the coming years of his reign.
Long life enough to oversee a stable transition of the kingdom to his own son when his time was complete.
context: Solomon's 'wisdom' became proverbial. The story of his judgment between two women claiming the same baby — offering to cut it in half, then giving it to the one who would rather see it spared — illustrated his discernment. Solomon's reign brought Israel to its largest territorial extent and built the first temple at Jerusalem. His later religious compromises (allowing his many foreign wives to bring their gods) led to the kingdom's division after his death.

question: John 11: at the tomb of Lazarus, Jesus 'wept.' What did this two-word verse become famous for?
answer: Being the shortest verse in many English Bible translations.
choices: Being the shortest verse in many English Bible translations.
Containing the first reference to Christian baptism.
Being the only verse in the Gospel of John without a subject.
Marking the beginning of Jesus's public ministry in Galilee.
context: John 11:35 — 'Jesus wept' — is the shortest verse in the King James Bible. It comes before Jesus raises Lazarus from the dead — moving readers to ask why he wept knowing what would follow. Augustine: he wept for our deaths, knowing he could only undo one. Bonhoeffer cited the verse in *Letters and Papers from Prison* as showing the God who suffers with us. The verse has shaped countless sermons on divine sympathy.

question: Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, was a disciple of John the apostle. He was martyred in 155 or 156 AD. What did he say when asked to deny Christ to spare his life?
answer: 'For eighty-six years I have served him, and he has done me no wrong; how can I blaspheme my king who saved me?'
choices: 'For eighty-six years I have served him, and he has done me no wrong; how can I blaspheme my king who saved me?'
'I deny only what is not true; my Lord is true, and I cannot deny him.'
'My life is not my own; I cannot trade it for what does not belong to me.'
'I have lived as a Christian; I will die as one; do as you must.'
context: Polycarp's *Martyrdom*, one of the earliest detailed accounts of a Christian martyr, preserves the dialogue. The proconsul tried to spare him — Polycarp was elderly, respected. Polycarp refused. He was burned at the stake; the flames are said not to have consumed him; he was finally killed with a dagger. The Martyrdom of Polycarp shaped the literary genre of saints' lives for fifteen centuries.

question: Norse cosmology held that the dwarves were made from what?
answer: The maggots in the corpse of the giant Ymir — given form and intelligence by the gods.
choices: The maggots in the corpse of the giant Ymir — given form and intelligence by the gods.
The clay of Midgard, fashioned by Odin and his brothers.
The stones of mountains, given life by their ancient lineage.
Spurned light-elves, banished from Alfheim and sent below ground.
context: Snorri's *Gylfaginning*: the gods gave the maggots in Ymir's flesh forms like men and granted them intelligence; they live in caves under the earth and are master smiths. The lower-class origin of the dwarves in Norse cosmology contrasts with their high cultural function — they made the gods' greatest treasures. The 'dark elves' (svartalfar) are sometimes identified with the dwarves and sometimes distinguished from them in the surviving texts.

question: In Exodus 3, the 80-year-old Moses — once an Egyptian prince, now an exiled Midianite shepherd — was tending Jethro's flocks near Mount Horeb. He saw a bush burning that was not consumed. A voice called his name twice, told him to remove his sandals (holy ground), and commissioned him: return to Egypt and deliver the Hebrews. Moses asked the voice its name. What was the answer?
answer: 'I AM THAT I AM' (Hebrew: ehyeh asher ehyeh) — translated YHWH, the name later considered too sacred to speak
choices: 'I AM THAT I AM' (Hebrew: ehyeh asher ehyeh) — translated YHWH, the name later considered too sacred to speak
'I am Adonai of Abraham' — the name later abbreviated El Shaddai in subsequent revelations to Israel
'I am El Elyon, the Most High' — the name Melchizedek had used to bless Abram in Salem
'I am Elohim of hosts' — a plural form indicating divine council and singular God of Israel
context: The Tetragrammaton (YHWH) became so sacred that observant Jews substitute 'Adonai' (Lord) when reading aloud. The 'I AM' formula echoes through the New Testament — Jesus's seven 'I am' statements in John deliberately invoke this Exodus 3 moment.

question: After the tenth plague, Pharaoh released the Hebrews — perhaps 600,000 men plus families — and they marched out. Within days he regretted it and sent 600 chariots in pursuit. The Hebrews found themselves trapped between the chariots and the Yam Suph (Sea of Reeds, traditionally Red Sea). They panicked. Moses stretched out his rod over the water. What happened?
answer: A strong east wind drove the sea back all night; the Hebrews crossed dry-shod; the waters returned and drowned the chariots
choices: A strong east wind drove the sea back all night; the Hebrews crossed dry-shod; the waters returned and drowned the chariots
A pillar of fire descended into the water and froze a bridge of ice across which the Hebrews walked at midnight
Sea monsters rose and dragged the Egyptian chariots down while the Hebrews crossed in fishing boats
The waters parted into seven channels and seven angels held back the floods until the last Hebrew was across
context: Exodus 14 describes the crossing; Exodus 15 is the Song of Moses, among the oldest poetry in the Bible. The miracle became the central paradigm of divine deliverance in Jewish memory, recited every Passover and echoed throughout Christian baptismal theology.

question: While Moses was on Sinai forty days receiving the law, the Hebrews grew restless. They came to Aaron — the high priest designate — and demanded gods to go before them. Aaron melted their gold earrings and fashioned a calf, built an altar, announced a feast. The people rose up to play. Moses descended carrying the two tablets, saw the dancing, and in fury threw the tablets and shattered them. What did he do next?
answer: Ground the calf to powder, scattered it on water, made the Hebrews drink it, then had the Levites kill 3,000 idolaters
choices: Ground the calf to powder, scattered it on water, made the Hebrews drink it, then had the Levites kill 3,000 idolaters
Banished Aaron from the camp forty years and personally re-cast the calf as a bronze serpent for healing
Demanded every Hebrew return the gold of Egypt and built a wall of dust between camp and altar
Called fire from heaven to consume the calf and the priests, sparing only the women and the children
context: Exodus 32. The golden calf is the archetypal Hebrew apostasy. Aaron's role is treated gently — he claimed the calf 'came out' of the fire on its own. The Levites' zeal in slaughtering idolaters confirmed their selection as the priestly tribe.

question: In the spring of the year — 'when kings go forth to battle' — David sent Joab to besiege the Ammonite capital while he remained in Jerusalem. From his rooftop he saw a woman bathing. He learned she was Bathsheba wife of Uriah the Hittite, one of his Thirty mighty men, sent for her, slept with her. When she conceived, David recalled Uriah and tried to get him to sleep with her. Uriah refused while his comrades slept in the field. What did David do next?
answer: Sent Uriah back to Joab with sealed orders to put him at the front of the hottest battle and withdraw support
choices: Sent Uriah back to Joab with sealed orders to put him at the front of the hottest battle and withdraw support
Confessed the affair to Uriah and offered him a province in compensation; Uriah accepted and went into exile
Had Uriah quietly poisoned at his own table during a victory banquet for the Ammonite campaign
Sent assassins to kill Bathsheba's father and brothers so she would have no protector but the king
context: 2 Samuel 11 is the great moral catastrophe of David's reign. Nathan confronted him with the parable of the rich man and the poor man's ewe lamb; David recognized himself and repented (Psalm 51). The child of the adultery died; Solomon was Bathsheba's later son.

question: Early in Solomon's reign — having just asked God for wisdom rather than wealth at Gibeon — two harlots came before the king with a dispute. They lived in the same house. Each had given birth within days of the other. One woman's baby died in the night; she had switched the dead child for the living one. Now both claimed the living infant. There were no witnesses. Solomon called for a sword and gave an order. What was it?
answer: 'Divide the living child in two and give half to one and half to the other' — to reveal the true mother by her horror
choices: 'Divide the living child in two and give half to one and half to the other' — to reveal the true mother by her horror
'Bring me a vessel of water and a vessel of wine' — to test which woman the child preferred in her arms
'Summon every woman who has nursed this year' — to identify the mother by milk and by scent
'Cast lots before the priest of Israel' — to leave the matter to the Lord and the Urim
context: 1 Kings 3 records the judgment that established Solomon's reputation for wisdom across the ancient world. The true mother said 'give her the living child, and in no wise slay it'; the false mother said 'let it be neither mine nor thine.' Solomon awarded the child to the woman willing to lose him.

question: Around 850 BC, Elijah challenged 450 prophets of Baal — Queen Jezebel's storm-god — to a contest on Mount Carmel. Each side would prepare a bull on an altar without fire and call on their deity. The prophets of Baal cried from morning to noon, leaping on the altar, cutting themselves. Nothing happened. Elijah mocked them — perhaps Baal slept or traveled. Then he prepared his altar and drenched it three times with water. What happened?
answer: Fire fell from heaven and consumed the offering, the wood, the stones, the dust, and licked up the water in the trench
choices: Fire fell from heaven and consumed the offering, the wood, the stones, the dust, and licked up the water in the trench
A whirlwind descended on the altar and tore the bull into seven pieces, scattering them across the mountainside
The earth opened and swallowed the prophets of Baal whole, leaving Elijah and the bull standing alone
A column of smoke rose without flame, in which Elijah saw the chariot of fire he later rode away
context: 1 Kings 18. After the fire fell, the people cried 'The Lord, he is the God.' Elijah had the 450 prophets seized and slaughtered at the brook Kishon. Jezebel swore his death; he fled to Horeb, where God appeared in the still small voice (1 Kings 19).

question: After his triumph on Carmel and Jezebel's death threat, Elijah fled into the wilderness, sustained by angelic bread and water, and traveled forty days to Horeb (Sinai). He hid in a cave. The word of the Lord came: 'What doest thou here, Elijah?' He complained he alone was left faithful. God commanded him to stand on the mountain. A great wind rent the rocks; an earthquake; a fire. But the Lord was not in any of these. After the fire came something else. What was it?
answer: A still small voice — at which Elijah wrapped his face in his mantle and went out to the cave's mouth
choices: A still small voice — at which Elijah wrapped his face in his mantle and went out to the cave's mouth
A voice of trumpets from the four corners — at which Elijah fell on his face and could not rise
A choir of seraphim singing the Trisagion — the same song Isaiah would hear in his Temple vision
A column of fire that took him up alive into heaven without going down to the grave at all
context: 1 Kings 19. The Hebrew 'qol demamah daqqah' is sometimes translated 'a sound of sheer silence' or 'a still small voice' (KJV). The passage became foundational for Christian mystical theology — God meets the soul not in spectacle but in stillness.

question: In October 539 BC, the Babylonian regent Belshazzar held a feast for a thousand of his lords. Drunk, he called for the gold and silver vessels his grandfather Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the Jerusalem Temple, and drank from them praising gods of gold and stone. In that hour the fingers of a man's hand appeared and wrote on the plaster. His knees smote together. None could read it. The queen mother recalled Daniel. What did the writing say?
answer: MENE MENE TEKEL UPHARSIN — 'Numbered, numbered, weighed, divided' — your kingdom is given to the Medes and Persians
choices: MENE MENE TEKEL UPHARSIN — 'Numbered, numbered, weighed, divided' — your kingdom is given to the Medes and Persians
ENOSH ENOSH SARIS ABYSSI — 'Mortal, mortal, eunuch, abyss' — your line ends tonight and your gods cannot help
MELEKH MELEKH KETHEM KASHAH — 'King, king, gold, hard' — the gold gods you praise are as deaf as stone
RA RA SHAMAYIM SHEOL — 'Evil, evil, heaven, hell' — judgment falls before the next dawn over Babylon
context: Daniel 5 dates the writing to the night Cyrus's forces diverted the Euphrates, walked under the river-gate, and entered Babylon. Belshazzar was slain that night and Darius the Mede received the kingdom. The phrase 'the writing is on the wall' entered English as a metaphor for inescapable doom.

question: Around 740 BC, the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah received his commissioning vision. He saw the Lord on a throne high and lifted up, train of his robe filling the Temple. Seraphim — six-winged — cried 'Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.' Doorposts shook; the house filled with smoke. Isaiah cried 'Woe is me; I am a man of unclean lips.' What happened next?
answer: A seraph flew with a live coal from the altar, touched his lips, and pronounced his iniquity taken away and sin purged
choices: A seraph flew with a live coal from the altar, touched his lips, and pronounced his iniquity taken away and sin purged
The Lord descended from the throne, raised Isaiah by the hand, and crowned him with a fillet of beaten Temple gold
The smoke filled Isaiah's lungs and he fell as dead; he was found three days later still breathing on the floor
A scroll appeared in his hand written front and back with lamentation; he was commanded to swallow it whole
context: Isaiah 6 is among the most influential theophanies in scripture. The Trisagion ('Holy, holy, holy') passed into Christian liturgy and the Sanctus of the Mass. After the coal-cleansing, Isaiah heard 'Whom shall I send?' and answered 'Here am I; send me' — the paradigmatic prophetic response.

question: Around 580 BC, during the Babylonian exile, the priest-prophet Ezekiel was set down by the Spirit in the midst of a valley full of bones — very many and very dry. The Lord asked: 'Son of man, can these bones live?' Ezekiel answered: 'O Lord God, thou knowest.' He was commanded to prophesy to the bones. As he spoke, something began to happen. What was it?
answer: A rattling — bones came together bone to bone, sinews and flesh covered them, breath came, they stood an exceeding great army
choices: A rattling — bones came together bone to bone, sinews and flesh covered them, breath came, they stood an exceeding great army
A whirlwind descended into the valley and the bones rose into the air, forming a single skeleton ten times life size
The bones turned to flesh first, then sinews, then bone — reversing creation order to display God's reverse-creation power
The bones became birds and flew away, then returned as living men who sang the Song of Moses together in chorus
context: Ezekiel 37 — God's promise to resurrect the dead nation from exile. Read in Christian tradition as also pointing to bodily resurrection generally. The Hebrew word 'ruach' means both 'breath' and 'spirit' — the same Spirit that hovered over the waters in Genesis 1.

question: The Nazarite Samson — strongest of the judges — fell for Delilah. The Philistine lords offered her 1,100 silver pieces for his secret. Three times she asked, three times he lied. The fourth, worn down, he told her: his uncut hair. While he slept she shaved his head. The Philistines bound, blinded, and forced him to grind grain. What was his end?
answer: Brought into the temple of Dagon to entertain 3,000 Philistines, he gripped the two pillars and brought down the roof on himself and them
choices: Brought into the temple of Dagon to entertain 3,000 Philistines, he gripped the two pillars and brought down the roof on himself and them
He escaped the mill at night, took up the jawbone of an ass once more, slew the Philistine king before dying of wounds
He prayed for death; the temple collapsed without his touch, killing only the Philistines and sparing Samson for old age
Delilah repented and shaved her own head to give him hair; his strength returned and he slew her ambushers in their bed
context: Judges 16 — Samson taking more Philistines in his death than in his life. Hebrews 11:32 lists him in the faith hall of fame despite the moral disasters. His Nazarite vow (Numbers 6) forbade wine, contact with the dead, and cutting his hair; the haircut was the breach.

question: In the days when the word of the Lord was precious in Israel, the boy Samuel ministered before Eli at Shiloh, where the Ark rested. Samuel slept in the temple near the ark. One night a voice called 'Samuel, Samuel.' Three times he ran to Eli, thinking the old priest called. Eli, nearly blind, finally perceived the Lord had called the child. He told Samuel: if the voice came again, what should he say?
answer: 'Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth' — and Samuel heard prophecy that Eli's house would be cut off for his sons' sins
choices: 'Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth' — and Samuel heard prophecy that Eli's house would be cut off for his sons' sins
'Hosanna in the highest; thy servant trembleth' — and Samuel was anointed with oil by the angel of the Temple
'Lord, depart from me; thy servant is too young' — and Samuel was caught up in a whirlwind to the throne of God
'Behold the handmaid of the Lord' — and Samuel saw the seven lamps of the menorah trembling and ascending
context: 1 Samuel 3 records Samuel's call. The phrase 'Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth' became a touchstone of spiritual receptivity in Christian tradition. Samuel grew up to be the last judge and the prophet who anointed both Saul and David — the transition figure from judges to kings.

question: In the third year of Xerxes I (c. 480 BC) at Susa, his queen Esther — Jewish, her descent kept secret — heard of vizier Haman's plot to exterminate the Jews on 13 Adar. Her uncle Mordecai sent word: 'Who knoweth whether thou art come for such a time as this?' Approaching the king uninvited was death. Esther fasted three days and went in. What was the outcome?
answer: The king extended his scepter; she invited him and Haman to two banquets; she revealed the plot; Haman was hanged on his own gallows
choices: The king extended his scepter; she invited him and Haman to two banquets; she revealed the plot; Haman was hanged on his own gallows
The king turned away; Esther was executed; Mordecai led an uprising that overthrew the Persian regime in three years
The king pardoned the Jews but executed Esther for entering uninvited; the festival commemorates her martyrdom on 14 Adar
The king ratified Haman's decree; the Jews fought back on 13 Adar; 75,000 Persian provincials died and the empire fell
context: The book of Esther is the only book in the Hebrew Bible that does not mention God by name. Purim (the festival of lots) commemorates the Jews' deliverance. The custom of drinking until one cannot distinguish 'cursed be Haman' from 'blessed be Mordecai' is rabbinic. Haman's ten sons were hanged after him.

question: Job of Uz — perfect, upright, fearing God — owned 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen. Satan challenged that Job served God only because God had hedged him about with blessings. The Lord permitted testing. In a single day Job lost his herds (Sabeans, fire, Chaldeans) and his ten children. His body was smitten with boils. His wife said: 'curse God, and die.' What was Job's reply?
answer: 'What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?' — and in all this Job sinned not with his lips
choices: 'What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?' — and in all this Job sinned not with his lips
'My redeemer liveth, and shall stand at the latter day upon the earth' — though his children were dead and his herds gone
'I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear; but now mine eye seeth thee' — repenting in dust and ashes already
'Behold, I am vile; what shall I answer thee? I will lay mine hand upon my mouth' — bowing before the divine prerogative
context: Job 2:10 — among the foundational verses for theodicy. Dialogues (chapters 3-37) feature three friends (Eliphaz, Bildad, Zophar) plus young Elihu insisting Job must have sinned; Job insisting his innocence. The whirlwind speech (38-41) reframes the question; Job is vindicated, his fortunes doubled.

question: Traditionally ascribed to Solomon, the Song of Songs is among the shortest books in the Hebrew Bible — eight chapters of erotic poetry with no mention of God, law, covenant, or Israel. 'Behold, thou art fair, my love... my beloved is unto me as a cluster of camphire in the vineyards of Engedi.' Its place in the canon perplexed both Jewish and Christian readers. Rabbi Akiva (c. 50-135 AD) defended it. How did he frame it?
answer: 'All the writings are holy, but the Song of Songs is the Holy of Holies' — read as God's love for Israel, sealed at Sinai
choices: 'All the writings are holy, but the Song of Songs is the Holy of Holies' — read as God's love for Israel, sealed at Sinai
'A bridal song for the daughters of Zion' — purely earthly poetry useful only for instruction in propriety
'A satire on the corruptions of Solomon's harem' — read as criticism of the very king to whom it is ascribed
'The whisperings of Eve to Adam in Eden' — read as the original prelapsarian love before the introduction of sin
context: Akiva's defense secured the Song's canon. The allegorical reading (God/Israel for Jews; Christ/Church or Christ/soul for Christians) became standard through medieval mysticism — Bernard of Clairvaux wrote 86 sermons on the first two chapters. Akiva himself died flayed alive by the Romans in 135 AD during the Bar Kokhba revolt.

question: Per Luke 1, in Elizabeth's sixth month of pregnancy with John the Baptist, Gabriel was sent to Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to Joseph of the house of David. Her name was Mary. He said 'Hail, thou that art highly favoured.' She was troubled. He told her she would conceive a son, Jesus, who would inherit the throne of David. She asked how, since she knew no man. What was his answer, and her response?
answer: 'The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee' — and Mary replied 'Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word'
choices: 'The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee' — and Mary replied 'Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word'
'A man of Bethlehem shall be sent' — and Mary replied 'I am too young; let the favor pass to my cousin Elisabeth'
'The seraphim shall stand watch over thee' — and Mary replied 'Show me a sign, and I will believe and obey thy word'
'Thou shalt drink the wine of heaven' — and Mary replied 'I will go up to the temple to receive thy gift in offering'
context: The Annunciation (Luke 1:26-38) is among the most painted scenes in Western art — Fra Angelico's San Marco fresco, Botticelli, Leonardo. Mary's fiat ('be it unto me') became foundational for Catholic Marian theology. The feast of the Annunciation is celebrated March 25, nine months before Christmas.

question: According to Matthew 2, in the reign of Herod the Great — most likely 6 or 5 BC by modern reckoning — Magi (Persian astrologer-priests, perhaps Zoroastrian) arrived in Jerusalem asking 'Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east.' Herod was troubled. His chief priests pointed to Bethlehem (Micah 5:2). The Magi went, found the child, fell down and worshipped, and opened their treasures. What did they offer?
answer: Gold, frankincense, and myrrh — interpreted as gifts to a king, to God, and to one destined to die
choices: Gold, frankincense, and myrrh — interpreted as gifts to a king, to God, and to one destined to die
Wheat, oil, and salt — the staples of the priestly offering, dedicating the child as a Temple servant
Silver, cedar, and lapis — building goods of David and Solomon, dedicating the child as a kingly architect
Bread, fish, and wine — the Temple meal-offering, dedicating the child as the New Passover lamb at birth
context: Matthew 2 records the visit. Tradition fixed their number at three from the three gifts, named them Caspar, Melchior, and Balthasar by the 6th century, and crowned them as kings (though the text says only 'Magi'). The Feast of the Epiphany (January 6) commemorates their visit; Eastern Christmas falls on this date.

question: According to Luke 2, every year Joseph and Mary went up to Jerusalem for Passover. When Jesus was twelve, they went with the usual caravan. On the return, after a day's travel, they realized he was not among kinsfolk. They returned to Jerusalem and after three days found him. Where was he, and what was he doing?
answer: In the Temple, sitting among the doctors, both hearing them and asking them questions — all that heard him were astonished
choices: In the Temple, sitting among the doctors, both hearing them and asking them questions — all that heard him were astonished
In the synagogue of Capernaum, having traveled north alone; teaching elders from the Torah of Moses by memory
In the courtyard of the High Priest, debating the priests about the cleanness of the Temple sacrifices and offerings
In the workshop of a carpenter, having pledged himself as an apprentice to a master of the cedars of Lebanon
context: Luke 2:41-52 records the only canonical episode from Jesus's adolescence. When Mary asked why he had treated them so, he replied 'wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?' (or 'in my Father's house'). The next narrative jump is to his baptism around age 30.

question: Per John 2, three days after Jesus had called his first disciples, there was a marriage in Cana of Galilee. Jesus, his disciples, and Mary were there. The wine ran out. Mary informed Jesus. He replied 'Woman, mine hour is not yet come.' Mary, undeterred, told the servants 'whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.' Six stone waterpots stood by, each 20-30 gallons. What did Jesus instruct?
answer: Fill the waterpots with water; draw out and bear to the governor — water had become wine of better quality than the first
choices: Fill the waterpots with water; draw out and bear to the governor — water had become wine of better quality than the first
Empty the waterpots into the well; the water would draw up wine for the bridegroom to taste and to discern
Crush the grapes outside the gate; the new wine would be aged in a single hour to match the best vintage
Hide the waterpots under the table; the bridegroom would find skins of new wine where they had stood
context: John 2 records the first 'sign' (semeion) — water made wine, perhaps 120-180 gallons of it. The governor, not knowing the source, called the bridegroom and remarked that normally the good wine is served first; here the best had been kept till last. John presents the signs not as marvels but as windows onto Christ's identity.

question: In John 4, Jesus came to a Samaritan city called Sychar near Jacob's well. Wearied, he sat at the well at noon while his disciples were off buying food. A Samaritan woman came to draw water. He asked for a drink. She was startled — Jews and Samaritans had no dealings. The conversation touched on living water, her five husbands, the place to worship. She asked about the coming Messiah. What did Jesus say?
answer: 'I that speak unto thee am he' — the first explicit Messianic self-disclosure in the Fourth Gospel, given to a Samaritan woman
choices: 'I that speak unto thee am he' — the first explicit Messianic self-disclosure in the Fourth Gospel, given to a Samaritan woman
'Behold the day cometh' — postponing the disclosure to Jerusalem and the Festival of Tabernacles three months later
'Believe in the Father' — refusing the Messianic title at this point and pointing her instead to general theism
'Thou art the Messiah' — turning the disclosure back to the woman as a prophetic riddle she must solve herself
context: John 4:26. The woman left her water jar, ran into the city, and brought back many Samaritans who believed. The episode is striking — Jesus's longest recorded one-on-one conversation, given to a woman, a Samaritan, of disreputable marital history, with a Messianic claim he gave to almost no one else.

question: When Jesus heard of John the Baptist's death, he departed by ship to a desert place. The multitude followed on foot. He had compassion and healed their sick. As evening drew on, the disciples urged him to send them away. He refused. He asked Philip 'Whence shall we buy bread?' Andrew brought a lad with five barley loaves and two fishes. Jesus told the people — about 5,000 men plus women and children — to sit. What happened?
answer: He blessed and brake, distributed by the disciples; all ate and were filled; twelve baskets of fragments remained
choices: He blessed and brake, distributed by the disciples; all ate and were filled; twelve baskets of fragments remained
He multiplied only the loaves and the fish appeared transformed into wine for the elders of the assembly
He commanded an angel to fly to Jerusalem and return with loaves from the Temple altar of shewbread
He sent the disciples to a Roman supply caravan a mile distant which surrendered its provisions without protest
context: The feeding of the 5,000 is the only miracle (besides the Resurrection) in all four Gospels. The twelve baskets — one for each disciple — became a symbol of Eucharistic abundance. John 6 follows it with the 'Bread of Life' discourse, the most explicit Eucharistic teaching in the Gospels.

question: After the feeding, Jesus sent the disciples ahead by boat across the Sea of Galilee while he went alone into a mountain to pray. About the fourth watch (3-6 AM) the boat was in mid-sea, wind contrary. Jesus came walking on the sea. They cried out, supposing it a ghost. He said 'Be of good cheer; it is I.' Peter answered 'Lord, if it be thou, bid me come.' Jesus said 'Come.' What happened?
answer: Peter walked on the water toward Jesus, then saw the wind, was afraid, began to sink, cried 'Lord, save me'; Jesus caught his hand
choices: Peter walked on the water toward Jesus, then saw the wind, was afraid, began to sink, cried 'Lord, save me'; Jesus caught his hand
Peter took a step onto the water, looked down, and sank to his waist; Jesus called him back to the boat from a distance
Peter declined to step out, recognizing his lack of faith; Jesus boarded the boat and the storm immediately ceased
Peter ran across the water to Jesus, embraced him, and the two walked together to the boat without any incident
context: Matthew 14:22-33. The rebuke 'O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?' became a refrain for Christian discipleship — the call is always to fix the eyes on Christ rather than the wind. Mark 6 and John 6 contain the walking on water without Peter's failed attempt.

question: In John 11, Mary and Martha of Bethany sent word that their brother Lazarus was sick. Jesus deliberately delayed two days. When he arrived, Lazarus had been dead four days. Martha met him: 'Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.' Jesus said he was the resurrection. At the tomb he ordered the stone removed. Martha protested — by now he stinketh. Jesus prayed aloud, then cried with a loud voice. What was the cry?
answer: 'Lazarus, come forth' — and Lazarus came out bound hand and foot with graveclothes and a napkin over his face
choices: 'Lazarus, come forth' — and Lazarus came out bound hand and foot with graveclothes and a napkin over his face
'Lazarus, awake' — and the dead man rose up walking, the graveclothes falling away of themselves outside the cave
'Spirit, return' — and Lazarus stood breathing inside the tomb, calling for his sisters before he came out
'Talitha cumi' — and Lazarus was lifted from the slab by an angel; his sisters dressed him and led him out
context: John 11:43-44 — the seventh and climactic sign in John's Gospel, immediately precipitating the Sanhedrin's decision to put Jesus to death. 'Jesus wept' (John 11:35) is the shortest verse in the English Bible. Lazarus appears once more in John 12, eating at table with Jesus.

question: After the Last Supper, Jesus went with his disciples to a garden at the foot of the Mount of Olives called Gethsemane ('oil press'). He took Peter, James, and John apart and began to be sorrowful. 'My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death; tarry ye here, and watch with me.' He went a stone's throw, fell on his face, and prayed. Three times he returned and found the disciples asleep. What did he pray?
answer: 'O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt'
choices: 'O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt'
'O my Father, take me up to the bosom of Abraham, lest the cup overwhelm thy servant in the hour of weakness'
'O my Father, behold the cup is heavy: send me twelve legions of angels to support me in the bearing of it'
'O my Father, the disciples sleep, they know not the cup: turn aside the cup, and let Peter taste it instead'
context: Matthew 26, Mark 14, Luke 22 all record the agony. Luke adds his sweat was as great drops of blood (hematidrosis, a real if rare phenomenon under extreme stress). The 'cup' is the prophets' figure for the wrath of God (Jeremiah 25, Isaiah 51). The acceptance is the hinge of the Passion.

question: At the Last Supper, Jesus had warned Peter: 'before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice.' Peter protested he would die first. After the arrest in Gethsemane, Peter followed afar off into the courtyard of Caiaphas the high priest. Three times he was challenged — by a maid, by another, by bystanders. Three times he denied. What broke him?
answer: The cock crew the second time; Jesus, being led across the courtyard, turned and looked at him; Peter went out and wept
choices: The cock crew the second time; Jesus, being led across the courtyard, turned and looked at him; Peter went out and wept
The maid herself was Mary Magdalene, who recognized him from his denials and rebuked him by name before the soldiers
A soldier struck him with the flat of his sword and recognized the wound he had given Malchus by the same blade
John the Beloved, also in the courtyard, called Peter's name from across the fire, and Peter realized he had been seen
context: Luke 22:61-62 records 'the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter,' the look that broke him. Peter's denial — and Christ's later threefold restoration in John 21 ('Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?') — became foundational for Catholic doctrine of the papacy. The church of St. Peter in Gallicantu commemorates it.

question: Friday morning, the chief priests delivered Jesus bound to Pontius Pilate, Roman prefect of Judea. Pilate examined him and found no fault. He sought to release him by Passover custom. The crowd, stirred by the priests, demanded Barabbas — a robber — instead. Pilate offered Jesus repeatedly; each time they shouted 'Crucify him.' He took water and washed his hands. What did he say?
answer: 'I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it' — and the people answered 'His blood be on us, and on our children'
choices: 'I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it' — and the people answered 'His blood be on us, and on our children'
'I have judged him not guilty of capital crime: take ye him' — and the crowd seized Jesus and dragged him out themselves
'I am bound by the law of Caesar: my hands are tied' — and the soldiers led him out without further inquiry from the prefect
'Crucify your king then, if such be your demand' — taunting them with the title before granting the death sentence
context: Matthew 27:24-25. Hand-washing was a Jewish ritual gesture (Deuteronomy 21:6-9); Pilate, knowing the custom, appropriated it. The phrase 'his blood be on us' was tragically misused for centuries to justify Christian violence against Jews; Vatican II's Nostra Aetate (1965) repudiated that reading.

question: Hanging on the cross from about 9 AM to 3 PM, Jesus spoke seven recorded sayings. To the Father: 'Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.' To the repentant thief: 'Today shalt thou be with me in paradise.' To his mother and John: 'Woman, behold thy son; behold thy mother.' The fourth, in the ninth hour, was a cry with a loud voice. What was it?
answer: 'Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani' — 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' — the opening line of Psalm 22
choices: 'Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani' — 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' — the opening line of Psalm 22
'Maranatha, maranatha' — 'Come, O Lord' — the Aramaic prayer that became a closing of early Christian letters
'Hosanna in excelsis Deo' — 'Glory to God in the highest' — taken up later by the angels at the empty tomb
'Berakhah, berakhah' — 'Blessed, blessed' — the priestly blessing he had received as a child in the Temple
context: Matthew 27:46, Mark 15:34. Whether read as despair or as the trustful opening of Psalm 22 (which ends in vindication), it remains the most theologically charged of the seven words. The other three: 'I thirst,' 'It is finished' (tetelestai), 'Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit.'

question: On the evening of the first day, the disciples gathered in a locked room. Jesus came and stood in the midst, showing his hands and side. Thomas (Didymus, the Twin) was absent. The others told him: 'We have seen the Lord.' Thomas refused — 'except I shall put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe.' Eight days later, with Thomas present, Jesus appeared. What did he say?
answer: 'Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; thrust thy hand into my side: and be not faithless, but believing'
choices: 'Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; thrust thy hand into my side: and be not faithless, but believing'
'Stand back, thou doubter; the others have believed and so shalt thou: keep thy hands at thy side until the morn'
'Thomas, twin of my own thought; thou shalt see when thou hast first taught the others' doubt away from them'
'Bring forth the centurion's spear; pierce me again, and prove to thy own hand that I am no spirit of the night'
context: John 20:24-29. Thomas's response — 'My Lord and my God' — is the highest Christological confession in the Gospel. Jesus's reply — 'blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed' — became the touchstone for all later faith. Caravaggio's painting (c. 1601) captures the moment with shocking physicality.

question: On the same first day, two disciples (Cleopas and a companion) walked the seven miles from Jerusalem to Emmaus. A stranger joined them; they did not recognize him. They told him about Jesus's crucifixion and the women's empty-tomb report. Beginning at Moses and the prophets, he expounded what scripture said of the Christ. At Emmaus they urged him to stay. He sat at meat. What happened?
answer: He took bread, blessed and brake, and gave to them; their eyes were opened, they recognized him, and he vanished
choices: He took bread, blessed and brake, and gave to them; their eyes were opened, they recognized him, and he vanished
He drew from his side and showed them the wound; they fell at his feet; he laid hands on them and disappeared
He drank the cup and said 'Peace be unto you'; they recognized his voice; he ascended through the ceiling above
He told the parable of the Good Samaritan once more; they recognized his teaching style and he was taken away
context: Luke 24:13-35 — the disciples saying 'did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?' The moment of recognition 'in the breaking of bread' became foundational for Eucharistic theology. The two returned to Jerusalem that same night to tell the eleven.

question: Luke 15 contains three parables of lost things. The Lost Sheep — shepherd leaves ninety-nine. The Lost Coin — woman sweeps her house. The longest: a man had two sons. The younger demanded his portion, took his journey into a far country, wasted his substance in riotous living. A famine arose; he was reduced to feeding swine. He came to himself and resolved to return as a hired servant. While he was yet afar off, what did his father do?
answer: Saw him afar off, had compassion, ran, fell on his neck, kissed him; called for the best robe, ring, fatted calf
choices: Saw him afar off, had compassion, ran, fell on his neck, kissed him; called for the best robe, ring, fatted calf
Sent the elder son to meet him; demanded restitution; received him only after a year of laboring as servant
Stood at the gate and made the younger son walk the last mile on his knees through the gathered village
Refused to see him; the mother received him secretly; only after seven years was the father reconciled
context: Luke 15:11-32. Rembrandt's painting (c. 1668) and Nouwen's book Return of the Prodigal Son made the parable resonant in modern devotional literature. The elder son's complaint — 'these many years do I serve thee' — and the father's reply ('Son, thou art ever with me') give the parable its dual structure.

question: A lawyer asked Jesus 'who is my neighbour?' Jesus answered with a parable. A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among thieves who stripped, wounded, and left him half dead. A priest passed by on the other side. A Levite likewise. Then a Samaritan — a despised group — had compassion, bound his wounds, set him on his beast, brought him to an inn, paid for his care. Jesus asked the lawyer which was neighbor. What was the answer?
answer: 'He that shewed mercy on him' — at which Jesus replied 'Go, and do thou likewise'
choices: 'He that shewed mercy on him' — at which Jesus replied 'Go, and do thou likewise'
'He that paid the innkeeper most generously' — refusing to name the Samaritan even in confession of mercy
'He that was nearest by ethnicity, were he Hebrew' — failing to grasp the parable's substantive force
'He that bound up the wounds in the prescribed manner' — naming only the action and not the man himself
context: Luke 10:25-37. The parable inverted ethnic and religious assumptions — the despised heretic outdoes the religious establishment in love of neighbor. The term 'good Samaritan' entered English; 'Good Samaritan laws' protect rescuers from liability. The road from Jerusalem to Jericho descends 3,300 feet through wilderness, still a robbery hotspot in Jesus's day.

question: Near Caesarea Philippi at the foot of Mount Hermon — a region famous for its pagan shrines, including a great cave to Pan — Jesus asked the disciples 'whom do men say that I the Son of man am?' They answered: some say John the Baptist; some, Elias; others, Jeremias, or one of the prophets. He pressed: 'But whom say ye that I am?' Simon Peter answered. What did he say, and what was Jesus's reply?
answer: 'Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God' — and Jesus replied 'thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church'
choices: 'Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God' — and Jesus replied 'thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church'
'Thou art the prophet greater than Moses' — and Jesus replied 'thou hast spoken from the Spirit; tarry yet a season'
'Thou art the king of Israel come from David' — and Jesus replied 'the kingdom is not yet; speak not of it openly'
'Thou art the Logos that was with the Father' — and Jesus replied 'the Father hath revealed his Word to thee'
context: Matthew 16:13-19. The wordplay — Petros (Peter, stone) and petra (rock) — became the foundation of Catholic papal theology: Peter as first pope, the rock on which the Church is built. Protestants typically read 'this rock' as Peter's confession rather than Peter himself. The episode marks a turning point — from public ministry to the journey to the cross.

question: Per Acts 2, fifty days after Passover — the Jewish feast of Shavuot — the disciples were gathered in one place in Jerusalem. Suddenly there came a sound as of a rushing mighty wind. Cloven tongues like fire sat on each of them. They were filled with the Holy Ghost. Devout Jews from every nation under heaven heard the noise and gathered. What perplexed them?
answer: Each heard the disciples speaking in his own native language — Parthians, Medes, Elamites, Cretans, Arabians, all understood
choices: Each heard the disciples speaking in his own native language — Parthians, Medes, Elamites, Cretans, Arabians, all understood
Each saw the same tongue of flame standing over Peter alone — the others appeared invisible from outside the upper room
Each tasted unleavened bread and wine on his tongue without having eaten — a sensory miracle without spoken words
Each felt himself rising above the ground — the entire upper room was levitating two cubits in plain sight
context: Acts 2 records Pentecost, traditionally the birthday of the Church. Peter's sermon — citing Joel 2 and Psalm 16 — added about 3,000 souls that day. The reversal of Babel (Genesis 11: languages divided) is deliberate: in Christ the nations are gathered. Western Christians commemorate Pentecost the seventh Sunday after Easter.

question: Around 60 AD, having appealed to Caesar following his arrest in Jerusalem, Paul was being shipped to Rome as a prisoner under centurion Julius. The voyage proved disastrous. Despite Paul's warning at Fair Havens on Crete, the captain pushed on. A typhoon-like 'Euroclydon' wind drove the ship for fourteen days. The crew gave up hope.
