Paul prophesied no loss of life, only the ship. Where did they finally make landfall?
answer: Malta — they ran the ship aground; all 276 souls reached land; Paul was bitten by a viper but suffered no harm
choices: Malta — they ran the ship aground; all 276 souls reached land; Paul was bitten by a viper but suffered no harm
Sicily — they put in at Syracuse where Paul healed the governor's father of fever and dysentery for three days
Cyprus — they were driven back east; Paul preached three months in Salamis before continuing to Rome by overland route
Sardinia — they landed near Cagliari; Paul was held by the Roman garrison for forty days before sailing on to Rome
context: Acts 27-28 records the shipwreck. The Maltese chief Publius received them; Paul healed his father; many came for healing. They wintered three months on Malta, then sailed via Syracuse and Rhegium to Puteoli, and walked the Appian Way to Rome. Paul spent two years in Rome under house arrest awaiting his hearing.

question: William Tyndale (c. 1494-1536) was first to translate the New Testament from Greek into English and print it. He fled England for the Continent (1524); his NT was smuggled in from 1526; copies were burned at St. Paul's. He continued with parts of the OT from Hebrew. Betrayed in Antwerp, he was strangled and burned at Vilvoorde Castle (October 1536). What were his famous last words?
answer: 'Lord, open the King of England's eyes' — within months Henry VIII authorized an English Bible largely drawn from Tyndale
choices: 'Lord, open the King of England's eyes' — within months Henry VIII authorized an English Bible largely drawn from Tyndale
'Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani' — taking up Christ's own cry of dereliction at his execution
'Now Lord, I depart in peace' — Simeon's Nunc Dimittis from his own English New Testament translation
'Forgive them, Father' — taking up Christ's words of forgiveness toward his persecutors at the stake
context: Tyndale's prayer was answered: within a year, the King's Great Bible (1539) drew heavily on his translation. The King James Version (1611) reportedly retains 75-85% of Tyndale's New Testament phrasing — making him arguably the chief architect of English religious vocabulary. 'My brother's keeper,' 'salt of the earth,' 'fight the good fight,' 'a stranger in a strange land' — all Tyndale.

question: In summer 325 AD Emperor Constantine convened roughly 250-318 bishops at Nicaea. The controversy: the Alexandrian priest Arius had been teaching the Son was a created being — 'there was a time when he was not.' Bishop Alexander and his deacon Athanasius opposed him fiercely. The council produced a creed and condemned Arius. The decisive Greek term meant 'of the same substance.' What was the term?
answer: Homoousios — declaring the Son of one substance with the Father, rejecting Arian Christology and establishing the Trinitarian orthodoxy of later catholic Christianity
choices: Homoousios — declaring the Son of one substance with the Father, rejecting Arian Christology and establishing the Trinitarian orthodoxy of later catholic Christianity
Homoiousios — declaring the Son of similar substance with the Father, the moderate compromise that papered over the disagreement for several decades after Nicaea
Hypostasis — declaring the Son a distinct personhood from the Father, the term later central in the Cappadocian formula of one ousia in three hypostases
Theotokos — declaring Mary the Mother of God, the term that became the test of Christological orthodoxy at the Council of Ephesus a century later
context: The single Greek iota between homoousios and homoiousios gave us 'not an iota of difference.' Arianism persisted under Constantius II and dominated among Germanic tribes for centuries. Athanasius was exiled five times defending the Nicene formula.

question: On October 27, 312 AD two Roman armies converged on a bridge over the Tiber north of Rome. On one side was Maxentius; on the other Constantine. The night before, according to Eusebius, Constantine saw a cross of light over the sun with the words 'In this sign, conquer.' He ordered the Chi-Rho painted on his soldiers' shields. He won; Maxentius drowned. What was the lasting result?
answer: The Edict of Milan in 313 legalized Christianity throughout the empire, ending three centuries of persecution and beginning the path to Theodosius making it official in 380
choices: The Edict of Milan in 313 legalized Christianity throughout the empire, ending three centuries of persecution and beginning the path to Theodosius making it official in 380

question: On October 6, 1536, at Vilvoorde near Brussels, a 42-year-old English priest was strangled and his body burned. His crime: translating the New Testament into English from Erasmus's Greek (1526 Worms edition) and part of the Old Testament from Hebrew. His final reported words: 'Lord! Open the King of England's eyes.' The King James (1611) drew 75-83% of its New Testament from his phrasings. Who was he?
answer: William Tyndale — whose translation gave English 'let there be light,' 'salt of the earth,' 'fight the good fight,' shaping English as much as any writer except Shakespeare

John Wycliffe — whose Lollards produced English translations of the Latin Vulgate in the 1380s, prompting Arundel's Constitutions of 1409 against vernacular Bibles

question: On October 16, 1978, cardinals elected the 58-year-old archbishop of Kraków, Karol Wojtyła. He took the name John Paul II — first non-Italian pope in 455 years, first Slavic pope ever. He had grown up under Nazi occupation, entered an underground seminary in 1942. In June 1979 he made his first papal visit to Poland — three million at the Kraków Mass. What was the strategic effect?
answer: It catalyzed Solidarity in 1980 — first independent labor union in the Eastern Bloc — beginning the chain leading to the 1989 collapse of communism in Eastern Europe
choices: It catalyzed Solidarity in 1980 — first independent labor union in the Eastern Bloc — beginning the chain leading to the 1989 collapse of communism in Eastern Europe

question: On July 8, 1741, in the meetinghouse at Enfield, Connecticut, a 37-year-old Northampton minister rose to preach a sermon. As he read in his flat delivery, the congregation began to weep, then cry out, then grip the pews in terror that the floor would open beneath them. He had to pause and ask for silence. The sermon became the most famous in American religious history. Who was he?
answer: Jonathan Edwards — a Calvinist holding humans hang over hell by a slender thread; his theology fused Enlightenment philosophical sophistication with Reformed orthodoxy
choices: Jonathan Edwards — a Calvinist holding humans hang over hell by a slender thread; his theology fused Enlightenment philosophical sophistication with Reformed orthodoxy

Theodore Frelinghuysen — the Dutch Reformed whose New Jersey revivals of the 1720s-30s pioneered the emotional preaching style Edwards adopted for the New England Puritan audience
Gilbert Tennent — the Presbyterian whose Danger of an Unconverted Ministry (1740) pushed the Awakening into conflict with established New England leadership at the Enfield sermon

His later works — Religious Affections (1746), Freedom of the Will (1754), The End for Which God Created the World (1765) — remain serious philosophical works. He died of a smallpox inoculation as president of Princeton.

question: On May 24, 1738, at about a quarter before nine in the evening, a 34-year-old Church of England priest reluctantly attended a small Moravian society meeting on Aldersgate Street in London. He had been a missionary to Georgia (1736-37), had returned in failure. Someone was reading aloud from Luther's preface to Romans. The priest later wrote: 'I felt my heart strangely warmed. question: On June 8, 793 AD, a small fleet of longships from Norway appeared off the coast of Northumbria in northeast England. They beached at the island of Lindisfarne, a Celtic Christian monastic center founded by St. Aidan from Iona in 635. The raiders killed monks, smashed altars, and carried off treasures and slaves. The English scholar Alcuin of York, then at Charlemagne's court, wrote in horror: 'Never before has such terror appeared in Britain as we have now suffered from a pagan race.' What did the raid mark?
answer: The traditional beginning of the Viking Age — three centuries of Scandinavian raiding, trading, and settlement across Britain, Ireland, France (Normandy), Russia
choices: The traditional beginning of the Viking Age — three centuries of Scandinavian raiding, trading, and settlement across Britain, Ireland, France (Normandy), Russia

The first appearance of Saxon shipping technology — the Northumbrians copied the raiders' shallow-draft

question: Among the most widely-copied texts in ancient Egypt — from the New Kingdom (c. 1550 BC) onward, written on papyrus rolls placed in tombs to guide the dead through the afterlife — was a collection of spells, prayers, and instructions. At the climactic moment, the deceased's heart was weighed on a scale against a single object. If the heart was lighter, the deceased proceeded to the field of reeds (Egyptian paradise). If heavier, the heart was eaten by the demon Ammit. What was on the other pan of the scale?
answer: The feather of Maat — the goddess of truth, justice, and cosmic order — embodying the principle of righteousness against which the moral life was weighed; the deceased
choices: The feather of Maat — the goddess of truth, justice, and cosmic order — embodying the principle of righteousness against which the moral life was weighed; the deceased
The heart of the deceased's mother — a measure of filial piety as the principal Egyptian moral criterion, the wider
The ankh of the deceased's father — a measure of paternal blessing as the principal criterion of life-after-death, the wider pattern
The crown of the pharaoh under whom the deceased lived — a measure of political loyalty as the principal Egyptian moral criterion
context: The 'Weighing of the Heart' is depicted in many surviving papyri (the Papyrus of Hunefer at the British Museum is famous). Maat — order, truth, justice — is one of the deepest Egyptian theological concepts: the gods themselves are bound by maat, and pharaoh's principal duty was to maintain it against chaos (isfet).

question: On July 6, 1415, in a field outside the city of Constance (Konstanz) on the south shore of Lake Constance, a Czech reformer was led to a stake. He had been promised imperial safe-conduct by Sigismund of Luxembourg. He was given a final chance to recant. He refused. As the fire was lit, he was reportedly heard to pray, 'Lord Jesus, son of the living God, have mercy on me.' His ashes were thrown in the Rhine to prevent their veneration. Who was he, and what was the wider impact?
answer: Jan Hus (c. 1369-1415) — and the Hussite Wars (1419-1434) followed, with the Czech Hussites under Jan Žižka and Prokop the Bald defeating five papal crusades; Hus's followers eventually compromised with Rome

context: Hus was a Wycliffite reformer — Czech Bohemia and English Oxford had been intellectually linked. The Hussite Wars devastated central Europe.

question: At Horeb the 80-year-old former Egyptian prince now shepherding his father-in-law Jethro's flock saw a thornbush blazing yet unconsumed. From the fire a voice called him by name. He asked: when the Israelites ask who sent me, what is your name? The answer became foundational for Jewish, Christian, and Islamic theology. What name did the voice give?
answer: Ehyeh asher ehyeh — I AM that I AM, rendered YHWH in the consonantal tetragrammaton, the name so holy later Jews substituted Adonai or HaShem when reading aloud
choices: Ehyeh asher ehyeh — I AM that I AM, rendered YHWH in the consonantal tetragrammaton, the name so holy later Jews substituted Adonai or HaShem when reading aloud

question: Late one afternoon King David walked his palace roof and saw a woman bathing. He sent for her. She conceived. Her husband Uriah the Hittite was at the siege of Rabbah; David recalled him hoping he would mask the paternity. Uriah slept at the palace gate refusing comfort while comrades fought. David sent him back with sealed orders to die. How did the prophet Nathan confront David?
answer: A parable of a rich man with many flocks who took a poor man's one beloved ewe lamb for a guest — David flared in anger at the rich man before Nathan said 'You are the man'

question: Around 870 BC the prophet Elijah challenged 450 prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel before Ahab and Jezebel. Each side would prepare a bull; whichever god answered by fire was God. The Baal prophets cried from morning to noon, gashing themselves; nothing. Elijah mocked them: perhaps Baal is sleeping. He drenched his altar with twelve jars of water. What happened next?
answer: Fire fell consuming the bull, the wood, the stones, the dust, and the water in the trench — the people fell saying YHWH he is God, and Elijah ordered the Baal prophets killed

question: Commanded to preach repentance to the Assyrian capital Nineveh, the prophet Jonah fled the opposite direction, boarding a ship for Tarshish (somewhere west, perhaps Spain). A great storm rose. The sailors cast lots; the lot fell on Jonah. He told them to throw him overboard. They did. The sea calmed. What happened next, and how does the book end?
answer: A great fish swallowed him three days; he prayed; the fish vomited him on shore; he preached; Nineveh repented; God spared the city; Jonah sulked under a withered plant — the book ends mid-rebuke

question: In Bethany, two miles from Jerusalem, Lazarus had been dead four days and was already in the tomb when Jesus arrived. His sisters Martha and Mary met him with grief and reproach: if you had been here. Jesus wept — the shortest verse in the English Bible. He ordered the stone rolled away despite Martha's warning of the smell. He cried in a loud voice. What happened?
answer: Lazarus came out bound in graveclothes; Jesus said 'Unbind him and let him go' — the raising became the trigger for the Sanhedrin's decision (John 11:53) to kill Jesus rather than risk Rome

question: Six days after Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi, Jesus took Peter, James, and John up a high mountain (traditionally Mount Tabor, possibly Hermon). His face shone like the sun; his garments became dazzling white. Two figures appeared speaking with him. Peter, terrified, offered to build three tents. answer: Moses and Elijah — representing the Law and the Prophets together bearing witness to Jesus, and (in the older tradition) the two figures who did not see ordinary death

question: Around 33-35 AD a young Pharisee from Tarsus named Saul, trained under Gamaliel and consenting to Stephen's stoning, obtained letters authorizing arrests in Damascus. question: On August 24, 410 AD Alaric and the Visigoths sacked Rome for three days — the first time in 800 years the city had fallen. question: In late 1224 a man dying of stomach cancer, near-blind from trachoma, having received the stigmata at La Verna, dictated a Umbrian-Italian hymn from his sickbed at San Damiano. The piece is the oldest surviving work of literary Italian. Earlier verses praise Brother Sun, Sister Moon, Brother Fire, Sister Water. He added two stanzas in the last weeks. What were they about?
answer: Forgiveness of injury for love of God — settling a quarrel between Assisi's bishop and mayor; and Sister Bodily Death herself praising God, added when his death was at hand in October 1226

question: Around 1078 a 45-year-old Benedictine prior at Bec in Normandy spent a sleepless night on a single argument. He wrote it as a prayer to God: faith seeking understanding. He defined God as 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived' (id quo maius cogitari nequit). The fool of Psalm 14 grasps this concept. What conclusion did Anselm draw?
answer: If God exists only in the understanding, a greater being can be conceived — one existing in reality — so God must exist, else God would not be that than which nothing greater can be conceived

question: In 1535 a 57-year-old Lord Chancellor of England was executed by Henry VIII for refusing to swear the Oath of Supremacy. On the scaffold he reportedly said he died 'the king's good servant, but God's first.' Twenty years earlier (1516) he had published in Latin a satirical fiction set on a fictional island. What was its title?
answer: Utopia — Greek for 'no place'; a fictional traveler's account describing an ideal commonwealth and (more cuttingly) satirizing English abuses; the word became the genre
choices: Utopia — Greek for 'no place'; a fictional traveler's account describing an ideal commonwealth and (more cuttingly) satirizing English abuses; the word became the genre

question: At sunset on a day in May or June 399 BC, after a trial in spring and a delay during the Athenian sacred mission to Delos, a 70-year-old philosopher sat with his friends in the state prison. He had been convicted of impiety and corrupting the youth. The Eleven brought the cup of hemlock. He drank. He walked. He felt his legs grow cold. What were his last words?
answer: Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius; pay the debt and do not forget — a sacrifice the god of healing was owed, perhaps meaning that death was a cure for life rather than the disease

question: From 995 to 1000 a Viking-king turned Christian missionary forcibly converted Norway. Earlier he had raided Britain; he had been baptized in the Scilly Isles by a hermit who prophesied his kingship. As king he gave Norwegians a choice: baptism or death. He pressured Iceland and the Faroes to convert. Who was he?
answer: Olaf Tryggvason — king of Norway 995-1000, who pressured Iceland's Althing of 1000 to adopt Christianity (Thorgeir Ljosvetningagodi negotiated the compromise); died at the sea-battle of Svolder

context: Both Olaf Tryggvason (995-1000) and Olaf Haraldsson (1015-30) — the two Olafs — completed Norway's Christianization between them. Saint Olaf's body at Trondheim became the great northern Christian pilgrimage site of the Middle Ages. Snorri's Heimskringla provides the saga-narratives.

question: Around 1000 AD Leif Eriksson (son of Eirik the Red, who had founded Greenland in 985-986) sailed west and discovered three lands. The first was a rocky waste (Helluland, probably Baffin Island). The second was forested (Markland, probably Labrador). The third had wild grapes. What did he call this third land, and what was found in 1960?
answer: Vinland — the wine-land; L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland was excavated by the Ingstads from 1961, confirming a Norse outpost of c. 1000 AD with longhouses, ironworks, and characteristic artifacts

question: Around 520 AD a south Indian Buddhist monk traveled to China and was granted audience with Emperor Wu of Liang. Wu boasted of his merit; the monk replied 'no merit.' question: In the oldest substantial literary work (Sumerian fragments from c. 2100 BC, full Akkadian version c. 1200 BC), the king of Uruk was 2/3 divine, 1/3 mortal and oppressed his subjects. answer: Enkidu (the wild man, civilized by the priestess Shamhat) was the friend; Humbaba (the monstrous guardian, slain after Shamash sent the winds to subdue him) was the guardian killed
